questions.prompt: Skip count by 5s: 35, 40, 45, ___. What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Added 1 instead of the jump of 5.
Skipped a jump — 55 comes after 50.
Repeated the last term instead of jumping on.

questions.explanation: Each jump adds 5: 35, 40, 45, 50. Counting by 5s always lands on numbers ending in 5 or 0.

questions.prompt: Is 23 even or odd — and why?

options.text: Odd, because the ones digit 3 is odd — one counter is left without a pair
Even, because 2 is an even digit
Even, because 23 can be split into two parts
options.diagnosis: Any number splits into two parts; even needs two EQUAL parts with none left over.

options.text: Odd, because it is a smallish number
options.diagnosis: Size has nothing to do with even and odd.

questions.explanation: Pair up 23 objects: 11 pairs form and 1 is left alone, so 23 is odd. Shortcut: look only at the ones digit — 3 is odd, so 23 is odd.

questions.prompt: A pattern goes 3, 8, 13, 18, ... What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Added 1 instead of the pattern's jump of 5.
Jumped 6 — check each earlier jump: they are all exactly 5.

questions.explanation: Every jump is +5: 3 → 8 → 13 → 18 → 23. Skip counting can start anywhere — the rule is the jump, not the starting number.

micros.title: Skip Counting by 2s, 5s and 10s
micros.description: Make equal jumps on the number line starting from the jump number: 2, 4, 6...; 5, 10, 15...; 10, 20, 30... Spot the ending-digit patterns each family makes.
outcomes: Can skip count by 2s, 5s and 10s from their own multiples
Can describe the ending-digit pattern of each count

micros.title: Skip Counting from Any Start
micros.description: The rule of a skip pattern is the JUMP SIZE — the starting stone is free. Jumping +5 from 3 lands on 3, 8, 13, 18, and that is a perfectly good pattern.
outcomes: Can continue a skip pattern that starts away from the skip number
Can state a pattern's jump size from its first few terms

question.prompt: A pattern goes 3, 8, 13, 18, ... What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Added 1 instead of the pattern's jump of 5.
Jumped 6 — check the earlier jumps: each one is exactly 5.

question.explanation: Every jump is +5: 3 → 8 → 13 → 18 → 23. Skip counting can start anywhere — the rule is the jump, not the starting number.

micros.title: Even and Odd by Pairing
micros.description: A number is even if its counters all pair up with none left over, and odd if one is left alone. Numbers ending in 0 pair up perfectly too — they are even.
outcomes: Can decide even or odd by pairing up counters
Can show that numbers like 30 are even because nothing is left over

question.prompt: Pair up 30 counters, two by two. What happens — and is 30 even or odd?

options.text: Every counter finds a partner, none left over — 30 is EVEN
30 is neither even nor odd — it ends in nothing
One counter is left alone — 30 is odd
options.diagnosis: Try it: 15 pairs form and nothing is left over.

options.text: You cannot pair up such a big number
options.diagnosis: Pairing works for any number — and the ones digit gives a shortcut.

question.explanation: 30 counters make exactly 15 pairs with none left over, so 30 is even. Even endings are 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 — zero belongs on the list!

micros.title: The Ones-Digit Shortcut
micros.description: Only the ONES digit decides even or odd, because tens and hundreds always split into pairs. 21 is odd since 1 is odd — the 2 in front has no say.
outcomes: Can decide even or odd for any 2- or 3-digit number using the ones digit
Can explain why the other digits do not matter

question.prompt: Is 21 even or odd — and why?

options.text: Odd, because the ones digit 1 is odd — one counter would be left without a pair
Even, because 21 can be split into two parts
options.diagnosis: Any number splits into two parts; even needs two EQUAL parts with none left over.

options.text: Neither — some numbers are in between
options.diagnosis: Every whole number is exactly one of even or odd.

question.explanation: The 2 tens make 10 pairs by themselves, so only the ones digit decides: 1 is odd, so 21 is odd.

micros.title: Describing and Extending Pattern Rules
micros.description: Say the rule out loud — 'add 10 each time', 'the numbers go even, odd, even, odd' — then use it to extend the pattern and to invent new patterns of your own.
outcomes: Can state the rule of a number pattern in words
Can extend a pattern by its rule and make up a new pattern from a given rule

nodes.title: Tables and Simple Bar Charts
nodes.description: A table lines data up in rows and columns; a bar chart turns those numbers into bars whose heights we can compare at a glance. To read a bar we follow its top across to the scale — and when one step of the scale stands for 2 or more, we must multiply, not just count steps. Charts help us answer questions with evidence.
learning_outcomes: Can record counts in a table using tally marks
Can read values from a simple bar chart using its scale
Can answer most/least and how-many-more questions from a chart
Can draw a bar chart from a small table of data

misconceptions.description: Bars are read by counting steps as ones, ignoring the scale — a 5-step bar on a 2-per-step scale is read as 5.
misconceptions.signal: All answers are exactly half (or a fixed fraction) of the true values on scaled charts.
misconceptions.remedy: Write the scale in a box at the top BEFORE reading anything, and count along the axis aloud: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Re-plot the same data at 1-per-step and 2-per-step and compare.

misconceptions.description: 'How many more?' is answered with the name of the bigger category, not a number — or with the bigger value itself.
misconceptions.signal: Q: 'How many more chose cricket than carrom?' A: 'Cricket!' (or '12').
misconceptions.remedy: Model difference as a climb: put a finger on the shorter bar's top and count up to the taller bar's top. The answer to 'how many more' is always a NUMBER of steps, not a name.

misconceptions.description: Questions about the data are answered from opinion or memory instead of the chart.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'football is most popular because everyone loves football' while the chart shows cricket.
misconceptions.remedy: Enforce point-to-prove: every answer needs a finger on the bar that shows it. Ask 'what does the CHART say?' and celebrate answers that go against personal favourites.

real_world_hooks: Class survey: how do you come to school?
Runs per over as a bar chart
Favourite ice-cream flavours at a party
Vehicles passing the school gate in 10 minutes
teaching.video_search: reading bar graphs with scale tally marks grade 3

questions.prompt: Favourite games of Class 3 — Cricket: 12, Kho-kho: 8, Carrom: 6, Football: 10. How many children chose kho-kho?

options.diagnosis: Read the biggest value instead of the row asked about.
Read the neighbouring row (carrom) — check labels carefully.
Added all the values instead of reading one row.

questions.explanation: Find the kho-kho row and read its number: 8 children chose kho-kho.

questions.prompt: In the same data (Cricket 12, Carrom 6), HOW MANY MORE children chose cricket than carrom?

options.diagnosis: Named the bigger category — but 'how many more' asks for a number.
Added the two values instead of finding the difference.
Compared cricket with kho-kho (12 − 8) instead of carrom.

questions.explanation: 'How many more' means find the difference: 12 − 6 = 6. Six more children chose cricket than carrom.

questions.prompt: In a bar chart, each step on the scale stands for 2 children. The 'tea' bar is 5 steps tall. How many children does it show?

options.diagnosis: Counted the steps but ignored the 2-per-step scale.
Added the scale to the steps (5 + 2) instead of multiplying.
Miscounted 6 steps before doubling — recount the steps.

questions.explanation: Each step is worth 2, so 5 steps show 5 × 2 = 10 children. Always read the scale before reading the bars!

micros.title: Tally Marks and Tables
micros.description: Record counts as tally marks in bundles of five — four sticks and a gate — and line the totals up in a neat table of rows and columns.
outcomes: Can record a count with tally marks in fives
Can fill and read a simple data table

micros.title: Reading a Bar Chart
micros.description: Follow a bar's top across to the scale to read its value, and answer questions from what the CHART says — point to the bar that proves your answer, not to your favourite.
outcomes: Can read values from a simple bar chart
Can answer most/least questions using the chart as evidence

question.prompt: A chart of favourite fruits shows: Mango 9, Apple 5, Banana 7. Which fruit did the MOST children choose?

options.text: Mango — its bar is the tallest, at 9

options.diagnosis: Answered from opinion — the chart says only 5 chose apple.
Second tallest — compare all the bars before choosing.

options.text: You cannot tell from a chart
options.diagnosis: The chart is exactly the evidence — follow the tallest bar.

question.explanation: Compare the bars: 9 > 7 > 5. The mango bar is tallest, so mango was chosen most. Always answer from the chart, not from memory!

micros.title: When One Step Stands for 2
micros.description: Check the scale BEFORE reading any bar: when one step stands for 2 or more, multiply the steps by the scale — never just count steps as ones.
outcomes: Can read a bar chart whose scale is 2 or more per step
Can explain why the scale must be read first

question.prompt: In a bar chart, each step on the scale stands for 2 children. The 'milk' bar is 5 steps tall. How many children does it show?

options.diagnosis: Counted the steps but ignored the 2-per-step scale.
Added the scale to the steps (5 + 2) instead of multiplying.
Miscounted 6 steps before doubling — recount the steps.

question.explanation: Each step is worth 2, so 5 steps show 5 × 2 = 10 children. Read the scale before reading the bars!

micros.title: How Many More? Comparing Bars
micros.description: 'How many more' asks for a NUMBER, not a name: put a finger on the shorter bar's top and count the climb to the taller bar's top — that climb is the difference.
outcomes: Can answer how-many-more questions with a number found by subtracting
Can compare two categories from a chart or table

question.prompt: A chart shows how children come to school: Bus 14, Cycle 9. HOW MANY MORE children come by bus than by cycle?

options.diagnosis: Named the bigger category — but 'how many more' asks for a number.
Gave the bigger value itself instead of the difference.
Added the two values instead of finding the difference.

question.explanation: 'How many more' means find the difference: 14 − 9 = 5. Five more children come by bus than by cycle.

micros.title: Drawing a Bar Chart
micros.description: Turn a small table into a bar chart: label the categories, choose a scale, draw each bar to the right height with equal widths and equal gaps, and give the chart a title.
outcomes: Can draw a bar chart from a small table of data
Can choose and label a sensible scale

nodes.title: 5-digit Numbers: Place Value and the Indian System
nodes.description: Numbers up to 1,00,000 open the door to real-world quantities like town populations, distances between cities and prices of scooters. You will read, write, compare and order 5-digit numbers, and use the Indian system of commas (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands). Knowing what each digit is worth is the key skill that all later arithmetic is built on.
learning_outcomes: Can read and write 5-digit numbers in figures and words using Indian-system commas
Can state the place value and face value of any digit in a 5-digit number
Can compare and order 5-digit numbers by first counting digits, then comparing place by place
Can expand a number as ten thousands + thousands + hundreds + tens + ones and rebuild it

misconceptions.description: Compares numbers by their leftmost digit regardless of length, e.g. thinks 8,754 > 12,345 because 8 > 1.
misconceptions.signal: Declares a 4-digit number bigger than a 5-digit number; never mentions the number of digits when comparing.
misconceptions.remedy: Make digit-count the explicit first step: line both numbers up right-justified in a place-value chart so the empty ten-thousands column is visible, then compare column by column from the left.

misconceptions.description: Writes numbers from words by transcribing each spoken chunk in full and joining them, e.g. 'forty thousand five hundred six' becomes 40,0005006 or 405006.
misconceptions.signal: Written numerals have too many digits; zeros appear in strange clusters that echo the spoken words.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a blank place-value frame (TTh Th H T O) and fill each spoken part into its column, writing 0 in every untouched column before reading the final numeral.

misconceptions.description: Treats a digit's value as its face value wherever it sits, e.g. says the 7 in 74,568 is 'worth 7'.
misconceptions.signal: Answers place-value questions with the bare digit; expanded form comes out as 7 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 8.
misconceptions.remedy: Trade games with play money: exchange a '7' card placed in the ten-thousands column for seven 10,000-rupee notes, so position visibly multiplies value.

real_world_hooks: Odometer of a car crossing 49,999 km on a highway trip
Prices of scooters and motorbikes in rupees (₹68,499 vs ₹72,150)
Populations of nearby towns on a district map
Attendance figures at a big cricket stadium
teaching.video_search: 5 digit numbers place value Indian system class 4

questions.prompt: What is the place value of the digit 7 in 74,568?

options.diagnosis: Named the thousands place instead of ten thousands; miscounted the columns from the right.
Called the leftmost digit the hundreds digit — a habit left over from 3-digit numbers; places must be counted from the ones end.

questions.explanation: In 74,568 the 7 sits in the ten-thousands place, so its place value is 7 × 10,000 = 70,000. Its face value is just 7 — position is what multiplies a digit's worth.

questions.prompt: Write 'forty thousand five hundred six' in figures.

options.diagnosis: Pushed the 'five hundred' into the thousands place; place-value frame not used.
Placed 5 and 6 in the wrong columns — wrote 'fifty-six' instead of 'five hundred six'.

questions.explanation: Fill a place-value frame: 4 ten-thousands, 0 thousands, 5 hundreds, 0 tens, 6 ones → 40,506. The zero in the tens column must be written even though no tens are spoken.

questions.prompt: Ravi says, '8,754 is greater than 12,345 because 8 is greater than 1.' Which statement gives the correct answer with the correct reason?

options.text: Ravi is wrong — 12,345 has 5 digits and 8,754 has only 4, so 12,345 is greater
Ravi is right — 8 is greater than 1, so 8,754 is greater
Ravi is right — the digits of 8,754 add up to more
options.diagnosis: Uses digit-sum to compare sizes; the sums are true (24 vs 15) but digit-sum does not decide which number is larger.

options.text: 12,345 is greater because 5 is greater than 4 in the ones place
options.diagnosis: Right conclusion by the wrong rule — compares ones digits first; this rule fails for e.g. 19 vs 25.

questions.explanation: First count digits: any 5-digit number is at least 10,000, and every 4-digit number is at most 9,999. So 12,345 > 8,754. Only when digit counts match do we compare from the leftmost place.

micros.title: The Ten-Thousands Place: Crossing 9,999
micros.description: What happens one step after 9,999: a new column opens up. Build 10,000 from ten thousands and meet the five-column place-value frame (TTh Th H T O).
outcomes: Can say what number comes after 9,999 and explain why a new column is needed
Can place the digits of a 5-digit number into a TTh Th H T O frame

micros.title: Reading and Writing 5-digit Numbers
micros.description: Read 5-digit numbers aloud, write them from words, and place Indian-system commas (last three digits, then pairs). Zeros hold empty places and must be written.
outcomes: Can write a spoken or worded number in figures using a place-value frame
Can read a 5-digit numeral aloud correctly, including ones with middle zeros
Can place Indian-system commas correctly in a 5-digit number

question.prompt: Write 'sixty thousand three hundred nine' in figures.

options.diagnosis: Transcribed each spoken chunk in full and glued them together, producing extra digits.
Pushed the 'three hundred' up into the thousands place; the place-value frame was not used.
Wrote 'ninety' instead of 'nine' — the final 9 belongs in the ones column, with 0 holding the tens.

question.explanation: Fill the frame: 6 ten-thousands, 0 thousands, 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 9 ones → 60,309. Every untouched column gets a 0 before you read the numeral off.

micros.title: Place Value and Face Value
micros.description: A digit's face value is the digit itself; its place value is digit × the worth of its column. The same digit is worth different amounts in different positions.
outcomes: Can state the place value and the face value of any digit in a 5-digit number
Can explain why the two 5s in 55,000 are worth different amounts

question.prompt: What is the place value of the digit 5 in 52,346?

options.diagnosis: Gave the face value; position multiplies a digit's worth.
Named the thousands place instead of ten thousands; columns miscounted from the right.
Counted positions from the left instead of from the ones place.

question.explanation: The 5 sits in the ten-thousands column, so it is worth 5 × 10,000 = 50,000. Its face value is just 5 — the position does the multiplying.

micros.title: Expanded Form: Breaking and Rebuilding Numbers
micros.description: Write a 5-digit number as ten-thousands + thousands + hundreds + tens + ones, and rebuild the numeral from an expansion — even a jumbled one.
outcomes: Can expand a 5-digit number as a sum of place values
Can rebuild the numeral from an expansion given in any order
Can spot a wrong expansion such as 7 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 8 for 74,568

micros.title: Comparing and Ordering 5-digit Numbers
micros.description: Compare numbers by first counting digits — more digits means a bigger number — and only then comparing place by place from the left. Order sets of numbers ascending and descending.
outcomes: Can compare two numbers by counting digits first, then comparing from the leftmost place
Can order four or five large numbers from smallest to greatest

question.prompt: Meera says, '9,876 is greater than 12,345 because 9 is greater than 1.' Which statement is correct?

options.text: Meera is wrong — 12,345 has 5 digits and 9,876 has only 4, so 12,345 is greater
Meera is right — 9 beats 1, so 9,876 is greater
options.diagnosis: Compared leftmost digits without first counting how many digits each number has.

options.text: Meera is right — the digits of 9,876 add up to more
options.diagnosis: Digit-sum (30 vs 15) does not decide which number is larger.

options.text: 9,876 is greater because its ones digit 6 beats 5
options.diagnosis: Compares ones digits first; that rule fails even for 19 vs 25.

question.explanation: Count digits first: every 5-digit number is at least 10,000, and every 4-digit number is at most 9,999. So 12,345 > 9,876 before we look at any digit.

micros.title: Making the Largest and Smallest Numbers from Digits
micros.description: Given a set of digits, arrange them to build the largest and the smallest possible 5-digit number — including the trick that 0 cannot lead.
outcomes: Can build the largest number by placing the biggest digit in the highest place
Can build the smallest number, moving a 0 to second place instead of first

nodes.title: Addition and Subtraction of Larger Numbers
nodes.description: Adding and subtracting 4- and 5-digit numbers lets you handle real quantities — ticket sales, populations, bank balances. The column method works exactly as it did for small numbers; the new challenges are carrying and borrowing across several places, especially across zeros. Estimation first tells you whether your exact answer is sensible.
learning_outcomes: Can add two numbers up to 5 digits with regrouping in any column
Can subtract with borrowing, including across one or more zeros
Can solve two-step word problems involving addition and subtraction
Can estimate a sum or difference to check whether an exact answer is reasonable

misconceptions.description: In subtraction, always takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column, regardless of which number is on top (52 − 38 = 26).
misconceptions.signal: Never borrows; answers to subtractions are too big; checking by adding back never happens.
misconceptions.remedy: Act the subtraction out with bundled sticks or money: to take 8 ones away when you only have 2, you must break a ten. Then require the add-back check (answer + subtracted number = start) on every problem for a week.

misconceptions.description: Treats carrying as optional bookkeeping — writes the ones digit of a column sum and drops the carry.
misconceptions.signal: Sums come out too small by 10, 100 or 1,000; the little carry marks are missing above the columns.
misconceptions.remedy: Slow the algorithm down with place-value discs: physically move ten ones into the tens pile so the carry is an object, not a mark; then reinstate the written carry as the record of that move.

misconceptions.description: When borrowing across a zero, takes the 10 but never reduces the column it came from (5,000 − 2,637 = 3,363-type errors).
misconceptions.signal: Errors cluster on problems with zeros in the top number; middle digits of the answer are exactly 1 too big, or the leading digit is.
misconceptions.remedy: Rename the whole block first: read 5,000 as 4 thousands + 9 hundreds + 9 tens + 10 ones before subtracting, so every reduction is done in one visible step.

real_world_hooks: Tickets left at a cricket stadium after a big sale
Money collected in a school fete versus the target
Distance still to travel on a Delhi–Mumbai train journey
Comparing populations of two villages
teaching.video_search: addition subtraction 4 digit numbers regrouping borrowing across zeros

options.diagnosis: Added an extra carry into the thousands column.
Dropped the carry from the ones column into the tens (wrote 5 + 7 = 12 → 2 without the carried 1) while keeping the later carry — regrouping applied inconsistently.

questions.explanation: Ones: 6 + 8 = 14, write 4 carry 1. Tens: 5 + 7 + 1 = 13, write 3 carry 1. Hundreds: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Thousands: 3 + 2 = 5. Answer: 5,834.

options.diagnosis: Single borrow slip in the tens column; the overall method is intact.

questions.explanation: Rename 5,000 as 4 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones. Then 10 − 7 = 3, 9 − 3 = 6, 9 − 6 = 3, 4 − 2 = 2, giving 2,363. Check: 2,363 + 2,637 = 5,000. ✓

questions.prompt: A cricket stadium holds 65,000 people. So far 48,750 tickets have been sold. How many tickets are still left?

options.diagnosis: Hundreds-column slip while borrowing; estimate-and-check would catch this.

micros.title: Estimate Before You Calculate
micros.description: Round each number to a friendly nearby thousand or hundred and add or subtract in your head, so you know roughly what the exact answer must be before you start.
outcomes: Can give a rough estimate for a sum or difference of 4- and 5-digit numbers
Can use the estimate to reject an answer that is clearly too big or too small

micros.title: Column Addition with Carrying
micros.description: Add 4- and 5-digit numbers in columns, carrying into the next place whenever a column sum reaches 10 — sometimes in several columns of the same sum.
outcomes: Can add two numbers up to 5 digits with carrying in any or all columns
Can explain what the small carry mark records (ten ones traded for one ten)

options.diagnosis: Wrote each column's ones digit and dropped every carry.
Dropped only the tens-column carry; regrouping is applied inconsistently.
Added an extra carry into the thousands column.

question.explanation: Ones: 7 + 6 = 13, write 3 carry 1. Tens: 6 + 7 + 1 = 14, write 4 carry 1. Hundreds: 5 + 8 + 1 = 14, write 4 carry 1. Thousands: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Answer: 8,443.

micros.title: Column Subtraction with Borrowing
micros.description: Subtract large numbers in columns. When the top digit is smaller, break one from the next place into ten — never just flip the digits around.
outcomes: Can subtract numbers up to 5 digits with borrowing in one or more columns
Can explain why 52 − 38 is not 26: you must borrow, not take smaller from larger

options.diagnosis: Took the smaller digit from the larger in every column instead of borrowing.
Single borrowing slip in the tens column; the method is otherwise intact.
Borrowing slip in the hundreds column; check by adding back would catch it.

question.explanation: Ones: borrow to make 13 − 8 = 5. Tens: 3 − 7 needs another borrow, 13 − 7 = 6. Hundreds: 1 − 5 needs a borrow, 11 − 5 = 6. Thousands: 5 − 2 = 3. Answer: 3,665. Check: 3,665 + 2,578 = 6,243.

micros.title: Borrowing Across Zeros
micros.description: Subtracting from numbers like 7,000 means borrowing across several zeros. Rename the whole block first (7,000 = 6 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones), then subtract place by place.
outcomes: Can subtract from a number with one or more zeros in the top row
Can rename a round number as thousands-hundreds-tens-ones before subtracting

options.diagnosis: Borrowed the 10 but never reduced the thousands column it came from — the leading digit is 1 too big.
Took the smaller digit from the larger in every column; no borrowing at all.
Slip in the hundreds column while borrowing; the renaming step was rushed.

question.explanation: Rename 7,000 as 6 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones. Then 10 − 8 = 2, 9 − 5 = 4, 9 − 4 = 5, 6 − 3 = 3, giving 3,542. Check: 3,542 + 3,458 = 7,000.

micros.title: Checking Answers by Adding Back
micros.description: Every subtraction can be checked: answer + number subtracted must give the starting number. Make the add-back check a habit that catches borrowing mistakes.
outcomes: Can check a subtraction with the add-back rule and say whether the answer stands
Can find which column went wrong when the check fails

micros.title: Two-step Word Problems
micros.description: Real problems often need two moves — add first, then subtract, or the other way round. Plan the steps, estimate the answer, compute, and check it makes sense in the story.
outcomes: Can plan and solve a word problem that needs both an addition and a subtraction
Can state the answer in a sentence with the right unit and sense-check it

question.prompt: A school fete collected ₹23,450 on Saturday and ₹18,600 on Sunday. The target was ₹50,000. How much MORE money was needed to reach the target?

options.diagnosis: Borrowed across the zeros of 50,000 without reducing the column the 10 came from.
Stopped after step one — that is the total collected, not the shortfall.
Added the target instead of subtracting from it; the question words were not re-read.

question.explanation: Step 1: 23,450 + 18,600 = 42,050 collected. Step 2: 50,000 − 42,050 = 7,950. Estimate check: about 42,000 collected of 50,000, so roughly 8,000 short — 7,950 fits.

nodes.title: Multi-digit Multiplication
nodes.description: Multiplying 2- and 3-digit numbers lets you scale things up fast: chairs in a hall, sticks of chalk in a delivery, rupees earned per day over a month. The big idea is breaking a number into tens and ones, multiplying each part, and adding the partial products — the written algorithm is just a tidy record of that.
learning_outcomes: Can multiply a 2- or 3-digit number by a 1-digit number with carrying
Can multiply two 2-digit numbers using partial products or the column method
Can explain why a zero placeholder appears when multiplying by the tens digit
Can solve multiplication word problems and check answers by estimating

misconceptions.description: Omits the placeholder zero when multiplying by the tens digit, so 27 × 34 becomes 108 + 81 instead of 108 + 810.
misconceptions.signal: Answers to 2-digit × 2-digit problems are far too small; the second partial-product row starts in the ones column.
misconceptions.remedy: Reconnect the algorithm to meaning: the second row is 27 × 30, not 27 × 3. Have the student write '× 30' beside the row and compute it as 27 × 3 × 10 before returning to the compact form.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies columns independently like addition: 23 × 45 is done as 3 × 5 and 2 × 4 with the results written side by side.
misconceptions.signal: Works right to left multiplying digit under digit only; never produces two partial-product rows.
misconceptions.remedy: Use an area (box) model: split 23 × 45 into a 20 + 3 by 40 + 5 grid, find all four partial areas, and show that column-under-column captures only two of the four.

misconceptions.description: Adds the carried digit before multiplying instead of after: for 34 × 6, does (3 + 2) × 6 = 30 instead of 3 × 6 + 2 = 20.
misconceptions.signal: Errors only appear on problems that involve a carry; single-digit facts are otherwise solid.
misconceptions.remedy: Verbalise the order every time: 'multiply first, then add the carry'. Write the carry small and circled, and have the student point to it only after saying the times fact aloud.

real_world_hooks: Rows of chairs in a wedding hall (36 rows × 24 chairs)
A newspaper seller's monthly earnings: papers per day × days
Total runs if a batter scores about 45 per match over 28 matches
Boxes of laddoos: sweets per box × number of boxes

options.diagnosis: Wrote 3 × 6 = 18 and 4 × 6 = 24 side by side instead of regrouping the partial products.
Carried 1 instead of 2 from 4 × 6 = 24; fact knowledge fine, carry recording slipped.

questions.explanation: 4 × 6 = 24: write 4, carry 2. Then 3 × 6 = 18, plus the carry 2 gives 20. Answer: 204. Multiply first, then add the carry.

options.diagnosis: Computed 27 × 4 as 98 instead of 108; a single fact/carry slip inside a correct method.

questions.explanation: 27 × 4 = 108 and 27 × 30 = 810. Add the partial products: 108 + 810 = 918. The second row must be 810, not 81 — you are multiplying by 30, not 3.

questions.prompt: A wedding hall has 36 rows of chairs with 24 chairs in each row. How many chairs are there in all?

options.diagnosis: Dropped the carry while finding 36 × 20 (6 × 2 = 12, wrote 2 but lost the carry, giving 620 instead of 720), then added 620 + 144 = 764 correctly.

questions.explanation: 36 × 24 = 36 × 20 + 36 × 4 = 720 + 144 = 864 chairs. Estimate check: 36 × 24 ≈ 40 × 25 = 1,000, so 864 is reasonable while 216 is far too small.

micros.title: Multiplying by 10, 100 and Tens
micros.description: Multiplying by 10 shifts every digit one place up, leaving a zero in the ones. Use this to compute 27 × 30 as 27 × 3 × 10 — the key fact behind the long multiplication algorithm.
outcomes: Can multiply any number by 10 or 100 and explain the zero pattern by place value
Can multiply by a multiple of ten, e.g. 27 × 30 = 810

micros.title: 2-digit × 1-digit with Carrying
micros.description: Multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number in columns. The rule to say aloud every time: multiply first, THEN add the carry.
outcomes: Can multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number with a carry
Can verbalise the order: times fact first, carry added after

options.diagnosis: Added the carry 5 to the 4 BEFORE multiplying: (4 + 5) × 8 = 72. Multiply first, then add the carry.
Wrote 32 and 56 side by side instead of regrouping the partial products.
Carried 4 instead of 5 from 7 × 8 = 56; the times fact is fine, the carry record slipped.

question.explanation: 7 × 8 = 56: write 6, carry 5. Then 4 × 8 = 32, plus the carry 5 gives 37. Answer: 376.

micros.title: 3-digit × 1-digit Numbers
micros.description: Extend column multiplication to 3-digit numbers, handling carries in more than one column and zeros inside the number (e.g. 305 × 7).
outcomes: Can multiply a 3-digit number by a 1-digit number with carries in several columns
Can handle a zero inside the 3-digit number correctly

micros.title: The Area (Box) Model and Partial Products
micros.description: Split each factor into tens and ones and draw a box: 23 × 45 becomes four small products (20×40, 20×5, 3×40, 3×5) that add to the answer. This is what the written algorithm secretly records.
outcomes: Can draw the box model for a 2-digit × 2-digit product and find all four partial products
Can explain why multiplying digit-under-digit misses two of the four boxes

question.prompt: To find 23 × 45 with the box model, you split 23 into 20 + 3 and 45 into 40 + 5. How many small products must you add up?

options.diagnosis: Only multiplies ones with ones and tens with tens — the two cross products are missing.
Thinks the box is just a picture of the final answer; each cell holds its own product.
Dropped one cross product; every part of one factor must meet every part of the other.

micros.title: 2-digit × 2-digit Column Method
micros.description: The compact written method: one row for the ones digit, one row for the tens digit ending in a placeholder zero because you are really multiplying by tens. Add the two partial products.
outcomes: Can multiply two 2-digit numbers with the column method, writing the placeholder zero
Can explain that the second row is 'times thirty', not 'times three'

options.diagnosis: Second row written as 86 instead of 860 — the placeholder zero for 'times twenty' was dropped.
Multiplied digit under digit (3×6 and 4×2) and wrote the results side by side.
Partial products right (258 and 860) but a small slip while adding them.

question.explanation: 43 × 6 = 258 and 43 × 20 = 860. Add: 258 + 860 = 1,118. The second row must end in 0 because it is 43 × 20, ten times bigger than 43 × 2.

micros.title: Estimating and Multiplication Word Problems
micros.description: Round the factors to estimate the product first, then solve rows-and-columns, price and earnings problems, using the estimate to spot answers that are far too small or big.
outcomes: Can estimate a product by rounding both factors to friendly numbers
Can solve a multiplication word problem and check the answer against the estimate

question.prompt: A shopkeeper packs 32 boxes with 25 pens in each box. How many pens is that in all?

options.diagnosis: Added 160 + 64 — the second partial product lost its placeholder zero (should be 640).
Multiplied digit under digit (3×2 and 2×5) and glued the results together.
Reported the estimate 30 × 25 as if it were the exact answer.

question.explanation: 32 × 25 = 32 × 20 + 32 × 5 = 640 + 160 = 800 pens. Estimate check: 30 × 25 = 750, so 800 is sensible while 224 is far too small.

nodes.title: Long Division with 1-digit Divisors and Remainders
nodes.description: Long division shares a big number into equal groups place by place: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down. The remainder tells you what is left over when the sharing cannot be completed — and in real problems, deciding what to do with that remainder is as important as the division itself.
learning_outcomes: Can divide a 2- or 3-digit number by a 1-digit number using long division
Can express and check an answer as quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend
Can explain why a remainder must be smaller than the divisor
Can interpret the remainder sensibly in word problems (round up, drop, or report it)

misconceptions.description: Stops dividing while the remainder is still as big as or bigger than the divisor, e.g. 57 ÷ 5 = 10 remainder 7.
misconceptions.signal: Written work shows remainders like 'r 7' when dividing by 5; the student never compares remainder with divisor.
misconceptions.remedy: Make 'Is what's left enough for one more group?' the final ritual question of every division. Model with counters: 7 leftover counters when sharing by 5 clearly fill one more plate.

misconceptions.description: Skips the zero in the quotient when a digit is too small to divide, so 612 ÷ 3 = 24 instead of 204.
misconceptions.signal: Quotients are missing a middle or final zero; answers are about ten times too small; no zero ever appears above a small digit.
misconceptions.remedy: Insist every digit of the dividend gets a digit written above it — even if that digit is 0. Estimate first (612 ÷ 3 is about 200) so a 2-digit answer immediately looks wrong.

misconceptions.description: Ignores or mechanically reports the remainder in context problems, e.g. answers '16 buses' when 2 students would be left behind.
misconceptions.signal: Word-problem answers are bare quotients or 'q r n' with no sentence; the student never asks what the leftover means.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort remainder problems into three piles — round up (buses), drop (full boxes), remainder is the answer (sweets left over) — and have the student justify the pile before computing.

real_world_hooks: Packing 130 students into vans that seat 8 for a school trip
Sharing a pot of ₹612 equally among 3 friends
Filling egg trays of 6 from a basket of 75 eggs
Distributing laddoos equally on plates at a festival
teaching.video_search: long division 1 digit divisor remainder class 4

options.diagnosis: Dropped the remainder — but 11 × 5 = 55, not 57; the 2 left over must be reported.
Chose a multiple that overshoots: 12 × 5 = 60 > 57. No check of quotient × divisor against the dividend.

questions.explanation: 5 × 11 = 55 and 57 − 55 = 2, so 57 ÷ 5 = 11 remainder 2. The remainder 2 is smaller than 5, so we are done. Check: 11 × 5 + 2 = 57. ✓

options.diagnosis: Wrote 1 in the tens place of the quotient even though 1 ÷ 3 gives 0; bring-down step confused.
Knew a zero was needed but appended it at the end instead of placing it above the tens digit.

questions.explanation: 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Then 1 ÷ 3 = 0 (write the 0!), carry the 1 to make 12. Finally 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Quotient: 204. Estimate: 612 ÷ 3 ≈ 600 ÷ 3 = 200, so 24 cannot be right.

questions.prompt: 130 students are going on a trip. Each van seats 8 students. How many vans are needed so that everyone gets a seat?

options.diagnosis: Division done correctly but not interpreted — a real-world answer cannot be 'remainder 2 vans'.
Added an extra van 'to be safe' without reasoning from the remainder.

questions.explanation: 130 ÷ 8 = 16 remainder 2. Sixteen vans seat 128 students, leaving 2 students without seats — so one more van is needed. Answer: 17 vans. Here the remainder forces us to round up.

micros.title: Division as Sharing and Grouping: Recap
micros.description: Warm up the two meanings of division — sharing equally among plates and making groups of a fixed size — and its link to multiplication facts (24 ÷ 6 asks '6 times what is 24?').
outcomes: Can model a division fact as sharing and as grouping with counters
Can find a division answer from the matching multiplication table fact

micros.title: Divide the Tens, Then the Ones
micros.description: Share a 2-digit number place by place: split 84 into 8 tens and 4 ones, share the tens first, then the ones. This place-by-place sharing is what long division writes down.
outcomes: Can divide a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number by sharing tens first, then ones
Can exchange leftover tens into ones and keep sharing

micros.title: What the Remainder Means
micros.description: Sometimes sharing does not come out even — the remainder is what is left. The golden rule: a remainder must always be SMALLER than the divisor, or one more group could still be made.
outcomes: Can find a quotient and remainder for a small division and say what each means
Can explain why a remainder equal to or bigger than the divisor signals an unfinished division

options.diagnosis: Stopped at 6 × 6 = 36 leaving 8 — but 8 leftover counters still fill one more group of 6.
Overshot: 8 × 6 = 48 is more than 44; the quotient must not overshoot the dividend.
Subtraction slip: 44 − 42 = 2, not 4. Check with 7 × 6 + remainder.

question.explanation: 6 × 7 = 42 and 44 − 42 = 2, so 44 ÷ 6 = 7 remainder 2. The remainder 2 is smaller than 6, so no more groups can be made. Check: 7 × 6 + 2 = 44.

micros.title: The Long Division Algorithm
micros.description: Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down — repeated for each digit of the dividend. Every digit of the dividend gets a digit written above it, even when that digit is 0.
outcomes: Can divide a 2- or 3-digit number by a 1-digit number using the written algorithm
Can place a 0 in the quotient when a digit is too small to divide
Can estimate the quotient first to catch missing-zero answers

options.diagnosis: Skipped the 0 above the tens digit; every digit of the dividend needs a digit in the quotient.
Knew a zero was needed but appended it at the end instead of above the tens digit.
Wrote 1 in the tens place even though 1 ÷ 4 gives 0; the bring-down step got confused.

question.explanation: 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Then 1 ÷ 4 = 0 (write the 0!) with 1 left over; bring down the 6 to make 16, and 16 ÷ 4 = 4. Quotient: 204. Estimate: 816 ÷ 4 is about 800 ÷ 4 = 200, so 24 cannot be right.

micros.title: Checking Division by Multiplying Back
micros.description: Every division can be verified: quotient × divisor + remainder must rebuild the dividend exactly. Use the check to catch remainder and missing-zero slips.
outcomes: Can check a division answer with quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend
Can use a failed check to find and fix the error

question.prompt: Asha worked out 74 ÷ 3 = 24 remainder 2. Which check shows her answer is right?

options.text: 24 × 3 + 2 = 74, so the answer rebuilds the dividend

options.diagnosis: Forgot the remainder in the check; 24 × 3 = 72, and the leftover 2 must be added back.
Added everything instead of multiplying; the check mirrors division with multiplication.
Reversed the roles of dividend and quotient; multiplying the dividend makes it bigger, not smaller.

question.explanation: Division undone is multiplication: 24 groups of 3 make 72, and adding the 2 left over gives 74 — exactly the starting number. So 24 r 2 is correct.

micros.title: Word Problems: What to Do with the Remainder
micros.description: In real problems the remainder must be interpreted: round up (everyone needs a seat), drop it (only full boxes count), or report it (sweets left over). The story decides.
outcomes: Can decide whether a problem needs rounding up, dropping, or reporting the remainder
Can state the final answer as a sensible sentence, not a bare 'q r n'

question.prompt: A farmer has 75 eggs and packs them into trays that hold 6 eggs each. How many FULL trays can she pack?

options.diagnosis: Reported the division mechanically — 'remainder 3 trays' is not a real-world answer; the 3 are loose eggs.
Rounded up, but the 13th tray would have only 3 eggs — not a FULL tray.
Reported the leftover eggs instead of the full trays; re-read what the question asks.

question.explanation: 75 ÷ 6 = 12 remainder 3. Twelve trays are completely full (72 eggs) and 3 eggs stay loose. The question asks for full trays, so the remainder is dropped: 12.

nodes.title: Fractions: Equal Parts, Comparing and Equivalence Intro
nodes.description: A fraction names equal parts of a whole: the bottom number tells how many equal parts the whole is cut into, and the top number tells how many of them we take. You will name fractions from pictures, compare simple fractions of the same whole, and meet the surprising idea that different-looking fractions like 1/2 and 3/6 can name the same amount.
learning_outcomes: Can explain why fraction parts must be equal, and reject unequal-part 'fractions'
Can name the fraction shown by a shaded region or a shared collection
Can compare unit fractions of the same whole (1/4 vs 1/6) with a reason
Can find a simple equivalent fraction using a picture or by doubling both numbers

misconceptions.description: Thinks any one of n parts is 1/n even when the parts are unequal — 'I cut it in 3 pieces, so each is a third.'
misconceptions.signal: Labels unequal pizza slices as thirds; shades any 3 of 4 unequal regions and writes 3/4.
misconceptions.remedy: Show fair-share disputes: cut a paper roti into obviously unequal 'thirds' and ask who would accept the small piece. Equal parts is the entry ticket to naming a fraction.

misconceptions.description: Believes a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction: 1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4.
misconceptions.signal: Orders unit fractions the same way as whole numbers; says 'eighths are more than quarters'.
misconceptions.remedy: Fold two same-size paper strips into quarters and eighths and physically compare one piece of each: more cuts means smaller pieces. Then generalise: for the same whole, more parts → smaller parts.

misconceptions.description: Treats numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers rather than one quantity — swaps them, or changes one without the other.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 4/3 for '3 of 4 parts'; claims 2/3 = 2/6 after 'doubling'; reads 3/4 as 'three and four'.
misconceptions.remedy: Always verbalise the roles: 'cut into __ equal parts, take __'. Use fraction-wall strips so that changing only the bottom number visibly changes the size of every piece.

real_world_hooks: Sharing a chapati or dosa fairly among friends
Half-litre and quarter-litre milk packets
Half-time in a football match, quarter of an hour
Cutting a birthday cake or barfi tray into equal pieces
teaching.video_search: fractions equal parts comparing unit fractions class 4

questions.prompt: A circle is divided into 4 equal parts and 3 of them are shaded. What fraction of the circle is shaded?

options.diagnosis: Named the unshaded part instead of the shaded part; read the picture, not the question.
Compared shaded parts to unshaded parts instead of to the whole circle.

questions.explanation: The whole is cut into 4 equal parts (denominator 4) and we take 3 of them (numerator 3), so the shaded fraction is 3/4.

questions.prompt: Ria eats 1/4 of a chapati. Sam eats 1/6 of the same chapati. Who ate more?

options.text: Ria — quarters are bigger pieces than sixths
Both ate the same — each ate exactly 1 piece
options.diagnosis: Counted pieces without attending to piece size — the bottom number tells how big each piece is, and a quarter piece is bigger than a sixth piece.

options.text: Cannot say without knowing the size of the chapati
options.diagnosis: Missed that both fractions are of the same whole, which is exactly what makes them comparable.

questions.explanation: Cutting the same chapati into 6 parts makes smaller pieces than cutting it into 4 parts. So 1/4 > 1/6, and Ria ate more. More parts means smaller parts.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is equivalent to (names the same amount as) 2/3?

options.diagnosis: Added 1 to both top and bottom — additive thinking; equivalence needs multiplying both by the same number.
Doubled only the denominator, which actually makes the fraction smaller.

questions.explanation: Cut each of the 3 parts in half: now there are 6 parts and the shaded 2 parts become 4. So 2/3 = 4/6 — both numbers are doubled together, and the amount does not change.

micros.title: Fractions Need EQUAL Parts
micros.description: A fraction only makes sense when the whole is cut into equal parts. Test cuttings of rotis, cakes and rectangles: equal parts earn fraction names, unequal parts do not.
outcomes: Can say whether a picture shows real fractions by checking the parts are equal
Can reject 'one of three pieces = one third' when the pieces differ in size

question.prompt: A cake is cut into 3 pieces: one big, one medium, one small. Rani takes the small piece. Did Rani get one third of the cake?

options.text: No — thirds must be 3 EQUAL pieces, and these are not equal
Yes — the cake is in 3 pieces, so each piece is a third
options.diagnosis: Counts the pieces but never checks that they are equal — the entry ticket to naming a fraction.

options.text: Yes, but only if she takes the middle-sized piece
options.diagnosis: Still accepts unequal cuts as fractions; no single unequal piece is a true third.

options.text: Only round cakes can be cut into thirds
options.diagnosis: Shape does not matter — any whole can be cut into 3 equal parts.

question.explanation: One third means the cake is shared into 3 equal parts and you take 1. With unequal pieces, nobody can say what fraction each piece is without measuring. Equal parts come first.

micros.title: Naming Fractions from Pictures
micros.description: Read a fraction off a picture: the bottom number counts the equal parts the whole is cut into, the top number counts the parts taken. Say it aloud: 'cut into __ equal parts, take __'.
outcomes: Can write the fraction for a shaded region or a shared collection
Can say which number is the denominator and what job it does

question.prompt: A strip is divided into 8 equal parts and 5 of them are shaded. What fraction of the strip is shaded?

options.diagnosis: Swapped numerator and denominator; the parts-in-the-whole number goes on the bottom.
Named the unshaded part instead of the shaded part.
Compared shaded parts to unshaded parts instead of to the whole strip.

question.explanation: The whole is cut into 8 equal parts (denominator 8) and 5 are taken (numerator 5): the shaded fraction is 5/8.

micros.title: Fractions of a Collection
micros.description: A fraction can also name part of a group: 1/4 of 12 marbles means sharing 12 into 4 equal groups and taking one group. Connect the denominator to dividing.
outcomes: Can find a unit fraction of a small collection by equal sharing
Can explain why 1/4 of 12 is found by dividing 12 by 4

micros.title: Comparing Unit Fractions of the Same Whole
micros.description: For the same whole, more parts means smaller parts: 1/4 of a chapati is bigger than 1/6 of it. Fold paper strips to see why the whole-number order flips for unit fractions.
outcomes: Can compare two unit fractions of the same whole and give the more-parts-smaller-parts reason
Can order three unit fractions such as 1/2, 1/5, 1/8

question.prompt: Arjun eats 1/5 of a chocolate bar. Priya eats 1/9 of the same bar. Who ate more?

options.text: Arjun — fifths are bigger pieces than ninths

options.diagnosis: Ordered the fractions like whole numbers; more parts actually means smaller parts.

options.text: Both the same — each ate exactly one piece
options.diagnosis: Counts pieces without minding their size; a piece's size depends on the denominator.

options.text: Cannot say without weighing the bar
options.diagnosis: Both fractions are of the SAME bar — that is exactly what makes them comparable.

question.explanation: Cutting the same bar into 9 parts makes smaller pieces than cutting it into 5. So 1/5 > 1/9 and Arjun ate more. For the same whole: more parts, smaller parts.

micros.title: Equivalent Fractions: Different Names, Same Amount
micros.description: Cutting every part in half doubles both numbers of a fraction but leaves the amount unchanged: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. Meet equivalence with pictures and the fraction wall.
outcomes: Can find an equivalent fraction by doubling (or tripling) both top and bottom
Can use a picture to explain why 1/2 and 3/6 name the same amount
Can spot false equivalents made by changing only one number

question.prompt: Which fraction names the SAME amount as 1/2?

options.diagnosis: Swapped top and bottom; 2/1 is two wholes, far more than a half.
Added 1 to both numbers — additive thinking; equivalence multiplies both by the same number.
Doubled only the denominator, which halves the amount instead of keeping it equal.

question.explanation: Cut each half into 3 smaller pieces: 6 pieces in all, and the 1 shaded half becomes 3 shaded pieces. So 1/2 = 3/6 — both numbers are multiplied by 3 together.

nodes.title: The Circle: Centre and Radius
nodes.description: A circle is the set of all points at the same distance from one special point, the centre. That fixed distance is the radius, and a line through the centre from edge to edge is the diameter — always twice the radius. This 'same distance all around' idea explains why wheels roll smoothly and why a compass draws a perfect circle.
learning_outcomes: Can identify and label the centre, radius and diameter of a circle
Can explain that all radii of a circle are equal, and use diameter = 2 × radius
Can draw a circle of a given radius with a compass
Can explain why wheels are circles using the equal-radius property

misconceptions.description: Does not accept that all radii of a circle are equal — thinks the distance from centre to edge can change with direction.
misconceptions.signal: Measures several radii 'to be sure'; says a spoke pointing down might be longer than one pointing up.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie a chalk to a string pinned at the centre and draw the circle: the string cannot stretch, so every point on the curve is exactly one string-length away. The equal radius is what MAKES it a circle.

misconceptions.description: Thinks any line joining two points on the circle is a diameter — misses that a diameter must pass through the centre.
misconceptions.signal: Labels chords as diameters; picks 'the longest-looking line' by eye rather than checking the centre.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw many chords in one circle and measure them: only the ones through the centre reach the maximum length, and they are all equal. Rule: no centre, no diameter.

misconceptions.description: Confuses radius and diameter — uses one when the other is needed, or treats them as the same length.
misconceptions.signal: Doubles when they should halve (or neither); sets a compass to the diameter to draw 'a circle of diameter 6 cm'.
misconceptions.remedy: Fold a paper circle in half: the crease is a diameter; fold again and the half-crease is a radius. Two radii lie along one diameter, so diameter = 2 × radius becomes something they have held.

real_world_hooks: Spokes of a bicycle or bullock-cart wheel
Drawing rangoli circles with string and chalk
Bangles, rotis and cricket ground boundary circles
Why manhole covers and wheels are round
teaching.video_search: circle centre radius diameter compass class 4

questions.prompt: The radius of a circle is 5 cm. What is its diameter?

options.diagnosis: Halved instead of doubled — the radius–diameter relationship is reversed.
Added radius and diameter together; the two lengths are being mixed, not related.

questions.explanation: A diameter runs from edge to edge through the centre, so it is made of two radii laid end to end: 5 cm + 5 cm = 10 cm.

questions.prompt: A line PQ joins two points on a circle but does NOT pass through the centre O. Is PQ a diameter?

options.text: No — a diameter must pass through the centre
Yes — any line joining two points on a circle is a diameter
Yes — as long as it looks like the widest line across
options.diagnosis: Judges by appearance instead of the defining property; needs the centre test, not the eye test.

options.text: Only if PQ is longer than the radius
options.diagnosis: Invented a length rule; many chords are longer than the radius without being diameters.

questions.explanation: PQ is a chord. A diameter is the special chord that passes through the centre — that is exactly what makes it the longest chord. Since PQ misses O, it is not a diameter.

questions.prompt: All the spokes of a cart wheel run from the centre to the rim. Spoke A is 30 cm long. How long is spoke B?

options.text: Exactly 30 cm — every spoke is a radius, and all radii are equal
It depends on which direction spoke B points
We cannot know without measuring spoke B
options.diagnosis: Does not yet use 'all radii equal' as a guaranteed property of circles; still treats it as a coincidence to verify.

questions.explanation: Each spoke goes from the centre to the rim, so each spoke is a radius. All radii of a circle are equal — that is what makes the wheel round and lets it roll smoothly. Spoke B is 30 cm.

micros.title: Centre, Radius, Diameter: Naming the Parts
micros.description: Meet the circle's special point (centre), the centre-to-edge distance (radius), the edge-to-edge line through the centre (diameter), and the boundary itself. Label them on drawings and real wheels.
outcomes: Can point out and label centre, radius and diameter on a circle
Can describe a circle as all points the same distance from the centre

micros.title: All Radii of a Circle Are Equal
micros.description: Draw a circle with string and chalk: the string cannot stretch, so every point of the curve is exactly one string-length from the centre. Equal radii are what MAKE a circle.
outcomes: Can state that all radii of one circle are equal, without measuring each one
Can use the string-and-chalk construction to justify the equal-radius property

question.prompt: O is the centre of a circle, and point A is on the circle with OA = 4 cm. Point B is also on the circle. How long is OB?

options.text: Exactly 4 cm — every centre-to-circle distance is a radius, and all radii are equal
It depends on which direction B lies from O
options.diagnosis: Thinks the centre-to-edge distance can change with direction; then the shape would not be a circle.
Doubled to the diameter; OB goes only from the centre to the edge, so it is a radius.

options.text: We cannot know without measuring OB
options.diagnosis: Treats equal radii as a coincidence to verify rather than the defining property of a circle.

question.explanation: A circle is exactly the set of points 4 cm from O. B is on the circle, so OB = 4 cm — guaranteed, no measuring needed.

micros.title: Diameter = 2 × Radius
micros.description: Fold a paper circle in half: the crease is a diameter, made of two radii laid end to end. Convert between radius and diameter in both directions.
outcomes: Can find the diameter from the radius and the radius from the diameter
Can show with a folded circle why the diameter is twice the radius

question.prompt: The diameter of a bangle is 12 cm. What is its radius?

options.diagnosis: Treats radius and diameter as the same length; the radius is half the diameter.
Doubled instead of halving — the conversion went the wrong way.
Halved twice; only one halving takes a diameter to a radius.

question.explanation: A diameter is two radii end to end, so radius = diameter ÷ 2 = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.

micros.title: No Centre, No Diameter
micros.description: Many lines can join two points on a circle (chords), but only the ones through the centre are diameters — and they are the longest. Test lines with the centre rule, not by eye.
outcomes: Can decide whether a line across a circle is a diameter by checking it passes through the centre
Can explain why the diameter is the longest chord

question.prompt: Which of these MUST be true for a line to be a diameter of a circle?

options.text: It joins two points on the circle AND passes through the centre
It just needs to join any two points on the circle
options.diagnosis: That describes a chord; without the centre it is not a diameter.

options.text: It needs to look like the widest line across
options.diagnosis: Judges by eye instead of the centre test; looks can deceive.

options.text: It must be the same length as the radius
options.diagnosis: A diameter is twice the radius, never equal to it.

question.explanation: The rule is: no centre, no diameter. Chords that miss the centre are shorter; only the chords through the centre reach the maximum length, 2 × radius.

micros.title: Drawing Circles with a Compass
micros.description: Set the compass opening to the RADIUS, plant the point at the centre, and sweep. Draw circles of a given radius — and of a given diameter, halving first.
outcomes: Can draw a neat circle of a given radius with a compass
Can set the compass correctly when the DIAMETER is given, by halving it first

question.prompt: You must draw a circle of diameter 8 cm with a compass. How wide should you open the compass?

options.text: 4 cm — the compass opening is the radius, half the diameter

options.diagnosis: Set the compass to the diameter; that draws a circle of diameter 16 cm.
Doubled instead of halving; the opening was pushed the wrong way twice.
Halved the diameter twice; radius = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm, halve only once.

question.explanation: The compass point sits at the centre and the pencil traces points one opening away — so the opening IS the radius: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm.

micros.title: Why Wheels Are Round
micros.description: Because all radii are equal, a rolling wheel keeps its axle at a constant height — that is why carts do not bump up and down. Connect the equal-radius property to wheels, bangles and manhole covers.
outcomes: Can explain a smooth wheel ride using the equal-radius property
Can predict what would happen with a square or oval wheel

nodes.title: Symmetry and Reflection
nodes.description: A shape has line symmetry when one half folds exactly onto the other — the fold line is the line of symmetry, and it acts like a mirror. You will find symmetry lines by folding and with mirrors, count them for common shapes and letters, and draw the mirror image of a simple figure.
learning_outcomes: Can test a proposed line of symmetry by folding or with a mirror
Can find all lines of symmetry of squares, rectangles, triangles and letters
Can draw the reflection of a simple shape across a mirror line
Can explain why equal halves are not always mirror halves (e.g. a rectangle's diagonal)

misconceptions.description: Thinks any line that cuts a shape into two equal-sized halves is a line of symmetry — e.g. the diagonal of a rectangle.
misconceptions.signal: Draws diagonals on rectangles and parallelograms and calls them symmetry lines; argues 'both halves are the same size'.
misconceptions.remedy: Fold it! Cut out a paper rectangle and fold along the diagonal: the triangles stick out and do not match. Equal area is not enough — the halves must land exactly on each other.

misconceptions.description: Only recognises vertical (upright) mirror lines; misses horizontal and slanted lines of symmetry, and rejects tilted shapes as 'not symmetric'.
misconceptions.signal: Finds 1 line for a square; says the letter E has no symmetry; symmetry answers change when the page is rotated.
misconceptions.remedy: Rotate the cut-outs: hand the student a square turned 45° and a letter E, with a small mirror. Hunting for fold lines in all directions breaks the 'mirror lines stand upright' habit.

misconceptions.description: Draws a reflection as a slide (translation) — copies the shape to the other side without flipping it.
misconceptions.signal: Mirror-image drawings face the same way as the original; letters like b reflect to b instead of d.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a real mirror on the mirror line, then trace what is actually seen. Follow with grid drawing: match each point's distance to the line on the opposite side, and check orientation reverses.

real_world_hooks: Rangoli and kolam designs outside homes
Ink-blot butterflies made by folding painted paper
The Taj Mahal's mirror-image architecture
Letters on an ambulance written in mirror form
teaching.video_search: lines of symmetry folding reflection mirror images grade 4

questions.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?

options.diagnosis: Found the upright lines (vertical and horizontal) but missed the two slanted diagonal lines of symmetry.
Counted each fold line twice (once per direction) or mixed in turns; each line is one line of symmetry.

questions.explanation: A square has 4 lines of symmetry: one vertical, one horizontal, and two diagonals. Folding along any of these four lines makes the halves match exactly.

questions.prompt: Is the diagonal of a rectangle (not a square) a line of symmetry?

options.text: No — the two halves are equal in size but do not fold exactly onto each other
Yes — it divides the rectangle into two equal parts
Yes — every straight line through the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry
options.diagnosis: Overgeneralised 'through the centre' to 'symmetry'; that works for a circle but almost nothing else.

options.text: No — a rectangle has no lines of symmetry at all
options.diagnosis: Overcorrection: a rectangle does have 2 lines of symmetry, through the midpoints of opposite sides.

questions.explanation: Fold a paper rectangle along its diagonal: the two triangles are the same size but their corners stick out — they do not coincide. A rectangle's real symmetry lines join the midpoints of opposite sides (2 lines).

questions.prompt: The letter 'b' is reflected in a vertical mirror standing to its right. What does the image look like?

options.diagnosis: Flipped top-to-bottom (horizontal mirror) instead of left-to-right.
Rotated the letter a half turn instead of reflecting it.

questions.explanation: A vertical mirror swaps left and right. The stick of 'b' is on the left with the bump on the right; in the mirror the bump moves to the left of the stick, giving 'd'. This is why AMBULANCE is written mirror-reversed on vans.

micros.title: The Fold Test for Symmetry
micros.description: A line of symmetry is a fold along which the two halves land EXACTLY on each other. Equal-sized halves are not enough — they must match point for point when folded.
outcomes: Can test a proposed line of symmetry by folding a cut-out or using a mirror
Can explain why a rectangle's diagonal cuts equal halves but is not a symmetry line

question.prompt: A line cuts a shape into two halves of exactly the same size. Is it always a line of symmetry?

options.text: No — the halves must also fold exactly onto each other, like the rectangle's diagonal shows
Yes — equal halves is exactly what symmetry means
options.diagnosis: Equal area is not enough; fold a rectangle on its diagonal and the corners stick out.

options.text: Only if the line stands straight up and down
options.diagnosis: Symmetry lines can be vertical, horizontal or slanted; direction is not the test, folding is.

options.text: Yes, as long as the line passes through the middle of the shape
options.diagnosis: Overgeneralises 'through the centre' to 'symmetry'; that works for a circle but almost nothing else.

question.explanation: The diagonal of a rectangle makes two equal triangles, but folding along it leaves corners sticking out — the halves do not coincide. Symmetry needs a perfect fold-match, not just equal size.

micros.title: Finding ALL the Lines of Symmetry
micros.description: Hunt for every fold line of squares, rectangles, triangles and circles — vertical, horizontal and slanted. Rotate the cut-out so tilted lines are not missed.
outcomes: Can find all lines of symmetry of common shapes (square 4, rectangle 2, equilateral triangle 3)
Can keep hunting after the first line is found, in every direction

question.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle (that is not a square) have?

options.diagnosis: Counted the diagonals too — they cut equal halves but fail the fold test.
Found only the upright fold and missed the horizontal one.
Overcorrection — the folds joining midpoints of opposite sides do work.

question.explanation: A rectangle folds onto itself along the two lines joining midpoints of opposite sides. Its diagonals are NOT symmetry lines — folding there leaves corners sticking out. So: 2 lines.

micros.title: Symmetry in Letters and Numbers
micros.description: Sort the alphabet by symmetry: A has a vertical line, E has a horizontal one, H and O have both, F has none. A small mirror makes the hunt a game.
outcomes: Can find vertical and horizontal symmetry lines in capital letters and digits
Can name letters with no line of symmetry

question.prompt: Which line of symmetry does the capital letter E have?

options.text: A horizontal line — the top half folds down exactly onto the bottom half

options.diagnosis: Folding E left-onto-right sends the arms away from the spine; they do not match.

options.text: None — symmetry lines must stand upright, and E has no upright one
options.diagnosis: Only accepts vertical mirror lines; horizontal and slanted folds count too.
Half right — test each fold separately; only the horizontal one works for E.

question.explanation: Fold E along a horizontal line through its middle arm: the top and bottom arms land exactly on each other. The vertical fold fails. Symmetry lines can lie in any direction.

micros.title: Drawing Mirror Images
micros.description: A reflection FLIPS a shape: each point moves to the same distance on the other side of the mirror line, and left-right (or top-bottom) reverses. Copying without flipping is a slide, not a reflection.
outcomes: Can draw the reflection of a simple shape or letter across a mirror line
Can check a reflection by matching point distances and reversed orientation

question.prompt: The letter 'p' is reflected in a vertical mirror standing to its right. What does the image look like?

options.diagnosis: Slid the letter across without flipping it; a mirror reverses left and right.
Flipped top-to-bottom (horizontal mirror) instead of left-to-right.
Rotated the letter a half turn instead of reflecting it.

question.explanation: A vertical mirror swaps left and right. The stick of 'p' with its bump on the right becomes a stick with the bump on the left: 'q'.

micros.title: Completing Symmetric Figures on a Grid
micros.description: Given half a figure and its mirror line on squared paper, draw the missing half: count each point's squares to the line and match them on the other side.
outcomes: Can complete a symmetric figure across a vertical or horizontal mirror line on a grid
Can verify the finished figure with the fold test or a mirror

nodes.title: Perimeter as Boundary Length
nodes.description: Perimeter is the total length of the boundary of a shape — the distance you would walk going once around it. You find it by adding all the side lengths. It answers real questions like how much fencing a field needs or how much lace goes around a tablecloth, and it is measured in units of length (cm, m).
learning_outcomes: Can find the perimeter of any straight-sided shape by adding all its side lengths
Can find the perimeter of rectangles and squares, using the repeated sides
Can solve fencing/border word problems, including finding a missing side from the perimeter
Can explain that shapes with the same area can have different perimeters

misconceptions.description: Confuses perimeter with area — multiplies the sides or counts inside squares when asked for the boundary.
misconceptions.signal: Answers perimeter questions with length × width; gives answers in square units; the words are used interchangeably.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor each word to a body action: walk the boundary of the playground for perimeter, count floor tiles to cover it for area. 'Fence or paint?' becomes the first question for every problem.

misconceptions.description: For a rectangle, adds only the two labelled sides (length + width) and stops, forgetting each appears twice.
misconceptions.signal: Rectangle perimeters come out exactly half the true value; diagrams with two labels get two-number sums.
misconceptions.remedy: Trace the full trip around the rectangle with a finger, saying each side aloud: 'long, short, long, short — four sides'. Then connect to the shortcut 2 × (length + width).

misconceptions.description: Believes shapes with the same area (same number of squares) must have the same perimeter.
misconceptions.signal: Says two pentomino-style shapes 'must have the same boundary because both use 5 squares'; skips measuring.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a 1×4 row and a 2×2 square from the same 4 tiles and count boundary units of each (10 vs 8). Same tiles, different boundary — measure, don't assume.

real_world_hooks: Fencing a vegetable field or school garden
Lace border sewn around a dupatta or tablecloth
One lap around the school playground
Marking the boundary line of a kabaddi court
teaching.video_search: perimeter of shapes fencing problems grade 4

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. What is its perimeter?

options.diagnosis: Added only three sides (8 + 8 + 5); lost track while going around the shape.

questions.explanation: Walk all the way around: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm, or use 2 × (8 + 5) = 26 cm. 40 comes from 8 × 5, which is the area (in square cm), not the boundary.

questions.prompt: A square field has sides of 12 m. How many metres of fencing are needed to go all the way around it?

options.diagnosis: Added only three sides; the walk around the field was not completed.

questions.explanation: A square has 4 equal sides, so the fence is 4 × 12 = 48 m. 144 is 12 × 12 — that is the field's area in square metres, not the length of its boundary.

questions.prompt: Garden A is a row of 4 square patches (1 × 4). Garden B is a square of 4 patches (2 × 2). Each patch has 1 m sides. Which garden needs more fencing around it?

options.text: Garden A — its boundary is 10 m, while Garden B's is only 8 m
Both need the same, because both are made of 4 patches
Garden B — a square shape always has the bigger boundary
options.diagnosis: Visual guess without counting boundary units; in fact the compact square has the SHORTER boundary.

options.text: 4 m each — one metre for each patch

questions.explanation: Count the outside edges: the 1 × 4 row has 4 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 10 edge-metres; the 2 × 2 square has 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. Same area (4 square metres), different perimeters — stretched-out shapes have longer boundaries.

micros.title: Perimeter Is the Walk Around the Boundary
micros.description: Perimeter is the total distance once around a shape — the length of fence, lace or one lap. It is measured in length units (cm, m). First question for any problem: fence or paint?
outcomes: Can explain perimeter as boundary length and give real examples (fencing, lace, laps)
Can say that perimeter is measured in cm or m, not square units

micros.title: Adding All the Sides
micros.description: For any straight-sided shape, trace the whole trip around it and add EVERY side length — triangles, quadrilaterals and odd shapes, including ones with an unlabelled repeated side.
outcomes: Can find the perimeter of a triangle or irregular shape by adding all side lengths
Can keep track of sides so none is missed or counted twice

question.prompt: A triangle has sides 7 cm, 9 cm and 12 cm. What is its perimeter?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied two sides (7 × 9) as if finding a covering; perimeter adds the boundary.
Added only 7 + 9 and missed the third side; the trip around was not completed.
Adding slip; re-add 7 + 9 + 12 carefully.

question.explanation: Walk the whole boundary: 7 + 9 + 12 = 28 cm. Every side is part of the trip around.

micros.title: Perimeter of a Rectangle
micros.description: A rectangle's trip goes long-short-long-short: each labelled side appears TWICE. Add all four sides, then meet the shortcut 2 × (length + width).
outcomes: Can find a rectangle's perimeter using all four sides
Can use and explain the shortcut 2 × (length + width)

question.prompt: A rectangle is 9 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its perimeter?

options.diagnosis: Added only the two labelled sides; each side of a rectangle appears twice.
Multiplied 9 × 4 — that is the area in square cm, not the boundary.
Added three sides (9 + 4 + 9) and stopped before the last width.

question.explanation: Go all the way around: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 cm, or 2 × (9 + 4) = 26 cm.

micros.title: Perimeter of a Square
micros.description: A square's four sides are equal, so its perimeter is 4 × side. Solve fencing problems and reverse ones: given the perimeter, find the side.
outcomes: Can find a square's perimeter with 4 × side
Can find the side of a square from its perimeter by dividing by 4

question.prompt: A square garden has sides of 15 m. How many metres of fencing go all the way around it?

options.diagnosis: Added only two sides; a square has four equal sides to fence.
Computed 15 × 15 — the garden's area in square metres, not the fence length.
Added three sides; the walk around the garden was not finished.

question.explanation: Four equal sides: 4 × 15 = 60 m of fencing. 225 answers a different question — how much ground the garden covers.

micros.title: Finding a Missing Side from the Perimeter
micros.description: Work backwards: if the perimeter and some sides are known, subtract to find the missing side. For rectangles, remember the missing width appears twice in the total.
outcomes: Can find a missing side of a shape when the perimeter and other sides are given
Can solve rectangle problems where the unknown side occurs twice

question.prompt: A rectangle has perimeter 30 cm and length 9 cm. What is its width?

options.diagnosis: Did 30 − 9, as if the perimeter were just one length plus one width.
Subtracted both lengths (30 − 18 = 12) but forgot that the 12 covers TWO widths.
Halved the perimeter but never subtracted the length.

question.explanation: The two lengths use 9 + 9 = 18 cm, leaving 30 − 18 = 12 cm for TWO widths. So each width is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm. Check: 2 × (9 + 6) = 30. ✓

micros.title: Same Tiles, Different Boundary
micros.description: Build different shapes from the same square tiles and count their boundary units: a stretched-out row has a longer boundary than a compact block. Same covering does not mean same perimeter.
outcomes: Can count boundary units of tile shapes on a grid
Can show with an example that equal tile counts can give different perimeters

question.prompt: Two gardens are built from six 1 m × 1 m patches: Garden A is a 1 × 6 row, Garden B is a 2 × 3 block. Which needs more fencing around it?

options.text: Garden A — its boundary is 14 m, while Garden B's is only 10 m
Both need the same, because both use 6 patches
options.diagnosis: Same tile count means same area, not same boundary — stretched shapes have longer edges.

options.text: Garden B — blocky shapes always have bigger boundaries
options.diagnosis: Backwards: compact shapes have SHORTER boundaries; count the edges to see it.

options.text: 6 m each — one metre of fence for each patch
options.diagnosis: Counted patches (covering) instead of walking the boundary.

question.explanation: Count outside edges: the 1 × 6 row has 6 + 1 + 6 + 1 = 14 edge-metres; the 2 × 3 block has 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10. Same six patches, different fences.

nodes.title: Area by Counting Squares
nodes.description: Area measures how much surface a shape covers, and we measure it by counting unit squares that tile the shape. Full squares count as 1, two half squares make 1, and rows of squares can be counted quickly with multiplication. Area answers 'how much carpet, paint or land?' — a different question from how long the boundary is.

chapters: How Many Squares? (Class 5 — nearest genuine NCERT chapter; Class 4 Math-Magic has no dedicated area-by-counting-squares chapter, and 'Fields and Fences' covers perimeter)

learning_outcomes: Can find the area of a shape on squared paper by counting unit squares, combining half squares
Can use rows × columns to count squares in a rectangle quickly
Can compare areas of different shapes drawn on the same grid
Can explain the difference between area (covering) and perimeter (boundary)

misconceptions.description: Confuses area with perimeter — counts boundary edges or adds side lengths when asked how much a shape covers.
misconceptions.signal: Grid-shape 'areas' equal the boundary count; answers given in cm instead of square units.
misconceptions.remedy: Colour the inside to find area, trace the rim to find perimeter — two different colours, two different questions. Then compare the two numbers for the same shape to cement that they measure different things.

misconceptions.description: Counts every partly-covered square as a whole one (or throws all of them away), instead of pairing halves.
misconceptions.signal: Areas of slanted or curved shapes come out clearly too big (or too small); half squares are tallied as 1 each.
