misconceptions.remedy: Physically cut two half-squares from squared paper and lay them on one full square. Establish the rule set: full = 1, two halves = 1, less than half ≈ 0, more than half ≈ 1 for estimates.

misconceptions.description: Believes a bigger perimeter always means a bigger area (and vice versa).
misconceptions.signal: Ranks shapes by boundary length when asked about covering; is sure a long thin shape 'must be bigger' than a compact one.
misconceptions.remedy: Give a fixed loop of string (fixed perimeter) on a pegboard and make different rectangles: count the enclosed squares each time. Same boundary, different areas — seeing it collapses the belief.

real_world_hooks: How many tiles cover the kitchen floor
Comparing two handkerchiefs or two leaves by tracing on squared paper
Farm plots of different shapes on a village map
How much paper is needed to cover a notebook
teaching.video_search: area by counting squares grid paper grade 4

questions.prompt: A rectangle drawn on squared paper is 5 squares long and 3 squares wide. What is its area?

options.diagnosis: Added 5 + 3 instead of counting the full array of squares.
Counted only the squares touching the border and missed the 3 inside ones.

questions.explanation: The squares sit in 3 rows of 5, so there are 3 × 5 = 15 squares. 16 is the number of edge units around the shape — that is its perimeter, not its area.

questions.prompt: A leaf traced on squared paper covers 6 full squares and 4 half squares. What is its area?

options.diagnosis: Ignored the half squares entirely; partial squares still cover surface.
Paired the halves incorrectly — 4 halves make 2 whole squares, not 1.

questions.explanation: Four half squares pair up into 4 ÷ 2 = 2 full squares. Total area = 6 + 2 = 8 square units.

questions.prompt: A 12 m rope is bent into a 1 m × 5 m rectangle, and then re-bent into a 3 m × 3 m square. Do the two shapes enclose the same area?

options.text: No — the square encloses 9 square metres but the rectangle only 5
Yes — the same rope means the same space inside
Yes — area is just length + width, which is 6 for both
No — the 1 × 5 rectangle has more area because it is longer
options.diagnosis: Attends to one dimension only; length alone does not decide how much is covered.

questions.explanation: Both shapes have perimeter 12 m, but 3 × 3 = 9 square metres while 1 × 5 = 5 square metres. Equal boundary does NOT mean equal area — compact shapes enclose more.

micros.title: Area Is How Much a Shape Covers
micros.description: Area answers 'how much carpet, paint or land?' and is measured in square units by covering the shape with unit squares — a different question from the boundary walk.
outcomes: Can tell an area question (covering) from a perimeter question (boundary)
Can say that area is measured in square units

question.prompt: Which of these questions is about AREA?

options.text: How many tiles are needed to cover the kitchen floor?
How long is the fence around the field?
options.diagnosis: Fencing follows the boundary — that is perimeter, measured in metres.

options.text: How far is one lap around the playground?
options.diagnosis: A lap traces the boundary; that is perimeter again, not covering.

options.text: How many corners does the room have?
options.diagnosis: Counting corners is about the shape's form, not about covering or boundary.

question.explanation: Tiling the floor covers the surface, so it asks for area (in square units). Fences and laps go around the edge — those are perimeter questions.

micros.title: Counting Unit Squares
micros.description: Find the area of grid shapes by counting the unit squares they cover, marking each counted square so none is missed or double-counted — including L-shapes and staircases.
outcomes: Can find the area of a grid shape by counting full unit squares
Can compare two shapes on the same grid by their square counts

micros.title: Handling Half Squares
micros.description: Slanted and curved shapes cover partial squares. Rule set: full square = 1, two halves = 1; for estimates, more than half ≈ 1 and less than half ≈ 0.
outcomes: Can find the area of a shape with half squares by pairing them up
Can estimate the area of a curved shape (like a leaf) on squared paper

question.prompt: A shape traced on squared paper covers 5 full squares and 6 half squares. What is its area?

options.diagnosis: Counted each half square as a whole one; two halves make one square.
Threw the half squares away; partial squares still cover surface.
Paired the halves wrongly — 6 halves make 3 whole squares, not 1.

question.explanation: Six half squares pair into 6 ÷ 2 = 3 full squares. Total area = 5 + 3 = 8 square units.

micros.title: Counting Squares Fast: Rows × Columns
micros.description: In a rectangle the squares sit in equal rows, so multiply rows by columns instead of counting one by one. This shortcut is the seed of the area formula met in Class 5.
outcomes: Can find a grid rectangle's area with rows × columns
Can explain why multiplying counts exactly the same squares as counting one by one

question.prompt: A rectangle on squared paper is 6 squares long and 4 squares wide. What is its area?

options.diagnosis: Counted the boundary units around the shape — that is its perimeter.
Added 6 + 4 instead of counting the full array of squares.
Counted only the squares touching the border and missed the inside ones.

question.explanation: The squares sit in 4 rows of 6: 4 × 6 = 24 squares. The boundary count, 2 × (6 + 4) = 20, answers the perimeter question instead.

micros.title: Same Boundary, Different Area
micros.description: Bend one loop of string into different rectangles and count the enclosed squares: the boundary stays the same but the area changes. Equal perimeter does NOT mean equal area.
outcomes: Can show with one string loop that equal perimeters can enclose different areas
Can explain why compact shapes enclose more than stretched ones

question.prompt: A 20 cm loop of string is first shaped into a 1 cm × 9 cm rectangle, then re-shaped into a 5 cm × 5 cm square. Do the two shapes enclose the same area?

options.text: No — the square encloses 25 square cm but the rectangle only 9
Yes — the same string must enclose the same space inside
options.diagnosis: Equal boundary does not mean equal covering; count the squares inside each shape.

options.text: Yes — area is length + width, which is 10 for both
options.diagnosis: Adding sides gives (half) the perimeter; area multiplies to count the covering squares.

options.text: No — the 1 × 9 rectangle has more area because it is longer
options.diagnosis: Length alone does not decide covering; the thin shape encloses far less.

question.explanation: Both have perimeter 20 cm, but 5 × 5 = 25 square cm while 1 × 9 = 9 square cm. The same boundary can hold very different areas — compact shapes hold more.

nodes.title: Elapsed Time and the 24-hour Clock
nodes.description: Elapsed time is how long something lasts — from a movie's start to its end, or a train's departure to its arrival. Because an hour has 60 minutes (not 100), adding and subtracting times needs care at the hour boundary. The 24-hour clock, used in railway timetables, removes the confusion between morning and evening times.
learning_outcomes: Can convert between 12-hour (am/pm) and 24-hour clock times
Can add a duration to a start time, regrouping 60 minutes into 1 hour
Can find the elapsed time between two clock times, including across noon
Can read a railway timetable and answer duration questions from it

misconceptions.description: Treats clock time as base-10: adds and subtracts minutes as if 100 minutes make an hour (2:45 + 30 min = 2:75).
misconceptions.signal: Writes impossible times like 2:75 or 3:80; column-subtracts times like ordinary numbers.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a visible number line of minutes marked in hops of 15 to the next hour: 2:45 + 15 lands on 3:00, then 15 more lands on 3:15. Rule on the wall: minutes roll over at 60, never 100.

misconceptions.description: Converts 24-hour times by subtracting 10 instead of 12 (17:00 read as 7 pm).
misconceptions.signal: Afternoon conversions are consistently 2 hours too late (or too early); 15:00 becomes 5 pm.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor to noon = 12:00: after noon the clock keeps counting 13, 14, 15... Have the student build the double-scale clock face (13 under 1, 14 under 2 ...) so 'subtract 12' is read off, not memorised.

misconceptions.description: Finds elapsed time across noon by subtracting the clock numbers directly (9:30 am to 1:15 pm = 9 − 1 = 8 hours).
misconceptions.signal: Durations spanning 12 o'clock come out wildly wrong; the student never splits the interval at 12:00.
misconceptions.remedy: Teach the bridge strategy on an empty time line: jump from the start to 12:00, then from 12:00 to the finish, and add the jumps. Alternatively convert both to 24-hour times first.

real_world_hooks: Indian Railways timetables written in 24-hour time
How long a cricket T20 innings or a movie lasts
School timetable: length of each period and lunch break
Cooking times: pressure-cooker whistles and biryani in the oven
teaching.video_search: elapsed time number line 24 hour clock word problems

questions.prompt: A railway board shows a departure at 17:00. What time is that on a 12-hour clock?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 12 correctly but dropped the am/pm meaning — times after 12:00 are afternoon/evening.
Off-by-one while counting on from 12; likely counted 12 itself as the first hour.

questions.explanation: After noon the 24-hour clock keeps counting: 13:00 = 1 pm, 14:00 = 2 pm, ... so 17:00 = 17 − 12 = 5 pm.

questions.prompt: A cartoon show starts at 2:45 pm and lasts 30 minutes. When does it end?

options.diagnosis: Added a whole hour instead of 30 minutes.
Crossed the hour but only added 20 minutes; lost 10 minutes at the boundary.

questions.explanation: Split the 30 minutes at the hour: 2:45 + 15 min = 3:00, then 15 more minutes gives 3:15 pm. There is no such time as 2:75 — minutes roll over at 60.

questions.prompt: A train leaves Agra at 9:30 am and reaches Jhansi at 1:15 pm the same day. How long does the journey take?

options.diagnosis: Counted 9:30 to 1:30 as 4 hours, then mishandled the extra 15 minutes — it should be subtracted, not added.
Counted 9:30 to 12:30 as 3 hours, then added only the ':15' of 1:15 — but 12:30 to 1:15 is 45 minutes, not 15.

questions.explanation: Bridge at noon: 9:30 am → 12:00 noon is 2 h 30 min; 12:00 → 1:15 pm is 1 h 15 min. Total: 3 h 45 min. Subtracting clock numbers (9 − 1) gives nonsense because the clock restarts at 12.

micros.title: The 24-hour Clock
micros.description: After noon the railway clock keeps counting: 13:00, 14:00, ... 23:59. Convert both ways between am/pm times and 24-hour times using the anchor noon = 12:00.
outcomes: Can convert a 24-hour time to am/pm by subtracting 12 after noon
Can convert an afternoon or evening time to 24-hour form by adding 12

question.prompt: A railway board shows a train at 15:30. What time is that on a 12-hour clock?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 10 instead of 12; the clock restarts at noon = 12, so take away 12.
Subtracted 12 correctly but dropped the meaning — times after 12:00 are afternoon (pm).
Subtracted 13; the anchor is 12:00 noon, so subtract exactly 12.

question.explanation: After noon the 24-hour clock keeps counting: 13:00 = 1 pm, 14:00 = 2 pm, 15:00 = 3 pm. So 15:30 = 3:30 pm.

micros.title: Adding Minutes Inside One Hour
micros.description: Add a duration to a start time when the sum of minutes stays under 60 — 3:10 + 25 minutes = 3:35. Reading durations in minutes and relating them to quarter and half hours.
outcomes: Can add minutes to a time when no hour boundary is crossed
Can use quarter-hour landmarks (15, 30, 45 minutes) fluently

micros.title: Crossing the Hour: 60 Minutes, Not 100
micros.description: When minutes pass 60 they roll into a new hour — there is no such time as 4:75. Split the added minutes at the next o'clock on a number line of minutes.
outcomes: Can add a duration that crosses an hour boundary by splitting at the next o'clock
Can explain why times like 4:75 are impossible

question.prompt: A TV show starts at 4:50 pm and lasts 25 minutes. When does it end?

options.diagnosis: Added minutes as if 100 make an hour; minutes roll over at 60, so 4:75 is not a time.
Crossed to 5:00 but then added the whole 25 minutes again, forgetting 10 were already used.
Added only 15 minutes after the hour; 25 − 10 = 15 was miscomputed.

question.explanation: Split at the hour: 4:50 + 10 minutes = 5:00, and the remaining 15 minutes land on 5:15 pm.

micros.title: Elapsed Time on an Empty Number Line
micros.description: Find how long something lasts by hopping on a time line: jump to the next o'clock, hop whole hours, then the final minutes. Works for any two times on the same side of noon.
outcomes: Can find the duration between two times using jumps on an empty time line
Can add the hour and minute jumps into a total like 2 h 30 min

micros.title: Elapsed Time Across Noon
micros.description: Durations that cross 12 o'clock cannot be found by subtracting clock numbers. Bridge at noon: start → 12:00, then 12:00 → finish, and add the two jumps.
outcomes: Can find a duration from a morning time to an afternoon time with the noon bridge
Can explain why subtracting the clock numbers directly gives nonsense

question.prompt: A bus leaves at 10:45 am and arrives at 2:30 pm. How long is the journey?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the clock numbers (10:45 − 2:30) directly; the clock restarts at 12, so bridge at noon instead.
Counted 10:45 to 2:45 as 4 hours, then mishandled the last 15 minutes — they must come off, not on.
Jumped 10:45 → 12:00 as 1 h 15 min but then took 12:00 → 2:30 as only 2 h.

question.explanation: Bridge at noon: 10:45 → 12:00 is 1 h 15 min; 12:00 → 2:30 pm is 2 h 30 min. Total: 3 h 45 min.

micros.title: Reading Railway Timetables
micros.description: Use real timetables in 24-hour time: find departures and arrivals, compute journey lengths, and compare trains. All the elapsed-time skills come together here.
outcomes: Can read departure and arrival times from a 24-hour timetable
Can compute a journey's duration from timetable times
Can answer comparison questions (which train is faster, which reaches first)

question.prompt: A train departs at 11:30 and arrives at 14:15. How long is the journey?

options.diagnosis: Column-subtracted the times like ordinary numbers, borrowing 100 minutes instead of 60.
Counted 11:30 → 14:30 as 3 hours and then ADDED the 15 minutes instead of taking them off.
Took the hours (11 → 14 minus a bit) and just copied the arrival's 15 minutes.

question.explanation: Hop on a time line: 11:30 → 12:00 is 30 min, 12:00 → 14:00 is 2 h, 14:00 → 14:15 is 15 min. Total: 2 h 45 min. An answer with 85 minutes is impossible — minutes roll over at 60.

nodes.title: Unit Conversions: Length, Weight, Capacity
nodes.description: Metres and centimetres, kilograms and grams, litres and millilitres — the metric system connects big and small units by factors of 100 and 1000. Converting between them means multiplying when going to smaller units and dividing when going to bigger ones. Mixed measures like 3 m 5 cm must be handled place by place, not glued together.
learning_outcomes: Can state the key metric relations: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 L = 1000 mL
Can convert a measure to a smaller unit by multiplying, and to a larger unit by dividing
Can express mixed measures (3 m 5 cm) as a single unit correctly
Can choose sensible units and estimate everyday lengths, weights and capacities

misconceptions.description: Converts in the wrong direction — multiplies when going to a bigger unit (250 cm = 25,000 m).
misconceptions.signal: Answers absurd on the face of it (a table 25,000 m long); the operation is chosen by habit, not by unit size.
misconceptions.remedy: Insist on a sense-check sentence before converting: 'a metre is BIGGER than a centimetre, so I need FEWER of them — divide.' Pair every conversion with an estimate of whether the answer should be a bigger or smaller number.

misconceptions.description: Uses the wrong conversion factor — treats all metric relations as ×10 or ×100 (1 kg = 100 g, 1 m = 1000 cm).
misconceptions.signal: Off-by-ten answers; the same factor is used for every unit pair.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a reference card from real objects: a 1 kg sugar pack holds 1000 g, a metre stick shows 100 cm, a 1 L bottle fills 1000 mL. Verify each factor physically once, then keep the card visible during practice.

misconceptions.description: Glues mixed measures together as digits or decimals: 3 m 5 cm becomes 3.5 m or 35 cm.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 3 m 5 cm = 350 cm; reads '5 cm' as '50 cm' or '0.5 m' when combining.
misconceptions.remedy: Convert each part separately and then add: 3 m = 300 cm, plus 5 cm, is 305 cm. A place-value-style frame for m | cm makes the missing tens position visible.

real_world_hooks: Buying 250 g of masala or 1.5 kg of rice at the kirana shop
A 500 mL water bottle versus a 1 L bottle for the school bag
Measuring cloth in metres and centimetres at the tailor
Distance boards on the highway in kilometres
teaching.video_search: metric unit conversion km m cm kg g litre ml class 4

questions.prompt: How many grams are there in 1 kilogram?

options.diagnosis: Overgeneralised a pattern of tens; metric jumps here are by thousands, not tens.
Confused 1 kg with the common half-kg shop pack.

questions.explanation: 'Kilo' means one thousand: 1 kg = 1000 g. Check with a sugar packet — a 1 kg pack is labelled 1000 g.

questions.prompt: A rope is 250 cm long. What is its length in metres?
questions.explanation: 100 cm make 1 m, so 250 cm = 250 ÷ 100 = 2 whole metres with 50 cm left over: 2 m 50 cm. Going to a bigger unit means fewer of them — divide.

questions.prompt: A ribbon is 3 m 5 cm long. How long is it in centimetres?

options.diagnosis: Stuck the digits 3 and 5 together with no unit reasoning at all.

questions.explanation: Convert the metres first: 3 m = 3 × 100 = 300 cm. Then add the 5 cm: 300 + 5 = 305 cm. Writing 350 treats '5 cm' as '50 cm' — the empty tens place must be held by a zero.

micros.title: The Metric Fact Family
micros.description: Fix the four key relations with real objects: 1 m = 100 cm (metre stick), 1 km = 1000 m (distance boards), 1 kg = 1000 g (sugar pack), 1 L = 1000 mL (water bottle).
outcomes: Can state the four key metric relations from memory
Can name a real object that proves each relation

question.prompt: How many millilitres are there in 1 litre?

options.diagnosis: Used the metre–centimetre factor; litres and millilitres jump by 1000.
Overgeneralised a pattern of tens; check the label on a 1 L bottle.
Confused 1 L with the common half-litre bottle.

question.explanation: 'Milli' means a thousandth: 1 L = 1000 mL. A 1-litre water bottle is labelled 1000 mL.

micros.title: Converting to a Smaller Unit: Multiply
micros.description: A smaller unit needs MORE of them, so multiply by the factor: 7 m = 700 cm, 4 kg = 4000 g. Say the sense-check sentence aloud before computing.
outcomes: Can convert m→cm, km→m, kg→g and L→mL by multiplying by the right factor
Can justify the direction: smaller units means a bigger count

question.prompt: A cloth piece is 7 m long. How long is it in centimetres?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 10; a metre holds 100 centimetres — check the metre stick.
Used the 1000 factor that belongs to km, kg and L, not to metres and centimetres.
Added 100 instead of multiplying by 100.

question.explanation: Centimetres are smaller than metres, so we need more of them: 7 × 100 = 700 cm.

micros.title: Converting to a Bigger Unit: Divide
micros.description: A bigger unit needs FEWER of them, so divide by the factor: 5000 m = 5 km, 300 cm = 3 m. An absurd-looking answer (a 25,000 m table!) means the direction was wrong.
outcomes: Can convert cm→m, m→km, g→kg and mL→L by dividing by the right factor
Can catch a wrong-direction conversion by sense-checking the answer's size

question.prompt: A morning walk track is 5,000 m long. How long is that in kilometres?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied when moving to a BIGGER unit; kilometres are bigger, so we need fewer — divide.
Divided by 100; the metre–kilometre factor is 1000.
Divided by 10 only; a 500 km walk should ring the alarm bell — sense-check the size.

question.explanation: A kilometre is bigger than a metre, so we need fewer of them: 5,000 ÷ 1000 = 5 km. A walking track millions of kilometres long is absurd — the sense-check catches it.

micros.title: Mixed Measures: 2 kg 50 g Is Not 250 g
micros.description: Convert mixed measures like 3 m 5 cm or 2 kg 50 g to a single unit: convert the big-unit part first, THEN add the small part. Never glue the digits together.
outcomes: Can express a mixed measure in the smaller unit by converting then adding
Can explain the zero that holds the empty place (3 m 5 cm = 305 cm, not 35 or 350)

question.prompt: A parcel weighs 2 kg 50 g. What is its weight in grams?

options.diagnosis: Glued the digits 2 and 50 together; the 2 kg must first become 2,000 g.
Read '50 g' as '500 g' when combining — the empty hundreds place needs its zero.
Converted with the wrong factor and glued the parts; 1 kg is 1000 g, not 100.

question.explanation: Convert the kilograms first: 2 kg = 2 × 1000 = 2,000 g. Then add the 50 g: 2,000 + 50 = 2,050 g.

micros.title: Choosing Sensible Units and Estimating
micros.description: Pick the right unit for the job — km for city distances, g for a pencil — and estimate everyday measures: a door is about 2 m, an apple about 150 g, a bucket about 10 L.
outcomes: Can choose the sensible unit for a given object or distance
Can give a reasonable estimate for everyday lengths, weights and capacities

question.prompt: Which is the best estimate for the weight of one apple?

options.diagnosis: That is about three big rice bags; the unit is far too heavy for one apple.
That is about one small biscuit; an apple is clearly heavier.
That is about two grown-ups; compare with things you have lifted.

question.explanation: An apple sits comfortably in one hand — around 150 g. Anchors help: a 1-rupee coin is about 4 g, a bag of sugar is 1 kg (1000 g).

micros.title: Word Problems with Unit Conversions
micros.description: Solve shopping and measuring problems where quantities come in mixed units: total cloth bought in m and cm, milk in L and mL. Convert to one unit before adding or comparing.
outcomes: Can bring all quantities to one unit before adding or comparing
Can answer with the sensible unit and sense-check the size of the result

nodes.title: Patterns and Rules
nodes.description: A pattern is a sequence built by a rule — add the same number, double, or repeat a block of shapes. The mathematician's job is to find the rule, check it against EVERY step given, and then use it to predict what comes next (or far ahead) without drawing everything. This is the first step toward algebra.
learning_outcomes: Can find and state the rule of a number pattern and extend it
Can check a proposed rule against every given term, not just the first pair
Can identify the repeating unit of a shape pattern and predict a far-away term (e.g. the 20th shape)
Can create a pattern from a given rule and describe features of it

misconceptions.description: Guesses the rule from the first pair of terms only and never tests it on the rest (sees 3, 6 and locks in 'add 3' for 3, 6, 12, 24).
misconceptions.signal: Confidently extends with a rule that already fails at the third term; never looks back at the sequence.
misconceptions.remedy: Make 'check every step' a required move: write the candidate rule above each gap (3→6 ✓? 6→12 ✓?) before extending. A rule earns the right to predict only after it explains ALL the evidence.

misconceptions.description: Continues a repeating pattern by copying the last item instead of restarting the repeating unit.
misconceptions.signal: After red-red-blue ends on blue, predicts another blue 'because blue is going on'; cannot say what the repeating block is.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student bracket the repeating unit physically — circle [red red blue] groups with a pencil — then read the next term as 'position 1 of the next block'.

misconceptions.description: Believes patterns must grow — cannot handle decreasing or turning rules ('subtract 4' feels wrong, so they add).
misconceptions.signal: Extends 40, 36, 32 with 36 or 40; says a shrinking sequence is 'not a pattern'.
misconceptions.remedy: Present growing and shrinking patterns side by side from the start (savings growing, water level dropping). Rule language should be neutral: 'what is DONE to each term to get the next?'

real_world_hooks: Rangoli border patterns and tile designs
House numbers on one side of a street (2, 4, 6, ...)
Cricket scoreboard rising in fours and sixes
Beads strung in a repeating necklace design
teaching.video_search: number patterns find the rule repeating patterns grade 4

questions.prompt: What is the next number in the pattern 5, 10, 15, 20, __?

options.diagnosis: Jumped two steps ahead; the rule was right but applied twice.
Switched to 'add 1' at the end; lost hold of the rule while extending.

questions.explanation: Each term is 5 more than the last: +5, +5, +5. So the next is 20 + 5 = 25. 'Double it' fits 5→10 but fails 10→15 — a rule must work for every step.

questions.prompt: What is the next number in the pattern 3, 6, 12, 24, __?

options.diagnosis: Repeated the last difference (+12) instead of noticing the differences themselves double.
Used an earlier difference (+6); treated the gaps as constant when they are growing.

questions.explanation: Each term is double the one before: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48. 'Add 3' fits only the first step (3→6) and already fails at 6→12, so it cannot be the rule.

questions.prompt: A necklace repeats the block: red bead, red bead, blue bead — over and over. What colour is the 10th bead?

options.text: Red — 10 beads make 3 full blocks of 3, then the 10th starts a new block with red
Blue — the 9th bead is blue, so blue continues
Blue — the beads simply alternate red, blue, red, blue
options.diagnosis: Identified the wrong repeating unit; the block is [red, red, blue], length 3, not length 2.

options.text: You can only tell by drawing all 10 beads
options.diagnosis: No unit-based strategy yet — counting one by one works here but fails for the 100th bead.

questions.explanation: The repeating block [red, red, blue] has length 3. Since 10 = 3 × 3 + 1, the 10th bead is in position 1 of a block — red. This block-counting trick answers 'what is the 100th bead?' without drawing.

micros.title: Finding the Repeating Unit
micros.description: In a repeating pattern, first bracket the block that repeats — [red red blue] — and then continue by restarting the block, not by copying the last item.
outcomes: Can circle the repeating block of a shape or colour pattern
Can extend a repeating pattern by restarting its block

question.prompt: A border pattern repeats the block star-star-moon. The first seven stamps are: star, star, moon, star, star, moon, star. What is the 9th stamp?

options.text: Moon — 9 stamps make exactly 3 full blocks, and each block ends with a moon
Star — the 7th stamp was a star, so stars keep going
options.diagnosis: Copied the last item instead of restarting the [star, star, moon] block.

options.text: Cannot tell without stamping all nine
options.diagnosis: No block strategy yet; counting works here but fails for the 90th stamp.

options.text: Either one — after a while the pattern becomes random
options.diagnosis: A repeating pattern never becomes random; the block fixes every position forever.

question.explanation: The block [star, star, moon] has length 3. Since 9 = 3 × 3, the 9th stamp is the last item of a block: moon.

micros.title: Predicting a Far-away Term
micros.description: Use the block length to leap ahead: for a block of 3, the 20th item is found from 20 = 6 blocks + 2, so it matches position 2 — no drawing twenty items.
outcomes: Can find a far-away term of a repeating pattern using full blocks and leftovers
Can explain the method as division with remainder in disguise

micros.title: Finding the Rule of a Number Pattern
micros.description: Ask 'what is DONE to each term to get the next?' — add the same number, or multiply. Find the rule and use it to extend the pattern.
outcomes: Can state the rule of an adding or doubling pattern
Can extend a number pattern two or three terms using its rule

question.prompt: What is the rule of the pattern 2, 6, 18, 54?

options.diagnosis: Fits only the first step (2 → 6) and already fails at 6 → 18; a rule must survive every step.
Fits only 6 → 18; the gaps are growing, so the rule is not a fixed addition.
2 doubled is 4, not 6 — this rule was never checked against even the first step.

question.explanation: Test each step: 2 × 3 = 6, 6 × 3 = 18, 18 × 3 = 54. 'Multiply by 3' works everywhere; 'add 4' dies at the second step.

micros.title: A Rule Must Work at EVERY Step
micros.description: A candidate rule earns the right to predict only after it explains every given step. Write the rule over each gap and tick it — one failure and the rule is out.
outcomes: Can test a proposed rule against all the given terms, not just the first pair
Can reject a rule with a counterexample step

question.prompt: Which rule works for EVERY step of the pattern 1, 2, 4, 8?

options.text: Double each time — it works at 1→2, 2→4 and 4→8

options.diagnosis: Fits only 1 → 2 and was never checked at 2 → 4; one look ahead breaks it.
Fits only 2 → 4; a rule must survive every single step.
Fits only 4 → 8; picking the rule from one convenient gap is not enough.

question.explanation: Check every gap: 1 × 2 = 2 ✓, 2 × 2 = 4 ✓, 4 × 2 = 8 ✓. Every 'add' rule fails at some step, so doubling is the only rule that explains all the evidence.

micros.title: Patterns Can Shrink Too
micros.description: Rules can subtract as well as add: 50, 45, 40 keeps dropping by 5. Practise decreasing patterns beside growing ones so 'pattern' does not mean 'goes up'.
outcomes: Can find and continue a decreasing number pattern
Can describe a rule neutrally, e.g. 'subtract 5 each time'

question.prompt: What is the next number in the pattern 50, 45, 40, 35, __?

options.diagnosis: Turned the pattern back upward, as if patterns must grow; the rule is 'subtract 5' all the way.
Applied the −5 rule twice in one step.
Switched to 'subtract 1' at the end; the rule slipped while extending.

question.explanation: Each term is 5 less than the last: −5, −5, −5, −5. So the next is 35 − 5 = 30. Shrinking sequences are patterns too.

micros.title: Creating Patterns from a Rule
micros.description: Turn a given rule into a pattern of your own — 'start at 7, add 6' or a repeating block you design — and describe its features (all odd? every third term?).
outcomes: Can generate a pattern from a stated starting number and rule
Can notice and describe a feature of the pattern that the rule creates

nodes.title: Reading and Drawing Bar Charts
nodes.description: A bar chart shows data as bars whose heights stand for amounts, read off a scaled axis. The crucial skill is using the scale: when one division stands for 5 or 10, you multiply divisions by the scale instead of counting lines. You will read values, compare categories, answer 'how many more' questions and draw your own charts from a table.
learning_outcomes: Can read a value from a bar chart whose scale is 2, 5 or 10 per division
Can compare two bars and find 'how many more/less' as a difference of values
Can draw a bar chart from a data table, choosing a sensible scale
Can answer multi-step questions (totals, differences) from one chart

misconceptions.description: Ignores the scale — counts gridline divisions as if each stood for 1, whatever the axis says.
misconceptions.signal: Reads a 7-division bar as '7' when the scale is 5 per division; never glances at the axis numbers.
misconceptions.remedy: Start every chart-reading with a 'scale check' ritual: touch the axis, say '1 division = __' aloud, and write it above the chart before answering anything.

misconceptions.description: Answers 'which/what' questions with the number instead of the category, or the category instead of the number — the bar's label and its value are not linked.
misconceptions.signal: Asked 'which fruit is most popular?', answers '40'; asked 'how many chose mango?', answers 'mango'.
misconceptions.remedy: Practice two-part answers: every reading is stated as 'CATEGORY has VALUE' (mango has 40 votes). Then the question decides which half of the sentence to report.

misconceptions.description: Answers 'how many more A than B?' with A's value instead of the difference A − B.
misconceptions.signal: Comparison questions get single bar readings as answers; no subtraction appears in the working.
misconceptions.remedy: Show the comparison visually: shade the part of the taller bar that pokes above the shorter one — THAT stub is 'how many more'. Then connect the stub's height to subtraction.

real_world_hooks: Runs scored per over in a cricket match
Favourite fruit or ice-cream flavour survey in class
Vehicles passing the school gate in an hour
Rainfall by month in your city
teaching.video_search: reading bar graphs with scale grade 4

questions.prompt: In a bar chart of favourite fruits, each division stands for 5 children. The banana bar is 7 divisions tall. How many children chose banana?

options.diagnosis: Added 7 + 5 instead of multiplying divisions by the scale.
Multiplied but miscounted the divisions as 6; scale understood, reading slipped.

questions.explanation: Each division = 5 children, so 7 divisions = 7 × 5 = 35 children. Counting divisions alone gives 7 — the scale must multiply the count.

questions.prompt: In the same chart (1 division = 5), mango's bar reaches 40 and orange's bar reaches 20. How many MORE children chose mango than orange?

options.diagnosis: Added the two values instead of subtracting; 'more than' compares by difference.

questions.explanation: 'How many more' asks for the difference: 40 − 20 = 20 children. Answering 40 just reports mango's bar; answering 4 counts the extra divisions (8 − 4) but forgets each stands for 5.

questions.prompt: You are drawing a bar chart where 1 division stands for 10 votes. The bar for 'cricket' must show 45 votes. How tall should you draw it?

options.diagnosis: Rounded down and silently lost 5 votes; parts of a division are allowed and needed.
Rounded up to the nearest line, over-reporting by 5 votes; the chart must show the data exactly.

questions.explanation: 45 ÷ 10 = 4.5, so the bar rises 4 full divisions plus half of the next one. Drawing 45 divisions ignores the scale; rounding to 4 or 5 divisions misrepresents the data by 5 votes.

micros.title: Reading Bars When One Division = 1
micros.description: Recap bar charts where each gridline step stands for exactly 1: read values, find the tallest and shortest bars, and connect each bar to its label.
outcomes: Can read values from a bar chart with a 1-per-division scale
Can identify the largest and smallest categories from bar heights

micros.title: Reading Scaled Bar Charts
micros.description: When one division stands for 2, 5 or 10, a bar's value is divisions × scale. Start every reading with the scale-check ritual: touch the axis, say '1 division = __'.
outcomes: Can read a value from a chart whose scale is 2, 5 or 10 per division
Can perform the scale check before answering any question

question.prompt: In a chart of library books, each division stands for 2 books. The storybook bar is 6 divisions tall. How many storybooks are there?

options.diagnosis: Counted divisions as if each stood for 1; the axis says each is worth 2.
Added 6 + 2 instead of multiplying divisions by the scale.
Divided by the scale instead of multiplying.

question.explanation: Each division = 2 books, so 6 divisions = 6 × 2 = 12 books. The scale multiplies the count.

micros.title: Category or Value: Answering What Is Asked
micros.description: Every bar carries two facts: its label (category) and its height (value). 'Which fruit?' wants the label; 'how many?' wants the number. Practise the two-part sentence 'mango has 40 votes'.
outcomes: Can answer 'which' questions with the category and 'how many' questions with the value
Can state any bar as a full sentence linking label and value

question.prompt: A chart shows votes for fruits: mango 30, apple 25, banana 40. Which fruit is the most popular?

options.diagnosis: Gave the value when the question asks WHICH fruit — the label answers this question.
Picked the first bar instead of the tallest one.
Added all the votes; the question asks for one category, not a total.

question.explanation: The tallest bar is banana's (40 votes). The question asks WHICH fruit, so the answer is the category 'banana' — the number 40 answers a different question.

micros.title: How Many More? Comparing Two Bars
micros.description: 'How many more A than B?' asks for the difference A − B — the stub of the taller bar poking above the shorter one — not A's value. Read both bars, then subtract.
outcomes: Can answer 'how many more/fewer' questions by subtracting two bar values
Can point to the difference as the part of the taller bar above the shorter one

question.prompt: In a sports survey, 35 children chose cricket and 20 chose football. How many MORE children chose cricket than football?

options.diagnosis: Reported cricket's whole bar; 'how many more' asks for the difference between the bars.
Added the two values; 'more than' compares by subtracting.
Reported football's bar; neither single bar answers a comparison question.

question.explanation: 'How many more' is the difference: 35 − 20 = 15 children — the part of cricket's bar that rises above football's.

micros.title: Drawing a Bar Chart from a Table
micros.description: Turn a data table into a chart: choose a sensible scale, label the axes, and draw each bar to exactly the right height — including half divisions when the data demands them.
outcomes: Can choose a sensible scale for the given data
Can draw bars of exactly the right height, using part divisions where needed

question.prompt: You are drawing a chart where 1 division stands for 5 votes. The 'kho-kho' bar must show 35 votes. How many divisions tall should it be?

options.diagnosis: Drew one division per vote, ignoring that each division holds 5.
Drew the scale number itself instead of dividing the value by the scale.
Division slip: 35 ÷ 5 = 7; six divisions would show only 30 votes.

question.explanation: Height in divisions = value ÷ scale = 35 ÷ 5 = 7. A 35-division bar would mean 35 × 5 = 175 votes.

micros.title: Totals and Multi-step Chart Questions
micros.description: Combine readings: totals across all bars, differences chained with sums ('how many children in all?', 'how many more on the two busiest days?'). Read each bar with the scale first, then compute.
outcomes: Can find a total across several bars of a scaled chart
Can solve a two-step question mixing addition and subtraction of bar values

question.prompt: A chart (1 division = 5) shows books read: Monday 20, Tuesday 35, Wednesday 15. How many books were read in the three days altogether?

options.diagnosis: Added the division counts (4 + 7 + 3) and forgot each division stands for 5 books.
Added only Monday and Tuesday; Wednesday's bar was missed.
Reported the tallest bar instead of adding all three.

question.explanation: Add the three values: 20 + 35 + 15 = 70 books. Adding raw divisions gives 14 — that number still needs the ×5 scale.

nodes.title: Large Numbers: Lakhs, Comparing, Rounding
nodes.description: Beyond ten thousand come lakhs (1,00,000) and ten lakhs — the numbers of city populations, fish-catch tonnages and film box-office collections. You will read and write 6- and 7-digit numbers in the Indian system, compare and order them, and round them to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand to make them easy to talk about.
learning_outcomes: Can read and write numbers up to ten lakh using Indian-system commas
Can compare and order large numbers by digit count, then place-by-place
Can round a number to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand using the digit to the right
Can use rounded numbers to estimate sums and to sense-check calculations

misconceptions.description: Rounds by truncating — chops off the lower digits and always rounds down (3,47,568 to the nearest thousand becomes 3,47,000 regardless of the 568).
misconceptions.signal: Rounded answers never go up; the digit to the right of the rounding place is never inspected.
misconceptions.remedy: Put the number on an empty number line between its two 'neighbour' thousands (3,47,000 and 3,48,000) and ask which neighbour is closer. Rounding is about closeness, not cutting.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the lakh with other landmarks — writes 1 lakh with the wrong number of zeros, or equates lakh with million.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 1 lakh as 10,000 or 10,00,000; places Indian-system commas at international positions.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a landmark ladder the student recites and writes: 1,000 (thousand) → 10,000 → 1,00,000 (lakh) → 10,00,000 (ten lakh = 1 million). Practise placing commas from the right: three digits first, then pairs.

misconceptions.description: Compares large numbers by the leftmost digit alone, ignoring how many digits each number has (9,87,654 called bigger than 10,23,456 because 9 > 1).
misconceptions.signal: A 6-digit number is declared bigger than a 7-digit number; digit count is never mentioned.
misconceptions.remedy: Right-align both numbers in a place-value chart so the missing crore/ten-lakh column shows as empty. Rule: count digits first; only equal-length numbers are compared digit by digit.

real_world_hooks: Populations of Indian cities in a census table
Box-office collections of films in lakhs and crores
The Fish Tale: how many kilograms of fish a trawler catches in a season
Prices of cars and flats in lakhs of rupees
teaching.video_search: Indian place value lakhs comparing rounding large numbers class 5

questions.prompt: How is one lakh written in figures?

options.diagnosis: Wrote ten lakh (1 million); lakh and million are being blended into one landmark.
Confused lakh with thousand; the landmark ladder needs rebuilding.

questions.explanation: One lakh = 100 thousands = 1,00,000 (a 1 followed by five zeros). In the Indian system the commas go 1,00,000; ten lakh is 10,00,000, which equals one million.

questions.prompt: Round 3,47,568 to the nearest thousand.

options.diagnosis: Rounded to the nearest ten thousand instead of the nearest thousand.
Rounded to the nearest ten; the target place was misread.

questions.explanation: The number sits between 3,47,000 and 3,48,000. Look at the hundreds digit: 5, so we round up to 3,48,000. Since 568 is more than half of 1000, 3,48,000 is genuinely the closer thousand.

questions.prompt: Two towns report their populations: Rampur 9,87,654 and Sundarpur 10,23,456. Which town has more people?

options.text: Sundarpur — it has 7 digits while Rampur has only 6, so it is past ten lakh

options.diagnosis: Compared inner digit pairs without first aligning the numbers by place value.

options.text: They are about equal, so we cannot tell
options.diagnosis: No comparison strategy applied; 'big numbers all look alike' — digit count settles it immediately.

questions.explanation: Count digits first: 10,23,456 has 7 digits (over ten lakh), while 9,87,654 has 6 digits (under ten lakh). So Sundarpur is larger — no digit-by-digit comparison is even needed.

micros.title: The Lakh Landmark
micros.description: Meet 1,00,000 as one lakh: how many zeros it has, where it sits on the number ladder, and where the Indian-system commas go (three digits from the right, then pairs).
outcomes: Can write 1 lakh and 10 lakh in figures with correct Indian-system commas
Can recite the landmark ladder: 1,000 -> 10,000 -> 1,00,000 -> 10,00,000

question.prompt: How is FIVE LAKH written in figures?

options.diagnosis: Wrote fifty lakh — one landmark step too far up the ladder.
Confused lakh with thousand; the landmark ladder needs rebuilding.

question.explanation: One lakh is 1,00,000 (a 1 with five zeros), so five lakh is 5,00,000. Indian commas go three digits from the right, then in pairs: 5,00,000.

micros.title: Reading and Writing 6- and 7-digit Numbers
micros.description: Read and write numbers up to ten lakh in figures and in words, using a place-value frame (TL L TTh Th H T O) and filling untouched columns with zeros.
outcomes: Can write a spoken 6- or 7-digit number in figures with every zero in place
Can read a 6- or 7-digit numeral aloud in words using lakhs and thousands

question.prompt: Write 'three lakh forty thousand six' in figures.

options.diagnosis: Pushed the 6 into the thousands block; a place-value frame keeps each spoken part in its own column.
Dropped a place — three lakh needs six more digits after the 3, with zeros holding the empty columns.

question.explanation: Fill the frame: 3 lakhs, 4 ten-thousands, 0 thousands, 0 hundreds, 0 tens, 6 ones — 3,40,006. Zeros must be written for every column that is not spoken.

micros.title: Comparing and Ordering Large Numbers
micros.description: Compare and order numbers up to ten lakh: count digits first, and only when the digit counts match, compare place by place from the left.
outcomes: Can state which of two large numbers is greater, giving digit count as the first reason
Can order four or five large numbers from smallest to greatest

question.prompt: Which number is greater: 8,76,543 or 12,34,567?

options.text: 12,34,567 — it has 7 digits while 8,76,543 has only 6

options.diagnosis: Compared inner digit pairs without lining the numbers up by place value first.

options.text: They are equal — both are in lakhs
options.diagnosis: No comparison strategy applied; digit count settles it at once.

question.explanation: Count digits first: 12,34,567 has 7 digits, so it is past ten lakh, while 8,76,543 is below ten lakh. Any 7-digit number beats any 6-digit number.

micros.title: Rounding to the Nearest Ten, Hundred and Thousand
micros.description: Round a number by finding its two neighbours at the rounding place and choosing the closer one, using the digit to the right to decide. Rounding is about closeness, not chopping.
outcomes: Can round any number to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand
Can show a rounding decision on an empty number line between the two neighbours

question.prompt: Round 45,678 to the nearest HUNDRED.

options.diagnosis: Rounded to the nearest ten; the target place was misread.
Rounded to the nearest thousand instead of the nearest hundred.

question.explanation: 45,678 sits between 45,600 and 45,700. The tens digit is 7, so 45,678 is closer to 45,700 — it rounds UP. Chopping off '78' always rounds down, which is not rounding.

micros.title: Estimating with Rounded Numbers
micros.description: Use rounded numbers to estimate sums and differences before calculating exactly, and use the estimate to sense-check the exact answer.
outcomes: Can estimate a sum or difference by rounding each number first
Can spot an unreasonable exact answer by comparing it with an estimate

nodes.title: Multiplication and Division with Larger Numbers
nodes.description: Now the numbers grow: multiplying 3-digit numbers by 2-digit numbers, multiplying by tens and hundreds using zero patterns, and dividing by 2-digit numbers. The methods are the same ones you know — partial products and divide-multiply-subtract-bring-down — applied with more care, and always sanity-checked with estimation.
learning_outcomes: Can multiply by 10, 100 and their multiples using zero patterns correctly
Can multiply a 3-digit number by a 2-digit number using partial products
Can divide by a 2-digit divisor, with the remainder smaller than the divisor
Can estimate products and quotients first, and verify division by multiplying back

misconceptions.description: Omits the placeholder zero in the second partial product, so 245 × 32 is computed as 245 × 2 plus 245 × 3 (instead of 245 × 30).
misconceptions.signal: 2-digit-multiplier products come out several times too small; second row of working starts in the ones column.
misconceptions.remedy: Estimate before multiplying (245 × 32 ≈ 250 × 30 = 7,500) so an answer near 1,000 is instantly suspect. Re-derive the second row as ×30 = ×3 then ×10, writing the 0 first.

misconceptions.description: Stops a division while the remainder is still equal to or bigger than the divisor (984 ÷ 24 = 40 remainder 24).
misconceptions.signal: Remainders as large as the divisor appear in written work and are not questioned.
misconceptions.remedy: End every division with the two-part check: (1) is the remainder smaller than the divisor? (2) does quotient × divisor + remainder rebuild the dividend? Make both checks non-optional for a fortnight.

misconceptions.description: Miscounts zeros when multiplying multiples of ten — 60 × 400 gets one zero too few or too many.
misconceptions.signal: Answers like 2,400 or 2,40,000 for 60 × 400; zeros are appended by feel rather than counted.
misconceptions.remedy: Separate the fact from the zeros explicitly: 6 × 4 = 24, then attach the zeros from 60 (one) and 400 (two) — three zeros, 24,000. Have the student annotate each zero's origin.

real_world_hooks: A fishing boat's season: kilograms of fish per trip × number of trips
School annual-day snacks: 245 boxes at ₹32 each
Packing 984 mangoes into crates of 24 for the mandi
Bricks needed for a wall: bricks per row × rows
teaching.video_search: multiply 3 digit by 2 digit long division 2 digit divisor class 5

options.diagnosis: Attached one zero too many; zeros must be counted from the factors (1 + 2 = 3), not estimated.
Added the numbers instead of multiplying; operation misread.

questions.explanation: 6 × 4 = 24. Now attach the zeros: one from 60 and two from 400, three in all: 24,000.

options.diagnosis: Computed 245 × 30 = 7,350 and stopped; the 245 × 2 partial product was never added.
Both partial products right (7,350 and 490) but a regrouping slip while adding them.

questions.explanation: 245 × 32 = 245 × 30 + 245 × 2 = 7,350 + 490 = 7,840. Estimate check: 250 × 30 = 7,500, so 7,840 is sensible while 1,225 is far too small — that comes from treating the 3 as 3 instead of 30.

questions.prompt: A trader packs 984 mangoes into crates that hold 24 mangoes each. How many full crates does she pack?

options.diagnosis: An extra zero slipped into the quotient during bring-down; estimation (about 1000 ÷ 25 = 40) would flag a 3-digit answer.
Quotient never verified — 24 × 36 = 864, which leaves 120 mangoes unpacked; the multiply-back check is missing.

questions.explanation: 984 ÷ 24: try 24 × 40 = 960, leaving 24 — exactly one more crate. So 24 × 41 = 984 with remainder 0: 41 full crates. A remainder of 24 can never be left over, because it fills another whole crate.

micros.title: Multiplying by Tens and Hundreds (Zero Patterns)
micros.description: Multiply numbers like 60 x 400 by separating the basic fact from the zeros: do 6 x 4, then attach exactly the zeros that came from each factor.
outcomes: Can multiply by 10, 100 and their multiples using counted zeros
Can explain where each zero in the answer came from

options.diagnosis: Attached one zero too many; the zeros must be counted from the factors (1 + 2 = 3), not guessed.
Added the numbers instead of multiplying; the operation was misread.

question.explanation: 3 x 5 = 15. Now attach the zeros: one from 30 and two from 500, three in all — 15,000.

micros.title: Estimating Products and Quotients
micros.description: Round the numbers to friendly tens and hundreds to estimate a product or quotient before computing, so a wildly wrong exact answer is caught immediately.
outcomes: Can estimate a product like 245 x 32 as about 250 x 30
Can use an estimate to reject an answer that is far too big or too small

micros.title: Multiplying 3-digit by 2-digit Numbers
micros.description: Multiply a 3-digit number by a 2-digit number using partial products, writing the second row as a multiplication by tens — with its placeholder zero written first.
outcomes: Can compute a 3-digit x 2-digit product with both partial products
Can explain why the second partial-product row must end in zero

options.diagnosis: Computed 132 x 20 = 2,640 and stopped; the 132 x 4 partial product was never added.
Both partial products right (2,640 and 528) but a regrouping slip while adding them.

question.explanation: 132 x 24 = 132 x 20 + 132 x 4 = 2,640 + 528 = 3,168. Estimate first: 130 x 25 is about 3,250, so 792 is far too small — it comes from multiplying by 2 instead of 20.

micros.title: Dividing by a 2-digit Divisor
micros.description: Run long division with 2-digit divisors like 21 and 24: estimate each quotient digit by trying multiples of the divisor, then divide-multiply-subtract-bring-down as usual.
outcomes: Can divide a 3-digit number by a 2-digit divisor
Can choose a sensible first quotient digit by trying multiples of the divisor

question.prompt: 672 divided by 21 = ?

options.diagnosis: An extra zero slipped into the quotient during bring-down; estimating (about 660 / 22 = 30) flags a 3-digit answer.
Quotient never verified — 21 x 22 = 462, leaving 210 unaccounted for; the multiply-back check is missing.

question.explanation: 21 x 32 = 672 exactly, so 672 / 21 = 32 with remainder 0. Stopping at 31 leaves remainder 21, which is as big as the divisor — one more 21 still fits.

micros.title: Checking Division: Remainder Rule and Multiply-back
micros.description: Finish every division with two checks: the remainder must be smaller than the divisor, and quotient x divisor + remainder must rebuild the dividend.
outcomes: Can verify a division answer using quotient x divisor + remainder = dividend
Can spot and fix a division that stopped with a remainder as big as the divisor

question.prompt: Asha divides 850 by 25 and writes: '33 remainder 25'. What should she notice?

options.text: The remainder 25 is not smaller than the divisor — one more 25 fits, so the answer is exactly 34
Nothing — 33 remainder 25 is a finished answer
She should add the remainder to the quotient: 33 + 25 = 58
options.diagnosis: Remainder and quotient measure different things; they can never be added together.

options.text: She must start again — 850 cannot be divided by 25
options.diagnosis: The division is possible; only the final remainder check was skipped.

question.explanation: 25 x 33 = 825, leaving 25 — but 25 fills one more whole group. So 850 / 25 = 34 exactly (25 x 34 = 850). A remainder must always be SMALLER than the divisor.

nodes.title: Factors, Multiples and Prime Numbers Intro
nodes.description: A factor of a number divides it exactly; a multiple is what you get by multiplying it. Factors come in pairs and stop at the number itself, while multiples go on forever. Numbers with exactly two factors — 1 and themselves — are the primes, the building blocks of all whole numbers.

chapters: Be My Multiple, I'll be Your Factor

learning_outcomes: Can list all factors of a number systematically using factor pairs
Can list multiples of a number and decide whether one number is a multiple of another
Can explain the difference between a factor and a multiple of a number
Can identify prime and composite numbers up to 100 by testing small divisors

misconceptions.description: Believes all odd numbers are prime (and often that 1 is prime too) — 9, 15 and 21 get called prime because they 'look odd and lonely'.
misconceptions.signal: Prime lists include 9, 15, 21, 27; the only test applied is 'is it even?'.
misconceptions.remedy: Test odd candidates against 3 and 7 explicitly: build 9 as a 3 × 3 array and 21 as 3 × 7. Then settle 1 by the two-factor definition: 1 has only ONE factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.

misconceptions.description: Swaps factors and multiples — asked for factors of 6, lists 6, 12, 18, 24.
misconceptions.signal: The words are used interchangeably; 'factor' answers grow bigger than the number itself.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor with size: factors FIT INSIDE the number (never bigger than it), multiples are the times-table of the number (never smaller). Sort a pile of number cards into 'factors of 12' and 'multiples of 12' bins.

misconceptions.description: Assumes a bigger number must have more factors.
misconceptions.signal: Ranks numbers by size when asked which has most factors; sure that 100 beats every smaller number.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student fully list factors of 36 (nine factors) and 97 (two — it is prime). Factor count depends on how a number is built from primes, not on its size.

real_world_hooks: Arranging 24 laddoos into equal rows — every arrangement shows a factor pair
The 'Be my multiple' circle game: clap on every multiple of 3
Sharing a bill exactly among friends: which group sizes work?
Tiling a 36-tile floor into equal rectangular patches
teaching.video_search: factors multiples prime numbers arrays class 5

questions.prompt: Which of these is a factor of 12?

options.diagnosis: Used an addition partner (8 + 4 = 12) instead of a divisor; factors must divide 12 exactly.
No divisibility test applied — 12 ÷ 7 leaves remainder 5.

questions.explanation: 4 divides 12 exactly: 12 ÷ 4 = 3, or 4 × 3 = 12. The full factor list of 12 is 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 — note 24 is a MULTIPLE of 12, not a factor.

questions.prompt: Which of these numbers is prime?

options.diagnosis: Odd, so assumed prime — but 15 = 3 × 5; oddness alone is not a primality test.
Missed 21 = 3 × 7; candidates must be tested against 3 and 7, not just 2.

questions.explanation: 17 has exactly two factors, 1 and 17 — no number from 2 to 16 divides it. The others fail: 9 = 3 × 3, 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7. Odd numbers can still be composite.

questions.prompt: Anu says: '100 is bigger than 36, so 100 must have more factors.' Count and decide who is right.

options.text: They tie — both have exactly 9 factors
Anu is right — bigger numbers always have more factors
100 has more because it ends in zero, and zeros mean extra factors
options.diagnosis: Surface-feature reasoning; ending in 0 guarantees the factors 2, 5 and 10 but says nothing about the total count.

options.text: Numbers this big have too many factors to count
options.diagnosis: No systematic pairing strategy — factor pairs (1×100, 2×50, 4×25, 5×20, 10×10) make the count quick and finite.

questions.explanation: Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36 — nine. Factors of 100: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50, 100 — also nine. Size does not decide factor count: the prime 97 is bigger than 36 but has only two factors.

micros.title: Finding Factors with Factor Pairs
micros.description: List all factors of a number systematically by finding pairs that multiply to it (1 x 12, 2 x 6, 3 x 4), using rectangle arrays of counters as the picture.
outcomes: Can list all factors of a number up to 50 using factor pairs
Can show a factor pair as a rectangle arrangement of counters

question.prompt: Which of these is a factor of 20?

options.diagnosis: No divisibility test applied — 20 / 3 leaves remainder 2.
Used a near fact (4 x 6 = 24?); 20 / 6 leaves remainder 2, so 6 does not divide 20 exactly.

question.explanation: 5 divides 20 exactly: 5 x 4 = 20. The full factor list of 20 is 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20. Note 40 is a MULTIPLE of 20 — factors never go above the number itself.

micros.title: Multiples: The Never-ending Times Table
micros.description: List multiples of a number by skip counting, and decide whether a given number is a multiple of another by testing exact division. Multiples go on forever; factors stop at the number.
outcomes: Can list the first several multiples of any number up to 12
Can decide whether one number is a multiple of another and justify it

question.prompt: Which of these is a multiple of 6?

options.diagnosis: Looks close to the 6 times table but 26 / 6 leaves remainder 2; nearness is not divisibility.
Ends in 6, but 16 / 6 leaves remainder 4 — the last digit alone cannot decide multiples of 6.

question.explanation: 42 = 6 x 7, so 42 is a multiple of 6. The number 3 is a FACTOR of 6, not a multiple — multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, ... and are never smaller than 6.

micros.title: Factor or Multiple? Keeping Them Apart
micros.description: Contrast the two ideas with the size rule: factors of a number fit inside it (never bigger), multiples are its times table (never smaller). Sort numbers into 'factors of n' and 'multiples of n' bins.
outcomes: Can classify given numbers as factors of n, multiples of n, or neither
Can state that n itself is both a factor and a multiple of n

question.prompt: Ravi is asked for the factors of 6 and writes: 6, 12, 18. What went wrong?

options.text: He listed multiples of 6 — the factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6
Only the 6 is wrong — a number can never be its own factor
options.diagnosis: 6 IS a factor of itself (6 x 1 = 6); the wrong entries are 12 and 18.

options.text: He stopped too soon — 24 should also be in the list
options.diagnosis: Continues the multiples list; the question asked for factors, which never exceed 6.

question.explanation: Factors of 6 divide it exactly and are never bigger than 6: they are 1, 2, 3, 6. The list 6, 12, 18 is the start of the MULTIPLES of 6 — the times table of 6.

micros.title: Prime and Composite Numbers
micros.description: A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Test candidates by trying small divisors (2, 3, 5, 7), and settle the special case: 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
outcomes: Can identify primes and composites up to 100 by testing small divisors
Can explain why 1 is neither prime nor composite
Can show a composite number as a rectangle array with more than one row

question.prompt: Which of these numbers is prime?

options.diagnosis: Missed 21 = 3 x 7; odd candidates must be tested against 3 and 7, not just 2.
1 has only ONE factor (itself), so it is neither prime nor composite — primes need exactly two factors.

question.explanation: 23 has exactly two factors, 1 and 23 — no number from 2 to 22 divides it. But 27 = 3 x 9 and 21 = 3 x 7: odd numbers can still be composite.

micros.title: Who Has More Factors? Size Doesn't Decide
micros.description: Count factors of several numbers and discover that bigger does not mean more factors: a small number like 12 can beat a bigger one like 25, and huge primes have only two.
outcomes: Can count and compare the number of factors of two numbers
Can give an example showing a bigger number with fewer factors

question.prompt: Which number has MORE factors: 12 or 25?

options.text: 12 — it has six factors (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12) while 25 has only three (1, 5, 25)
25 — it is the bigger number, so it must have more factors
They have the same number — both are composite
options.diagnosis: Being composite says 'more than two factors', not 'the same count'; the lists must actually be made.

options.text: Cannot tell without dividing by every number up to 25
options.diagnosis: Factor pairs make the count quick: each divisor found brings its partner with it.

question.explanation: List them: 12 has 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 — six factors. 25 has only 1, 5, 25 — three. How many factors a number has depends on how it is built, not on how big it is.

nodes.title: Equivalent Fractions and Comparison
nodes.description: Different fractions can name the same amount: 1/2, 2/4 and 3/6 all sit at the same point. You make equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing BOTH the numerator and denominator by the same number. With equivalence in hand you can compare any two fractions — by common denominators, by same numerators, or by clever benchmarks like 'how far from one whole?'.
learning_outcomes: Can generate equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing both terms by the same number
Can reduce a fraction to its simplest form
Can compare fractions with the same denominator, the same numerator, or neither
Can use benchmarks (1/2, 1 whole, distance from 1) to compare fractions mentally

misconceptions.description: Makes 'equivalent' fractions by adding the same number to top and bottom: 3/4 = 4/5 = 5/6.
misconceptions.signal: Equivalence chains built by +1; when checked on a fraction wall the amounts visibly creep upward.
misconceptions.remedy: Test the claim on a fraction wall or by halving a chapati: 3/4 and 4/5 clearly do not match. Equivalence is re-cutting every existing piece into the same number of sub-pieces — which is multiplication, not addition.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction, comparing denominators like whole numbers.
misconceptions.signal: Claims 2/7 > 2/5 'because 7 > 5'; ignores that sevenths are smaller pieces.
misconceptions.remedy: Same-numerator comparisons with paper strips: 2 pieces of a 5-strip versus 2 pieces of a 7-strip. More parts → smaller parts, so with equal counts the bigger denominator LOSES.

misconceptions.description: Compares fractions by the gap between numerator and denominator: 5/6 and 7/8 called equal because both are '1 away'.
misconceptions.signal: Says 3/4 = 7/8 = 99/100 'since each is one piece short'; subtraction of top from bottom appears in the working.
misconceptions.remedy: Focus on the SIZE of the missing piece: 5/6 is missing 1/6, 7/8 is missing only 1/8, and 1/8 < 1/6, so 7/8 is closer to the whole. The gap counts pieces; it ignores how big the pieces are.

real_world_hooks: Half a large pizza vs three-sixths of the same pizza
Cricket: winning 3 of 4 matches vs 7 of 8 — which record is better?
Measuring cups in cooking: 2/4 cup is the same as 1/2 cup
Sharing sugarcane pieces fairly among different group sizes
teaching.video_search: equivalent fractions comparing fractions fraction wall class 5

questions.prompt: Which fraction is equivalent to 3/4?

options.diagnosis: Doubled only the denominator — that halves the fraction instead of preserving it.
Doubled only the numerator — that doubles the fraction; both terms must change together.

questions.explanation: Multiply top and bottom by the same number: 3/4 = (3×2)/(4×2) = 6/8. Adding 1 to both terms gives 4/5, which sits at a different point — check it on a fraction wall.

questions.prompt: Which is greater: 2/5 or 2/7?

options.text: 2/5 — fifths are bigger pieces than sevenths, and there are 2 of each
They are equal — both have numerator 2
options.diagnosis: Compared numerators only; the denominators say how big each piece is.

options.text: They cannot be compared without making the denominators the same
options.diagnosis: Procedure-bound: common denominators always work, but same-numerator reasoning settles this instantly.

questions.explanation: Both take 2 pieces, but a fifth of a roti is bigger than a seventh of it. So 2/5 > 2/7. (Common denominators agree: 14/35 > 10/35.)

questions.prompt: Team A won 5/6 of its matches; Team B won 7/8 of its matches. Whose record is better?

options.text: Team B — it is missing only 1/8 of a full record, and 1/8 is less than 1/6
They are equal — each is exactly one win short of a perfect record
Team A — sixths are bigger than eighths, so 5/6 must be more
options.diagnosis: Right fact, wrong conclusion — bigger pieces also make the MISSING piece bigger, pulling 5/6 further below 1.
Additive pattern-matching on the digits with no thought about piece size.

questions.explanation: Compare distances from 1 whole: 5/6 = 1 − 1/6 and 7/8 = 1 − 1/8. Since 1/8 < 1/6, Team B is closer to a perfect record, so 7/8 > 5/6. Check: 5/6 = 20/24 and 7/8 = 21/24.

micros.title: Making Equivalent Fractions
micros.description: Generate fractions that name the same amount by multiplying BOTH the numerator and denominator by the same number — re-cutting every piece into equal sub-pieces on a fraction wall.
outcomes: Can generate equivalent fractions by multiplying both terms by the same number
Can explain with a picture why multiplying both terms keeps the amount unchanged

question.prompt: Which fraction is equivalent to 2/5?

options.diagnosis: Doubled only the denominator — that halves the fraction instead of preserving it.
Doubled only the numerator — that doubles the fraction; both terms must change together.

question.explanation: Multiply top and bottom by the same number: 2/5 = (2x2)/(5x2) = 4/10. Adding 1 to both terms gives 3/6, which equals 1/2 — a different amount. Check both on a fraction wall.

micros.title: Reducing to Simplest Form
micros.description: Run equivalence backwards: divide both terms by the same number until no common divisor is left, giving the fraction in its simplest form.
outcomes: Can reduce a fraction like 6/8 to its simplest form
Can check that a fraction is fully simplified by hunting for common divisors

question.prompt: What is 6/8 in its simplest form?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 2 from both terms — additive change moves the amount (4/6 = 2/3, not 6/8).
Swapped numerator and denominator; flipping a fraction changes its value completely.

question.explanation: Divide both terms by 2: 6/8 = 3/4, and 3 and 4 share no common divisor, so it is fully simplified. Subtracting 1 from both terms gives 5/7 — a different point on the number line.

micros.title: Comparing with Same Denominators or Same Numerators
micros.description: Two quick comparison rules: same denominator — more pieces wins; same numerator — the bigger denominator means smaller pieces, so it LOSES.
outcomes: Can compare fractions with equal denominators by comparing numerators
Can compare fractions with equal numerators by reasoning about piece size

question.prompt: Which is greater: 3/5 or 3/8?

options.text: 3/5 — fifths are bigger pieces than eighths, and there are 3 of each
They are equal — both have numerator 3
options.diagnosis: Compared numerators only; the denominators say how big each piece is.

options.text: They cannot be compared without a common denominator
options.diagnosis: Common denominators always work, but same-numerator reasoning settles this instantly.

question.explanation: Both take 3 pieces, but a fifth of a roti is bigger than an eighth of it. So 3/5 > 3/8. (Common denominators agree: 24/40 > 15/40.)

micros.title: Comparing Any Two Fractions with a Common Denominator
micros.description: When neither the tops nor the bottoms match, rewrite both fractions with a common denominator using equivalence, then compare the numerators.
outcomes: Can compare two unlike fractions by rewriting both over a common denominator
Can pick a sensible common denominator for a pair of fractions

question.prompt: Which is greater: 2/3 or 3/5?

options.text: 3/5 — because 5 is greater than 3, fifths beat thirds
3/5 — because 3 is greater than 2 on top
options.diagnosis: Compared numerators of fractions with DIFFERENT denominators; the pieces are not the same size.

options.text: They are equal — 2/3 becomes 3/5 by adding 1 to top and bottom

question.explanation: Rewrite both over 15: 2/3 = 10/15 and 3/5 = 9/15, so 2/3 is greater. Adding 1 to both terms does NOT keep a fraction equal — it slides it to a new point.

micros.title: Benchmark Tricks: Half and Distance from One Whole
micros.description: Compare fractions mentally against benchmarks: is each more or less than 1/2? For near-whole fractions like 5/6 and 7/8, compare the SIZE of the missing piece instead of the count.
outcomes: Can decide whether a fraction is more or less than 1/2 without computing
Can compare near-whole fractions by comparing their distances from 1

question.prompt: Which is greater: 7/8 or 9/10?

options.text: 9/10 — it is missing only 1/10, and 1/10 is smaller than the missing 1/8
They are equal — each is exactly one piece short of a whole
7/8 — eighths are bigger pieces than tenths
options.diagnosis: Right fact, wrong conclusion — bigger pieces make the MISSING piece bigger too, pulling 7/8 further below 1.
Distance-from-one settles it mentally: compare the missing pieces 1/8 and 1/10.

nodes.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions (Like and Related Denominators)
nodes.description: Fractions can only be added or subtracted when the pieces are the same size — the same denominator. With like denominators you simply add or subtract the counts of pieces. When one denominator is a multiple of the other (halves and quarters, thirds and sixths), you first re-cut one fraction into the finer pieces, then combine. Wholes join in by renaming 1 as 4/4, 8/8 and so on.
learning_outcomes: Can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator, keeping the denominator fixed
Can add and subtract fractions where one denominator is a multiple of the other
Can rename a whole as an equivalent fraction to subtract from it
Can solve one-step fraction word problems about sharing food, time and lengths

misconceptions.description: Adds (or subtracts) tops and bottoms separately: 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/16, or 1/2 + 1/4 = 2/6.
misconceptions.signal: Denominators change during addition of like fractions; answers are visibly smaller than one of the addends.
misconceptions.remedy: Say the denominator as a NAME, not a number: '3 eighths + 2 eighths = 5 eighths', just like '3 mangoes + 2 mangoes = 5 mangoes'. Adding the bottoms is like adding the word 'mangoes' to itself.

misconceptions.description: When making denominators match, changes the denominator but forgets to scale the numerator: 1/2 becomes 1/4, so 1/2 + 1/4 = 2/4.
misconceptions.signal: Working shows denominators edited in place with numerators untouched; answers are too small.
misconceptions.remedy: Force the equivalence step to be written and checked separately first (1/2 = 2/4, verify on a strip) before any adding happens. Re-cutting a half into quarters gives TWO quarters, not one.

misconceptions.description: Cannot operate with a whole — believes you cannot take 3/8 away from 1 because '1 is not a fraction'.
misconceptions.signal: Freezes on 1 − 3/8; or answers such problems by adding; never rewrites 1 as 8/8.
misconceptions.remedy: Cut a full paper roti into 8 parts to see 1 = 8/8 physically, then remove 3. Practise renaming 1 with several denominators until it feels like the same whole in different clothes.

real_world_hooks: Eating 3/8 of a pizza and then 2/8 more — how much is gone?
Half a glass of milk plus a quarter glass more
A recipe needing 1/2 cup dal plus 1/4 cup extra
How much of the water tank is left after using 3/8 of it

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the numerators — the operation sign was misread.
Multiplied the numerators (3 × 2 = 6); a times-table fact intruded on addition.

questions.explanation: 3 eighths + 2 eighths = 5 eighths, so the answer is 5/8. The denominator is the NAME of the piece — it does not get added, just like 3 mangoes + 2 mangoes is 5 mangoes, not 5 'double-mangoes'.

options.diagnosis: Found the right numerator total (2 + 1 = 3) but then added the denominators too — a hybrid of the correct method and top-plus-bottom adding.

questions.explanation: Re-cut the half into quarters: 1/2 = 2/4. Then 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. Note the renaming gives TWO quarters — changing only the denominator (1/2 → 1/4) silently shrinks the fraction.

questions.prompt: Meena's family ate 3/8 of a whole pizza. How much of the pizza is left?

options.text: It cannot be worked out — you cannot take 3/8 away from 1

options.diagnosis: Added instead of subtracting; 'left over' means removing the eaten part from the whole.
Reported the part eaten; the question asks for the remaining part.

questions.explanation: Rename the whole pizza: 1 = 8/8. Then 8/8 − 3/8 = 5/8 of the pizza is left. Any whole can be rewritten as a fraction over the denominator you need.

micros.title: Adding and Subtracting Like Fractions
micros.description: With the same denominator, only the counts of pieces are added or subtracted — the denominator is the NAME of the piece and stays put: 3 eighths + 2 eighths = 5 eighths.
outcomes: Can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator
Can explain why the denominator does not change during the operation

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the numerators (2 x 3 = 6); a times-table fact intruded on addition.
Subtracted the numerators — the operation sign was misread.

question.explanation: 2 sevenths + 3 sevenths = 5 sevenths = 5/7. The denominator is the piece's name — it never gets added, just as 2 mangoes + 3 mangoes is 5 mangoes.

micros.title: Adding with Related Denominators
micros.description: When one denominator is a multiple of the other (halves and quarters, thirds and sixths), first re-cut the coarser fraction into the finer pieces using equivalence, then add like fractions.
outcomes: Can add fractions where one denominator is a multiple of the other
Can write and verify the renaming step (1/2 = 2/4) before adding

options.diagnosis: Subtracted instead of adding: 1/3 - 1/6 = 1/6; the operation sign was misread.

question.explanation: Re-cut the third into sixths: 1/3 = 2/6. Then 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. Changing only the denominator (1/3 into 1/6) silently shrinks the fraction — the numerator must scale too.

micros.title: Subtracting with Related Denominators
micros.description: Subtract fractions like 3/4 - 1/8 by first renaming the coarser fraction into the finer pieces (3/4 = 6/8), then subtracting the counts.
outcomes: Can subtract fractions where one denominator is a multiple of the other
Can check a fraction subtraction by adding back

micros.title: Taking a Fraction Away from a Whole
micros.description: Rename 1 as 4/4, 8/8 or whatever denominator is needed — the same whole in different clothes — so that fractions can be subtracted from wholes.
outcomes: Can rewrite 1 (or 2, 3, ...) as an equivalent fraction with any denominator
Can subtract a fraction from a whole number

question.prompt: A water tank is full. The family uses 2/5 of it in one day. How much of the tank is left?

options.text: It cannot be worked out — you cannot take 2/5 away from 1

options.diagnosis: Reported the part USED; the question asks for the part remaining.
Added instead of subtracting; using water removes it from the whole.

question.explanation: Rename the full tank: 1 = 5/5. Then 5/5 - 2/5 = 3/5 of the tank is left. Any whole can be rewritten as a fraction over the denominator you need.

micros.title: Fraction Word Problems: Food, Time and Lengths
micros.description: Solve one-step story problems about sharing food, cooking measures, time and lengths by choosing add or subtract, renaming where needed, and sanity-checking the answer against the whole.
outcomes: Can translate a one-step fraction story into an addition or subtraction
Can judge whether a fraction answer is sensible (not bigger than the whole, etc.)

question.prompt: A recipe needs 1/2 cup of dal plus 1/4 cup extra. How much dal is that in all?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the fractions instead of adding them; 'plus extra' means addition.

question.explanation: Re-cut the half into quarters: 1/2 = 2/4. Then 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4 cup. Adding tops and bottoms (2/6) gives less than the 1/2 cup you started with — impossible when you are adding more.

nodes.title: Decimals: Tenths and Hundredths
nodes.description: Decimals extend place value to the right of the ones: tenths and hundredths, separated by the decimal point. 0.7 means 7 tenths (7/10), and 0.07 means 7 hundredths — ten times smaller. Decimals run our money (₹ and paise), our measurements (metres and centimetres) and every price tag, so reading them correctly matters every day.
learning_outcomes: Can read and write tenths and hundredths as fractions and as decimals
