Can place decimals like 0.3 and 0.45 on a number line between whole numbers
Can compare two decimals by comparing place by place, not by digit count
Can connect decimals to money (₹1 = 100 paise) and measures (1 m = 100 cm)

misconceptions.description: Longer decimal means larger number: 0.25 > 0.5 because 25 > 5.
misconceptions.signal: Reads the digits after the point as a whole number; orders 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 as increasing.
misconceptions.remedy: Give both decimals the same number of places by appending zeros — 0.5 = 0.50, and 50 hundredths beats 25 hundredths. Reinforce with money: ₹0.50 is 50 paise, clearly more than 25 paise.

misconceptions.description: Shorter-is-larger overcorrection: believes more decimal digits always make a number smaller because hundredths are 'tiny things'.
misconceptions.signal: Claims 0.3 > 0.45 'because 0.45 is in hundredths'; a rule about digit COUNT replaces place-by-place comparison.
misconceptions.remedy: Shade both on a hundred-square grid: 0.3 covers 30 small squares, 0.45 covers 45. Comparison must go place by place from the tenths, never by counting digits.

misconceptions.description: Ignores what the decimal point does — reads 0.7 as 'seven', or treats 0.30 and 3.0 as the same number.
misconceptions.signal: Says 'zero point seven, so seven'; moves the point around casually; sees 0.30, 3.0 and 30 as one family of equals.
misconceptions.remedy: Name every digit by its place aloud ('7 tenths, not 7'), and locate 0.7, 7 and 0.07 on the same number line to dramatise how the point pins each digit to a column.

real_world_hooks: Rupees and paise on a price tag: ₹7.50
A cricketer's batting average of 54.35
Petrol pump display counting litres in hundredths
Heights on a measuring tape: 1.4 m vs 1.35 m
teaching.video_search: decimals tenths hundredths place value number line class 5

questions.prompt: Which decimal shows the fraction 7/10?

options.diagnosis: Placed the 7 in the hundredths column; 7/10 is 7 TENTHS, one place after the point.
Wrote numerator-point-denominator; a decimal is not the fraction's two numbers glued around a dot.
Appended the denominator's digits after the numerator; the denominator 10 is shown by POSITION, not written out.

questions.explanation: 7/10 is 7 tenths. The first place after the decimal point is the tenths place, so 7/10 = 0.7. (0.07 would be 7/100 — ten times smaller.)

questions.prompt: Which is greater: 0.5 or 0.25?

options.text: 0.5 — it equals 0.50, and 50 hundredths is more than 25 hundredths
0.25 — hundredths are more exact, so it is the bigger number
options.diagnosis: Conflates precision with size; extra decimal places refine a measurement, they do not enlarge it.

options.text: They are equal — both begin with 0
options.diagnosis: Compared only the whole-number parts and stopped; the tenths digits (5 vs 2) decide it.

questions.explanation: Line up the places: 0.5 = 0.50. Comparing tenths first: 5 tenths > 2 tenths, so 0.5 > 0.25. With money: 50 paise is more than 25 paise.

questions.prompt: Which number is exactly the same as 0.30?

options.diagnosis: Treated the zero's position as decoration — but 0.03 is 3 hundredths, ten times smaller than 30 hundredths.
Dropped the decimal point and read the digits as thirty.

questions.explanation: 0.30 is 30 hundredths = 3 tenths = 0.3. A zero at the RIGHT END after the point changes nothing (0.3 = 0.30), but moving the point or shifting digits (0.03, 3, 30) changes the number entirely.

micros.title: Tenths on the Number Line
micros.description: Cut the gap between whole numbers into ten equal hops: each hop is one tenth, written 0.1. Read and place numbers like 0.4 and 2.7 on the number line and connect them to fractions like 4/10.
outcomes: Can write tenths as both fractions (7/10) and decimals (0.7)
Can place and read tenths on a number line between whole numbers

question.prompt: On a number line, each hop from 0 is one tenth. What number do you reach after 4 hops?

options.diagnosis: Landed in the hundredths column; one hop of a tenth is 0.1, not 0.01.
Glued the count and the denominator together; the 10 is shown by the digit's POSITION, not written out.

question.explanation: Four hops of one tenth is 4 tenths = 4/10 = 0.4 — still less than 1. Reaching the number 4 would take forty hops.

micros.title: Hundredths and Money
micros.description: Split each tenth into ten again to get hundredths: 0.07 is 7/100, ten times smaller than 0.7. Money makes it concrete — 1 rupee is 100 paise, so 45 paise is Rs 0.45.
outcomes: Can write hundredths as fractions and decimals and tell them apart from tenths
Can convert between rupees-and-paise and decimal rupee amounts

question.prompt: 1 rupee = 100 paise. How do you write 45 paise in rupees?

options.diagnosis: Wrote 45 TENTHS of a rupee — that is 4 rupees 50 paise, ten times too much.
Slid the digits one place too far; 45 out of 100 sits in the tenths and hundredths columns.

question.explanation: 45 paise is 45 out of 100 paise, so it is 45/100 of a rupee = Rs 0.45. Dropping the decimal point turns 45 paise into 45 whole rupees — a hundred times too much.

micros.title: Extending the Place-value Table Past the Point
micros.description: Add tenths and hundredths columns to the right of the ones: each step right divides by 10. Name every digit by its column, and see why 0.30 equals 0.3 but 0.03 does not.
outcomes: Can state the place value of any digit in a number like 3.65
Can explain why a zero at the right end after the point changes nothing

question.prompt: In the number 3.65, what is the value of the digit 6?

options.diagnosis: Counted one column too far right; the first place after the point is tenths.
Read the digits 65 as a whole number sitting after the 3; the point pins each digit to a column.

question.explanation: The first column after the decimal point is tenths, so the 6 in 3.65 is worth 6 tenths = 0.6. The 5 next to it is 5 hundredths.

micros.title: Comparing Decimals Place by Place
micros.description: Compare decimals by lining up the places and comparing from the left, padding with zeros so both have the same number of places — never by counting digits.
outcomes: Can compare two decimals by padding to equal places and comparing place by place
Can order a mixed list like 0.5, 0.45, 0.7 from smallest to largest

question.prompt: Which is greater: 0.6 or 0.42?

options.text: 0.6 — it equals 0.60, and 60 hundredths is more than 42 hundredths
0.42 — more decimal places always make a bigger number
options.diagnosis: Digit COUNT is being used instead of place value; extra places refine a number, they do not enlarge it.

options.text: They are equal — both start with 0
options.diagnosis: Compared only the whole-number parts and stopped; the tenths digits (6 vs 4) decide it.

question.explanation: Pad to equal places: 0.6 = 0.60. Comparing tenths first: 6 tenths beats 4 tenths, so 0.6 > 0.42. On a hundred-square grid, 0.6 shades 60 small squares and 0.42 only 42.

micros.title: Decimals and Fractions: Two Names, One Number
micros.description: Translate both ways between decimals and fractions with denominators 10 and 100 (0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4), and place both forms at the same point on the number line.
outcomes: Can convert tenths and hundredths between fraction and decimal form both ways
Can show that a decimal and its fraction sit at the same point on the number line

question.prompt: Which fraction is exactly equal to 0.25?

options.diagnosis: Used the digits 2 and 5 as top and bottom; 2/5 = 0.4, a different number.
Turned the digits into a denominator; 0.25 means 25 parts OF a hundred, not 1 part of 25.

question.explanation: Two places after the point means hundredths: 0.25 = 25/100, which simplifies to 1/4. Writing 25/10 would be 25 tenths = 2.5 — the point's position matters.

nodes.title: Adding and Subtracting Decimals
nodes.description: Adding and subtracting decimals works exactly like whole numbers — as long as you line up the decimal points so tenths sit under tenths and hundredths under hundredths. Appending zeros (4.5 = 4.50) makes ragged numbers tidy. These are the calculations of shopkeepers and shoppers: totals, change and measurements every single day.
learning_outcomes: Can add and subtract decimals by aligning the decimal points
Can pad with trailing zeros to equalise decimal places before computing
Can regroup across the decimal point (10 tenths = 1 one)
Can solve money and measurement problems, including making change

misconceptions.description: Right-aligns the digits and ignores the decimal points, so 4.5 + 2.35 is set up as 45 + 235.
misconceptions.signal: Written columns show the last digits aligned regardless of the points; answers are out by a factor of ten.
misconceptions.remedy: Rule: points in a vertical line FIRST, then pad the gaps with zeros (4.5 → 4.50). Squared paper with a dedicated 'point column' rebuilds the habit fast.

misconceptions.description: Adds the decimal parts as separate whole numbers: 0.8 + 0.6 = 0.14, or 4.5 + 2.35 = 6.40 (because 5 + 35 = 40).
misconceptions.signal: Fractional parts are computed in isolation and pasted after a point; carries never cross the decimal point.
misconceptions.remedy: Show the carry crossing the point with base-ten blocks: 8 tenths + 6 tenths = 14 tenths = 1 whole and 4 tenths. The point separates places, not two unrelated numbers.

misconceptions.description: Handles the whole part and decimal part in separate compartments when subtracting, so 50 − 49.25 becomes '50 − 49 = 1, keep the .25' = 1.25.
misconceptions.signal: Change calculations come out too big; borrowing never crosses the decimal point.
misconceptions.remedy: Count up instead: from 49.25 to 50 is 0.75 (0.05 to 49.30, 0.70 to 50). Then revisit column subtraction writing 50 as 50.00 so the borrow visibly crosses the point.

real_world_hooks: Adding up a kirana bill: ₹12.50 + ₹36.75
Making change from a ₹50 note
Relay race timings: adding 12.6 s and 11.85 s
Adding weights: 1.5 kg of rice and 0.75 kg of dal
teaching.video_search: adding subtracting decimals lining up decimal point money class 5

options.diagnosis: Lost the decimal point entirely and answered in whole numbers.
Addition-fact slip (8 + 6 taken as 12); the decimal handling itself is right.

questions.explanation: 8 tenths + 6 tenths = 14 tenths = 1 whole and 4 tenths = 1.4. Writing 0.14 keeps the 14 trapped after the point — the ten tenths must carry over into the ones.

options.diagnosis: Dropped the hundredths digit; padding 4.5 to 4.50 keeps every column accounted for.

questions.explanation: Line up the points and pad: 4.50 + 2.35. Hundredths: 0 + 5 = 5; tenths: 5 + 3 = 8; ones: 4 + 2 = 6. Answer: 6.85. Right-aligning the raw digits (45 under 235) mixes tenths with hundredths.

questions.prompt: Riya buys a pen for ₹12.50 and a notebook for ₹36.75. She pays with a ₹50 note. How much change does she get?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the whole parts, then reported the bill's paise as the change; the subtraction was never completed.
Reported the total bill instead of the change; the final subtraction step was skipped.

questions.explanation: Bill: 12.50 + 36.75 = ₹49.25. Change: 50.00 − 49.25 = ₹0.75. Counting up confirms it: 49.25 + 0.75 = 50. The '50 − 49 = 1, keep .25' shortcut double-counts the paise.

micros.title: Lining Up the Decimal Points
micros.description: Set up decimal additions in columns with the decimal points in one vertical line, padding ragged numbers with trailing zeros (4.5 becomes 4.50) so every column is complete.
outcomes: Can set up and add decimals with different numbers of places correctly
Can explain why right-aligning the digits (ignoring the points) gives wrong answers

options.diagnosis: Shifted 3.2 one column over (added 3.2 to 14.5); the points must sit in one vertical line.
Dropped the 5 hundredths; padding 3.2 to 3.20 keeps every column accounted for.

question.explanation: Line up the points and pad: 3.20 + 1.45. Hundredths: 0 + 5 = 5; tenths: 2 + 4 = 6; ones: 3 + 1 = 4. Answer: 4.65. Right-aligning the raw digits computes 32 + 145 and lands on 1.77.

micros.title: Carrying Across the Decimal Point
micros.description: See the carry cross the point: 8 tenths + 6 tenths = 14 tenths = 1 whole and 4 tenths. The point separates columns, not two different numbers.
outcomes: Can add decimals where tenths regroup into ones (and hundredths into tenths)
Can explain a carry across the point using tenths language

options.diagnosis: Lost the decimal point entirely and answered in whole numbers.
Addition-fact slip (7 + 5 taken as 13); the decimal handling itself is right.

question.explanation: 7 tenths + 5 tenths = 12 tenths = 1 whole and 2 tenths = 1.2. Writing 0.12 traps the 12 after the point — ten of those tenths must carry into the ones.

micros.title: Subtracting Decimals with Borrowing
micros.description: Subtract decimals in columns, padding with zeros (6 becomes 6.00) so borrows can visibly cross the decimal point, and check by adding back or counting up.
outcomes: Can subtract decimals including borrows that cross the decimal point
Can check a decimal subtraction by counting up from the smaller number

options.diagnosis: A single borrow slip in the tenths column; the overall method is intact.
Borrowed from the ones twice; write 6 as 6.00 and track each borrow once.

question.explanation: Write 6 as 6.00, then subtract: 6.00 - 2.75 = 3.25. Check by counting up: 2.75 + 0.25 = 3, and 3 + 3 = 6, so the gap is 3.25. Doing '6 - 2 = 4, keep the .75' counts the 75 hundredths the wrong way.

micros.title: Bills and Change with Money
micros.description: Total a shopping bill in rupees and paise and work out the change from a note, using column work or the shopkeeper's counting-up method.
outcomes: Can total a bill of two or three decimal money amounts
Can compute change from a note, borrowing across the point correctly

question.prompt: Arun's bill at the kirana shop is Rs 63.50. He pays with a Rs 100 note. How much change should he get?

options.diagnosis: A borrow slip in the tens column; estimate first — the change should be a bit less than 40.
Reported the bill instead of the change; the subtraction from 100 was never done.

question.explanation: 100.00 - 63.50 = 36.50. Count up to check: 63.50 + 0.50 = 64, and 64 + 36 = 100, so the change is Rs 36.50. The shortcut '100 - 63 = 37, keep the .50' double-counts the 50 paise.

micros.title: Adding and Subtracting Measures
micros.description: Apply decimal addition and subtraction to real measures — race timings in seconds, weights in kilograms, lengths in metres — keeping units consistent throughout.
outcomes: Can add and subtract decimal measurements of length, weight and time
Can state the answer with its correct unit

nodes.title: Angles: Right Angles and Degree Intuition
nodes.description: An angle measures a TURN — how far one arm swings away from the other. A right angle (a square corner) is 90 degrees, a straight angle is 180, and a full turn is 360. Angle size depends only on the amount of turn, not on how long the arms are drawn or which way the corner faces.
learning_outcomes: Can identify right, acute and obtuse angles in shapes and surroundings
Can state the degree landmarks: 90 (right), 180 (straight), 360 (full turn)
Can compare two angles by amount of turn, ignoring arm length and orientation
Can estimate everyday angles (clock hands, open doors, scissors) against the 90-degree benchmark

misconceptions.description: Thinks longer arms make a bigger angle — judges the angle by the size of the drawing, not the turn.
misconceptions.signal: Picks the angle drawn with longer rays as 'bigger' even when it is visibly narrower; measures arm length with a ruler.
misconceptions.remedy: Use two pairs of scissors — small ones opened wide, big ones nearly shut. Overlay tracing-paper copies of angles so only the OPENING is compared; extend the arms of the small angle live to show nothing changes.

misconceptions.description: Only accepts angles in standard orientation — a tilted right angle 'is not really a right angle'.
misconceptions.signal: Right angles are recognised only when one arm is horizontal; rotating the page changes the student's answers.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a paper right-angle tester (folded corner) on angles in every orientation — door corners, kite corners, tilted set-squares. The tester fits or it doesn't; the tilt is irrelevant.

misconceptions.description: Muddles the degree landmarks — assigns 100 to a right angle or 180 to a full turn.
misconceptions.signal: Says a right angle 'must be 100, degrees work like tens'; calls a straight line a full turn.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor with the body and the clock: a quarter turn of your body = 90, half turn = 180, full spin = 360. Four square corners tiled around a point complete the full 360 — count them: 90 × 4.

real_world_hooks: Clock hands at 3:00, 6:00 and other times
How wide a door or a laptop lid is opened
Scissors, divider and compass openings
Corners in carrom boards, kites and rangoli designs
teaching.video_search: angles right angle acute obtuse degrees turn class 5

questions.prompt: How many degrees are there in a right angle?

options.diagnosis: Named the straight angle instead; a right angle is only half of a straight one.
Gave half a right angle; possibly thinking of the diagonal fold of a square corner.

questions.explanation: A right angle — the corner of a book or a door — measures 90 degrees. Two right angles make a straight angle (180), and four make a full turn (360).

questions.prompt: A small pair of scissors (arms 5 cm) is opened very wide. A large pair (arms 20 cm) is opened just a little. Which pair makes the bigger angle?

options.text: The small pair — the angle is the amount of opening, not the length of the blades
The large pair — its arms are much longer
Both the same — scissors always open to the same angle
options.diagnosis: Treats the angle as a fixed property of the object rather than of how far it is turned open.

options.text: Impossible to compare without a protractor
options.diagnosis: No turn-based intuition yet; wide-versus-narrow can be compared directly by eye or by overlaying.

questions.explanation: An angle measures the TURN between the arms. The small scissors are swung far apart (a wide turn), the big ones barely at all. Arm length only changes how big the picture is — not the angle.

questions.prompt: A set-square's right angle is rotated so that both its arms point diagonally. Is the angle still a right angle?

options.text: Yes — turning the whole angle does not change how open it is
No — a right angle needs one horizontal arm and one vertical arm
No — tilting it makes it acute
options.diagnosis: Perceives rotation as partially 'closing' the angle; the opening between the arms is unchanged.

options.text: Only if it is drawn on squared paper
options.diagnosis: Ties the property to the representation; an angle's size does not depend on the paper beneath it.

questions.explanation: Rotating an angle moves both arms together, so the opening between them stays exactly 90 degrees. A paper corner-tester still fits perfectly however the angle is tilted.

micros.title: An Angle Is a Turn
micros.description: An angle measures how far one arm swings away from the other — the opening, not the drawing. Longer arms do not make a bigger angle.
outcomes: Can compare two angles by their openings, ignoring arm length
Can demonstrate an angle as a turn with arms, scissors or clock hands

question.prompt: Angle P is drawn with arms 10 cm long but a narrow opening. Angle Q has arms only 3 cm long but is opened much wider. Which angle is bigger?

options.text: Angle Q — the angle is the amount of opening between the arms
Angle P — its arms are much longer
They are equal — both have two arms
options.diagnosis: Counting arms tells you it IS an angle; the amount of turn between them is what is measured.

options.text: Impossible to compare without a protractor
options.diagnosis: Wide-versus-narrow can be compared by overlaying tracings; no measuring is needed.

question.explanation: An angle measures the TURN between its arms. Extending or shortening the arms changes the picture's size, not the opening. Q is opened wider, so Q is the bigger angle.

micros.title: Right Angles in Every Direction
micros.description: Make a folded-paper corner tester and use it to find right angles around you — including tilted ones. The tester fits or it doesn't; the tilt is irrelevant.
outcomes: Can test any corner for a right angle with a folded-paper tester
Can recognise right angles in non-standard orientations

question.prompt: A kite's corner is a right angle, but the kite hangs tilted so neither arm is horizontal or vertical. Is the corner still a right angle?

options.text: Yes — tilting the whole corner does not change how open it is
No — a right angle needs one flat arm and one upright arm
No — tilting squeezes it into an acute angle
options.diagnosis: Rotation moves both arms together; the opening between them never changes.

options.text: Only if you redraw it on squared paper
options.diagnosis: An angle's size belongs to the angle, not to the paper beneath it.

question.explanation: A folded-paper corner tester still fits the kite's corner perfectly however it hangs. Turning an angle moves both arms together, so the 90-degree opening is unchanged.

micros.title: Degree Landmarks: 90, 180, 360
micros.description: Anchor the three big degree landmarks with body turns and the clock: a quarter turn is 90 (right angle), a half turn is 180 (straight angle), a full spin is 360.
outcomes: Can state the degrees in a right angle, straight angle and full turn
Can show that four square corners fill a full turn (4 x 90 = 360)

question.prompt: How many degrees are there in a FULL turn (spinning all the way around)?

options.diagnosis: Degrees do not work in hundreds like money; a full turn is four right angles, 4 x 90 = 360.
Named the quarter turn (right angle); a full spin is four of those.

question.explanation: Face north and spin all the way back to north: that is 360 degrees. Half way (facing south) is 180, and a quarter (facing east) is 90 — four square corners tile a full turn.

micros.title: Acute, Right, Obtuse, Straight
micros.description: Classify angles against the 90-degree benchmark: smaller than a right angle is acute, bigger (but less than straight) is obtuse. Use the corner tester as the judge.
outcomes: Can classify a drawn angle as acute, right, obtuse or straight
Can find one angle of each type in the classroom

question.prompt: An angle measures 120 degrees. What kind of angle is it?

options.text: Obtuse — bigger than 90 but less than 180

options.diagnosis: Acute means SMALLER than a right angle; 120 is past the 90 benchmark.
A right angle is exactly 90; 120 overshoots it by 30.
A straight angle is exactly 180 — a full straight line; 120 is short of that.

question.explanation: Compare with the landmarks: 90 < 120 < 180, so the angle is obtuse — wider than a square corner but not yet a straight line.

micros.title: Estimating Everyday Angles
micros.description: Estimate the angles made by clock hands, door openings, scissors and laptop lids by comparing them with the 90-degree benchmark and its half, 45.
outcomes: Can estimate a real-world angle to the nearest landmark (45, 90, 180)
Can state the angle between clock hands at o'clock times like 3:00 and 6:00

question.prompt: At exactly 3:00, what angle do the clock's two hands make?

options.text: 90 degrees — a right angle, a quarter of the clock face

options.diagnosis: Counted the 15 minutes between the hands; minutes are not degrees — 15 minutes is a quarter of the face, which is 90 degrees.
Read the hour number as the angle; the angle comes from the turn between the hands.

question.explanation: At 3:00 the hands point to 12 and 3 — a quarter of the way around the face. A quarter of the full 360 is 90 degrees, a perfect right angle. (6:00 gives the straight 180.)

nodes.title: 3D Shapes, Boxes and Nets
nodes.description: A net is a flat pattern that folds up into a solid — unfold a toothpaste box and you are looking at its net. You will count faces, edges and corners of cubes and cuboids, decide which arrangements of squares fold into a cube and which do not, and sketch boxes on flat paper. This is the skill of packaging designers everywhere.
learning_outcomes: Can count faces, edges and vertices of cubes and cuboids
Can decide by mental folding whether a given arrangement of squares is a net of a cube
Can match a box to its net and mark which faces end up opposite each other
Can draw a simple net for an open or closed box

misconceptions.description: Thinks ANY arrangement of six squares folds into a cube — six squares is treated as the whole test.
misconceptions.signal: Accepts a 1×6 strip or a 2×3 block as a cube net without folding; counts squares and stops thinking.
misconceptions.remedy: Hand over cut-outs and have them actually fold: the 1×6 strip wraps around leaving two open holes and two doubled faces. Six squares is necessary but the ARRANGEMENT decides.

misconceptions.description: Counts only the faces that show in a drawing — a cube 'has 3 faces' (or 4), the hidden ones do not exist.
misconceptions.signal: Face counts match what is visible in the sketch; answers change depending on the picture used.
misconceptions.remedy: Stamp each face of a real dice or box with paint onto paper, counting the prints: six prints, always. Then revisit drawings and mark hidden faces with dotted shading.

misconceptions.description: Expects the net to LOOK like the solid — rejects valid cross-shaped cube nets because 'a cube is square, this is a plus sign'.
misconceptions.signal: Chooses the most compact/symmetric arrangement as 'the net'; calls the T and Z shaped nets wrong on sight.
misconceptions.remedy: Unfold several identical boxes along different edges to collect visibly different nets of the SAME box. A net records the unfolding path, not the solid's silhouette — there are 11 different cube nets!

real_world_hooks: Unfolding a toothpaste or mithai box flat
Designing a gift box for Diwali sweets
Dice: opposite faces of a dice always add to 7
Flattened cartons stacked at the kirana shop for recycling
teaching.video_search: nets of a cube folding boxes faces edges vertices class 5

questions.prompt: How many faces does a cube have?

options.diagnosis: Counted the corners (vertices) instead of the faces.
Counted the edges instead of the faces.

questions.explanation: A cube has 6 square faces (top, bottom, and 4 sides), 12 edges and 8 vertices. In a drawing only 3 faces show — the other 3 are hidden behind.

questions.prompt: Six squares are joined in one straight strip (1 × 6). Will this fold into a cube?

options.text: No — it wraps around the cube, doubling some faces and leaving two faces uncovered
Yes — it has exactly 6 squares, which is all a cube needs
Yes — any 6-square shape works if you fold it carefully enough
options.diagnosis: No mental (or physical) folding test performed; care cannot fix an impossible layout.

options.text: No — a cube's net needs 8 squares
options.diagnosis: Wrong face count for a cube; the issue with the strip is its arrangement, not the number 6.

questions.explanation: Fold the strip and it rolls around like a ring: four squares form the sides, then the last two land on faces already covered, while the two end holes stay open. Six squares are needed, but only certain arrangements (11 of them) fold into a cube.

questions.prompt: A sweet shop wants an OPEN box (no lid) shaped like a cube. How many square faces does its net need?

options.diagnosis: Included the lid — the box is open on top, so one face is deliberately missing.
Counted the corners of a cube instead of its faces.

questions.explanation: A closed cube has 6 faces; removing the lid leaves 5 — one base and four walls. Its net is 5 squares, for example a plus-sign shape with the centre square as the base.

micros.title: Faces, Edges and Vertices of Boxes
micros.description: Count the 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices of cubes and cuboids using real boxes and paint-stamping, remembering that a drawing hides half the faces.
outcomes: Can count faces, edges and vertices of cubes and cuboids, including hidden ones
Can mark the hidden faces on a sketch of a box

question.prompt: How many faces does a closed cuboid box (like a toothpaste carton) have?

options.diagnosis: Counted the edges instead of the faces.
Counted the corners (vertices) instead of the faces.

question.explanation: Every cuboid has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back and two sides. A drawing can only show 3 of them — stamp each face of a real box in paint and you always get 6 prints.

micros.title: Will It Fold into a Cube?
micros.description: Test arrangements of six squares by real and mental folding. Six squares are necessary but not enough — the ARRANGEMENT decides whether it closes into a cube.
outcomes: Can decide by folding (mental or paper) whether a 6-square arrangement is a cube net
Can explain why a 1x6 strip and a 2x3 block fail as cube nets

question.prompt: Six squares are joined in a 2 x 3 block (two rows of three). Will this fold into a cube?

options.text: No — folding makes squares land on top of each other, leaving some faces uncovered
Yes — it has exactly 6 squares, which is all a cube needs
Yes — any six squares work if you fold gently
options.diagnosis: No folding test was performed; care cannot fix an impossible layout.

options.text: No — a cube's net needs 8 squares
options.diagnosis: Wrong face count; a cube needs 6 squares — the 2 x 3 block fails because of its arrangement.

question.explanation: Fold the 2 x 3 block and squares overlap while two faces of the cube stay open. Six squares are needed, but only 11 special arrangements fold into a cube — count and layout both matter.

micros.title: Many Nets, One Box
micros.description: Unfold identical boxes along different edges to collect different-looking nets of the same cube — cross, T and Z shapes are all valid. A net records the unfolding path, not the solid's silhouette.
outcomes: Can accept and verify unfamiliar-looking valid cube nets
Can produce two different nets of the same box by unfolding along different edges

question.prompt: A net is drawn as a cross: a column of four squares, with one square attached to each side of the second square. Can it fold into a cube?

options.text: Yes — the four column squares wrap around, and the two side squares close the ends
No — a cube is square-shaped, and this looks like a plus sign
No — only a 2 x 3 rectangle of squares folds into a cube
options.diagnosis: Reversed: the compact 2 x 3 block is one of the arrangements that FAILS; the cross is a classic valid net.

options.text: Only if the cross is drawn upright
options.diagnosis: Rotating a net changes nothing about how it folds.

question.explanation: Fold the column of four into a ring (front, bottom, back, top), then the two side squares swing up to become the left and right faces. A net never looks like the solid — it records an unfolding.

micros.title: Opposite Faces on a Net
micros.description: Predict which faces of a net end up opposite each other after folding, and check with a dice — opposite faces of a dice always add up to 7.
outcomes: Can mark pairs of opposite faces on a cube net before folding
Can use the opposite-faces-sum-to-7 rule of a dice

micros.title: Drawing Nets and Box Sketches
micros.description: Draw a correct net for an open or closed box and make a simple 3D sketch of a box on flat paper, choosing the right number of faces for each design.
outcomes: Can draw a net for a closed box (6 faces) and an open box (5 faces)
Can sketch a cuboid showing its hidden edges with dotted lines

question.prompt: You are drawing the net for a CLOSED cuboid gift box. How many rectangle faces must the net contain?

options.diagnosis: Left out the lid — 5 faces is the net of an OPEN box, but this one is closed.
Counted edges instead of faces; the net needs one rectangle per face.

question.explanation: A closed box has 6 faces, so its net needs all 6 rectangles — including the bottom and back you cannot see in a sketch. An open box would need only 5.

nodes.title: Symmetry, Turns and Tiling Patterns
nodes.description: Some shapes look exactly the same after a quarter turn (90°) or a half turn (180°) — that is turning (rotational) symmetry, a cousin of mirror symmetry but not the same thing. Turns also build patterns: many rangoli, tile and border designs repeat a single motif by rotating it again and again. You will predict what a shape looks like after a turn and continue turn-based patterns.
learning_outcomes: Can state that a quarter turn is 90°, a half turn 180° and a full turn 360°
Can predict what a shape or letter looks like after a quarter or half turn
Can test whether a figure looks the same after a given turn, and distinguish this from mirror symmetry
Can continue and create tiling/border patterns built from repeated turns of one motif

misconceptions.description: Mixes up reflection and rotation — assumes a shape with a mirror line must also look the same after a turn, and turns figures by flipping them.
misconceptions.signal: Says E looks the same after a half turn 'because it is symmetric'; rotation tasks produce mirror images (b turned becomes d).
misconceptions.remedy: Physically contrast the two motions with one letter cut-out: FLIP the E across its mirror line (matches) versus TURN it 180° (upside-down E — does not match). One motion lifts the paper over; the other spins it flat.

misconceptions.description: Assumes a shape returns to itself after a half turn as long as it looks 'regular' or balanced.
misconceptions.signal: Claims triangles, hearts and the letter A all 'look the same upside down'; never actually rotates the figure.
misconceptions.remedy: Make trace-and-turn the required test: trace the figure, pin the centre, rotate the tracing 180° and see whether it truly matches. Balance to the eye is a guess; the tracing is evidence.

misconceptions.description: Confuses turn amounts — treats a quarter turn as 180° or as 'a little tilt', and half turns as full turns.
misconceptions.signal: Turns the figure the wrong amount in drawings; says a quarter turn brings a shape back to the start.
misconceptions.remedy: Link turns to the clock and the body: facing north, a quarter turn faces east (90°), another quarter faces south (180° in all). Four quarter turns — and only four — bring you home.

real_world_hooks: Rangoli and kolam motifs repeated by quarter turns
Fan blades and the wheel of a ship — same after part turns
Playing cards that look identical upside down
Floor tiling patterns in temples and railway stations
teaching.video_search: rotational symmetry half turn quarter turn patterns class 5

questions.prompt: A quarter turn is a turn of how many degrees?

options.diagnosis: Mapped 'quarter' to 25 as in 25 paise out of 100; a turn's whole is 360°, and a quarter of 360 is 90.
Halved a right angle instead — a quarter turn is a quarter of the full 360° turn, which is 90°, not 45°.

questions.explanation: A full turn is 360°. A quarter of it is 360 ÷ 4 = 90° — the turn from facing north to facing east, or the clock's minute hand moving 15 minutes.

questions.prompt: The letter 'b' is given a half turn (rotated 180°). What does it look like now?

options.diagnosis: Flipped the letter top-to-bottom (a reflection in a horizontal mirror) instead of turning it.

questions.explanation: A half turn spins the letter around its centre: the stick that pointed up now points down, and the bump swaps sides — 'b' becomes 'q'. A mirror flip would give 'd', which is a different motion.

questions.prompt: A border pattern repeats one arrow tile, giving it a quarter turn each time: UP, RIGHT, DOWN, LEFT, ... What is the 5th tile?

options.text: UP — after four quarter turns the arrow is back to the start
RIGHT — a quarter turn from LEFT flips it to the opposite side
LEFT — the last tile simply repeats
options.diagnosis: Copied the previous item instead of applying the turn rule again; the pattern's rule is 'turn', not 'stay'.

options.text: Any direction — the tiles are placed randomly
options.diagnosis: The rotation rule was never spotted; check each step: every arrow is the previous one turned 90° clockwise.

questions.explanation: Each tile is the previous one turned 90°: up → right → down → left → up. Four quarter turns make a full 360°, so the 5th tile matches the 1st. Turning LEFT by only a quarter gives UP; jumping to RIGHT would need a half turn.

micros.title: Quarter, Half and Full Turns
micros.description: Connect turn words to degrees and directions: a quarter turn is 90, a half turn 180, a full turn 360 — and turns add up, so two quarter turns make a half turn.
outcomes: Can state the degrees for quarter, half and full turns
Can combine turns (two quarters make a half; four quarters return home)

question.prompt: Riya makes two quarter turns in the same direction. How far has she turned in all?

options.text: A full turn — she is back where she started

options.diagnosis: Each new turn was treated as starting over; turns in the same direction add up.
Halved a quarter turn instead of doubling it; 90 + 90 = 180.

question.explanation: Each quarter turn is 90 degrees, so two of them make 90 + 90 = 180 — a half turn. Facing north, Riya now faces south. It takes FOUR quarter turns to get back to the start.

micros.title: Predicting a Shape After a Turn
micros.description: Predict what a letter or shape looks like after a quarter or half turn using trace-and-turn: trace it, pin the centre, rotate the tracing. Turning is spinning flat — not flipping over.
outcomes: Can draw or pick the image of a shape after a 90 or 180 degree turn
Can distinguish the result of a turn from the result of a mirror flip

question.prompt: Which of these letters looks EXACTLY the same after a half turn (180 degrees)?

options.text: E — it is symmetric, so it must look the same
A — it is balanced, so it looks the same upside down
b — every letter survives a half turn
options.diagnosis: Turn it and check: b spins into q; trace-and-turn is the test, not a guess.

question.explanation: Trace N, pin its centre and spin it 180 degrees: it lands exactly on itself. E has a MIRROR line but spins into a backwards E; A turns upside down; b becomes q. Mirror symmetry and turning symmetry are different tests.

micros.title: The Trace-and-Turn Symmetry Test
micros.description: Test whether a figure has turning symmetry: trace it, rotate the tracing a quarter or half turn, and see if it truly matches — and notice this is independent of mirror symmetry.
outcomes: Can test a figure for quarter-turn and half-turn symmetry with a tracing
Can give an example with turning symmetry but no mirror line (like S), and the reverse

question.prompt: The letter S has no mirror line at all. Does it look the same after a half turn?

options.text: Yes — spin S half way around and it lands exactly on itself
No — without a line of symmetry it cannot have turning symmetry

options.diagnosis: That is what a mirror FLIP does to S; a flat spin keeps its curves hooked the same way.

options.text: Only shapes with straight sides can have turning symmetry
options.diagnosis: Curved figures can have turning symmetry too — test with a tracing, not a rule about sides.

question.explanation: Trace S, pin the centre and rotate 180 degrees: it matches itself perfectly. Mirror symmetry and turning symmetry are separate properties — S has the second without the first.

micros.title: Patterns Built from Turns
micros.description: Continue and create border and tiling patterns made by repeating one motif with a quarter or half turn each time, as in rangoli and railway-station floors.
outcomes: Can continue a border pattern whose rule is 'turn the motif 90 degrees each time'
Can design a four-tile motif pattern using repeated quarter turns

nodes.title: Area and Perimeter of Rectangles (Formulas)
nodes.description: Counting squares one by one is slow — for rectangles, multiplication does it instantly: area = length × width, because the squares sit in equal rows. Perimeter has its own shortcut: 2 × (length + width). The two formulas answer two different questions (covering vs surrounding), use different units (square cm vs cm), and mixing them up is the classic trap.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the area of a rectangle as length × width and justify it with rows of squares
Can compute the perimeter of a rectangle as 2 × (length + width)
Can attach the correct units: square units for area, length units for perimeter
Can find a missing side given the area or perimeter, and compare rectangles with equal perimeter

misconceptions.description: Swaps the formulas — multiplies sides for perimeter or adds-and-doubles for area; treats 'area and perimeter' as one interchangeable idea.
misconceptions.signal: The right numbers go into the wrong formula; answers to 'fencing' problems come out in square metres.
misconceptions.remedy: Re-derive each formula from its meaning every time for a while: area = rows of squares (3 rows of 9 squares → 3 × 9); perimeter = walk around the boundary (9 + 4 + 9 + 4). The question 'cover it or go around it?' picks the formula.

misconceptions.description: Believes rectangles with the same perimeter must have the same area (and same area means same perimeter).
misconceptions.signal: Given a fixed fence length, says all possible plots 'hold the same amount'; skips computing areas separately.
misconceptions.remedy: Fix a 24-unit loop of string and build 1×11, 4×8 and 6×6 rectangles on a pegboard, recording area each time (11, 32, 36). Same fence, wildly different areas — squarer is roomier.

misconceptions.description: Ignores or swaps units — reports area in cm and perimeter in square cm, or drops units entirely.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 'area = 36 cm'; unit choice looks random and survives unchallenged.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie the unit to the measuring object: perimeter is measured by laying down 1 cm STICKS (cm), area by covering with 1 cm SQUARES (sq cm). Require the unit-object to be named with every answer.

real_world_hooks: Fencing a plot vs buying grass to cover it
Tiles for the kitchen floor vs skirting along its walls
A farmer choosing the roomiest field shape for a fixed fence
Framing a photo (perimeter) vs the glass to cover it (area)
teaching.video_search: area perimeter rectangle formula same perimeter different area class 5

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 9 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its AREA?

options.diagnosis: Added the two sides once (9 + 4); neither the area nor the perimeter recipe was completed.

questions.explanation: Area = length × width = 9 × 4 = 36 square cm — four rows of nine unit squares. 26 cm is the perimeter, 2 × (9 + 4); and area must carry SQUARE units because it counts squares.

questions.prompt: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 7 m wide. How much fencing is needed for its PERIMETER?

options.diagnosis: Computed length + width but forgot to double it — only half the boundary was walked.
Doubled only the length (2 × 12); the two widths went missing.

questions.explanation: Perimeter = 2 × (12 + 7) = 2 × 19 = 38 m. Multiplying 12 × 7 = 84 gives the area in square metres — how much ground the garden covers, not the fence around it.

questions.prompt: A farmer has exactly 24 m of fencing. Which rectangular plot gives her the MOST area: 1 m × 11 m, 4 m × 8 m, or 6 m × 6 m?

options.text: 6 m × 6 m — its area is 36 sq m, beating 32 and 11
All three hold the same area — they use the same 24 m of fence
1 m × 11 m — the longest side wins
options.diagnosis: Maximised one dimension only; a long thin strip encloses very little ground.

options.text: 4 m × 8 m — a square does not count as a rectangle
options.diagnosis: A square IS a rectangle (all right angles, opposite sides equal) — excluding it discards the best option.

questions.explanation: All three have perimeter 24 m, but the areas differ: 1 × 11 = 11, 4 × 8 = 32, 6 × 6 = 36 sq m. Equal perimeter does not mean equal area — the squarer the rectangle, the more it encloses.

micros.title: Area Formula from Rows of Squares
micros.description: Turn square-counting into multiplication: a rectangle's unit squares sit in equal rows, so area = length x width. The formula is a fast way of counting squares, and its unit is SQUARE units.
outcomes: Can compute a rectangle's area with length x width and justify it with rows
Can attach square units (sq cm, sq m) to every area answer

question.prompt: A rectangle is 7 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its AREA?

options.diagnosis: Added the two sides (7 + 3) instead of multiplying the rows of squares.

question.explanation: Area = 7 x 3 = 21 square cm — three rows of seven unit squares. 20 comes from the perimeter recipe 2 x (7 + 3); and area must carry SQUARE units because it counts squares, not sticks.

micros.title: Perimeter Formula: 2 x (Length + Width)
micros.description: Walk the boundary — long, short, long, short — and compress it into the shortcut perimeter = 2 x (length + width), measured in plain length units.
outcomes: Can compute a rectangle's perimeter with 2 x (length + width)
Can explain the formula as walking all four sides

question.prompt: A rectangular garden is 10 m long and 6 m wide. How much fencing does its PERIMETER need?

options.diagnosis: Computed length + width but forgot to double — only half the boundary was walked.
Doubled only the length (2 x 10 + 6); both widths must be counted too.

question.explanation: Perimeter = 2 x (10 + 6) = 2 x 16 = 32 m. Multiplying 10 x 6 = 60 gives the AREA in square metres — the grass inside, not the fence around it.

micros.title: Cover It or Go Around It? Choosing Formula and Unit
micros.description: Sort real problems by the question they ask — covering (area, square units) or surrounding (perimeter, length units) — before touching any numbers.
outcomes: Can decide whether a word problem needs area or perimeter
Can pick the correct unit (cm vs sq cm, m vs sq m) for each answer

question.prompt: You want to know how much carpet covers a room's floor. Which unit should the answer be in?

options.text: Square metres — carpet covers a surface

options.diagnosis: Cubic units measure filled SPACE (volume); a carpet covers a flat surface.
Litres measure liquid capacity; a floor is covered, not filled.

question.explanation: Covering questions are area questions, and area is measured by laying down unit SQUARES — so square metres. Plain metres would measure the skirting that runs AROUND the room (perimeter).

micros.title: Finding a Missing Side
micros.description: Run the formulas backwards: given a rectangle's area (or perimeter) and one side, find the other side by dividing (or halving then subtracting).
outcomes: Can find a missing side from the area and one side
Can find a missing side from the perimeter and one side

question.prompt: A rectangle has an AREA of 24 square cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 6 from 24; area is length TIMES width, so undoing it needs division.
Multiplied 24 by 6 instead of dividing; check — a 6 x 144 rectangle has a huge area, not 24.

question.explanation: Area = length x width, so width = 24 / 6 = 4 cm. Check: 6 x 4 = 24 square cm. Answering 6 comes from treating 24 as the PERIMETER: 2 x (6 + 6) = 24 — the wrong formula.

micros.title: Same Fence, Different Fields
micros.description: Explore rectangles sharing one perimeter and discover their areas differ — the squarer the rectangle, the more it encloses. Equal boundary never guarantees equal area.
outcomes: Can build several rectangles with the same perimeter and compute each area
Can explain why a fixed fence length can enclose different amounts of ground

question.prompt: Two plots each use exactly 20 m of fencing: Plot A is 2 m x 8 m and Plot B is 5 m x 5 m. Do they enclose the same area?

options.text: No — Plot B holds 25 sq m but Plot A only 16 sq m
Yes — the same fence means the same space inside
Plot A is bigger — it is longer
options.diagnosis: One long dimension does not decide coverage; the narrow 2 m width starves Plot A of area.

options.text: They cannot be compared without walking around both
options.diagnosis: The formulas settle it: 2 x 8 = 16 and 5 x 5 = 25 square metres.

question.explanation: Both perimeters are 20 m (2 x (2+8) = 20 and 4 x 5 = 20), but the areas are 16 and 25 square metres. Same fence, different fields — the squarer plot is roomier.

nodes.title: Volume Intuition with Unit Cubes
nodes.description: Volume measures how much space something fills, and we measure it by counting unit cubes — including the ones hidden inside and underneath. A box packs cubes in layers: cubes per layer × number of layers. Rearranging the same cubes into a tower or a slab changes the shape but never the volume.
learning_outcomes: Can find the volume of a cube-built solid by counting unit cubes, including hidden ones
Can use layers to count: cubes in one layer × number of layers
Can explain that rearranging cubes changes shape but not volume
Can compare volumes of two cube buildings and order containers by how much they hold

misconceptions.description: Counts only the cubes visible in a drawing — hidden and underneath cubes do not exist.
misconceptions.signal: A 2×2×2 stack drawn on paper is counted as 7 (or fewer); answers change with the viewing angle.
misconceptions.remedy: Build the drawn solid from real cubes, count by dismantling, and compare with the drawing count. Then practise 'X-ray counting': for each visible column, ask how many cubes stand in it top to bottom.

misconceptions.description: Stops at one layer — treats the base layer (or the taller-looking shape) as the whole volume.
misconceptions.signal: Multi-layer boxes get single-layer answers; 'taller' is declared 'more' without counting.
misconceptions.remedy: Fill a small open box with cube layers one at a time, pausing to record the running total: 12, 24, ... Volume = one layer × layers becomes something watched, not memorised.

misconceptions.description: Believes rearranging changes the amount — 12 cubes as a tall tower 'is more' than the same 12 as a flat slab (non-conservation).
misconceptions.signal: Judges quantity by height or spread; refuses to accept equality without recounting; wants to weigh them 'to be sure'.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student personally rebuild the SAME 12 cubes from tower to slab and back, counting each time. The cubes never left their hands — nothing was added or removed, so the volume is unchanged.

real_world_hooks: Stacking sugar cubes or Maggi packets into a carton
How many small mithai boxes fit in the shop's big carton
Bricks stacked in layers at a building site
Water displaced when you drop stones in a measuring jug
teaching.video_search: volume counting unit cubes layers class 5

questions.prompt: A box is filled with 2 layers of cubes. Each layer has 3 rows of 4 cubes. How many cubes are in the box?

options.diagnosis: Added 3 + 4 = 7 and doubled it — the layer needs 3 × 4 cubes, not 3 + 4.
Added all three numbers (3 + 4 + 2); the structure of layers-of-arrays was not used.

questions.explanation: One layer holds 3 × 4 = 12 cubes. Two layers hold 12 × 2 = 24 cubes. Layer count × cubes per layer is the fast way to count a box full of cubes.

questions.prompt: A drawing shows a 2 × 2 × 2 cube stack. Ravi counts 7 cubes because that is how many he can see. How many cubes are really there?

options.diagnosis: Counted one 2 × 2 face only; the stack is two such layers deep.
Counted the six faces of the big cube instead of the small cubes inside it.

questions.explanation: The stack is 2 layers of 2 × 2 = 4 cubes, so 4 × 2 = 8. One cube hides at the back bottom corner where the drawing cannot show it — hidden cubes still count.

questions.prompt: Meena builds a tall tower from 12 cubes. Arjun uses his own 12 identical cubes to make a flat 3 × 4 slab. Who has used more material?

options.text: Both the same — 12 cubes is 12 cubes, however they are arranged
Meena — the tower is taller, so it must be more
Arjun — the slab spreads over more of the table
options.diagnosis: Judged by footprint area; spreading out is the flip side of height, and neither changes the count.

options.text: Impossible to tell without weighing both

questions.explanation: Each build uses exactly 12 unit cubes, so the volumes are equal. Height and spread trade off against each other; rearranging cubes never creates or destroys any. (Weighing would just confirm 12 = 12.)

micros.title: Volume Is Counting Cubes
micros.description: Volume measures filled space, and its unit is a little cube — not a flat square. Find the volume of small cube buildings by counting every unit cube.
outcomes: Can find the volume of a simple cube building by counting unit cubes
Can state that volume is measured in cubes while area is measured in squares

micros.title: X-ray Counting: The Hidden Cubes
micros.description: Drawings hide cubes at the back and underneath, but they still count. Practise X-ray counting: for each visible column, count how many cubes stand in it top to bottom.
outcomes: Can count all cubes in a drawn stack, including hidden ones
Can verify a drawing count by building the solid from real cubes

question.prompt: A solid stack is 3 cubes long, 2 cubes wide and 2 cubes high. In the drawing, Ravi can see only 9 cubes, so he answers 9. How many cubes are really in the stack?

options.diagnosis: Counted only the front layer plus one; a 3-wide, 2-deep, 2-high block has two full layers of six.
Multiplied the wrong dimensions (perhaps 4 x 4); the block is 3 x 2 x 2.

question.explanation: Each layer holds 3 x 2 = 6 cubes, and there are 2 layers: 6 x 2 = 12. The cubes hidden at the back and bottom of the drawing are still there — a drawing shows at most three sides.

micros.title: Counting by Layers
micros.description: A box packs cubes in identical layers, so the fast count is cubes in one layer x number of layers — watched live by filling a real box layer by layer.
outcomes: Can compute a box's cube count as one layer x layers
Can find the cubes in one layer as rows x columns

question.prompt: A carton is filled with 3 layers of cubes. Each layer has 4 rows of 3 cubes. How many cubes fill the carton?

options.diagnosis: Added rows and columns first (4 + 3 = 7) then multiplied by layers; one layer holds 4 x 3 = 12 cubes.
Added all three numbers (4 + 3 + 3); the structure is layers OF arrays, which multiply.

question.explanation: One layer holds 4 x 3 = 12 cubes. Three layers hold 12 x 3 = 36 cubes. Stopping at 12 counts only the bottom layer — the box keeps filling upward.

micros.title: Rearranging Never Changes Volume
micros.description: Rebuild the same set of cubes from a tall tower into a flat slab and back: the shape changes, the count never does. Height and spread trade off; nothing is created or destroyed.
outcomes: Can state that rearranging cubes preserves volume, with a demonstration
Can reject 'taller means more' by counting both builds

question.prompt: Meena stacks 18 cubes into one tall tower. Arjun arranges his own 18 identical cubes into a low 3 x 3 x 2 block. Whose build takes up more space?

options.text: Both the same — 18 cubes is 18 cubes, however they are arranged
Meena's — the tower is taller, so it must be more
Impossible to tell without weighing both builds
Arjun's — his block covers more of the table
options.diagnosis: Judged by footprint; spreading out is the flip side of height, and neither changes the cube count.

question.explanation: Check Arjun's block: 3 x 3 x 2 = 18 cubes — exactly Meena's count. Rearranging never adds or removes a cube, so the volumes are equal. Weighing would only confirm 18 = 18.

micros.title: Comparing and Ordering Volumes
micros.description: Compare cube buildings by count (not by look) and order containers by how much they hold, previewing capacity: pouring and packing decide, not height alone.
outcomes: Can compare two cube buildings by computing both volumes
Can order three containers or builds from smallest to largest volume

nodes.title: Interpreting Tables, Bar Graphs and Simple Pie Charts
nodes.description: Data answers questions — if you read it correctly. You will pull values out of tables, read scaled bar graphs precisely (including part-divisions), and interpret simple pie charts where a slice is a fraction of the total. The golden rules: check the scale, and remember a pie slice is a fraction — its actual count depends on the total.
learning_outcomes: Can extract and compare values from a data table, including finding least and greatest
Can read bar graphs with scaled axes, including bars ending between gridlines
Can interpret a simple pie chart by applying its fractions (half, quarter) to the stated total
Can answer multi-step questions combining two or more readings from one display

misconceptions.description: Reads a pie slice's fraction as a raw count — 'half the circle' becomes '50 people' whatever the total is.
misconceptions.signal: Answers to pie-chart questions are 50, 25 and similar percent-flavoured numbers regardless of the stated total.
misconceptions.remedy: Always write the total above the pie first, then compute each slice AS a fraction OF that total: half of 60 is 30. Compare two pies with equal slices but different totals (half of 60 vs half of 200) to break the '50' reflex.

misconceptions.description: Ignores the axis scale on bar graphs — counts divisions as if each were 1, and rounds bars that end between gridlines to the nearest line.
misconceptions.signal: Bar readings match the gridline count, not the data; half-divisions are silently rounded away.
misconceptions.remedy: Keep the scale-check ritual ('1 division = __') and practise on bars deliberately drawn to end mid-division: the reading is divisions × scale, including the half.

misconceptions.description: Compares multi-digit values in a table by their first digits or by length of the written word, declaring 9 greater than 15.
misconceptions.signal: 'Least/greatest' answers contradict the numbers; single-digit entries beat teens in the student's ranking.
misconceptions.remedy: Route the comparison through place value: line the column's values up right-justified and compare digit counts first. Data reading is only as good as the number comparison underneath it.

real_world_hooks: Runs per over charts from an IPL match
Library register: books borrowed each day of the week
A pie chart of how a family's monthly budget is split
Rainfall or temperature tables from the newspaper
teaching.video_search: interpreting bar graphs pie charts tables class 5

questions.prompt: A table shows books borrowed from the library: Mon 12, Tue 15, Wed 9, Thu 21. On which day were the FEWEST books borrowed?

options.diagnosis: Picked the greatest value — the question asks for the fewest; 'least/most' words need flagging before reading.
Found the smallest value (9) but slipped a row when matching it back to its day — trace across the table with a finger to keep day and number together.

questions.explanation: Compare the four values: 9 < 12 < 15 < 21, so Wednesday (9 books) is the fewest. A single-digit number is always less than any two-digit number, even though 9 is a 'big' digit.

questions.prompt: In a bar graph of favourite sports, each division stands for 10 children. The kabaddi bar rises 4 and a half divisions. How many children chose kabaddi?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by the scale but dropped the half division — that half stands for 5 real children.
Rounded the bar up to the next gridline before scaling; the graph must be read exactly.

questions.explanation: 4.5 divisions × 10 children per division = 45 children. The half division is data too: it represents 5 children, not something to round away.

questions.prompt: A pie chart of 60 students' favourite fruit shows: half the circle for mango, a quarter for banana, a quarter for apple. How many students chose mango?

options.diagnosis: Computed a quarter of 60 instead of half — the slice fractions were swapped.
Reported the total number of students; the slice's fraction was never applied to it.

questions.explanation: The mango slice is half the circle, and half OF the 60 students is 30. A pie slice is a fraction, not a count — the same half-circle would mean 100 students if the total were 200.

micros.title: Reading Data Tables
micros.description: Pull the right value out of a table, then compare entries to find least and greatest — routing every comparison through place value, not first digits.
outcomes: Can extract a named value from a data table
Can find the least and greatest entries in a table column correctly

question.prompt: A table shows rainfall in mm: June 8, July 12, August 25, September 9. Which month had the MOST rain?

options.text: September — 9 is the biggest digit in the list

options.diagnosis: Picked the least value — the question asks for the most; flag least/most words before reading.
Compared 12 and 25 by their second digits; line values up and compare place by place from the left.

question.explanation: Compare all four: 8 < 9 < 12 < 25, so August (25 mm) had the most rain. A big single digit like 9 still loses to any two-digit number.

micros.title: Bar Graphs with Scaled Axes
micros.description: Read bar graphs where one division stands for 5, 10 or more: run the scale-check ritual first, and read bars that end between gridlines exactly — the half division is data too.
outcomes: Can state a bar graph's scale before reading any bar
Can read a bar ending mid-division as divisions x scale, including the half

question.prompt: On a runs-per-over graph, 1 division stands for 10 runs. The bar for over 3 rises 3 and a half divisions. How many runs were scored in over 3?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by the scale but dropped the half division — that half stands for 5 real runs.
Rounded the bar up to the next gridline before scaling; the graph must be read exactly.

question.explanation: 3.5 divisions x 10 runs per division = 35 runs. Counting gridlines as if each were 1 (and rounding the half away) throws away both the scale and part of the data.

micros.title: Pie Slices Are Fractions of the Total
micros.description: Read a simple pie chart by writing the total above it first, then computing each slice as a fraction OF that total: half of 80 is 40, a quarter of 80 is 20.
outcomes: Can compute the count for a half or quarter slice from the stated total
Can explain why the same slice means different counts for different totals

question.prompt: A pie chart shows the favourite games of 80 children. The cricket slice is a QUARTER of the circle. How many children chose cricket?

options.diagnosis: Took half of 80 instead of a quarter; the slice is one fourth of the circle.
Used the denominator of the fraction as the answer; the quarter must be applied TO the total of 80.

question.explanation: A quarter OF the 80 children is 80 / 4 = 20. The answer 25 treats 'quarter' as a fixed number (like 25 out of 100), but a slice is a fraction whose count depends on the total.

micros.title: Comparing Pie Charts with Different Totals
micros.description: Compare slices across two pie charts with different totals and discover that a smaller slice of a bigger total can beat a bigger slice of a smaller total.
outcomes: Can compare slice counts across two pies by applying each fraction to its own total
Can explain why slice size alone cannot be compared across pies

question.prompt: In School A's pie chart (100 students), HALF the circle likes mango. In School B's pie chart (400 students), only a QUARTER of the circle likes mango. Which school has more mango lovers?

options.text: School B — a quarter of 400 is 100, more than half of 100, which is 50
School A — half a circle always beats a quarter circle
They are equal — the slices balance out
options.diagnosis: No computation done; each fraction must be applied to its OWN total before comparing.

options.text: Cannot be answered from pie charts
options.diagnosis: It can — the totals are given, so each slice converts to a real count.

question.explanation: Half of 100 = 50 mango lovers at School A; a quarter of 400 = 100 at School B. The smaller-looking slice wins because its total is four times bigger — a slice is a fraction, not a count.

micros.title: Multi-step Questions from One Display
micros.description: Answer questions that need two or more readings from the same table or graph — totals across rows, differences between bars, and 'how many more' comparisons.
outcomes: Can combine two readings from one display into a total or difference
Can answer 'how many more' questions from tables and bar graphs

nodes.title: Knowing Our Numbers: Large Numbers and Estimation
nodes.description: You will read, write, compare and order large numbers in both the Indian (lakh, crore) and international (million, billion) systems, and use rounding to estimate sums, differences and products. Estimation is the everyday superpower of mathematics: it lets you sanity-check bills, budgets and news headlines in seconds.
learning_outcomes: Can read and write numbers up to crores using both Indian and international place-value systems, with correct comma placement
Can compare and order large numbers by aligning place values, not just by looking at leading digits
Can round a number to the nearest ten, hundred, thousand or lakh
Can estimate the result of an addition, subtraction or multiplication and judge whether an exact answer is reasonable

misconceptions.description: Compares numbers by their leading digits instead of by number of digits and place value (e.g. thinks 98,765 > 1,00,065 because 9 > 1).
misconceptions.signal: Says the number starting with the bigger digit is bigger, even when the other number has more digits.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student count digits first and stack numbers right-aligned in a place-value chart; compare column by column from the left only after digit counts match.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the Indian and international systems, e.g. believes 1 lakh = 1 million.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 10,00,000 when asked for one lakh, or reads 5,000,000 as 'five lakh'.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a two-row conversion strip (1 lakh = 100 thousand, 10 lakh = 1 million, 1 crore = 10 million) and practise re-punctuating the same digit string with both comma conventions.

misconceptions.description: When rounding, looks at the wrong digit (often the last digit) instead of the digit just below the rounding place.
misconceptions.signal: Rounds 8,468 to the nearest thousand as 9,000 'because it ends in 8'.
misconceptions.remedy: Teach an explicit two-step routine: underline the rounding place, circle the single digit to its right, and let only the circled digit decide up or down; verify on a number line showing which thousand is nearer.

misconceptions.description: Thinks estimation is random guessing rather than controlled rounding, so estimates wildly or refuses to estimate without computing exactly.
misconceptions.signal: Computes the exact answer first and then 'estimates' by copying it, or offers a guess unconnected to the numbers.
misconceptions.remedy: Give estimation-only tasks with a strict time budget where exact computation is impossible, then compare classmates' rounded estimates against the exact value to show the method's reliability.

real_world_hooks: Populations of Indian cities in a census table: which is bigger, 92,53,000 or 1,02,10,000?
IPL auction amounts: is 12 crore more or less than 120 million?
Estimating a monthly grocery bill before the shopkeeper totals it
teaching.video_search: large numbers Indian place value system lakhs crores estimation class 6

questions.prompt: Which of these numbers is the greatest?

options.diagnosis: Chose the number with the most repeated large digits; not attending to the number of digits at all.

questions.explanation: Count digits first: 1,00,065 has six digits while 98,765 and 99,999 have five and 9,999 has four. A six-digit number is always greater than any five-digit number, so 1,00,065 (one lakh sixty-five) is the greatest, even though it starts with 1.

questions.prompt: Round 8,468 to the nearest thousand.

options.diagnosis: Rounded to the nearest five hundred instead of the nearest thousand.
Rounded to the nearest ten; misread which place value was asked for.

questions.explanation: The thousands digit is 8. The digit just to its right (hundreds) is 4, which is less than 5, so we round down: 8,468 → 8,000. The final 8 in the ones place plays no role in rounding to the nearest thousand.

questions.prompt: A school collected ₹5,290 in week 1 and ₹17,986 in week 2. Estimate the total collection by rounding each amount to the nearest thousand.

options.diagnosis: Rounded both numbers down (truncated) instead of rounding to the nearest thousand.
Rounded both numbers up regardless of the hundreds digit.

questions.explanation: 5,290 rounds to 5,000 (hundreds digit 2 < 5) and 17,986 rounds to 18,000 (hundreds digit 9 ≥ 5). Estimated total: 5,000 + 18,000 = ₹23,000. Note ₹23,276 is the exact sum — a correct calculation, but not an estimate, which is what was asked.

micros.title: Place Value up to Lakhs: Recap and Warm-up
micros.description: Revise the Indian place-value chart up to lakhs: face value versus place value, and expanded form of 5- and 6-digit numbers.
outcomes: Can state the place value and face value of any digit in a 6-digit number
Can write a 6-digit number in expanded form and rebuild it from expanded form

micros.title: Reading and Writing Numbers up to Crores
micros.description: Extend the Indian system to ten lakh, crore and ten crore, placing commas after thousands, lakhs and crores (3-2-2 pattern) and reading number names aloud.
outcomes: Can insert commas correctly in the Indian system for numbers up to 10 crore
Can write the number name for a given numeral and the numeral for a given name

micros.title: The International System: Millions and Billions
micros.description: Read and write the same digit string in the international system (thousand, million, billion) and convert between lakhs/crores and millions.
outcomes: Can punctuate a number with international commas (groups of 3) and read it
Can convert between lakh/crore and hundred thousand/million (1 lakh = 100 thousand, 1 crore = 10 million)

question.prompt: Which of these is equal to 1 million?

options.diagnosis: Confused million with crore; 1 crore is 10 million, not 1 million.
That is 1 billion (1,000 million), several steps too large.

question.explanation: 1 million = 1,000,000 = 10,00,000 in Indian commas, which is ten lakh. A useful conversion strip: 1 lakh = 100 thousand, 10 lakh = 1 million, 1 crore = 10 million.

micros.title: Comparing and Ordering Large Numbers
micros.description: Compare large numbers by first counting digits, then comparing place by place from the left; order lists ascending and descending and build greatest/smallest numbers from given digits.
outcomes: Can compare two large numbers using digit count first, then leftmost differing digit
Can arrange four or more large numbers in ascending or descending order
Can form the greatest and smallest numbers from a set of digits

question.prompt: Which of these numbers is the greatest?

options.diagnosis: Picked a five-digit number by its large leading digits instead of counting digits first.
Chose a four-digit number; not attending to the number of digits at all.

question.explanation: Count digits first: 1,02,345 has six digits while 99,876 and 87,654 have five, and 9,876 has four. Any six-digit number beats every five-digit number, so 1,02,345 is the greatest even though it starts with 1.

micros.title: Rounding to Tens, Hundreds, Thousands and Lakhs
micros.description: Round a number to a chosen place by underlining the rounding place and letting only the single digit to its right decide up or down, verified on a number line.
outcomes: Can round any number to the nearest ten, hundred, thousand or lakh
Can justify a rounding decision by naming which two multiples the number lies between and which is nearer

question.prompt: Round 3,472 to the nearest hundred.

options.diagnosis: Used the ones digit (2) to decide instead of the tens digit (7).
Rounded to the nearest thousand instead of the nearest hundred.
Rounded to the nearest ten; misread which place was asked for.

question.explanation: The hundreds digit is 4. The digit just to its right is the tens digit 7, and 7 is 5 or more, so round up: 3,472 lies between 3,400 and 3,500 and is nearer 3,500.

micros.title: Estimating Sums, Differences and Products
micros.description: Use controlled rounding to estimate the result of an addition, subtraction or multiplication before (or instead of) computing exactly, and judge whether an exact answer is reasonable.
outcomes: Can estimate a sum or difference by rounding each number to a sensible place
Can estimate a product by rounding each factor and explain why the estimate is not a random guess

question.prompt: Estimate 4,317 + 2,896 by rounding each number to the nearest thousand.

options.diagnosis: Computed the exact sum instead of estimating; estimation means working with rounded numbers.
Truncated both numbers down instead of rounding to the nearest thousand.
Rounded both numbers up regardless of the hundreds digit.

question.explanation: 4,317 rounds to 4,000 (hundreds digit 3 < 5) and 2,896 rounds to 3,000 (hundreds digit 8 >= 5). Estimated sum: 4,000 + 3,000 = 7,000. The exact sum 7,213 confirms the estimate is close.

nodes.title: Whole Numbers and Their Properties
nodes.description: Whole numbers are the counting numbers together with zero. You will explore their behaviour on the number line and the properties of addition and multiplication — commutativity, associativity, distributivity and the special roles of 0 and 1 — and use these properties to compute cleverly instead of laboriously.
learning_outcomes: Can identify predecessors and successors and locate whole numbers on a number line
Can state which operations on whole numbers are commutative and associative, with counterexamples for subtraction and division
Can use distributivity and regrouping to simplify calculations such as 8 × 293 × 125 mentally
Can explain the roles of 0 and 1 as identities and why division by zero is undefined

misconceptions.description: Believes dividing by zero gives zero (or gives the number itself).
misconceptions.signal: Writes 7 ÷ 0 = 0 or 7 ÷ 0 = 7 without hesitation.
misconceptions.remedy: Recast division as 'how many groups?': 7 ÷ 0 asks how many groups of 0 make 7 — no number of empty groups ever reaches 7. Contrast with 0 ÷ 7 = 0, which does make sense.

misconceptions.description: Assumes subtraction and division are commutative like addition and multiplication.
misconceptions.signal: Claims 5 − 8 = 8 − 5 or rearranges a − b to b − a mid-calculation 'because order doesn't matter'.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student test each property with small concrete numbers before using it, and keep a personal 'property table' showing which operations pass and fail the order-swap test.

misconceptions.description: Thinks 1 (not 0) is the smallest whole number, or that zero is 'nothing' and not a number.
misconceptions.signal: Starts the whole-number list at 1, or refuses to place 0 on the number line.
misconceptions.remedy: Distinguish natural numbers from whole numbers explicitly, and use contexts where 0 is a meaningful value (0 runs scored, 0°C, floor 0) rather than an absence.

misconceptions.description: Misapplies distributivity, e.g. 4 × (25 + 3) = 4 × 25 + 3, distributing over only the first term.
misconceptions.signal: Multiplies only one addend inside the bracket by the outside factor.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the rectangle/area model: a 4-by-28 rectangle split into 4-by-25 and 4-by-3 parts makes visible that BOTH parts get multiplied by 4.

real_world_hooks: Mental math at a shop: 8 packets at ₹293 each, grouped as 8 × 125 tricks with round numbers
Cricket: a batter on 0 runs — zero as a real score, not 'nothing'
Splitting a UPI payment: why ₹0 sent leaves the balance unchanged (additive identity)
teaching.video_search: whole numbers properties commutative associative distributive class 6

questions.prompt: What is the smallest whole number?

options.diagnosis: Reaching ahead to integers; negative numbers are not whole numbers.

options.text: There is no smallest whole number
options.diagnosis: Confusing 'no largest' (true) with 'no smallest' (false) — the list stops going down at 0.

questions.explanation: Whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, … The collection has no largest member, but it does have a smallest: 0. (The natural numbers 1, 2, 3, … are the whole numbers without zero — that is where the '1' answer comes from.)

questions.prompt: Using a clever regrouping, find 8 × 293 × 125.

options.diagnosis: Correct method (8 × 125 = 1000) but dropped a zero when multiplying by 1000.
Correct method but added an extra zero when multiplying by 1000.
Treated 8 × 125 as 100 instead of 1000, then computed 2344 × 100.

questions.explanation: Multiplication is commutative and associative, so regroup: 8 × 125 = 1000, and 1000 × 293 = 293,000. The whole point of the properties is to pair numbers that make powers of ten.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true for EVERY whole number a?

options.diagnosis: Confusing a ÷ a (which is 1, when a ≠ 0) with a − a = 0.

questions.explanation: Subtracting zero changes nothing, so a − 0 = a always holds. Division by zero is undefined (not zero). Subtraction is not commutative, so 0 − a is not a for a > 0 (it is not even a whole number). And a ÷ a = 1 for a ≠ 0, while it is a − a that equals 0.

micros.title: Whole Numbers, Zero and the Number Line
micros.description: Meet the whole numbers as the counting numbers together with 0, locate them on the number line, and find successors and predecessors.
outcomes: Can explain that 0 is the smallest whole number and that every whole number has a successor
Can find the successor and predecessor of any whole number and model addition/subtraction as jumps on the number line

question.prompt: Which is the smallest whole number?

options.text: There is no smallest whole number
options.diagnosis: Confused smallest with largest; whole numbers have no largest member, but they do start at 0.
Negative numbers are integers but not whole numbers.

question.explanation: Whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, ... Zero is a genuine number (not 'nothing') and it is the smallest whole number. There is no largest whole number because adding 1 always gives another one.

micros.title: Commutativity and Associativity of Addition and Multiplication
micros.description: Discover that addition and multiplication can be done in any order and any grouping, and test whether subtraction and division share these properties (they do not).
outcomes: Can state and use a + b = b + a and (a + b) + c = a + (b + c), and the same for multiplication
Can give a counterexample showing subtraction and division are not commutative

question.prompt: Which statement is true for ALL whole numbers a and b?

options.text: a - b is always a whole number
options.diagnosis: Whole numbers are not closed under subtraction: 3 - 5 is not a whole number.

question.explanation: Addition is commutative: swapping the numbers never changes the sum. Subtraction and division are not: 5 - 3 = 2 but 3 - 5 is not 2, and 8 / 4 = 2 but 4 / 8 is not 2.

micros.title: The Special Roles of 0 and 1
