Constructions teach WHY figures have their properties — every arc is a statement about equal distances.
learning_outcomes: Can draw a circle of given radius and copy a line segment with compass and ruler
Can construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment and a perpendicular through a point
Can construct 60° and related angles (120°, 30°, 90°) and bisect a given angle
Can explain why a construction works in terms of equal radii (equal distances)

misconceptions.description: Thinks measuring with a protractor or marked ruler counts as 'construction', or that constructions are just careful drawing tricks with no reasoning behind them.
misconceptions.signal: Reaches for the protractor to 'construct' a 60° angle; cannot say why the compass method gives exactly 60°.
misconceptions.remedy: Reveal the hidden equilateral triangle: join the arc intersection points and measure the three equal sides. Constructions become logical arguments (equal radii ⇒ equal sides ⇒ 60°), not rituals.

misconceptions.description: Lets the compass width drift mid-construction, believing the radius doesn't need to stay fixed.
misconceptions.signal: Arcs that should intersect don't; bisectors come out visibly off-centre; the student shrugs and adjusts by eye.
misconceptions.remedy: Demonstrate a deliberate 'sabotaged' construction with changed radius and compare with a correct one. Teach the physical skills: tighten the hinge, hold by the handle, lean the compass in the direction of turn.

misconceptions.description: Thinks the perpendicular bisector is just any line through the midpoint (perpendicularity ignored), or just the midpoint itself.
misconceptions.signal: Marks the midpoint with a ruler and draws a slanted line through it, calling it the perpendicular bisector.
misconceptions.remedy: Emphasise both conditions with a checklist (passes through midpoint ✓, makes 90° ✓) and show that the equal-arcs construction guarantees both at once.

misconceptions.description: Believes the size of the arcs (compass opening) chosen during bisection changes the answer, so there is 'one right opening'.
misconceptions.signal: Asks 'how much should I open the compass?' expecting a specific number; erases work when a different opening is used.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student bisect the same angle three times with three different openings on tracing paper and overlay the results — the bisector lands in the same place every time (as long as the opening stays fixed WITHIN one step).

real_world_hooks: How a carpenter marks a perpendicular cut with just string and a pencil
Drawing a perfect circle for a cricket pitch or rangoli using a rope as compass
Finding the exact middle of a doorway or shelf without measuring numbers
teaching.video_search: ruler compass constructions perpendicular bisector 60 degree angle class 6

questions.prompt: To draw a circle of radius 4 cm, you should open the compass to:

options.diagnosis: Confused radius with diameter; the compass opening is the centre-to-edge distance.
Halved the radius, perhaps thinking the opening spans only half way.

options.text: Any width — you can adjust it while drawing

questions.explanation: The compass opening IS the radius: every point of the circle sits exactly that distance from the centre. Open it to 4 cm on the ruler and keep it fixed while you turn — changing it mid-turn breaks the equal-distance property that makes it a circle.

questions.prompt: In the compass construction of a 60° angle, why does the angle come out exactly 60°?

options.text: The two arcs and the base segment create an equilateral triangle, and each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°
Compasses are manufactured to draw 60° automatically
Because the first arc must be drawn exactly 6 cm wide
It is only approximately 60°; you fix it with a protractor afterwards

questions.explanation: Keeping the same compass opening makes three equal lengths: the base and the two arc radii. Equal sides force an equilateral triangle, whose angles are all 60°. The opening's actual size never matters — only that it stays the SAME.

questions.prompt: P is a point on the perpendicular bisector of segment AB. What must be true about P?

options.text: P is equidistant from A and B
P must be the midpoint of AB
P is at distance exactly AB from both A and B
options.diagnosis: Confuses 'equal distances' with one specific distance; points on the bisector are at ALL sorts of (equal) distances.

options.text: P is always closer to A than to B
options.diagnosis: Misses the symmetry entirely; the bisector is precisely the set of points that favour neither end.

questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisector is exactly the set of points equally far from A and B. The midpoint is just one such point — every other point on the line is also equidistant (that's why the equal-arc construction, which marks two points equidistant from A and B, produces this line).

micros.title: The Idea of Construction: Ruler-and-Compass Rules
micros.description: Learn what counts as a geometric construction - figures produced with an unmarked straightedge and a compass by steps that can be justified - as opposed to measuring with protractor or marked ruler.
outcomes: Can name the allowed tools and moves in ruler-and-compass construction
Can explain why constructing differs from measuring and drawing

question.prompt: Which of these counts as a ruler-and-compass CONSTRUCTION of a right angle?

options.text: Producing it with compass arcs and a straightedge, with each step justified
Measuring 90 degrees with a protractor and drawing the arm
Tracing the corner of a set-square
options.diagnosis: Copying a manufactured corner is measurement by proxy, not a reasoned construction.
However neat, freehand drawing has no guarantee of exactness and no justification.

question.explanation: A construction uses only an unmarked straightedge and a compass, and each step is exact by reasoning (equal radii give equal lengths). Protractors and set-squares measure or copy - useful, but not constructions.

micros.title: Drawing Circles with a Compass
micros.description: Draw circles of a given radius with a compass, keeping the opening fixed while rotating, and see the circle as all points at one fixed distance from the centre.
outcomes: Can draw a circle of given radius smoothly with a fixed compass opening
Can explain why a slipping compass opening spoils the circle

micros.title: Constructing and Copying a Line Segment
micros.description: Construct a segment of given length and copy a given segment onto another line using the compass as a distance-carrier, without reading a marked scale.
outcomes: Can copy a segment onto a given ray using only compass and straightedge
Can construct a segment equal to the sum or difference of two given segments

micros.title: Perpendicular to a Line Through a Point
micros.description: Construct the perpendicular to a given line through a point on the line, and through a point not on the line, using pairs of equal arcs.
outcomes: Can construct a perpendicular through a point on the line
Can construct a perpendicular from an external point and check it with a set-square

micros.title: The Perpendicular Bisector of a Segment
micros.description: Construct the perpendicular bisector with intersecting arcs from both endpoints, and understand it as the line that BOTH passes through the midpoint AND meets the segment at 90 degrees.
outcomes: Can construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment with equal arcs from both ends
Can state both defining properties (midpoint and right angle) and check them

question.prompt: Which of these describes the perpendicular bisector of segment AB?

options.text: The line through the midpoint of AB that meets AB at 90 degrees
Any line that passes through the midpoint of AB

options.diagnosis: The bisector is a whole line, not a single point.

options.text: Any line that meets AB at 90 degrees
options.diagnosis: Perpendicular, yes - but it must also cut AB exactly in half.

question.explanation: 'Perpendicular' and 'bisector' are two separate requirements: the line must cross AB at its midpoint (bisect) AND at a right angle (perpendicular). Infinitely many lines pass through the midpoint; only one of them is perpendicular to AB.

micros.title: Copying an Angle of Unknown Measure
micros.description: Copy a given angle onto a new ray using two arcs and a transferred chord distance - no protractor and no knowledge of the angle's degree measure needed.
outcomes: Can copy any given angle with compass and straightedge
Can explain which equal distances make the copy exact

micros.title: Bisecting an Angle
micros.description: Bisect an angle with an arc from the vertex and two equal arcs from the crossing points, and see that any sufficiently large compass opening gives the SAME bisector.
outcomes: Can bisect any angle with compass and straightedge and verify by measuring both halves
Can explain why the choice of arc radius does not change the bisector

question.prompt: While bisecting an angle, Riya uses a much wider compass opening for her arcs than Arjun does for the same angle. What happens?

options.text: Both get the same bisector - any sufficiently large opening works
They get different bisectors, because the arc size changes the answer
Only one 'correct' opening exists, so at most one of them is right
options.diagnosis: Believing there is a single magic radius; the construction works for every workable radius.

options.text: The wider opening makes the angle itself bigger
options.diagnosis: Arcs are scaffolding; they cannot change the angle being bisected.

question.explanation: The construction relies only on the arcs being EQUAL to each other, not on their particular size. Different radii produce crossing points at different distances, but all those crossing points lie on the same bisector ray.

nodes.title: Mensuration: Perimeter and Area of Squares and Rectangles
nodes.description: Perimeter measures the boundary of a figure; area measures the surface it covers. You will use the formulas for squares and rectangles, work with the right units (cm vs cm²), and discover that figures with the same perimeter can enclose very different areas.
learning_outcomes: Can compute perimeters of rectangles, squares and figures made of straight segments
Can compute areas of rectangles and squares, and of shapes decomposable into rectangles
Can attach correct units: linear units for perimeter, square units for area
Can explain with examples that equal perimeters do not force equal areas (and vice versa)

misconceptions.description: Confuses area and perimeter — uses the wrong formula or swaps the two concepts.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'area 26 cm' for an 8×5 rectangle, or multiplies sides when asked for the boundary length.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie each to a physical action: perimeter = walking the fence (add the walk), area = counting the tiles inside (multiply rows × columns). Have the student state WHICH action the problem asks for before computing.

misconceptions.description: Believes shapes with the same perimeter must have the same area (and same area forces same perimeter).
misconceptions.signal: Argues a 6×4 and an 8×2 rectangle 'must' have equal areas since both use 20 cm of boundary.
misconceptions.remedy: Give a fixed 20 cm loop of string on squared paper and record the areas of different rectangles it can bound (1×9 = 9 up to 5×5 = 25). The table itself refutes the belief memorably.

misconceptions.description: Writes area in linear units (cm) or perimeter in square units (cm²), treating units as decoration.
misconceptions.signal: Answers '49 cm' for the area of a 7 cm square.
misconceptions.remedy: Show that area counts unit SQUARES: each tile is 1 cm × 1 cm = 1 cm². Make unit-checking a final step of every answer: 'did I count steps (cm) or tiles (cm²)?'

misconceptions.description: Computes a rectangle's perimeter as just length + breadth, forgetting the figure has four sides.
misconceptions.signal: Gives 13 cm for the perimeter of an 8×5 rectangle.
misconceptions.remedy: Trace the full boundary with a finger, counting all four sides aloud: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5. Then compress the reasoning into the formula 2 × (l + b) so the doubling is understood, not memorised.

real_world_hooks: Fencing a vegetable patch vs buying grass to cover it — one is perimeter, the other area
Tiling a bathroom floor: how many 1-ft tiles for a 6 ft × 8 ft floor?
Photo frames (border) vs the photo itself (surface)
Boundary rope for a school sports ground
teaching.video_search: perimeter and area of rectangle square word problems class 6

questions.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 8 cm and breadth 5 cm.

options.diagnosis: Used 4 × 5, applying the square's perimeter formula to one side only.

questions.explanation: Perimeter = walk all four sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 2 × (8 + 5) = 26 cm. Multiplying 8 × 5 = 40 gives the AREA (in cm², not cm) — a different question entirely.

questions.prompt: What is the area of a square of side 7 cm?

options.diagnosis: Added two sides (7 + 7) instead of multiplying side × side.

questions.explanation: Area = side × side = 7 × 7 = 49, and since we are counting 1 cm × 1 cm tiles, the unit is cm². The option '28 cm²' comes from the perimeter calculation 4 × 7 = 28 — that number is the perimeter, not an area, whatever unit is pasted on. And 49 with unit 'cm' is wrong too — area is measured in square units.

questions.prompt: Rectangle A is 6 cm × 4 cm and rectangle B is 8 cm × 2 cm. Both have perimeter 20 cm. Do they have the same area?

options.text: No — A has area 24 cm² and B has area 16 cm²
Yes — same perimeter always means same area
It cannot be decided without drawing them
options.diagnosis: The formulas decide it exactly; measurement or drawing is not needed.

questions.explanation: Area A = 6 × 4 = 24 cm²; Area B = 8 × 2 = 16 cm². Equal perimeters, different areas: the same boundary length encloses more area the closer the rectangle is to a square. Perimeter and area measure genuinely different things.

micros.title: Perimeter as Distance Around
micros.description: Establish perimeter as the total length of the boundary - walked, fenced or traced - and find perimeters of arbitrary straight-sided figures by adding ALL the sides.
outcomes: Can find the perimeter of any polygon by summing every side
Can identify real situations (fencing, lace border, running a lap) that call for perimeter

micros.title: Perimeter Formulas for Rectangles and Squares
micros.description: Compress side-adding into formulas - rectangle: 2 x (length + breadth), square: 4 x side - remembering the shape has four sides, so length + breadth is only halfway there.
outcomes: Can apply P = 2(l + b) and P = 4s correctly with units
Can find a missing side given the perimeter

question.prompt: A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. What is its perimeter?

options.diagnosis: Added length + breadth only; that covers just two of the four sides.
Multiplied 8 x 5 - that is the area formula, not the perimeter.
Computed 8 + 8 + 5, forgetting one of the widths.

question.explanation: The boundary has four sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm, i.e. P = 2 x (8 + 5) = 2 x 13 = 26 cm. Length plus breadth (13 cm) is only half the way around.

micros.title: Area by Counting Unit Squares
micros.description: Measure area as the number of unit squares a region covers, counting full squares, half squares, and estimating for more-than-half / less-than-half squares on grid paper.
outcomes: Can find areas of grid figures including halves and irregular edges
Can explain area as covered surface, distinct from distance around

micros.title: Area Formulas for Rectangles and Squares
micros.description: Derive area = length x breadth from rows of unit squares, use area = side x side for squares, and attach SQUARE units (cm2, m2) because area counts squares, not lengths.
outcomes: Can compute areas of rectangles and squares with correct square units
Can find a missing side from the area and explain why area units are squared

question.prompt: What is the area of a square of side 6 cm?

options.diagnosis: Computed the perimeter (4 x 6) instead of the area.
Right number, wrong unit: area counts unit SQUARES, so it needs cm2.
Added 6 + 6 instead of multiplying 6 x 6.

question.explanation: Area = side x side = 6 x 6 = 36, measured in square centimetres: 36 cm2. The unit matters - 36 cm would describe a length, but area counts the 1 cm x 1 cm squares covering the surface.

micros.title: Same Perimeter, Different Area (and Vice Versa)
micros.description: Build different rectangles with equal perimeters and compare their areas (and equal areas with different perimeters), proving the two measures are independent.
outcomes: Can construct rectangles with the same perimeter but different areas
Can explain why knowing the perimeter does not determine the area

question.prompt: Rectangle P is 6 cm by 2 cm. Rectangle Q is 5 cm by 3 cm. Both have perimeter 16 cm. Which has the bigger area?

options.text: Q, because 5 x 3 = 15 cm2 is more than 6 x 2 = 12 cm2
They must have the same area, because their perimeters are equal

options.diagnosis: A longer shape with the same perimeter is thinner; length alone does not decide area.

options.text: It cannot be determined from the given information
options.diagnosis: Both areas can be computed directly: 12 cm2 and 15 cm2.

question.explanation: P: 6 x 2 = 12 cm2. Q: 5 x 3 = 15 cm2. Same perimeter (16 cm), different areas - the squarer the rectangle, the more area a fixed boundary encloses. Perimeter does not control area.

micros.title: Choosing Perimeter or Area in Word Problems
micros.description: Solve fencing, framing, tiling and painting problems by first deciding which measure the situation needs - boundary length (perimeter) or covered surface (area) - including cost calculations.
outcomes: Can classify a real problem as a perimeter or an area problem before computing
Can solve cost problems like fencing at Rs per metre or tiling at Rs per square metre

question.prompt: A square park has side 50 m. How much wire is needed to fence it once all around?

options.diagnosis: Computed the area 50 x 50; fencing follows the boundary, which is the perimeter.
Added only two sides (50 + 50); the fence must run along all four.
Used a single side; the fence goes all the way around.

question.explanation: Fencing runs along the boundary, so we need the perimeter: 4 x 50 = 200 m. The area (2,500 m2) tells how much ground the park covers - useful for laying grass, irrelevant for fencing.

nodes.title: Data Handling: Tally Marks, Pictographs, Bar Graphs
nodes.description: Data becomes useful when organised: you will record data with tally marks, and read and draw pictographs and bar graphs — including ones where a symbol or one unit of height stands for many items. Reading scales correctly is the key skill; it protects you from misleading graphs forever after.
learning_outcomes: Can record raw data in a frequency table using tally marks (bundles of five)
Can read and draw a pictograph where one symbol represents multiple units, including half symbols
Can read and draw a bar graph, choosing and using a sensible scale
Can answer comparison questions ('how many more…?') from a graph, applying the scale correctly

misconceptions.description: Miscounts tally bundles — treats the five-bar gate 卌 as 4 (or some other number of) strokes.
misconceptions.signal: Counts 卌 卌 || as 10 or 14 instead of 12.
misconceptions.remedy: Rebuild the convention physically: make four vertical strokes, then the diagonal 'gate' is the FIFTH. Practise skip-counting completed bundles by 5 before adding the loose strokes.

misconceptions.description: Ignores the scale of a bar graph, reading bar heights as raw counts (or comparing bars by grid squares only).
misconceptions.signal: Says 'this bar is 2 more' when it is 2 UNITS higher and each unit is 5, so the true gap is 10.
misconceptions.remedy: Always convert units to values at the axis before comparing: write the value at the top of each bar first. Show the same data drawn at two scales to prove the bars' look depends on scale.

misconceptions.description: Reads each pictograph symbol as one item even when the key says otherwise — counting a half symbol as one more whole item, or dropping it.
misconceptions.signal: Answers '3' or '4' for a row of 3½ symbols with key '1 symbol = 10 fans'.
misconceptions.remedy: Ritualise 'key first': circle the key before reading any row. Practise with keys of 2, 5, 10 and rows containing half symbols so multiplying by the key becomes automatic.

misconceptions.description: Answers 'how many more' questions by naming the bigger category or restating one value instead of finding the difference.
misconceptions.signal: Q: 'How many more students chose cricket than football?' A: 'Cricket' or the cricket total.
misconceptions.remedy: Model comparison as subtraction with the bars themselves: cover the common height of the two bars and count only the part that sticks out.

real_world_hooks: Class survey: favourite IPL team or favourite fruit, recorded live in tallies
Runs scored per over shown as a bar graph on TV — reading the scale
Vehicle count outside school for a traffic-safety project
Rainfall by month in your city as a pictograph
teaching.video_search: data handling tally marks pictograph bar graph scale class 6

questions.prompt: A tally record shows 卌 卌 || (two full bundles and two single strokes). What count does it represent?

options.diagnosis: Counted one bundle as 5 plus the 2 singles but overlooked the second bundle.
Treated each five-bar bundle as worth 10 instead of 5: 10 + 10 + 2 = 22.

questions.explanation: Each full five-bar gate 卌 is 5 (four strokes plus the crossing fifth). So 5 + 5 + 2 = 12. Counting a bundle as 4 gives 10; treating each bundle as 10 gives 22 — both come from misreading the convention.

questions.prompt: In a pictograph, one fan symbol = 10 fans sold. Monday's row shows 3 full symbols and 1 half symbol. How many fans were sold on Monday?

options.diagnosis: Applied the key to full symbols but dropped the half symbol (worth 5).
Multiplied by 100 instead of 10 — scale slip.

questions.explanation: Key first: each symbol is 10 fans, so a half symbol is 5. Total = 3 × 10 + 5 = 35 fans. Counting symbols without the key ('about 4') answers a different, useless question.

questions.prompt: On a bar graph, 1 unit of height = 5 students. Cricket's bar is 6 units tall and football's bar is 4 units tall. How many MORE students chose cricket than football?

options.diagnosis: Added the two values (30 + 20) instead of subtracting.

questions.explanation: Convert with the scale first: cricket = 6 × 5 = 30, football = 4 × 5 = 20. Difference = 30 − 20 = 10 students. Answering '2' compares grid units and forgets each unit is worth 5; '30' merely restates cricket's total.

micros.title: Collecting and Organising Data
micros.description: Gather raw data from a survey, and organise it into a frequency table so questions like 'which is most common?' can be answered at a glance.
outcomes: Can record survey responses and organise raw data into a frequency table
Can answer simple most/least/how-many questions from an organised table

micros.title: Recording with Tally Marks
micros.description: Use tally marks in bundles of five - four strokes and a fifth diagonal across - to record counts quickly and read them back by counting bundles, not strokes.
outcomes: Can record counts in five-bar tally bundles
Can read a tally accurately as 5 per full bundle plus leftover singles

question.prompt: A tally shows two full five-bar bundles and 3 single strokes. What count does it represent?

options.diagnosis: Counted each bundle as 4 strokes (4 + 4 + 3); the diagonal fifth stroke is part of the bundle.
Counted only the full bundles and ignored the 3 single strokes.
Counted the singles as a third full bundle of five.

question.explanation: Each full five-bar gate is 5 (four uprights plus the diagonal): 5 + 5 = 10, then add the 3 singles: 10 + 3 = 13.

micros.title: Reading and Drawing Pictographs
micros.description: Interpret and draw pictographs where one symbol stands for a scaled quantity given by the key, handling half-symbols as half the key value.
outcomes: Can read a pictograph by multiplying symbol count by the key value, including half symbols
Can choose a sensible key and draw a pictograph for given data

question.prompt: In a pictograph, one book symbol = 10 books. A row shows 3 full symbols and 1 half symbol. How many books is that?

options.diagnosis: Counted symbols as items (3 full + 1 half rounded to 4), ignoring the key of 10 per symbol.
Used the key for full symbols but dropped the half symbol worth 5.
Treated the half symbol as a full one; a half symbol means half the key value.

question.explanation: Each full symbol is 10 books and the half symbol is 5: 3 x 10 + 5 = 35 books. Always read the key first - symbols are counters of the key value, not of single items.

micros.title: Reading Bar Graphs with a Scale
micros.description: Read bar graphs whose axis uses a scale (1 unit = 10, 20, 100...), converting bar heights into actual values before answering any question.
outcomes: Can convert bar heights to values using the stated scale
Can answer comparison and total questions from a scaled bar graph

question.prompt: A bar graph uses the scale 1 unit = 20 students. The bar for Class 6 is 6 units tall. How many students does it show?

options.diagnosis: Read the bar height as the raw count, ignoring the scale.
Added the scale to the height (6 + 20) instead of multiplying.
Used a scale of 10 per unit instead of the stated 20.

question.explanation: Each unit of height stands for 20 students, so 6 units represent 6 x 20 = 120 students. The first step in reading any bar graph is to check the scale.

micros.title: Drawing Bar Graphs
micros.description: Draw bar graphs from frequency tables: choose an appropriate scale, keep bar widths and gaps equal, and label axes and title.
outcomes: Can choose a scale that fits the data on the grid
Can draw a correctly labelled bar graph with uniform bars and gaps

micros.title: Answering Comparison Questions from Graphs
micros.description: Answer 'how many more', 'how many fewer' and 'total' questions from bar graphs and pictographs by computing differences and sums of the actual values - not just naming the bigger category.
outcomes: Can answer how-many-more questions by subtracting the two values
Can combine values from a graph to answer total and two-step questions

question.prompt: A bar graph shows 40 students chose cricket and 25 chose football. HOW MANY MORE students chose cricket than football?

options.diagnosis: Named the bigger category; 'how many more' asks for the difference as a number.
Restated the larger value instead of subtracting the smaller from it.
Added the two values; the question asks for the difference, not the total.

question.explanation: 'How many more' means find the difference: 40 - 25 = 15. Fifteen more students chose cricket than football. Naming the winning category answers 'which is more', a different question.

nodes.title: Integers: Multiplication, Division and Properties
nodes.description: Building on integer addition and subtraction, you will multiply and divide integers, master the sign rules (and why they work), and use properties like distributivity with negative numbers. These rules power all of algebra — every bracket you expand later depends on them.
learning_outcomes: Can multiply integers with any combination of signs and justify the sign of the product
Can divide integers and connect division to multiplication facts
Can apply commutativity, associativity and distributivity with negative numbers
Can solve multi-step problems mixing all four operations with integers

misconceptions.description: Believes negative × negative = negative ('two bad things stay bad').
misconceptions.remedy: Use the pattern approach: 3×(−6)=−18, 2×(−6)=−12, 1×(−6)=−6, 0×(−6)=0 … each step ADDS 6, so (−1)×(−6) must be +6. Also frame as reversing a reversal: the opposite of −6, taken 4 times.

misconceptions.description: Over-applies 'minus and minus make plus' to ADDITION: (−3) + (−5) = +8.
misconceptions.signal: Turns sums of two negatives positive, citing the multiplication rule.
misconceptions.remedy: Separate the contexts explicitly: the two-negatives rule belongs to multiplication/division only. Re-anchor addition in debts: owing ₹3 and owing ₹5 more is owing ₹8, never gaining.

misconceptions.description: Distributes a minus sign to only the first term: −(3 + 4) = −3 + 4.
misconceptions.signal: Bracket expansions where only the first term changes sign.
misconceptions.remedy: Read −(3+4) as (−1) × (3+4) and distribute the −1 to BOTH terms; check numerically: −(7) must equal −3 − 4 = −7, not +1.

misconceptions.description: Drops the sign in division (or applies sign rules inconsistently there): (−36) ÷ 4 = 9.
misconceptions.signal: Correct magnitudes but random or missing signs in quotients.
misconceptions.remedy: Convert every division to its multiplication check: (−36) ÷ 4 = q means q × 4 = −36, forcing q = −9. Same sign rules govern both operations.

real_world_hooks: Quiz scoring: +5 per correct answer, −2 per wrong answer — final scores
A water tank draining 3 litres per minute: level change after 8 minutes as (−3) × 8
Temperature dropping 2°C per hour through the night
Rewinding a video at 2× speed: reversing a reversal as negative × negative
teaching.video_search: multiplying dividing integers sign rules why negative times negative is positive class 7

questions.prompt: Compute: (−4) × (−6)

options.diagnosis: Added the magnitudes and kept a negative sign — treated × as +.
Added the magnitudes and applied the sign rule — right rule, wrong operation.

questions.explanation: Negative × negative = positive, so (−4) × (−6) = +24. One way to see it: (−4) × (−6) is the opposite of 4 × (−6) = −24, and the opposite of −24 is 24.

questions.prompt: Compute: (−36) ÷ 4

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 4 from 36 instead of dividing.
Multiplied instead of dividing.

questions.explanation: Check by multiplication: what times 4 gives −36? Since (−9) × 4 = −36, the quotient is −9. Unlike signs (negative ÷ positive) always give a negative result.

questions.prompt: In a quiz, each correct answer scores +5 and each wrong answer scores −2. Rahul got 6 answers correct and 7 wrong. What is his total score?

options.diagnosis: Assigned the negative to the correct answers instead of the wrong ones.
Counted only the correct answers; ignored the penalty entirely.

questions.explanation: Score = 6 × 5 + 7 × (−2) = 30 + (−14) = 16. Treating the penalty as +2 gives 30 + 14 = 44 — dropping the sign changes a penalty into a reward.

micros.title: Warm-up: Adding and Subtracting Integers
micros.description: Revise integer addition and subtraction with the number line and debt model, firmly separating them from the multiplication sign rules to come.
outcomes: Can add and subtract any two integers fluently
Can explain why (−3) + (−5) = −8 using the debt model

question.prompt: Compute: (−3) + (−5)

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the magnitudes (5 − 3) and kept a minus sign.
Subtracted the magnitudes and dropped the sign entirely.

question.explanation: Owing ₹3 and then owing ₹5 more means owing ₹8: (−3) + (−5) = −8. 'Minus and minus make plus' belongs to MULTIPLICATION, not addition — two debts never add up to a gain.

micros.title: Multiplying a Positive by a Negative
micros.description: Build 4 × (−3) as repeated addition of debts, and (−3) × 4 via commutativity, establishing that unlike signs give a negative product.
outcomes: Can compute products of one positive and one negative integer
Can justify the negative sign using repeated addition or a real context

micros.title: Why Negative × Negative Is Positive
micros.description: Use the descending pattern 3×(−6), 2×(−6), 1×(−6), 0×(−6), ... to force (−1)×(−6) = +6, and frame negative × negative as reversing a reversal.
outcomes: Can multiply two negative integers correctly
Can justify the sign of the product with the pattern argument

question.prompt: Compute: (−7) × (−3)

options.diagnosis: Added the magnitudes and kept a minus — treated × as +.
Added the magnitudes, then applied the sign rule — right rule, wrong operation.

question.explanation: Negative × negative = positive: (−7) × (−3) is the opposite of 7 × (−3) = −21, so it is +21. The pattern 3×(−3)=−9, 2×(−3)=−6, 1×(−3)=−3, 0×(−3)=0 keeps adding 3, so negative multipliers must continue into positives.

micros.title: Dividing Integers with Sign Rules
micros.description: Connect every division to its multiplication check — (−36) ÷ 4 = q means q × 4 = −36 — so the same sign rules govern quotients.
outcomes: Can divide integers with any combination of signs
Can verify a quotient's sign via the multiplication check

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 6 from 48 instead of dividing, and kept a minus.
Multiplied instead of dividing.

question.explanation: Check by multiplication: what times (−6) gives −48? Since 8 × (−6) = −48, the quotient is +8. Like signs (negative ÷ negative) always give a positive result — the same rule as multiplication.

micros.title: Properties of Operations and Opening Brackets
micros.description: Use commutativity, associativity and distributivity with negatives, reading −(a + b) as (−1) × (a + b) so the minus reaches EVERY term inside.
outcomes: Can use distributivity to simplify computations like (−4) × 103
Can expand −(a + b) correctly to −a − b and check numerically

question.prompt: Simplify: −(9 + 4)

options.diagnosis: Dropped the leading minus after adding.
Changed only the second term's sign, computing 9 − 4.

question.explanation: Read −(9 + 4) as (−1) × (9 + 4) and distribute to BOTH terms: −9 − 4 = −13. Check directly: the bracket is 13, and the opposite of 13 is −13 — so −5 (minus reaching only the 9) cannot be right.

micros.title: Multi-step Problems with All Four Operations
micros.description: Solve real contexts — quiz scoring, draining tanks, falling temperatures — that mix addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of integers.
outcomes: Can translate a signed real-world situation into an integer expression
Can evaluate multi-step integer expressions respecting order of operations

question.prompt: At 10 pm the temperature is 4°C and it falls 2°C every hour. What is the temperature 6 hours later?

options.diagnosis: Computed the total drop 6 × (−2) but forgot the starting 4°C.
Subtracted the 6 hours instead of the 12-degree total drop.

question.explanation: Final = 4 + 6 × (−2) = 4 − 12 = −8°C. Dropping the sign turns the fall into a rise and gives 4 + 12 = 16°C — a warm night instead of a freezing one.

nodes.title: Fractions and Decimals: Multiplication and Division
nodes.description: You will multiply and divide fractions and decimals, understand 'of' as multiplication, and see why dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal. Along the way you will confront a big surprise: multiplying can make numbers smaller, and dividing can make them bigger.
learning_outcomes: Can multiply fractions (including mixed numbers) and interpret 'of' as multiplication
Can divide by a fraction using the reciprocal, and explain why the method works
Can multiply and divide decimals, placing the decimal point by counting decimal places
Can predict whether a product/quotient will be bigger or smaller than the starting number

misconceptions.description: When dividing fractions, inverts the wrong fraction (or both), e.g. 3/4 ÷ 1/2 computed as 4/3 × 1/2.
misconceptions.signal: Sometimes right, sometimes wrong on division — the flip lands on a random fraction.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor the rule in meaning: a ÷ (1/2) asks 'how many halves fit in a?' — so the DIVISOR is what gets inverted (keep–change–flip, in that fixed order). Verify each answer by multiplying back.

misconceptions.description: Believes multiplication always makes numbers bigger and division always makes them smaller.
misconceptions.signal: Rejects 8 × 1/2 = 4 as impossible; picks the larger option by instinct on any multiplication.
misconceptions.remedy: Use 'of' language with areas: 1/2 of 8 is visibly 4. Build a prediction table: multiplying by more than 1 grows, by exactly 1 keeps, by less than 1 shrinks — then test with a calculator.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies fractions by cross-multiplying or by first finding common denominators (mixing up the addition procedure).
misconceptions.signal: Computes 2/3 × 4/5 as 10/12, or converts to fifteenths before multiplying.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two procedures side by side on the same pair of fractions, with an area-model picture for multiplication (a 2/3-by-4/5 shaded rectangle has area 8/15) so 'tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms' has an image behind it.

misconceptions.description: Places the decimal point in a product by vertical alignment (as in addition): 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.6.
misconceptions.signal: Products of two decimals keep one decimal place; the student never counts places.
misconceptions.remedy: Route through fractions: 0.3 × 0.2 = 3/10 × 2/10 = 6/100 = 0.06. Then formalise: the product has as many decimal places as the two factors COMBINED. Estimation check: 0.3 × 0.2 must be less than 0.3.

real_world_hooks: Half of three-quarters of a pizza: 'of' as multiplication
How many 0.5 L bottles can you fill from a 3.75 L can?
Petrol at ₹104.50 per litre: cost of 2.4 litres
Scaling a recipe down to 2/3 for fewer guests
teaching.video_search: multiplying dividing fractions reciprocal decimal multiplication class 7

questions.prompt: Compute: 2/3 × 4/5

options.diagnosis: Added the fractions (10/15 + 12/15) instead of multiplying.
Added numerators and added denominators — neither multiplication nor correct addition.

questions.explanation: Multiply straight across: (2 × 4)/(3 × 5) = 8/15. Cross-multiplying (giving 10/12) belongs to comparing fractions, not multiplying them. Note 8/15 is smaller than both factors' larger one — taking 2/3 OF something shrinks it.

questions.prompt: Compute: 0.3 × 0.2

options.diagnosis: Added the decimals instead of multiplying.
Multiplied 3 × 2 and ignored both decimal points.

questions.explanation: 3 × 2 = 6, and the factors have 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places between them, so the product has two: 0.06. Fraction check: 3/10 × 2/10 = 6/100. Sense check: 0.3 of 0.2 must be SMALLER than 0.2 — so 0.6 cannot be right.

questions.prompt: A jug holds 3/4 litre of juice. How many half-litre glasses' worth of juice is that — that is, what is 3/4 ÷ 1/2?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 1/2 instead of dividing — forgot to invert the divisor.
Inverted BOTH fractions before multiplying.

questions.explanation: Keep–change–flip: 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 3/4 × 2/1 = 6/4 = 3/2 = 1½. Meaning: one full half-litre glass fits in 3/4 L, with 1/4 L left — exactly half of another glass. Notice the quotient is BIGGER than 3/4: dividing by a number less than 1 enlarges.

micros.title: 'Of' Means Multiply: Fraction of a Quantity
micros.description: Interpret 3/4 of 20 as 3/4 × 20 with pictures and sharing, meeting the first surprise: taking a fraction OF something makes it smaller.
outcomes: Can find a fraction of a whole-number quantity
Can explain why multiplying by a fraction less than 1 shrinks the result

micros.title: Multiplying Fractions with the Area Model
micros.description: Multiply fractions 'tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms', backed by the shaded-rectangle area model so the rule has an image behind it.
outcomes: Can multiply two fractions and simplify the product
Can draw an area model showing why 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15

question.prompt: Compute: 3/5 × 2/7

options.diagnosis: Added the fractions (21/35 + 10/35) instead of multiplying.
Added numerators and added denominators — a rule that fits neither operation.

question.explanation: Multiply straight across: (3 × 2)/(5 × 7) = 6/35. Cross-multiplying (3 × 7 over 5 × 2 = 21/10) belongs to comparing fractions, not multiplying — and 21/10 is bigger than 1, impossible for a product of two fractions below 1.

micros.title: Multiplying Mixed Numbers
micros.description: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying, and see with numbers why multiplying whole and fraction parts separately undercounts.
outcomes: Can multiply mixed numbers via improper fractions
Can estimate the product first to catch conversion errors

micros.title: Dividing by a Fraction: Keep–Change–Flip and Why
micros.description: Anchor a ÷ (1/2) in 'how many halves fit in a?', then formalise: keep the dividend, change ÷ to ×, flip the DIVISOR — and verify by multiplying back.
outcomes: Can divide fractions by inverting the divisor only
Can explain the reciprocal rule with a fitting-in picture and check answers by multiplication

question.prompt: Compute: 5/6 ÷ 2/3

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 2/3 without flipping anything.
Inverted BOTH fractions before multiplying.

question.explanation: Keep–change–flip: 5/6 ÷ 2/3 = 5/6 × 3/2 = 15/12 = 5/4. Only the DIVISOR is inverted. Check: 5/4 × 2/3 = 10/12 = 5/6 ✓. Flipping the dividend instead gives 6/5 × 2/3 = 4/5, which fails the check.

micros.title: Multiplying Decimals: Counting Decimal Places
micros.description: Route decimal products through fractions (0.3 × 0.2 = 3/10 × 2/10 = 6/100), then formalise: the product carries as many decimal places as both factors combined.
outcomes: Can multiply decimals and place the point by counting places
Can catch place-value errors with an estimation check

question.prompt: Compute: 0.4 × 0.6

options.diagnosis: Multiplied 4 × 6 and ignored both decimal points.
Added the decimals instead of multiplying.

question.explanation: 4 × 6 = 24, and the factors have 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places between them, so the product has two: 0.24. Fraction check: 4/10 × 6/10 = 24/100. Sense check: 0.4 of 0.6 must be SMALLER than 0.6, ruling out 2.4.

micros.title: Dividing Decimals
micros.description: Divide decimals by whole numbers, then by decimals by scaling both numbers by the same power of 10 until the divisor is whole.
outcomes: Can divide a decimal by a whole number keeping the point aligned
Can divide by a decimal by shifting both points equally (3.6 ÷ 0.4 = 36 ÷ 4)

micros.title: Will the Answer Be Bigger or Smaller?
micros.description: Build the prediction habit: multiplying by a number less than 1 shrinks, dividing by a number less than 1 enlarges — overturning the primary-school instinct.
outcomes: Can predict whether a product or quotient exceeds the starting number before computing
Can state the boundary role of 1 in both operations

question.prompt: WITHOUT computing exactly, which expression has a value GREATER than 60?

options.diagnosis: Multiplying by a number below 1 shrinks: this is 45.
Dividing by a number above 1 shrinks: this is 50.

question.explanation: Dividing by 0.9 asks how many 0.9s fit in 60 — more than 60 of them (≈66.7). Multiplying by 0.9 takes nine-tenths OF 60, which is less (54). The instinct 'multiplication enlarges, division shrinks' only holds for numbers greater than 1.

nodes.title: Rational Numbers: Representation and Comparison
nodes.description: Rational numbers are all numbers expressible as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0 — uniting integers, fractions and their negatives into one family. You will write rationals in standard form, place them on the number line, compare them, and find rationals between any two given ones.
learning_outcomes: Can write a rational number in standard form (positive denominator, lowest terms)
Can place positive and negative rationals on the number line
Can compare and order rational numbers, including negatives
Can find rational numbers between two given rational numbers

misconceptions.description: Orders negative rationals by magnitude: −3/4 > −1/2 'because 3/4 > 1/2'.
misconceptions.signal: Ranks negative fractions in the same order as their positive counterparts.
misconceptions.remedy: Plot both on a number line: −3/4 sits further LEFT than −1/2, so it is smaller. Rehearse the reflection principle: comparing negatives reverses the comparison of their positives.

misconceptions.description: Believes there are no (or only finitely many) rational numbers between two given rationals.
misconceptions.signal: Says 'nothing lies between 1/3 and 1/2' or counts a fixed handful.
misconceptions.remedy: Average the two numbers to exhibit one in between, then average again — the process never ends. Rewrite with bigger denominators (1/3 = 10/30, 1/2 = 15/30) to make room visibly.

misconceptions.description: Thinks integers (and terminating decimals) are not rational numbers.
misconceptions.signal: Sorts 5 or −3 outside the 'rational' circle in a classification task.
misconceptions.remedy: Write each as p/q: 5 = 5/1, −3 = −3/1, 0.7 = 7/10. Draw the nested-sets diagram: integers sit inside the rationals.

misconceptions.description: Treats −5/8, 5/−8 and −(5/8) as three different numbers, or misplaces the sign in standard form.
misconceptions.signal: Cannot decide whether 12/−18 is positive or negative; leaves negative denominators in answers.
misconceptions.remedy: Establish that one negative sign anywhere makes the whole number negative, and standard form parks the sign in the numerator; verify equivalence by dividing on a calculator.

real_world_hooks: Temperatures between −1°C and 0°C on a winter night in the hills
Profit/loss per share on the stock ticker: −2.5, +0.75
Sea level as 0: heights and depths as positive and negative rationals
Zooming into a digital measuring scale: always more marks between marks
teaching.video_search: rational numbers standard form number line comparison class 7

questions.prompt: Write 12/−18 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: Moved the sign correctly but only divided by 2; standard form needs lowest terms.
Inverted the fraction while simplifying.

questions.explanation: One negative sign makes the number negative: 12/−18 = −12/18. Divide top and bottom by HCF 6: −2/3. Standard form = negative sign (if any) on top, denominator positive, lowest terms. Note −6/9 is the same VALUE as −2/3 — but the question asks for standard form, so the answer is matched by the exact form written: it must be in lowest terms.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the GREATEST: −1/2, −3/4, −7/8, −1?

options.diagnosis: Partial ordering: beat some options but still compared magnitudes the wrong way round.

questions.explanation: All four are negative, so the one CLOSEST to zero is greatest. On the number line from left to right: −1, −7/8, −3/4, −1/2. Hence −1/2 is greatest — for negatives, bigger magnitude means smaller number.

questions.prompt: Which rational number lies between 1/3 and 1/2?

options.text: There is no rational number between them

options.diagnosis: 2/6 equals 1/3 itself — equivalent fractions overlooked; 'between' must be strictly between.
Arithmetic slip while averaging: 7/12 is bigger than 1/2 = 6/12, so it lies outside the interval.

questions.explanation: Convert to twelfths: 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/2 = 6/12, so 5/12 sits strictly between. (It is exactly their average.) Between ANY two distinct rationals there are infinitely many more — just keep averaging.

micros.title: What Counts as a Rational Number
micros.description: Define rationals as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0, and show integers and terminating decimals joining the family via 5 = 5/1 and 0.7 = 7/10.
outcomes: Can decide whether a given number is rational and write it as p/q
Can draw the nested-sets picture: integers inside rationals

question.prompt: Which statement about the number 5 is true?

options.text: It is a rational number, because 5 = 5/1
It is not rational, because it is not written as a fraction
It is an integer, so it cannot also be rational
It is rational only when written as 5.0
options.diagnosis: How a number is WRITTEN doesn't change what it is; 5, 5.0 and 5/1 are the same number.

question.explanation: A rational number is any number expressible as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0. Since 5 = 5/1, it qualifies. Every integer is rational — the integers sit INSIDE the rational family, they are not excluded from it.

micros.title: Standard Form: Where the Sign Lives
micros.description: Establish that −5/8, 5/−8 and −(5/8) are one number, and write rationals in standard form: sign in the numerator, positive denominator, lowest terms.
outcomes: Can rewrite any rational with a positive denominator in lowest terms
Can recognise equivalent forms of the same negative rational

question.prompt: Write −8/−12 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: Left a negative denominator and stopped short of lowest terms.
Inverted the fraction while simplifying.

question.explanation: Two negative signs cancel: −8/−12 = 8/12. Divide top and bottom by the HCF 4: 2/3. The number is POSITIVE — a negative over a negative is like (−8) ÷ (−12), and like signs give a positive quotient.

micros.title: Rationals on the Number Line
micros.description: Place positive and negative rationals by subdividing the gaps between integers, locating numbers like −3/4 between −1 and 0.
outcomes: Can plot any rational number by subdividing unit intervals
Can read off the rational represented by a marked point

micros.title: Comparing and Ordering Rationals
micros.description: Compare rationals via common denominators and the number line, mastering the reflection principle: comparing negatives reverses the comparison of their positives.
outcomes: Can order a mixed list of positive and negative rationals
Can explain why −3/4 < −1/2 although 3/4 > 1/2

question.prompt: Which number is SMALLER: −2/3 or −1/3?

options.diagnosis: Different numerators over the same denominator are different numbers.
Every pair of rationals can be compared — the number line orders them all.

question.explanation: On the number line −2/3 sits further LEFT than −1/3, so it is smaller. For negatives, bigger magnitude means a smaller number — the comparison of 2/3 > 1/3 gets REVERSED by the minus signs.

micros.title: Finding Rationals Between Rationals
micros.description: Use averaging and denominator enlargement (1/3 = 10/30, 1/2 = 15/30) to exhibit rationals between any two given ones — and see the supply never ends.
outcomes: Can find several rationals between two given rationals
Can argue that infinitely many rationals lie between any two distinct rationals

question.prompt: How many rational numbers lie between 1/4 and 1/2?

options.text: None — they are next to each other
Only the ones with denominator up to 8
options.diagnosis: Denominators can be as large as you like — 9/32, 100/399, ... keep appearing forever.

question.explanation: The average 3/8 lies between them; then the average of 1/4 and 3/8 lies between THOSE; and so on without end. Rewriting as 8/32 and 16/32 already shows seven thirty-secondths strictly between — and finer denominators reveal ever more.

nodes.title: Comparing Quantities: Percentage, Profit and Loss, Simple Interest
nodes.description: Percentages turn every comparison into 'per hundred', making unlike things comparable. You will convert between fractions, decimals and percents, compute percentage increase/decrease, profit and loss on cost price, and simple interest. These are the most-used school mathematics in adult life.
learning_outcomes: Can convert fluently between fractions, decimals and percentages
Can find a percentage of a quantity and express one quantity as a percentage of another
Can compute profit/loss and profit/loss percent on the cost price
Can compute simple interest with SI = P × R × T / 100 and find the amount

misconceptions.description: Compares or adds percentages of DIFFERENT bases as if they were plain numbers ('10% of my money plus 10% of yours = 20%').
misconceptions.signal: Claims a 50% score in one test and 50% in another 'add to 100%', or that 20% off a cheap item beats 10% off an expensive one automatically.
misconceptions.remedy: Force the base into every statement: '20% OF WHAT?' Compute rupee values side by side (20% of ₹100 = ₹20 vs 10% of ₹500 = ₹50) until percent-without-base sounds incomplete.

misconceptions.description: Computes profit percent on the selling price instead of the cost price.
misconceptions.remedy: Fix the reference: profit percent answers 'how much did the money INVESTED grow?' — the base is what you paid. Label CP explicitly as the base in every problem before computing.

misconceptions.description: Treats the percent number as a rupee/quantity answer (25% of 200 is '25'), or drops the /100 in formulas.
misconceptions.signal: Answers with the rate itself; simple-interest answers off by a factor of 100.
misconceptions.remedy: Translate percent to a fraction EVERY time before computing: 25% = 25/100 = 1/4, so 25% of 200 = 200/4 = 50. Keep units attached: percent is a rate, rupees are money.

misconceptions.description: Believes an x% increase followed by an x% decrease returns to the original value.
misconceptions.signal: Says a price raised 10% then cut 10% is unchanged.
misconceptions.remedy: Compute a concrete case: ₹100 → ₹110 → ₹99. Discuss why: the 10% cut acts on a BIGGER base than the 10% rise did. This previews successive-change problems in Class 8.

real_world_hooks: Sale season: '25% OFF' tags and comparing final UPI amounts across shops
A shopkeeper buys at wholesale (CP) and sells at retail (SP) — profit percent
Bank FD or post-office savings: simple interest on a deposit
Exam scores: 18/25 vs 68/100 — which is better?
teaching.video_search: percentage profit loss simple interest word problems class 7

questions.prompt: Find 25% of 200.

options.diagnosis: Divided 200 by 25 instead of taking 25 hundredths of it.
Subtracted 25 from 200 — treated the percent as a rupee amount to remove.

questions.explanation: 25% means 25/100 = 1/4. One quarter of 200 is 50. The rate '25' is not itself the answer — it must act on the base 200.

questions.prompt: A trader buys a bag for ₹400 (CP) and sells it for ₹500 (SP). What is the profit percent?

options.diagnosis: Reported the rupee profit (₹100) with a percent sign attached.
Computed SP as a percent of CP but forgot to subtract the original 100%.

questions.explanation: Profit = 500 − 400 = ₹100. Profit% = profit/CP × 100 = 100/400 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by SP gives 20% — but the base for profit percent is always the cost price, the money originally put in.

questions.prompt: Meera deposits ₹5,000 at 8% per annum simple interest. How much interest does she earn in 2 years?

options.diagnosis: Computed one year's interest; forgot to multiply by the time (2 years).
Reported the total amount (principal + interest) instead of the interest alone.

questions.explanation: SI = P × R × T / 100 = 5000 × 8 × 2 / 100 = ₹800. The amount she would hold at the end is 5000 + 800 = ₹5,800, but the question asks only for the interest earned.

micros.title: Fractions, Decimals and Percents: One Family
micros.description: Convert fluently between the three notations — 3/5 = 0.6 = 60% — reading percent as 'per hundred' throughout.
outcomes: Can convert any of fraction, decimal, percent into the other two
Can recall benchmark equivalents (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 1/10)

micros.title: Finding a Percent of a Quantity
micros.description: Compute p% of a quantity by translating the percent into a fraction EVERY time: 15% of 400 = 15/100 × 400 — the rate must act on the base.
outcomes: Can find a given percent of a quantity
Can keep the rate (%) and the result (units) clearly separate

question.prompt: Find 15% of 400.

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 15 from 400 — treated the percent as an amount to remove.

question.explanation: 15% = 15/100, so 15% of 400 = (15 × 400)/100 = 60. Answering '15' repeats the rate without applying it; 6000 comes from 15 × 400 with the /100 dropped — off by exactly a factor of 100.

micros.title: Expressing One Quantity as a Percent of Another
micros.description: Turn part/whole comparisons into percents to compare unlike bases fairly — 18 out of 25 versus 68 out of 100 — always asking 'percent OF WHAT?'.
outcomes: Can express one quantity as a percentage of another
Can compare quantities with different bases by converting both to percents

question.prompt: Ria scored 18 out of 25 in one test; Sam scored 68 out of 100 in another. Who did better?

options.text: Sam — 68 marks is more than 18 marks

options.diagnosis: 72% ≠ 68%; equal raw gaps do not mean equal shares of different totals.

options.text: Scores from different tests can never be compared
options.diagnosis: That is exactly what percentages are FOR — converting to the common base 100.

question.explanation: Convert both to the base 100: 18/25 = 72/100 = 72%, while Sam has 68%. Comparing the raw marks 68 vs 18 ignores that the totals differ — percent-of-different-bases must be converted before comparing.

micros.title: Percentage Increase and Decrease
micros.description: Compute percent change on the ORIGINAL value, and discover with ₹100 → ₹110 → ₹99 why an x% rise followed by an x% cut does not return home.
outcomes: Can compute percentage increase or decrease of a quantity
Can explain why successive +10% and −10% changes do not cancel

question.prompt: A price of ₹200 is raised by 10%, and the new price is then reduced by 10%. What is the final price?

options.diagnosis: Applied only the increase and stopped.
Took both 10% amounts from the ORIGINAL ₹200; the cut acts on ₹220.

question.explanation: ₹200 + 10% = ₹220; then ₹220 − 10% of 220 = 220 − 22 = ₹198. The rise and cut use DIFFERENT bases (200, then 220), so they cannot cancel — you end ₹2 below the start.

micros.title: Profit and Loss Percent on the Cost Price
micros.description: Compute profit or loss in rupees and as a percent whose base is always the COST price — the money originally invested.
outcomes: Can compute profit/loss and profit/loss percent from CP and SP
Can find SP given CP and a profit percent (and vice versa in simple cases)

question.prompt: A shopkeeper buys a lamp for ₹250 (CP) and sells it for ₹300 (SP). What is the profit percent?

options.diagnosis: Reported the rupee profit (₹50) with a percent sign attached.
Computed SP as a percent of CP but forgot to subtract the original 100%.

question.explanation: Profit = 300 − 250 = ₹50. Profit% = 50/250 × 100 = 20%. Dividing by the selling price (50/300 ≈ 16.7%) uses the wrong base — profit percent measures how much the money INVESTED grew, so the base is CP.

micros.title: Simple Interest and the Amount
micros.description: Use SI = P × R × T / 100 for deposits and loans, keeping interest and the final amount (principal + interest) clearly distinct.
outcomes: Can compute simple interest given principal, rate and time
Can find the amount and solve for one missing quantity in the formula

nodes.title: Exponents and Powers: Laws and Standard Form
nodes.description: Exponents compress repeated multiplication: 10⁵ instead of 10×10×10×10×10. You will evaluate powers, use the laws of exponents (product, quotient, power of a power), and write large numbers in standard form. Exponents are the language of both astronomy and algebra.
learning_outcomes: Can evaluate powers with whole-number exponents, including powers of negative bases
Can apply a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n) and (a^m)^n = a^(mn) with justification
Can use a⁰ = 1 (a ≠ 0) and explain it via the quotient pattern
Can express large numbers in standard form k × 10^n with 1 ≤ k < 10

misconceptions.description: Multiplies exponents when multiplying same-base powers: a^m × a^n = a^(mn).
misconceptions.signal: Writes 3⁴ × 3² = 3⁸.
misconceptions.remedy: Expand once fully: (3·3·3·3) × (3·3) is six 3s multiplied, so 3⁶. Derive each law from expansion at least once before allowing shortcut use.

misconceptions.description: Reads a power as base × exponent: 2³ = 6.
misconceptions.signal: Small powers systematically wrong: 2³=6, 5²=10.
misconceptions.remedy: Verbalise '2 used as a factor 3 times' and contrast the pair 2³ = 8 vs 2×3 = 6 explicitly; drill with cases where the two differ dramatically (10² vs 10×2).

misconceptions.description: Thinks a⁰ = 0 (or a⁰ = a).
misconceptions.signal: Writes 7⁰ = 0.
misconceptions.remedy: Walk down the ladder: 7³=343, 7²=49, 7¹=7 — each step divides by 7, so 7⁰ = 7/7 = 1. Also via the quotient law: 7² ÷ 7² = 7⁰ and any number divided by itself is 1.

misconceptions.description: In standard form, counts only the zeros (or the digits) to pick the power of 10.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 384,000 = 3.84 × 10³ 'because there are three zeros'.
misconceptions.remedy: Teach the decimal-shift method: count how many places the decimal point moves from after the leading digit to the end — for 384,000 it is 5 moves, so 10⁵. Verify by multiplying back.

real_world_hooks: Distance from Earth to Sun ≈ 1.5 × 10⁸ km — why scientists refuse to write all the zeros
Viral forwarding: one WhatsApp message forwarded to 3 people, each forwards to 3 more — powers of 3
Folding a paper in half repeatedly: thickness doubles as 2ⁿ
India's population written in standard form
teaching.video_search: laws of exponents standard form large numbers class 7

questions.prompt: What is 2³?

options.diagnosis: Swapped base and exponent: computed 3².
Added base and exponent.

questions.explanation: 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 — the base 2 used as a factor three times. It is NOT 2 × 3; that confusion gives 6.

questions.prompt: Simplify: 3⁴ × 3²

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the bases as well; with the same base, the base stays put.

questions.explanation: 3⁴ × 3² = (3·3·3·3) × (3·3) = six 3s multiplied = 3⁶. When multiplying powers of the SAME base, add the exponents (4 + 2 = 6); the base does not change.

questions.prompt: Write 384,000 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: Equal in value, but standard form requires the first factor to be at least 1 and less than 10.
Off by one: counted all six digits instead of the five decimal shifts.

questions.explanation: Place the decimal after the leading digit: 3.84. The point moves 5 places to restore 384,000, so the power is 10⁵: 384,000 = 3.84 × 10⁵. Counting only the three zeros undercounts the shifts. Note 38.4 × 10⁴ has exactly the same VALUE — but the question asks for standard form, so the answer is matched by the exact form written: the first factor must be at least 1 and less than 10.

questions.prompt: Why does 5⁰ equal 1 (and not 0)?

options.text: The quotient law gives 5³ ÷ 5³ = 5⁰, and any nonzero number divided by itself is 1
An exponent of 0 means there are no fives at all, and having nothing means the value is 0
It doesn't — 5⁰ equals 5, because raising to the power 0 leaves the base unchanged
Because 5⁰ means 5 multiplied by 0, which should give 0, so mathematicians just define it as 1

questions.explanation: Walk down the power ladder: 5³ = 125, 5² = 25, 5¹ = 5 — each step down divides by 5, so the next step is 5⁰ = 5 ÷ 5 = 1. Equivalently, the quotient law says 5³ ÷ 5³ = 5³⁻³ = 5⁰, and 125/125 = 1. The exponent counts factors, it is not a multiplier: 5⁰ is an EMPTY product, and an empty product is 1 (the multiplicative identity), not 0.

micros.title: Reading and Writing Powers
micros.description: Read a^n as 'a used as a factor n times', evaluating small powers and contrasting 2³ = 8 with 2 × 3 = 6 until the two never blur.
outcomes: Can evaluate powers with whole-number bases and exponents
Can express a repeated product in exponential form and identify base and exponent

question.prompt: What is 3⁴?

options.diagnosis: Swapped base and exponent: computed 4³.
Added base and exponent.

question.explanation: 3⁴ means 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81 — the base 3 used as a factor four times. It is NOT 3 × 4 = 12; compare 10² = 100 with 10 × 2 = 20 to feel how different the two are.

micros.title: Powers of Negative Bases
micros.description: Track the sign of (−a)^n through the sign rules: even exponents give positive results, odd exponents keep the minus — and (−2)⁴ differs from −2⁴.
outcomes: Can evaluate powers of negative integers
Can predict the sign of (−a)^n from the parity of n

micros.title: Product Law: Add the Exponents
micros.description: Derive a^m × a^n = a^(m+n) by expanding both powers into factors at least once, so the shortcut is earned rather than memorised.
outcomes: Can simplify products of same-base powers by adding exponents
Can justify the law by expansion and spot when it does NOT apply (different bases)

question.prompt: Simplify: 5³ × 5⁴

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the bases as well; with the same base, the base stays put.

question.explanation: 5³ × 5⁴ = (5·5·5) × (5·5·5·5) = seven 5s multiplied = 5⁷. Multiplying same-base powers ADDS the exponents (3 + 4 = 7); multiplying them (3 × 4 = 12) counts factors that are not there.

micros.title: Quotient Law and Why a⁰ = 1
micros.description: Derive a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n) by cancelling factors, then walk the ladder 7³, 7², 7¹, 7⁰ — each step divides by 7 — to land on a⁰ = 1.
outcomes: Can simplify quotients of same-base powers by subtracting exponents
Can explain via the ladder or quotient law why a⁰ = 1 for a ≠ 0

question.prompt: What is 9⁰?

options.diagnosis: Glued the digits together — the exponent is not a digit to append.

question.explanation: Walk down: 9² = 81, 9¹ = 9, and each step divides by 9 — so 9⁰ = 9/9 = 1. Or use the quotient law: 9² ÷ 9² = 9⁰, and any number divided by itself is 1.

micros.title: Power of a Power and Power of a Product
micros.description: Establish (a^m)^n = a^(mn) and (ab)^m = a^m b^m by expansion, completing the toolkit of exponent laws.
outcomes: Can simplify expressions like (2³)² and (3 × 5)²
Can choose the correct law when several could apply

micros.title: Standard Form for Large Numbers
micros.description: Write large numbers as k × 10^n with 1 ≤ k < 10, choosing the power by counting DECIMAL SHIFTS from after the leading digit — not by counting zeros.
outcomes: Can express large numbers in standard form and convert back
Can compare magnitudes of numbers given in standard form

question.prompt: Write 5,600,000 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: Equal in value, but standard form needs the first factor at least 1 and less than 10.
Off by one: counted all seven digits instead of the six decimal shifts.

question.explanation: Place the point after the leading digit: 5.6. The point must move 6 places to restore 5,600,000, so the power is 10⁶. Counting only the five zeros undercounts — the 6 after the 5 also gets crossed by the moving point.

nodes.title: Simple Equations: Solving One-variable Linear Equations
nodes.description: An equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. You will solve equations like 5x − 3 = 12 by systematic inverse operations (or transposition done with understanding), check solutions by substitution, and translate word problems into equations.
learning_outcomes: Can maintain balance: perform the same operation on both sides of an equation
Can solve one- and two-step linear equations in one variable, including with integer solutions
Can verify a solution by substituting it back into the original equation
Can set up and solve an equation from a word problem

misconceptions.description: Transposes terms without changing the operation/sign: from x + 7 = 15 gets x = 15 + 7.
misconceptions.signal: Moves numbers across '=' unchanged; answers consistently overshoot or undershoot.
misconceptions.remedy: Re-derive transposition from balance moves: subtract 7 from BOTH sides and watch the +7 'become' −7 on the other side. Ban blind rule-use until the student can narrate the both-sides version.

misconceptions.description: Applies an operation to only one side (or only one term) of the equation.
misconceptions.signal: From x/3 = 4 writes x = 4 (multiplied the left by 3 only), or halves a single term.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a physical or drawn pan balance: removing weight from one pan visibly tilts it. Insist on writing the operation on both sides on separate lines before simplifying.

misconceptions.description: Thinks '=' means 'the answer is', so the number on the right IS x, and an equation is an instruction to compute left-to-right.
misconceptions.signal: For x + 5 = 12 answers x = 12; resists equations written as 12 = x + 5.
misconceptions.remedy: Present equations in varied formats (12 = x + 5, x + 5 = 3 + 9) and use the balance metaphor: '=' states that two expressions weigh the same, it does not announce a result.

misconceptions.description: Does not check solutions; accepts any computed number even when substitution fails.
misconceptions.signal: Submits x = 9/5 for 5x − 3 = 12 without noticing 5(9/5) − 3 = 6 ≠ 12.
misconceptions.remedy: Make substitution the mandatory last step with a written ✓/✗; celebrate catches — a failed check is information, pointing back to the exact wrong move.

real_world_hooks: A pan balance with hidden-mass bags: physically solving 2x + 1 = 7
Mobile recharge puzzle: after spending ₹37 you have ₹63 — what did you start with?
Auto fare: total ₹85 at ₹25 base plus ₹12/km — how far did you ride?
'Think of a number' magic tricks reversed step by step
teaching.video_search: solving simple linear equations balance method transposition class 7

questions.prompt: Solve: x + 7 = 15

options.diagnosis: Echoed the other visible number; no solving move was made.

questions.explanation: Subtract 7 from both sides: x + 7 − 7 = 15 − 7, so x = 8. Check: 8 + 7 = 15 ✓. Moving the 7 across without flipping to subtraction gives 22 — and 22 + 7 is 29, not 15, so the check catches it.

questions.prompt: Solve: 5x − 3 = 12

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 5 in the last step instead of dividing — inverted the inverse operation.
Divided 15 by 3 (the wrong number) — coefficient and constant swapped roles.

questions.explanation: Add 3 to both sides: 5x = 15. Divide both sides by 5: x = 3. Check: 5(3) − 3 = 12 ✓. Transposing −3 without flipping gives 5x = 9, x = 1.8, and the check fails: 5(1.8) − 3 = 6 ≠ 12.

questions.prompt: The sum of three consecutive whole numbers is 63. What is the SMALLEST of them?

options.diagnosis: Solved 3x = 63 directly, forgetting the +1 and +2 — that gives the middle number, not the smallest.
Found the largest of the three numbers; misread which one was asked.
Stopped at 3x = 60 without dividing by 3.

questions.explanation: Let the numbers be x, x+1, x+2. Then 3x + 3 = 63, so 3x = 60 and x = 20. The numbers are 20, 21, 22 (sum 63 ✓); the smallest is 20. Note 21 is the middle number — the mean — not the smallest.

micros.title: What an Equation Says
micros.description: Read '=' as 'both sides weigh the same' — a statement, not an instruction to compute — using equations written in every orientation, including 12 = x + 5.
outcomes: Can state what an equation claims and identify its two sides
Can decide whether a given value makes an equation true or false

question.prompt: What does the equation 12 = x + 5 tell us?

options.text: That x + 5 and 12 are the same value — so x must be 7
That x is 12, since 12 is the answer written first
That the equation is written backwards and has no solution

options.diagnosis: Added 5 to 12 instead of asking what plus 5 gives 12.

question.explanation: '=' declares that the two sides balance; it does not announce a result. 12 = x + 5 and x + 5 = 12 say exactly the same thing, and the value keeping the balance is x = 7 (since 7 + 5 = 12).

micros.title: The Balance Model: Same Move on Both Sides
micros.description: Use a pan balance (drawn or physical) to see that adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing must hit BOTH sides, or the equation tips into falsehood.
outcomes: Can perform the same operation on both sides and keep the equation true
Can spot and explain the error when an operation touches only one side

question.prompt: To solve x/4 = 3, which move is correct?

options.text: Multiply BOTH sides by 4, giving x = 12
Multiply only the left side by 4, giving x = 3
Divide both sides by 4, giving x = 3/4
options.diagnosis: Chose the SAME operation instead of the inverse — dividing again buries x deeper.

options.text: Subtract 4 from both sides, giving x = −1
options.diagnosis: Treated the ÷4 as a +4; the inverse of dividing is multiplying.

question.explanation: x is divided by 4, so undo it by multiplying — but on BOTH sides: x/4 × 4 = 3 × 4 gives x = 12. Check: 12/4 = 3 ✓. Multiplying one side only changes what the equation says and breaks the balance.

micros.title: Solving by Inverse Operations
micros.description: Solve one- and two-step equations like 3x + 4 = 19 by peeling operations off in reverse order, deriving 'transposition' honestly from both-sides moves.
outcomes: Can solve two-step linear equations including negative solutions
Can narrate each transposition as its underlying both-sides operation

question.prompt: Solve: 3x + 4 = 19

options.diagnosis: Reached 3x = 15 but then multiplied by 3 instead of dividing.
Stopped at 3x = 15 and reported it as x.

question.explanation: Subtract 4 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3: x = 5. Check: 3(5) + 4 = 19 ✓. Moving the +4 across WITHOUT flipping it to −4 gives 3x = 23 and the wrong x = 23/3 — the check exposes it.

micros.title: Check Your Solution by Substitution
micros.description: Make substitution the mandatory last step of every solve: put the value back into the ORIGINAL equation and record a ✓ or ✗ — a failed check locates the wrong move.
outcomes: Can verify a proposed solution by substituting into the original equation
Can use a failed check to hunt down the erroneous step

question.prompt: A student claims x = 4 solves 5x − 3 = 12. Is the claim right?

options.text: No — substituting gives 5(4) − 3 = 17 ≠ 12; the real solution is x = 3
Yes — the working looked correct, so there is no need to check
No — because 5(4) = 9, so the left side is 6
options.diagnosis: Added 5 and 4 instead of multiplying; the check itself must be computed correctly.

options.text: It cannot be judged without re-solving the whole equation
options.diagnosis: Substitution alone settles it — that is the power of checking.

question.explanation: Substitute: 5(4) − 3 = 20 − 3 = 17, not 12, so x = 4 fails. Solving properly: 5x = 15, x = 3, and 5(3) − 3 = 12 ✓. A ten-second substitution catches errors that neat-looking working hides.

micros.title: First Steps with the Variable on Both Sides
micros.description: Solve equations like 5x = 2x + 9 by collecting the variable terms on one side with balance moves — a gentle preview of the Class 8 staple.
outcomes: Can solve simple equations with the variable appearing on both sides
Can decide which side to collect variable terms on and why

micros.title: From Words to Equations
micros.description: Translate word problems — fares, recharges, consecutive numbers — into equations: name the unknown, encode the relationships, solve, and answer the question actually asked.
outcomes: Can set up a linear equation from a word problem
Can solve it and interpret the solution back in context

question.prompt: When 7 is added to twice a number, the result is 25. What is the number?

options.diagnosis: Stopped at 2x = 18 without dividing by 2.
Divided 25 by 2 before subtracting the 7 — inverse operations applied in the wrong order.

question.explanation: The equation is 2x + 7 = 25. Subtract 7: 2x = 18; divide by 2: x = 9. Check: 2(9) + 7 = 25 ✓. Transposing +7 without flipping gives 2x = 32 and x = 16 — but 2(16) + 7 = 39, so the check rejects it.

nodes.title: Algebraic Expressions: Terms, Like Terms, Evaluation
nodes.description: You will take expressions apart into terms, factors and coefficients, combine like terms, add and subtract whole expressions, and evaluate them for given values — including negative ones. Fluency here is what makes equation-solving and identities feel easy next year.
learning_outcomes: Can identify terms, factors, coefficients, and classify monomials/binomials/trinomials
Can identify like terms and combine them correctly
Can add and subtract algebraic expressions, distributing the minus sign over every term
Can evaluate expressions at given values, including negative values

misconceptions.description: Combines unlike terms: 2a + 4b = 6ab, or x + x² = x³.
misconceptions.signal: Any sum collapses to a single term; variables get glued together.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the fruit-crate test carefully re-worded numerically: substitute a = 2, b = 3 and compare 2a + 4b = 16 with 6ab = 36. Sort terms into like-term bins by their exact variable part before adding.

misconceptions.description: When subtracting an expression, applies the minus sign only to the first term: (4a+3b) − (2a−b) = 4a + 3b − 2a − b.
misconceptions.signal: Sign of the second and later terms of the subtracted bracket left unchanged.
misconceptions.remedy: Rewrite subtraction as adding (−1) × (bracket) and distribute the −1 to EVERY term, drawing arrows to each one. Check with numbers afterwards.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles squares of negative values: (−2)² computed as −4.
misconceptions.signal: Evaluation errors whenever the substituted value is negative; confuses (−2)² with −2².
misconceptions.remedy: Bracket discipline: substitute with brackets ALWAYS — (−2)² = (−2)(−2) = 4. Contrast (−2)² and −(2²) explicitly as different expressions.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a lone variable has coefficient 0 (or that −x has coefficient 1).
misconceptions.signal: Says the coefficient of x in x + 5 is 0 'because nothing is written'.
misconceptions.remedy: Rewrite invisibly-coefficient terms explicitly: x = 1·x, −x = (−1)·x, then combine like terms with the coefficients visible.

real_world_hooks: Canteen orders: 3 samosas + 2 teas can't merge into '5 samosa-teas' — like terms only
Perimeter expressions for garden plots with unknown sides
Total marks formula across tests with different weightings
Simplifying a shopping bill written with x kg onions and y kg tomatoes
teaching.video_search: algebraic expressions like terms adding subtracting evaluating class 7

questions.prompt: Simplify: 5x + 3x

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the variables while adding coefficients; adding like terms never changes the power.
Multiplied the coefficients instead of adding them.
Dropped the variable; 5x + 3x means 5 x's plus 3 x's, which is 8 x's.

questions.explanation: 5x and 3x are like terms (same variable part x), so add the coefficients: (5 + 3)x = 8x. Think '5 mangoes + 3 mangoes = 8 mangoes' — the unit x stays as it is.

questions.prompt: Simplify: (4a + 3b) − (2a − b)

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the first expression from the second — order of subtraction reversed.

questions.explanation: Distribute the minus over BOTH terms of the second bracket: 4a + 3b − 2a + b. Combine like terms: (4a − 2a) + (3b + b) = 2a + 4b. Forgetting to flip −b to +b gives 2a + 2b — the classic slip.

questions.prompt: Evaluate 3x² + 2x when x = −2.

options.diagnosis: Dropped the sign in 2x: computed 12 + 4 instead of 12 − 4.
Computed (−2)² as −4 AND dropped the sign in 2x: −12 + 4 = −8 — two slips chained.

questions.explanation: Substitute with brackets: 3(−2)² + 2(−2) = 3(4) + (−4) = 12 − 4 = 8. The trap is (−2)²: squaring a negative gives POSITIVE 4. Writing −2² without brackets is how the −16 and −8 answers arise.

questions.prompt: A student claims that 2a + 3b simplifies to 5ab. What is the best way to test this claim, and what does the test show?

options.text: Substitute values such as a = 2, b = 3: then 2a + 3b = 13 but 5ab = 30, so unlike terms cannot be combined
No test is needed — the claim is correct, since 2 + 3 = 5 and the letters a and b join together to make ab
