options.diagnosis: Over-shifted: added three decimal places instead of two.

questions.explanation: (0.4)² = 0.4 × 0.4. Digits: 4 × 4 = 16; decimal places: 1 + 1 = 2, giving 0.16. Sense check: 0.4 is less than 1, so its square must be smaller than 0.4 — which rules out both 1.6 and 0.8.

questions.prompt: What is √(9 + 16)?

options.diagnosis: Added correctly but forgot to take the square root at all.

questions.explanation: Add first, THEN take the root: √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. The tempting shortcut √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7 is wrong — the square root does not distribute over addition. (This is the same trap as (a+b)² ≠ a² + b².)

nodes.title: Cubes and Cube Roots
nodes.description: Cubing a number multiplies it by itself three times — the volume of a cube of that side. You will recognise perfect cubes, use prime factorisation (triples of factors) to find cube roots, and exploit unit-digit patterns for quick mental roots. Unlike squares, cubes of negatives stay negative.
learning_outcomes: Can compute cubes and recognise perfect cubes up to 1000 (and 12³ = 1728)
Can find cube roots by grouping prime factors into triples
Can use unit-digit patterns to find cube roots of perfect cubes mentally
Can explain why cubes of negative numbers are negative, unlike squares

misconceptions.description: Treats cubing as multiplying by 3: 4³ = 12.
misconceptions.signal: Cube answers that are exactly 3× the base.
misconceptions.remedy: Build 4³ from unit cubes (or draw layers): a 4×4×4 block holds 64 cubes, not 12. Keep 'times 3' and 'to the power 3' as a contrasted pair: 4×3 = 12 vs 4³ = 64.

misconceptions.description: Believes the cube of a negative number is positive (over-extending the even-power rule).
misconceptions.signal: Writes (−5)³ = 125.
misconceptions.remedy: Track the signs one product at a time: (−5)(−5) = +25, then (+25)(−5) = −125. Generalise: an ODD count of negative factors leaves a negative product.

misconceptions.description: Finds cube roots by dividing by 3 (or halving), treating the root as inverse of multiplication.
misconceptions.remedy: Emphasise root-as-inverse-of-POWER: ask 'what number, multiplied by itself three times, gives 1728?' and verify candidate answers by cubing them, not by any division.

misconceptions.description: Assumes patterns for squares transfer to cubes (e.g. that cubes cannot end in 2, 3, 7, 8).
misconceptions.signal: Rejects 1728 as a perfect cube 'because it ends in 8'.
misconceptions.remedy: Cube the digits 0–9 and observe: EVERY digit 0–9 appears as a cube's unit digit (8³=512, 3³=27...). This contrast with squares also gives the handy unit-digit map for mental cube roots (2↔8, 3↔7).

real_world_hooks: Rubik's cube: 3×3×3 = 27 cubies
Water tank volumes: a cubical tank of side 2 m holds 8 m³
The Hardy–Ramanujan taxicab number 1729 = 12³ + 1 = 10³ + 9³
Storage boxes: how many 1-cm dice fit in a 5-cm cube?
teaching.video_search: cubes cube roots prime factorisation unit digit trick class 8

questions.prompt: What is 4³?

options.diagnosis: Squared instead of cubing — stopped one multiplication early.
Went one multiplication too far: that is 4⁴.

questions.explanation: 4³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 — picture a 4×4×4 stack of unit cubes. Multiplying by the exponent (4 × 3 = 12) is the classic trap.

questions.prompt: Find ∛1728.

options.diagnosis: Halved the number — treating the cube root as division by 2.
Close-recall slip: 13³ = 2197, not 1728. Verify by cubing.

questions.explanation: 1728 = 2⁶ × 3³ = (2² × 3)³, so ∛1728 = 2² × 3 = 12. Check: 12³ = 12 × 12 × 12 = 144 × 12 = 1728 ✓. Dividing 1728 by 3 gives 576 — but roots undo POWERS, not multiplication.

questions.prompt: What is (−5)³?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 3 AND lost the sign — two slips stacked.

questions.explanation: (−5)³ = (−5)(−5)(−5) = (+25)(−5) = −125. Three negative factors — an odd count — leave the product negative. Compare (−5)² = +25: only EVEN powers wipe out the sign.

nodes.title: Comparing Quantities: Discounts, Compound Interest
nodes.description: Real prices move in chains: marked price → discount → sales tax/GST → final bill, and savings grow by compound interest, where each year's interest itself earns interest. You will compute successive percentage changes correctly by multiplying growth factors — the single most useful trick in consumer maths.
learning_outcomes: Can compute discount, sale price, and tax/GST on a purchase
Can handle successive percentage changes by multiplying factors (×0.9, ×1.18, …)
Can compute compound interest annually (and half-yearly) using A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ
Can explain why compound interest exceeds simple interest after the first period

misconceptions.description: Adds successive percentages: a 10% discount followed by 20% is treated as 30% off.
misconceptions.signal: Combines percentage changes by addition regardless of order or base.
misconceptions.remedy: Convert each change to a multiplying factor and compose: ×0.9 then ×0.8 is ×0.72 — a 28% total drop, not 30%. Compute one concrete bill both ways and compare with the till receipt.

misconceptions.description: Computes compound interest as simple interest — interest on the original principal every year.
misconceptions.signal: CI answers equal P×R×T/100; no growth in the yearly interest amounts.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a year-by-year table: year 2's interest is computed on the NEW balance (principal + year-1 interest). Watching the interest column grow (800, 880, 968…) makes compounding concrete.

misconceptions.description: Believes an x% increase then x% decrease (or vice versa) restores the original value.
misconceptions.signal: Says a stock that fell 50% needs only a 50% rise to recover.
misconceptions.remedy: Test with ₹100: −50% → ₹50, then +50% → ₹75. The second change acts on a DIFFERENT base. Generalise via factors: 0.5 × 1.5 = 0.75 ≠ 1.

misconceptions.description: Confuses which price the discount acts on — applies discount percent to cost price or to the sale price instead of the marked price.
misconceptions.signal: Sets up discount = % of SP, or mixes MP, CP and SP freely.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the price pipeline: MP —discount→ SP —(compare with CP)→ profit. Label every rupee amount in a problem as MP, SP or CP before touching percentages.

real_world_hooks: Festival-sale stacking: '20% off + extra 10% off' — why it isn't 30%
GST at 18% on a restaurant bill after the discount
Fixed deposit vs simple-interest loan from a relative: comparing growth
Population growth of a town at 5% per year — same maths as compound interest
teaching.video_search: successive discounts compound interest formula class 8

questions.prompt: A kurta is marked ₹500 and the shop offers 20% discount. What is the sale price?

options.diagnosis: Computed the discount amount but forgot to subtract it from the marked price.
Treated 20% as ₹20 — subtracted the rate itself instead of 20/100 of the price.
Added the 20% instead of subtracting — direction of a discount reversed.

questions.explanation: Discount = 20% of 500 = ₹100. Sale price = 500 − 100 = ₹400. (Or in one step: 500 × 0.8 = 400.) The discount amount and the price you pay are different answers to different questions.

questions.prompt: A jacket marked ₹800 gets successive discounts of 25% and then 10%. What is the final price?

options.diagnosis: Applied only the 25% discount; the second discount was dropped.
Applied only the 10% discount; the first discount was dropped.

questions.explanation: Multiply the factors: 800 × 0.75 = 600, then 600 × 0.90 = ₹540. Adding the discounts (35% off → ₹520) overstates the saving, because the 10% acts on the already-reduced ₹600, not on ₹800.

questions.prompt: Find the compound interest on ₹8,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years, compounded annually.

options.diagnosis: Reported the final amount A, not the interest A − P.
Computed only the first year's interest.

questions.explanation: A = 8000 × (1.1)² = 8000 × 1.21 = ₹9,680, so CI = 9680 − 8000 = ₹1,680. Simple interest would give 8000×10×2/100 = ₹1,600 — the extra ₹80 is year-2 interest earned ON year-1's ₹800 interest. That is compounding.

nodes.title: Exponents and Powers: Negative Exponents, Scientific Notation
nodes.description: Negative exponents extend the power ladder below 1: 10⁻³ means 1/10³, letting scientific notation describe the very small (a bacterium's width) as easily as the very large. You will apply all the exponent laws with integer exponents and convert numbers to and from standard form in both directions.
learning_outcomes: Can evaluate powers with negative integer exponents via a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ
Can apply the laws of exponents across integer exponents, including a⁰ = 1
Can write very small numbers in standard form k × 10⁻ⁿ and convert back
Can compare magnitudes expressed in scientific notation

misconceptions.description: Thinks a negative exponent makes the VALUE negative: 2⁻³ = −8.
misconceptions.signal: Treats the minus in the exponent as the sign of the answer.
misconceptions.remedy: Walk the ladder downward: 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4 — each step divides by 2 and the values stay POSITIVE, just small. Negative exponent = reciprocal, not negative number.

misconceptions.description: Divides exponents when dividing powers: a⁸ ÷ a² = a⁴.
misconceptions.signal: Quotient-law answers with divided instead of subtracted exponents.
misconceptions.remedy: Expand once: (a·a·a·a·a·a·a·a)/(a·a) cancels two factors leaving six, so a⁶ — the exponents SUBTRACT. Derive, then drill the law with cases where subtracting and dividing differ.

misconceptions.description: Gets the sign of the exponent wrong in standard form: writes small numbers with positive powers (0.00052 = 5.2 × 10⁴).
misconceptions.signal: Standard-form conversions of decimals below 1 carry positive exponents, or vice versa.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor the rule in size: numbers ≥ 1 need positive powers, numbers between 0 and 1 need negative powers. Always multiply back to check: 5.2 × 10⁴ = 52,000, clearly not 0.00052.

misconceptions.description: Counts decimal shifts off by one when converting to scientific notation (counting zeros instead of shifts).
misconceptions.signal: Answers like 5.2 × 10⁻⁵ for 0.00052; consistently one power out.
misconceptions.remedy: Standardise the procedure: move the point until exactly one nonzero digit is left of it, COUNTING each hop. For 0.00052 the point hops 4 places right, so 10⁻⁴. Verify by shifting back.

real_world_hooks: Size of a red blood cell (≈ 7 × 10⁻⁶ m) vs distance to the Moon (≈ 3.84 × 10⁸ m)
Mobile data units: 1 KB, 1 MB, 1 GB as powers of 10 (and of 2)
A virus vs a cricket ball: how many powers of ten apart?
Interest rates and probabilities written as 10⁻² scale numbers
teaching.video_search: negative exponents scientific notation standard form small numbers class 8

questions.prompt: What is 2⁻³?

options.diagnosis: Computed 1/(2×3) — multiplied base by exponent instead of raising to the power.

questions.explanation: A negative exponent means reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8. The result is a small POSITIVE number — the minus sign moves the power downstairs; it never makes the value negative.

questions.prompt: Simplify: 5⁸ ÷ 5²

options.diagnosis: Divided the bases (5 ÷ 5 = 1) as well as handling exponents — the base stays 5.
Added the exponents — that is the rule for MULTIPLYING powers, not dividing.

questions.explanation: Dividing same-base powers subtracts exponents: 5⁸ ÷ 5² = 5⁸⁻² = 5⁶. Expanding shows why: eight 5s over two 5s cancels to six 5s. Dividing the exponents (8 ÷ 2 = 4) is the classic wrong move.

questions.prompt: Write 0.00052 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: Equal in value but not standard form — the leading factor must be at least 1 and less than 10.

questions.explanation: Move the decimal point 4 places right to get 5.2, so 0.00052 = 5.2 × 10⁻⁴. The exponent is negative because the number is less than 1, and it is 4 (not 5) because the point hops four places. Check: 5.2 ÷ 10⁴ = 0.00052 ✓. Note 52 × 10⁻⁵ has exactly the same VALUE — but the question asks for standard form, so the answer is matched by the exact form written: the leading factor must be at least 1 and less than 10.

questions.prompt: Continue the pattern 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1. What must 2⁻¹ be, and why?

options.text: 1/2 — each step down the ladder divides the value by 2, so the pattern forces 2⁻¹ = 1 ÷ 2
−2 — the minus sign in the exponent carries over and makes the value of the power negative
−1/2 — you take the reciprocal of the base and then attach the minus sign from the exponent
0 — the values 8, 4, 2, 1 keep shrinking, so the ladder must finally bottom out at zero here
options.diagnosis: Sees the shrinking but not its mechanism: each step HALVES the value, and repeatedly halving a positive number never reaches 0.

questions.explanation: Going down one rung of the ladder always divides by the base: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, each time ÷ 2. So the next rung is 2⁻¹ = 1 ÷ 2 = 1/2, and then 2⁻² = 1/4. A negative exponent means RECIPROCAL (a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ), not a negative value — every power of a positive base stays positive, just smaller and smaller.

nodes.title: Direct and Inverse Proportion
nodes.description: Two quantities are in direct proportion when their RATIO stays constant (double one, double the other) and in inverse proportion when their PRODUCT stays constant (double one, halve the other). The crucial skill is deciding which model — if either — fits a situation before computing.
learning_outcomes: Can test whether tabled data shows direct proportion (y/x constant) or inverse proportion (xy constant)
Can solve direct-proportion problems via the constant ratio or unitary method
Can solve inverse-proportion problems (workers–days, speed–time) via the constant product
Can identify situations that are NEITHER kind of proportion (e.g. age vs height)

misconceptions.description: Applies direct proportion everywhere, including to inverse situations: 'more workers, so multiply the days up'.
misconceptions.signal: Worker/speed problems answered with the quantities scaling the same way; more workers 'take longer'.
misconceptions.remedy: Install a direction check before any computation: 'if this goes UP, does that go UP or DOWN?' Sketch the situation (more taps filling a tank faster) and only then pick the model.

misconceptions.description: Handles inverse proportion additively: 2 more workers means 2 fewer days.
misconceptions.signal: Answers offset by a fixed difference rather than scaled by a factor.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the constant-product frame explicitly: total work = workers × days stays FIXED (6 × 12 = 72 worker-days), so 8 workers need 72 ÷ 8 = 9 days, not 10. Tabulate several (workers, days) pairs and watch the product.

misconceptions.description: Treats direct proportion as an additive relationship: y = x + k instead of y = kx.
misconceptions.signal: Extends tables by adding the same gap (4→12 becomes 10→18 'because +8').
misconceptions.remedy: Test the additive rule at zero: 0 cups of rice would still 'serve 8 people' under +8 — absurd. Check y/x down a real table to reveal the multiplicative constant.

misconceptions.description: In inverse proportion, keeps the RATIO constant instead of the product.
misconceptions.signal: Sets up y₁/x₁ = y₂/x₂ for speed–time problems.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two set-ups on the same problem and check which answer respects reality (faster speed must give LESS time). Memorise the pairings: direct ↔ equal ratios; inverse ↔ equal products.

real_world_hooks: Petrol and distance: double the fuel, double the kilometres (direct)
Workers building a wall, or pipes filling a tank (inverse)
Speed vs journey time to school (inverse)
Recipe quantities per guest (direct) — and why cooking TIME is not proportional to guests
teaching.video_search: direct and inverse proportion word problems class 8

questions.prompt: x and y are in DIRECT proportion, and when x = 4, y = 12. What is y when x = 10?

options.diagnosis: Applied the inverse-proportion model (constant product xy = 48) to a direct-proportion situation: 48 ÷ 10 = 4.8.
Multiplied 10 × 12 without using the given pair — no proportional set-up at all.

questions.explanation: Direct proportion keeps y/x constant: y/x = 12/4 = 3, so y = 3 × 10 = 30. The answer 18 comes from the additive pattern '+8', which fails the ratio test (18/10 ≠ 3); 4.8 keeps the product constant, which is the INVERSE model.

questions.prompt: 6 workers can finish a job in 12 days. How long will 8 workers take, working at the same rate?

options.diagnosis: Adjusted in the wrong direction — ADDED days when more workers must reduce them.

questions.explanation: Total work = 6 × 12 = 72 worker-days (constant product). With 8 workers: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 days. Direct-proportion setup gives 16 days — but more workers taking LONGER fails the common-sense direction check.

questions.prompt: A car covers a fixed route in 3 hours at 60 km/h. How long does the same route take at 90 km/h?

options.diagnosis: Assumed 1.5× speed simply halves the time; the factor is 60/90 = 2/3, not 1/2.

questions.explanation: The distance is fixed: 60 × 3 = 180 km. At 90 km/h, time = 180 ÷ 90 = 2 hours. Speed and time are inversely proportional (constant product 180), so time scales by 60/90 = 2/3: 3 × 2/3 = 2 h.

nodes.title: Playing with Numbers: General Form and Divisibility
nodes.description: Writing a two-digit number as 10a + b turns number tricks into algebra: you can PROVE why ab + ba is always divisible by 11, justify the divisibility tests for 3 and 9, and crack letter-for-digit puzzles. This chapter is a first taste of proof through generalisation.
learning_outcomes: Can express 2- and 3-digit numbers in general form (10a + b, 100a + 10b + c)
Can prove simple facts like 11 | (ab + ba) and 9 | (abc − cba variants) using the general form
Can justify the divisibility tests for 2, 3, 5, 9 and 10 from place value
Can solve letter-digit (cryptarithm) puzzles using digit constraints

misconceptions.description: Reads the two-digit numeral 'ab' as the product a × b instead of 10a + b.
misconceptions.signal: Substitutes ab = 6 when a = 2, b = 3 (instead of 23).
misconceptions.remedy: Expand notation aloud: the NUMERAL ab means 'a tens and b ones' = 10a + b; contrast with the algebra product ab = a×b. Use an overbar or colour for numeral-form until the distinction is stable.

misconceptions.description: Checks divisibility by 3 or 9 with the last digit, or believes a 9 anywhere in the number guarantees divisibility by 9.
misconceptions.signal: Says 19 is divisible by 9 'because it ends in 9'.
misconceptions.remedy: Derive the digit-sum test from general form: 10a + b = 9a + (a + b) — the 9a part is always divisible by 9, so everything hinges on the digit SUM. Test on 19 (1+9=10, not divisible).

misconceptions.description: Believes divisibility by 3 implies divisibility by 9.
misconceptions.signal: Concludes 9 | 12 or 9 | 15 after passing the '3' test.
misconceptions.remedy: Line up counterexamples (12, 15, 21 — divisible by 3, not 9) and show the containment goes the OTHER way: every multiple of 9 is a multiple of 3, not vice versa. Venn-diagram the two sets.

misconceptions.description: In digit puzzles, forgets digit constraints: lets a letter be more than 9, ignores carries, or allows a leading digit to be 0.
misconceptions.signal: Puzzle 'solutions' with impossible digits or unverified columns.
misconceptions.remedy: Solve column by column with explicit carry bookkeeping, then ALWAYS substitute the found digits back into the original sum to verify.

real_world_hooks: Number magic tricks: 'reverse and add' party tricks explained
Why the digit-sum trick for checking bills and roll-number sums works
Cryptic puzzles and escape-room codes as cryptarithms
Bank card checksums: real systems built on divisibility
teaching.video_search: general form of numbers divisibility proofs letter digit puzzles class 8

questions.prompt: A two-digit number has tens digit a and units digit b. Its value is:

options.diagnosis: Added the digits — that gives the digit sum, not the number.
Swapped the place values: this is the number with its digits REVERSED.

questions.explanation: The tens digit contributes ten times its face value: the number is 10a + b. For a = 2, b = 3 that is 23 — while a × b = 6, a + b = 5 and 10b + a = 32, all different things.

questions.prompt: For what digit x is the number 52x3 divisible by 9?

options.diagnosis: Assumed the existing digits already worked; their sum is 10, which is not a multiple of 9.

questions.explanation: Digit sum = 5 + 2 + x + 3 = 10 + x. For divisibility by 9 the sum must be a multiple of 9, so 10 + x = 18, giving x = 8. Note x = 2 makes the sum 12 — divisible by 3 but NOT by 9.

questions.prompt: In the puzzle A + A + A = BA (a two-digit number whose units digit is again A), what digit is A?

options.diagnosis: 0+0+0 = 0 is a single digit, not a two-digit number BA — the trivial case doesn't satisfy the puzzle.

questions.explanation: We need 3A to be a two-digit number ending in A: 3 × 5 = 15 ends in 5 ✓, so A = 5 and B = 1 (5+5+5 = 15). Check the others: 3×6 = 18 ends in 8, 3×2 = 6 isn't two-digit — verifying the units-digit condition is the step most solvers skip.

nodes.title: Linear Equations in One Variable: Variables on Both Sides
nodes.description: Equations now carry the variable on BOTH sides (2x + 5 = x + 9), and may involve fractions or expressions that need simplifying first. You will reduce them systematically to x = value, and use them to crack age, number, perimeter and money problems.
learning_outcomes: Can solve linear equations with variables on both sides
Can clear fractions by multiplying EVERY term by the common denominator
Can reduce word problems (ages, numbers, money) to linear equations and solve them
Can verify solutions by substitution and interpret them in context

misconceptions.description: Transposes constants without inverting the operation: from 2x + 5 = x + 9 gets x = 9 + 5.
misconceptions.signal: Constants cross the equals sign with their signs unchanged.
misconceptions.remedy: Slow down to both-sides moves: subtract 5 from both sides and WATCH it become −5 on the right. Require the check-by-substitution step, which exposes the error immediately (14 + 5 ≠ ...).

misconceptions.description: Moves variable terms across without changing sign: 2x + 5 = x + 9 becomes 2x + x = 9 − 5.
misconceptions.signal: Variable terms collected by ADDING coefficients that should subtract.
misconceptions.remedy: Treat x-terms exactly like number terms: subtract x from both sides explicitly. Colour-code x-terms and constants and move one colour at a time, writing every intermediate line.

misconceptions.description: When clearing fractions or brackets, multiplies only the fraction term, not EVERY term.
misconceptions.signal: From x/3 + 5 = 8 writes x + 5 = 24.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the multiplication as distributing over the whole side: 3(x/3 + 5) = 3×8 forces 3×5 too. Alternatively isolate the fraction first (x/3 = 3) so only one multiplication is ever needed.

misconceptions.description: Stops mid-solution (reports 4x = 56 as the answer) or answers a different unknown than the one asked.
misconceptions.signal: Final line is not of the form x = …, or gives the mother's age when the child's was asked.
misconceptions.remedy: End every solution with two rituals: (1) reduce to x = value, (2) re-read the question and answer THAT sentence in words ('Sahil is 14').

real_world_hooks: Two mobile plans reaching equal cost: 99 + 2x = 149 + x
Age puzzles across years: 'in 5 years the sum of our ages…'
Splitting prize money in a given ratio with a fixed bonus
Balancing weights on a two-pan scale with unknown packets on both pans
teaching.video_search: linear equations variables on both sides word problems class 8

questions.prompt: Solve: 2x + 5 = x + 9

options.diagnosis: Sign flipped in the final step; substitute back to catch it: 2(−4)+5 = −3 ≠ 5.

questions.explanation: Subtract x from both sides: x + 5 = 9. Subtract 5: x = 4. Check: 2(4)+5 = 13 and 4+9 = 13 ✓. Moving 5 across unchanged gives x = 14, whose check fails (33 ≠ 23) — always substitute back.

questions.prompt: Solve: x/3 + 5 = 8

options.diagnosis: Divided by 3 at the end instead of multiplying — inverse operation inverted.

questions.explanation: Isolate the fraction: x/3 = 8 − 5 = 3. Multiply both sides by 3: x = 9. Check: 9/3 + 5 = 8 ✓. Multiplying through by 3 but forgetting the 5 gives x + 5 = 24 → 19, and stopping at x/3 = 3 gives the unfinished '3'.

questions.prompt: Sahil is x years old and his mother is 3x years old. In 5 years, the sum of their ages will be 66. How old is Sahil NOW?

options.diagnosis: Ignored the two +5s for 'in 5 years' and solved 4x = 66 directly.

questions.explanation: In 5 years: (x+5) + (3x+5) = 66, so 4x + 10 = 66, 4x = 56, x = 14. Check: ages now 14 and 42; in five years 19 + 47 = 66 ✓. Forgetting the two +5s gives 4x = 66 → 16.5; '42' answers the mother's age; '56' stops at 4x.

nodes.title: Algebraic Expressions and Identities
nodes.description: You will multiply monomials, binomials and polynomials, and meet the standard identities: (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b², (a−b)² = a²−2ab+b², and (a+b)(a−b) = a²−b². Identities are equalities true for ALL values — and they turn ugly arithmetic like 103² into two-second mental maths.
learning_outcomes: Can multiply monomials and binomials, applying exponent rules to variables
Can expand using the three standard identities and recognise when they apply
Can distinguish an identity (true for all values) from an equation (true for some)
Can use identities for fast numeric computation (103², 98², 52 × 48)

misconceptions.description: Squares a sum term by term: (a+b)² = a² + b².
misconceptions.signal: The middle term 2ab never appears; 103² computed as 100² + 3².
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the (a+b)×(a+b) area square: it visibly contains a², b² AND two ab rectangles. Numerically test a = b = 1: (1+1)² = 4 but 1² + 1² = 2. Keep the picture on the wall until 2ab is automatic.

misconceptions.description: Extends the same error to differences: (a−b)² = a² − b², or muddles the sign of the middle term.
misconceptions.signal: Expansions of (a−b)² missing +b² or with −b²; middle term sign random.
misconceptions.remedy: Expand (a−b)(a−b) longhand once, tracking each of the four products with its sign: −ab appears twice (giving −2ab) and (−b)(−b) = +b². The LAST term of a square is always positive.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies binomials by pairing only firsts and lasts: (x+2)(x+3) = x² + 6.
misconceptions.signal: Products of binomials with two terms instead of (up to) four.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the 2×2 grid (area) method so all FOUR partial products get a cell; only then compress to the shortcut. Check by substituting x = 1: (3)(4) = 12 but 1 + 6 = 7.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles variables when multiplying monomials: 3x × 4x = 12x (or 7x²).
misconceptions.signal: Coefficients handled but exponents not added, or coefficients added while variables multiplied.
misconceptions.remedy: Split every product into (numbers) × (letters): 3x·4x = (3·4)(x·x) = 12x². Multiply coefficients, ADD exponents — rehearse the two rules as separate moves.

real_world_hooks: Mental-math party trick: 103² or 98 × 102 in your head via identities
Area of a square field extended by b metres on each side — where 2ab lives
Framing a square photo: the border area IS (a+b)² − a²
Quick checks for shop bills: 52 × 48 = 50² − 2²
teaching.video_search: algebraic identities a plus b whole square expansion area model class 8

questions.prompt: Multiply: 3x × 4x²

options.diagnosis: Added the coefficients instead of multiplying them (exponents handled correctly).

questions.explanation: Group numbers and letters: (3 × 4) × (x × x²) = 12x³. Coefficients multiply (3×4 = 12); exponents of the same base ADD (1 + 2 = 3).

questions.prompt: Expand: (x + 2)(x + 3)

options.diagnosis: Dropped the constant product 2 × 3 — three of the four partial products kept.
Swapped the roles of sum and product: the x-coefficient is 2+3 and the constant is 2×3, not the other way round.

questions.explanation: Four products: x·x + x·3 + 2·x + 2·3 = x² + 3x + 2x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6. Check at x = 1: (3)(4) = 12 and 1 + 5 + 6 = 12 ✓. Multiplying only 'firsts and lasts' loses the two middle products.

questions.prompt: Use an identity to evaluate 103².

options.diagnosis: Computed a² + 2ab but dropped the final b² = 9.
Used ab instead of 2ab for the middle term — halved the cross term.

questions.explanation: 103² = (100 + 3)² = 100² + 2(100)(3) + 3² = 10000 + 600 + 9 = 10609. Leaving out the cross term 2ab (giving 10009) is exactly the (a+b)² = a² + b² fallacy — the area model shows the two missing 100×3 rectangles.

nodes.title: Factorisation of Algebraic Expressions
nodes.description: Factorisation reverses expansion: rewriting an expression as a product of factors. You will take out common factors, regroup, apply the identities backwards (a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b)), split the middle term of x² + bx + c, and divide expressions cleanly — with a spotlight on the cancellation errors everyone must unlearn.
learning_outcomes: Can factor out the greatest common monomial factor completely
Can factorise using identities, especially the difference of squares
Can factorise trinomials x² + bx + c by splitting the middle term
Can divide a polynomial by a monomial correctly, term by term

misconceptions.description: Treats a difference of squares as the square of a difference: a² − b² = (a − b)².
misconceptions.signal: Factors x² − 25 as (x − 5)².
misconceptions.remedy: Expand (x−5)² = x² − 10x + 25 and compare with x² − 25 — the middle term betrays the difference. Verify the correct factorisation numerically: at x = 6, x² − 25 = 11 = (6+5)(6−5) ✓.

misconceptions.description: Cancels single terms across addition in a fraction: (5x + 10)/5 = x + 10.
misconceptions.signal: Cancellation strikes through one term of a sum while other terms ride along untouched.
misconceptions.remedy: Factor BEFORE cancelling: (5x + 10)/5 = 5(x + 2)/5 = x + 2. Rule: only common FACTORS of the whole numerator and denominator cancel. Numeric check at x = 1: 15/5 = 3 = 1 + 2 ✓, not 11.

misconceptions.description: Factors incompletely or unevenly — divides only some terms by the common factor: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 9).
misconceptions.signal: One term inside the bracket unchanged; expansion of the answer doesn't return the original.
misconceptions.remedy: Institute the expand-back check: multiply the factored form out and compare with the original expression, every single time. Divide each term by the common factor in writing.

misconceptions.description: When splitting the middle term of x² + bx + c, hunts for numbers with sum c and product b (roles swapped).
misconceptions.signal: x² + 5x + 6 factored as (x + 1)(x + 5) or similar.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor with expansion: (x+p)(x+q) = x² + (p+q)x + pq — SUM goes with x, PRODUCT is the constant. Practise listing factor pairs of c first, then testing their sums against b.

real_world_hooks: Un-multiplying: finding the dimensions of a rectangular plot from its area expression
Simplifying a formula before coding it into a spreadsheet
Splitting a bill of (5x + 10) rupees equally among 5 friends
teaching.video_search: factorisation common factors identities splitting middle term class 8

questions.prompt: Factorise: 6x + 9

options.diagnosis: Took out 6, but 9 is not divisible by 6 — expanding gives 6x + 18, not 6x + 9.
Took x common from a term that has no x; expanding gives 15x.

questions.explanation: HCF of 6x and 9 is 3: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3). Always expand back to check: 3 × 2x + 3 × 3 = 6x + 9 ✓. In 3(2x + 9) the second term was never divided by 3.

questions.prompt: Factorise: x² − 25
questions.explanation: Difference of squares: x² − 5² = (x + 5)(x − 5). Both square options fail the expansion check — (x−5)² = x² − 10x + 25 has a middle term that x² − 25 lacks. And x(x − 25) = x² − 25x, also wrong.

questions.prompt: Simplify: (5x + 10) ÷ 5

options.diagnosis: Combined 5x and 10 into 15x first — unlike terms cannot be added.

questions.explanation: Factor first: (5x + 10)/5 = 5(x + 2)/5 = x + 2 — EVERY term gets divided by 5. Cancelling the 5 against only one term gives x + 10 or 5x + 2; test x = 1: (15)/5 = 3, and only x + 2 gives 3.

nodes.title: Introduction to Graphs: Coordinates and Linear Graphs
nodes.description: The coordinate plane turns pairs of numbers into points and relationships into pictures. You will plot points, read line graphs, and draw the graphs of simple linear relationships like y = 2x — seeing for the first time that an equation IS a line. This bridge between algebra and geometry carries all of higher mathematics.
learning_outcomes: Can plot and read points (x, y), respecting the order of coordinates
Can locate points on the axes and state where axis points belong
Can check whether a point lies on the graph of a simple equation like y = 2x
Can interpret real line graphs (distance–time, cost–quantity) including rates as steepness

misconceptions.description: Ignores coordinate order: treats (3, 5) and (5, 3) as the same point.
misconceptions.signal: Plots x along the vertical axis at random; swapped points 'look fine'.
misconceptions.remedy: Fix the convention with the corridor-then-stairs story: along the corridor (x) FIRST, then up the stairs (y). Plot both (3,5) and (5,3) on one grid to see they are genuinely different places.

misconceptions.description: Misplaces axis points: thinks (0, 4) lies on the x-axis (matching the '0' with 'x').
misconceptions.signal: Points with a zero coordinate put on the wrong axis.
misconceptions.remedy: Reason by movement, not by symbol-matching: (0, 4) means move 0 along x — you stay put — then 4 up: you land ON the y-axis. Generalise: x = 0 IS the y-axis, y = 0 is the x-axis.

misconceptions.description: Believes only the plotted/tabled points belong to a line's graph — points in between 'don't count'.
misconceptions.signal: Denies that (1.5, 3) lies on y = 2x after plotting only integer points.
misconceptions.remedy: Zoom in: check (1.5, 3) in the equation (3 = 2 × 1.5 ✓) and plot it — it lands exactly on the line. The line is the set of ALL solutions, a continuous infinity of points.

misconceptions.description: Reads graphs without attending to axis labels or scales — comparing steepness across different scales, or joining discrete data meaninglessly.
misconceptions.signal: Concludes 'faster' from a steeper look alone; connects favourite-fruit bar categories with a line.
misconceptions.remedy: Always read the axes aloud first (units and scale). Show the same data plotted at two scales, and discuss when joining points means something (continuous quantities) and when it doesn't.

real_world_hooks: Battleship-style grid games: coordinates as addresses
Distance–time graph of your school bus with its stops (flat parts!)
Cinema seat numbers row-and-seat as ordered pairs
Mobile recharge: talktime vs amount as a straight line through the origin
teaching.video_search: coordinate plane plotting points linear graphs introduction class 8

questions.prompt: Where does the point (0, −4) lie?

options.diagnosis: Any zero coordinate read as 'the origin'; the origin is only (0, 0).
Points ON an axis belong to no quadrant; movement along x is zero here.

questions.explanation: From the origin, move 0 units horizontally (stay on the vertical axis), then 4 units DOWN. The point sits on the y-axis below the origin. Every point with x-coordinate 0 lies on the y-axis.

questions.prompt: Which point lies on the graph of y = 2x?

options.diagnosis: Treated 'y = 2x' as 'y = x + 2' — added 2 instead of doubling.
Satisfies x = 2y — the relationship was inverted (halving instead of doubling).

questions.explanation: Substitute: for (3, 6), y = 2x gives 6 = 2 × 3 ✓. For (6, 3): 3 ≠ 12 — swapping coordinates breaks the equation. A point lies on a graph exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation.

questions.prompt: A distance–time graph shows a cyclist moving in a straight line from (0 h, 0 km) to (2 h, 20 km). What is the cyclist's speed?

options.diagnosis: Inverted the slope: computed hours per kilometre instead of kilometres per hour.
Multiplied distance by time instead of dividing.

questions.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time = 20 km ÷ 2 h = 10 km/h — the slope (steepness) of the line. Reading the end value 20 as the speed ignores the time axis; slope always needs BOTH axes.

nodes.title: Understanding Quadrilaterals: Polygon Angle Sums and Parallelograms
nodes.description: The interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to (n−2)×180°, while exterior angles always total 360°. You will use these facts, then dive into the parallelogram family — opposite sides and angles equal, diagonals bisecting each other — and see how rectangle, rhombus and square refine it step by step.
learning_outcomes: Can compute interior angle sums of polygons via (n−2) × 180° and use the 360° exterior-angle fact
Can use parallelogram properties (opposite sides/angles equal, adjacent angles supplementary, diagonals bisect each other) to find unknowns
Can state which extra properties rectangles, rhombuses and squares add
Can place the special quadrilaterals in a correct hierarchy

misconceptions.description: Uses 360° as the interior angle sum of EVERY polygon, not just quadrilaterals.
misconceptions.signal: Pentagon angle problems solved with 360°; answers systematically 180° short per extra side.
misconceptions.remedy: Triangulate polygons from one vertex: a pentagon splits into 3 triangles, so 3 × 180° = 540°. Build the (n−2) pattern from a table of n = 3, 4, 5, 6 rather than as a bare formula.

misconceptions.description: Believes the diagonals of every parallelogram are equal (importing the rectangle's special property).
misconceptions.signal: Claims diagonals equal in a generic parallelogram or rhombus.
misconceptions.remedy: Measure the diagonals of a drawn slanted parallelogram — visibly unequal. Sort diagonal properties into a table: bisect each other (all parallelograms) vs equal (rectangles/squares) vs perpendicular (rhombus/square).

misconceptions.description: Thinks adjacent angles of a parallelogram are equal (instead of supplementary), confusing them with opposite angles.
misconceptions.signal: Given one angle 70°, writes the neighbouring angle as 70°.
misconceptions.remedy: Walk the parallel-lines connection: adjacent angles are co-interior angles between parallel sides, so they sum to 180°; OPPOSITE angles are the equal pair. Colour opposite angle pairs identically in diagrams.

misconceptions.description: Gets the quadrilateral hierarchy backwards: 'every rectangle is a square', or refuses 'a square is a rhombus'.
misconceptions.signal: Hierarchy questions answered by visual prototype rather than property lists.
misconceptions.remedy: Run each shape through property checklists: a square passes ALL rhombus tests (four equal sides) and all rectangle tests (four right angles). Draw the family tree with arrows meaning 'is a special kind of'.

real_world_hooks: Sliding gates and scissor lifts: parallelogram linkages in action
Why mobile screens and doors are rectangles — equal diagonals as a squareness check used by carpenters
Kite festival: the geometric kite and its diagonals
Floor tiles: which polygons tile because of their angle sums?
teaching.video_search: polygon angle sum parallelogram properties rectangle rhombus square hierarchy class 8

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon?

options.diagnosis: Used n instead of n−2 (or the hexagon's count) in (n−2) × 180°.
Estimated 100° per angle × 5 — plausible-looking but not a polygon fact.

questions.explanation: A pentagon splits into 5 − 2 = 3 triangles from one vertex, so its angles total 3 × 180° = 540°. The 360° figure is the QUADRILATERAL sum (and, separately, every polygon's EXTERIOR angle total).

questions.prompt: In a parallelogram, one angle measures 70°. What is the measure of the angle ADJACENT to it?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted from 90° — complement used where a supplement is needed.
Subtracted from 360°, the full quadrilateral sum, instead of from 180°.

questions.explanation: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram lie between the two parallel sides (co-interior), so they are supplementary: 180 − 70 = 110°. It is the OPPOSITE angle that equals 70°.

questions.prompt: Which quadrilateral always has diagonals that are EQUAL and bisect each other, without needing all four sides equal?

options.diagnosis: A general trapezium's diagonals are neither equal nor mutually bisecting — property list not checked.

questions.explanation: All parallelograms have diagonals that bisect each other, but EQUAL diagonals is the rectangle's special extra (from its right angles). A rhombus instead has perpendicular diagonals — equal only when it becomes a square. Carpenters exploit this: equal diagonals certify right angles.

nodes.title: Practical Geometry: Constructing Quadrilaterals
nodes.description: A quadrilateral needs five independent measurements to be pinned down — four sides alone leave it floppy. You will construct quadrilaterals from five given parts (e.g. four sides and a diagonal) by splitting them into two triangles, reusing everything you know about triangle construction.
learning_outcomes: Can explain why 5 measurements (suitably chosen) determine a quadrilateral while 4 do not
Can construct quadrilaterals given: 4 sides + 1 diagonal; 3 sides + 2 diagonals; 2 adjacent sides + 3 angles; 3 sides + 2 included angles
Can decompose the construction into two triangle constructions sharing a diagonal
Can detect impossible data (triangle inequality failing inside a component triangle)

misconceptions.description: Believes four sides determine a quadrilateral uniquely, as three sides do a triangle.
misconceptions.signal: Constructs from 4 sides only and is surprised the shape can be 'squashed' into different quadrilaterals.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a four-strip hinged frame (or straw model) and squash it: same four sides, many shapes. Contrast with a triangle frame, which cannot flex — rigidity needs the fifth measurement (a diagonal or angle).

misconceptions.description: Thinks ANY five measurements will do, regardless of which parts they are.
misconceptions.signal: Attempts constructions from data like four angles + one side, or five angles, and stalls.
misconceptions.remedy: Classify the workable data sets and trace each back to two constructible triangles. Show a failing case (four angles already forced by the 360° sum, so they carry less information).

misconceptions.description: Ignores feasibility checks: starts drawing without testing the triangle inequality in each half-triangle.
misconceptions.signal: Arcs fail to intersect mid-construction; student blames drawing accuracy rather than the data.
misconceptions.remedy: Before drawing, split the data into its two triangles and verify each satisfies the triangle inequality. Turn 'my compass slipped' moments into data-checking moments.

misconceptions.description: Draws by eye and adjusts: places vertices where they 'look right' instead of at arc intersections.
misconceptions.signal: No construction arcs visible; measurements of the finished figure drift from the given data.
misconceptions.remedy: Require all arcs to remain visible in submitted work and have students measure their own finished figure against the specification — accuracy becomes checkable, not aesthetic.

real_world_hooks: Why gates and grills get a diagonal brace — the fifth measurement in steel
Land records: a four-sided plot needs a diagonal measure to be mapped exactly
Foldable furniture and collapsible stalls: useful floppiness of 4-bar frames
Kite-making: fixing a quadrilateral's shape with its two diagonal sticks
teaching.video_search: constructing quadrilaterals four sides diagonal compass class 8

questions.prompt: How many measurements are needed, in general, to construct a unique quadrilateral?

options.diagnosis: Carried over the triangle's count; a quadrilateral has more independent parts to fix.

options.text: 8 (all four sides and all four angles)
options.diagnosis: That is every part — far more than needed; five suitably chosen parts suffice.

questions.explanation: Four sides leave a quadrilateral hinged and floppy — it can flex into infinitely many shapes. One more suitable measurement (say a diagonal) locks it, because the diagonal splits it into two rigid triangles. Hence 5.

questions.prompt: To construct quadrilateral ABCD given the four sides and the diagonal AC, the standard strategy is to:

options.text: Construct triangle ABC first, then triangle ACD on the same base AC
Draw the four sides in order and adjust until the figure closes
Begin by drawing all four angles
Draw both diagonals first and hang the sides on them
options.diagnosis: Only ONE diagonal is given; the second diagonal's length is an outcome, not data.

questions.explanation: The diagonal AC splits ABCD into triangles ABC (sides AB, BC, AC) and ACD (sides AC, CD, DA) — each constructible by SSS. Building two triangles on the shared base AC assembles the quadrilateral exactly.

questions.prompt: You are asked to construct quadrilateral ABCD with AB = 4 cm, BC = 5 cm and diagonal AC = 10 cm (plus suitable remaining data). What do you conclude?

options.text: The construction is impossible: in triangle ABC, AB + BC = 9 < 10 = AC
It must be possible, since five measurements are provided
It is possible if drawn very carefully with a sharp pencil
It is impossible because a diagonal can never be the longest given length
options.diagnosis: Right verdict, wrong rule — diagonals CAN be longest; the actual test is the triangle inequality.

questions.explanation: Triangle ABC must be built from sides 4, 5 and 10 — but 4 + 5 = 9 < 10 violates the triangle inequality, so the arcs can never meet. Five measurements only suffice when each component triangle is actually constructible.

nodes.title: Visualising Solid Shapes: Views and Euler's Relation
nodes.description: You will map solids from different viewpoints (top, front, side), read simple maps, and discover Euler's beautiful relation for polyhedra: F + V − E = 2 — faces plus vertices minus edges equals two, for EVERY polyhedron from a cube to a football. It is many students' first universal theorem about 3D space.
learning_outcomes: Can draw and match top, front and side views of solids and cube arrangements
Can distinguish polyhedra (flat faces) from non-polyhedra (cylinder, sphere, cone)
Can verify Euler's relation F + V − E = 2 on prisms and pyramids
Can use Euler's relation to find a missing count (e.g. faces from V and E)

misconceptions.description: Misremembers or distrusts Euler's relation: uses F + V − E = 0, F = V + E − 2, or believes the value changes from solid to solid.
misconceptions.signal: Plugs counts into a scrambled formula; answers 'it depends on the shape' for F + V − E.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a data table (cube, cuboid, triangular prism, square pyramid, tetrahedron) and compute F + V − E for each — the constant 2 emerges from the student's own data, then the formula is remembered as a discovered fact.

misconceptions.description: Confuses which view is which: expects the top view of a cylinder to be a rectangle, or draws the front view from above.
misconceptions.signal: Views swapped or blended; the same drawing offered for top and front.
misconceptions.remedy: Physically move: hold the object at eye level for the front view, then look straight down for the top view. Use a torch to cast the corresponding shadows and match each to its name.

misconceptions.description: Applies Euler's relation to non-polyhedra (cylinder, cone, sphere) or counts curved surfaces as 'faces'.
misconceptions.signal: Reports F + V − E ≠ 2 for a cylinder as a 'violation', counting its curved surface as a face.
misconceptions.remedy: Define polyhedron sharply: flat polygonal faces, straight edges. Sort solids into polyhedra / non-polyhedra BEFORE any counting; Euler's relation applies only to the first pile.

misconceptions.description: Miscounts hidden faces, edges or vertices when working from a 2D sketch.
misconceptions.signal: Counts of F, E, V systematically low; only visible parts tallied.
misconceptions.remedy: Count on a real model with a marker — tick each face/edge/vertex as it is counted. On sketches, draw hidden edges dashed and count the dashes too.

real_world_hooks: Building plans: floor plan (top view) vs elevation (front view) of a house
A football's pentagon-hexagon pattern satisfies F + V − E = 2
Minecraft-style block builds: drawing their three views
Reading a metro map vs an aerial photo — maps as chosen views
teaching.video_search: views of 3d shapes euler formula polyhedron F V E class 8

questions.prompt: For any polyhedron, F + V − E equals:
questions.explanation: Euler's relation: F + V − E = 2 for every polyhedron. Cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2. Square pyramid: 5 + 5 − 8 = 2. The astonishing part is precisely that it does NOT depend on the solid.

questions.prompt: What is the TOP view of a cylinder standing upright?

options.text: An oval that is longer than it is wide
options.diagnosis: Perspective drawing habit; looking straight down, the rim is a true circle.
A view is a flat 2D picture, not the solid itself.

questions.explanation: Looking straight down at an upright cylinder you see only its circular top: the top view is a circle. The rectangle is its FRONT view. Each view flattens the solid from one direction.

questions.prompt: A polyhedron has 6 vertices and 12 edges. How many faces does it have?

options.diagnosis: Assumed faces must equal vertices; the relation, not symmetry, decides.
Sign slip while rearranging: computed E − V − 2 instead of 2 − V + E.

questions.explanation: F + V − E = 2 ⟹ F = 2 − V + E = 2 − 6 + 12 = 8. (This solid is the octahedron.) Rearranging as F = V + E − 2 gives 16 — a scrambled formula; check any rearrangement against the cube's 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.

nodes.title: Mensuration: Trapezium, Polygon Areas; Surface Area and Volume
nodes.description: You will find areas of trapeziums and general quadrilaterals via triangles, then step into 3D: surface areas and volumes of cuboids and cylinders. Keeping 'how much to paint' (surface area) separate from 'how much it holds' (volume) — and their different units — is the chapter's central discipline.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the area of a trapezium as ½(a + b)h and of polygons by triangulation
Can compute lateral/total surface area of cuboids, cubes and cylinders
Can compute volumes of cuboids, cubes and cylinders
Can choose between surface area and volume from context, with correct units (cm² vs cm³)
Can reason about scaling: doubling an edge multiplies volume by 8

misconceptions.description: Drops the ½ in the trapezium formula (or forgets to add the parallel sides first).
misconceptions.signal: Trapezium areas exactly double, or computed as product of the parallel sides.
misconceptions.remedy: Derive the formula by duplication: two copies of the trapezium (one rotated) form a parallelogram of base (a+b) and the same height — so the trapezium is HALF of (a+b)×h.

misconceptions.description: Confuses surface area with volume — computes one when the context needs the other.
misconceptions.signal: Uses volume to answer painting/wrapping questions; units of the answer don't match the quantity.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort a batch of real questions into PAINT (area, cm²) vs FILL (volume, cm³) before any formula work. Wrapping a box vs filling it with water makes the split physical.

misconceptions.description: Uses the curved-surface-area formula 2πrh when volume πr²h is needed (and vice versa) for cylinders.
misconceptions.signal: Cylinder answers linear in r for volume questions; the two formulas treated as interchangeable.
misconceptions.remedy: Dimension-check every formula before use: volume needs three lengths multiplied (r·r·h), surface area needs two (r·h or r·r). Unroll a paper label to SEE 2πr × h as a rectangle.

misconceptions.description: Assumes measures scale linearly: doubling a side doubles area and volume.
misconceptions.signal: Answers ×2 for the volume of a doubled cube; surprised a tank 'twice as big' holds 8 times the water.
misconceptions.remedy: Build the 2×2×2 block from 8 unit cubes — the eightfold jump is countable. Tabulate side, area, volume for sides 1, 2, 3 and read off the ×n² and ×n³ patterns.

real_world_hooks: Water tanker cylinders: how many litres fit? (1 L = 1000 cm³)
Painting a room vs the air inside it — area vs volume in one scene
Trapezium-shaped fields and canal cross-sections
Why a 'double-size' popcorn tub holds far more than double
teaching.video_search: trapezium area surface area volume cuboid cylinder class 8

questions.prompt: A trapezium has parallel sides 8 cm and 6 cm, and the distance between them is 5 cm. Its area is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied all three numbers — no formula multiplies both parallel sides by the height.
Added all three measurements — a perimeter-style move, not an area one.

questions.explanation: Area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height = ½ × (8 + 6) × 5 = ½ × 70 = 35 cm². Two copies of this trapezium tile a parallelogram of area 70 — hence the ½.

questions.prompt: Taking π = 22/7, find the VOLUME of a cylinder with radius 7 cm and height 10 cm.

options.diagnosis: Computed πrh — one r missing from the volume formula πr²h.
Computed the base area πr² but forgot to multiply by the height.

questions.explanation: V = πr²h = (22/7) × 7 × 7 × 10 = 22 × 7 × 10 = 1540 cm³. The value 440 is the CURVED SURFACE AREA 2πrh = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × 10 — the label, not the contents. Volume must multiply three lengths.

questions.prompt: The edge of a cube is DOUBLED. What happens to its volume?

options.diagnosis: Applied the AREA scaling factor (2²) to volume; volume scales with the cube, 2³.
Reached for the cube's 6 faces — a count of faces, not a scaling factor.

questions.explanation: Volume = edge³. New volume = (2e)³ = 8e³ — eight times the old. Concretely, a 2×2×2 stack contains exactly 8 unit cubes. (Surface area, by contrast, becomes 4 times as large: it scales with the square.)

nodes.title: Data Handling: Histograms, Pie Charts, Probability Intro
nodes.description: You will group data into class intervals and draw histograms (bars touching — the scale is continuous), build and read pie charts where slices are proportional shares of 360°, and compute probabilities of equally likely outcomes — learning why a coin has no memory.
learning_outcomes: Can group raw data into class intervals and draw/read a histogram
Can explain why histogram bars touch while bar-graph bars do not
Can convert data shares into pie-chart angles (fraction × 360°) and read pie charts
Can compute probabilities as favourable/total for equally likely outcomes, and recognise independence of successive trials

misconceptions.description: Treats a histogram as a bar graph: leaves gaps between bars, or reads class intervals as separate categories.
misconceptions.signal: Gapped 'histograms'; asks what the 'category' 20–30 means.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two chart types on the same page: categories (fruit names) vs a continuous scale chopped into intervals (heights). The bars touch precisely because the intervals share endpoints on one number line.

misconceptions.description: Reads or draws pie-chart slices using the percentage AS the angle: a 25% share drawn as a 25° slice.
misconceptions.signal: Slice angles that total 100° instead of 360°.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor the conversion: the whole circle is 360°, so a share s becomes s × 360°. Quick benchmarks help: 50% = 180°, 25% = 90°, 10% = 36°.

misconceptions.description: Gambler's fallacy: believes past random outcomes change future probabilities ('four heads in a row, so tails is due').
misconceptions.signal: Adjusts predicted probabilities after streaks; talks of luck 'evening out' on the next toss.
misconceptions.remedy: Simulate long runs of tosses (or use class data): after a streak of heads, the NEXT toss still lands heads about half the time. The coin has no memory — discuss why each toss is physically identical.

misconceptions.description: Forms probabilities as part-to-part odds instead of part-to-whole: P(red) = 3/7 from 3 red and 7 blue.
misconceptions.signal: Denominators equal to the OTHER group's count rather than the total.
misconceptions.remedy: Always write the sample space size first: 3 + 7 = 10 equally likely balls, THEN count favourables. Probability compares favourable outcomes with ALL outcomes.

real_world_hooks: Class heights or daily screen-time grouped into intervals — a real histogram
Monthly family budget as a pie chart: food, rent, travel, savings
Cricket toss streaks: does losing five tosses make you 'due' to win?
Board-game dice: chances of rolling the six you need
teaching.video_search: histogram pie chart central angle probability basics class 8

questions.prompt: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a 3?

options.diagnosis: 'It happens or it doesn't' treated as two equally likely outcomes — but the six faces are the equally likely ones.
Counted the five faces that are NOT 3 as the favourable outcomes — computed the probability of the complementary event instead.

questions.explanation: Six equally likely faces, one favourable: P(3) = 1/6. The denominator counts ALL outcomes (6), not the unfavourable ones (5) — and 5/6 is the probability of NOT rolling a 3 (the complement), not of rolling one.

questions.prompt: In a pie chart of a family budget, food takes 25% of total spending. What central angle should the food slice have?

options.diagnosis: Halved the correct angle — possibly used 180° as the whole circle.
Computed 100 − 25 and then read the result as degrees — two confusions chained.

questions.explanation: The full circle is 360°, so 25% of it is 0.25 × 360 = 90°. Percentages and degrees are different scales for shares: 25 out of 100 corresponds to 90 out of 360.

questions.prompt: A fair coin has landed heads 4 times in a row. What is the probability that the NEXT toss is a head?

options.text: Less than 1/2, because tails is now 'due'
More than 1/2, because heads is on a hot streak

options.diagnosis: That is the probability of five heads in a row computed BEFORE any tosses — not the probability of the next single toss given four already happened.

questions.explanation: The coin has no memory: the next toss is the same physical experiment as always, so P(head) = 1/2. The streak's rarity (1/32 for five in advance) is irrelevant once four heads have already occurred — both 'due for tails' and 'hot streak' are versions of the gambler's fallacy.

nodes.title: Number Systems: Irrational Numbers, Real Number Line, Rationalisation
nodes.description: Not every number can be written as a fraction: numbers like √2 and π have decimal expansions that never end and never repeat. This node extends the number line to all real numbers, teaches you to spot rational versus irrational numbers from their decimal expansions, to locate irrationals like √2 on the number line, and to simplify expressions with surds by rationalising denominators. It is the foundation for all later algebra, since from now on 'number' means 'real number'.
learning_outcomes: Can classify a given number as natural, whole, integer, rational or irrational with justification
Can decide from a decimal expansion (terminating, recurring, non-recurring) whether a number is rational or irrational
Can represent numbers like √2 and √3 on the number line using right triangles
Can rationalise denominators of the form 1/(a+b√c) and simplify surd expressions using laws of exponents

misconceptions.description: Square roots distribute over addition: √(a+b) = √a + √b, and similarly √(a²+b²) = a+b.
misconceptions.signal: Writes √(9+16) = 3+4 = 7 instead of √25 = 5; simplifies √(x²+y²) to x+y.
misconceptions.remedy: Force a numeric collision: have the student compute √(9+16) both ways and confront the mismatch (5 vs 7). Generalise: root and addition do not commute; only multiplication passes through the root (√(ab)=√a·√b for a,b ≥ 0).

misconceptions.description: Anything written with a root sign is irrational.
misconceptions.signal: Classifies √25 or √(4/9) as irrational because 'it has a square root'.
misconceptions.remedy: Teach 'evaluate before you classify': simplify the expression first (√25 = 5). Card-sort a deck (√2, √25, √49/√4, √3+1...) into rational/irrational, requiring simplification before sorting.

misconceptions.description: Any non-terminating decimal is irrational (fails to distinguish recurring from non-recurring).
misconceptions.signal: Says 0.333... is irrational 'because it never ends', or says 0.101001000100001... is rational 'because there is a pattern'.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two side by side: convert 0.333... to 1/3 using the x = 0.333..., 10x − x trick, then show the same trick fails for 0.101001000... because no block repeats. Key distinction: a repeating BLOCK, not just any pattern.

misconceptions.description: The sum or product of two irrational numbers is always irrational.
misconceptions.signal: Claims √2 · √8 or (2+√3) + (2−√3) must be irrational because both factors/addends are.
misconceptions.remedy: Counterexample hunt: challenge the student to build a rational number out of two irrationals (√2·√2 = 2, √2 + (−√2) = 0). Contrast with rational + irrational, which IS always irrational, and ask why the proof works in one case but not the other.

real_world_hooks: π in every circle: a bicycle wheel's distance per revolution is never a 'clean' fraction of a metre
A4 paper's sides are in the ratio √2 : 1 — that's why folding it in half gives the same shape (A5)
The diagonal of a square field of side 100 m is exactly 100√2 m — no measuring tape gives it 'exactly'
Bank interest and UPI amounts are always rational; geometry keeps forcing irrationals on us
teaching.video_search: class 9 number systems irrational numbers rationalisation explained

questions.prompt: Which of the following numbers is irrational?

options.diagnosis: Believes 22/7 IS π and that π-like numbers stay irrational even when written as a fraction; 22/7 is a rational approximation of π.

questions.explanation: √7 is irrational because 7 is not a perfect square, so its decimal expansion is non-terminating and non-recurring. √16 = 4 is rational (evaluate before classifying!). 0.272727... has a repeating block (27), so it equals 27/99 = 3/11, a rational number. 22/7 is a ratio of integers, hence rational — it is only an approximation of π, not π itself.

questions.prompt: Rationalise the denominator: 1/(√5 − 2) equals

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by (√5 − 2)/(√5 − 2) — the same expression instead of the conjugate — which changes nothing useful.
Computed the denominator as (√5)² + 2² = 9 instead of (√5)² − 2² = 1; sign error in the difference-of-squares identity.
Computed the denominator as 5 − 2 = 3, forgetting to square the 2 in (√5−2)(√5+2) = 5 − 4.

questions.explanation: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate √5 + 2: 1/(√5−2) × (√5+2)/(√5+2) = (√5+2)/((√5)² − 2²) = (√5+2)/(5−4) = √5 + 2.

questions.prompt: Consider the number 0.101001000100001... (each block has one more zero than the last). This number is:

options.text: Irrational, because its expansion is non-terminating AND non-recurring
Rational, because its digits follow a clear pattern
options.diagnosis: Conflates 'any pattern' with 'a repeating block'. Rationality requires a fixed block that repeats forever; here the blocks keep growing.

options.text: Irrational, simply because it is non-terminating
Rational, because every decimal number can be written as p/q
options.diagnosis: Believes all decimals are fractions; only terminating or recurring decimals can be written as p/q with integers p, q.

questions.explanation: The expansion never terminates, and no fixed block of digits ever repeats (the runs of zeros keep lengthening), so the number cannot be written as p/q. Both conditions matter: 0.333... is also non-terminating but IS rational (1/3) because the block '3' repeats. Non-terminating + non-recurring together define irrationality.

nodes.title: Polynomials: Zeroes, Remainder and Factor Theorems, Identities
nodes.description: A polynomial is an expression built from a variable using only addition, subtraction and whole-number powers — the workhorse of algebra. Here you learn to evaluate polynomials, find their zeroes, use the Remainder and Factor Theorems to divide and factorise without long division, and wield algebraic identities like (a+b)², a³+b³ and (a+b+c)² to compute and factorise at speed. Everything from quadratic equations to calculus stands on this node.
learning_outcomes: Can identify polynomials, state their degree, and classify them as linear, quadratic or cubic
Can evaluate p(x) at a given value and verify whether a given number is a zero of p(x)
Can apply the Remainder Theorem (remainder of p(x) ÷ (x−a) is p(a)) and the Factor Theorem to factorise cubics
Can expand and factorise using standard identities including (a±b)², a²−b², (x+a)(x+b), (a+b+c)² and a³±b³

misconceptions.description: When dividing by (x − a), the remainder is p(−a) — the sign of a is mishandled.
misconceptions.signal: For p(x) ÷ (x − 3) evaluates p(−3); for p(x) ÷ (x + 2) evaluates p(2).
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor to the root idea: the remainder is p(value that makes the divisor zero). Always ask first 'what x kills x−3?' (x = 3). One-line habit: set divisor = 0, solve, substitute.

misconceptions.description: Powers distribute over sums: (a+b)² = a² + b².
misconceptions.signal: Expands (x+3)² as x²+9; claims x² + 1/x² = (x + 1/x)² without subtracting the cross term.
misconceptions.remedy: Area model: draw a square of side (a+b) and show the two ab rectangles that a²+b² ignores. Then test numerically: (2+3)² = 25 but 2²+3² = 13. Institute the reflex 'squaring a sum? — expect a middle term'.

misconceptions.description: The degree of a polynomial is the number of terms it has.
misconceptions.signal: Says 4x³ − x² + 7 has degree 3 'because it has three terms' (right answer, wrong reason — collapses on x⁵ + 1, which they call degree 2).
misconceptions.remedy: Diagnose with a two-term, high-degree example like x⁵ + 1. Redefine degree as the highest power of the variable, and practise on polynomials written in jumbled order (7 − x⁴ + 2x).

misconceptions.description: Every polynomial of degree n must have n distinct real zeroes.
misconceptions.signal: Insists x² + 1 has two real zeroes 'because it is quadratic', or is confused when (x−2)² has 'only one' zero.
misconceptions.remedy: Graph x²+1, x², and x²−1 together (interactive slider on c in x²+c): the parabola sliding up loses its x-intercepts. Degree bounds the NUMBER of zeroes (at most n); it does not guarantee them.

real_world_hooks: Mental-math party trick: 103 × 97 = (100+3)(100−3) = 9991 in two seconds using a²−b²
The height of a cricket ball tossed up is a quadratic polynomial in time
Box design: the volume of a carton folded from a sheet is a cubic polynomial in the cut size
Coding: polynomial hash functions decide which bucket a password lands in
teaching.video_search: class 9 polynomials remainder theorem factor theorem identities

questions.prompt: If p(x) = 3x² − 4x + 2, then p(−1) equals

options.diagnosis: Evaluated p(1) = 3 − 4 + 2, ignoring the negative sign of the input.
Treated (−1)² as −1, computing −3 + 4 + 2; squaring a negative gives a positive.
Dropped the constant term: computed 3(−1)² − 4(−1) = 7 and forgot the +2.

questions.prompt: The remainder when p(x) = x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1 is divided by (x − 2) is

options.diagnosis: Computed 2³ as 2 × 3 = 6 instead of 8; treated the power as multiplication.
Assumed the divisor is always a factor; remainder 0 happens only when p(a) = 0, which must be checked, not assumed.

questions.explanation: By the Remainder Theorem, the remainder is p(2), since x − 2 = 0 gives x = 2. p(2) = 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27. Evaluating p(−2) = −8 + 12 − 6 + 1 = −1 is the classic sign trap: substitute the value that makes the divisor zero.

questions.prompt: If x + 1/x = 5, the value of x² + 1/x² is

options.diagnosis: Knew a middle term exists but added it: computed 25 + 2 instead of 25 − 2.
Doubled instead of squared: treated x² + 1/x² as 2(x + 1/x).

questions.explanation: Square both sides: (x + 1/x)² = x² + 2·x·(1/x) + 1/x² = x² + 2 + 1/x². So 25 = x² + 1/x² + 2, giving x² + 1/x² = 23. Answering 25 means the cross term 2·x·(1/x) = 2 was forgotten — the (a+b)² = a²+b² trap.

nodes.title: Linear Equations in Two Variables
nodes.description: An equation like 2x + y = 7 does not have one answer — it has infinitely many solutions, each an ordered pair (x, y), and together they draw a straight line in the Cartesian plane. This node connects algebra to geometry: every solution is a point on the line, and every point on the line is a solution. Mastering this picture prepares you for solving pairs of such equations in Class 10 and for functions and graphs beyond.
learning_outcomes: Can write a linear equation in two variables in the standard form ax + by + c = 0 and identify a, b, c
Can find several solutions of a given equation and verify whether a given ordered pair is a solution
Can explain why such an equation has infinitely many solutions and why its graph is a straight line
Can graph equations including the special forms x = k and y = k

misconceptions.description: Every equation has exactly one solution, so a linear equation in two variables must too.
misconceptions.signal: Solves 2x + y = 7 by 'finding x', gets stuck, or reports a single pair like (2,3) as THE solution.
misconceptions.remedy: Solution-generating game: fix x = 0, 1, 2, −1... and compute y each time; plot the pairs and watch a line emerge. Contrast with 2x + 3 = 7 (one variable, one solution) to show what changed: one equation with two unknowns leaves one degree of freedom.

misconceptions.description: A solution is a single number, not an ordered pair.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'x = 2' or 'y = 3' when asked for a solution of 2x + y = 7; writes solutions without pairing.
misconceptions.remedy: Insist on the point language: a solution is a POINT (x, y) that sits on the line. Have the student check candidate points by substitution and mark them on the graph — the pair-ness becomes physical.

misconceptions.description: The order in an ordered pair doesn't matter: (2,3) and (3,2) are the same solution.
misconceptions.signal: Substitutes the y-value for x and vice versa when verifying; claims (3,2) solves 2x + y = 7 because (2,3) does.
misconceptions.remedy: Direct test: substitute both orders into 2x + y = 7 and watch (3,2) fail (6 + 2 = 8 ≠ 7). Reinforce the convention alphabetically — first slot is x, second is y — and connect to plotting, where (2,3) and (3,2) are visibly different points.

misconceptions.description: x = 3 is a horizontal line (or 'just a point'), confusing it with y = 3.
misconceptions.signal: Draws x = 3 parallel to the x-axis; or plots only the point (3, 0).
misconceptions.remedy: Reframe x = 3 as x + 0·y = 3: y is free, so list solutions (3,0), (3,1), (3,−2)... and plot them — they stack vertically. Rule of thumb built from evidence, not memory: the graph of x = k CUTS the x-axis.

real_world_hooks: Auto fare: total = ₹30 + ₹15 per km is a line relating fare and distance
Splitting ₹100 between data packs at ₹20 and talk-time at ₹10: 20x + 10y = 100
Cricket: ways to reach 7 runs off the last over with fours (x) and singles (y): 4x + y = 7
Budget lines: any combination of samosas and chai that spends exactly ₹50
teaching.video_search: class 9 linear equations in two variables graph solutions

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a solution of 2x + y = 7?

options.diagnosis: Ignored the coefficient of x: checked x + y = 7 instead of 2x + y = 7.
Halved the constant while setting x = 0; with x = 0 the equation gives y = 7, not 7/2.

questions.explanation: Substitute each pair with x first, y second. (2,3): 2(2) + 3 = 7 ✓. (3,2): 2(3) + 2 = 8 ✗ — order matters. (3,4): 2(3) + 4 = 10 ✗ (it only 'works' if you forget to double x, since 3 + 4 = 7). (0, 3.5): 2(0) + 3.5 = 3.5 ✗; the y-intercept is (0, 7).

questions.prompt: In the Cartesian plane, the graph of the equation x = 3 is

options.text: A vertical line parallel to the y-axis, passing through (3, 0)
A horizontal line parallel to the x-axis
A line through the origin with slope 3
options.diagnosis: Confused x = 3 with y = 3x; the equation here fixes x and says nothing about y.

questions.explanation: x = 3 means x + 0·y = 3: x must be 3 but y can be anything. Solutions include (3, 0), (3, 1), (3, −5)... which stack up into a vertical line through (3, 0). It is a full line (infinitely many solutions), not one point, and it runs parallel to the y-axis.

questions.prompt: If the point (2, k) lies on the graph of 3x − 2y = 4, then k equals

options.diagnosis: Sign slip in the last step: from 6 − 2k = 4 reached k = −1 by mishandling the negative coefficient.
Moved the 4 to the wrong side: solved 2k = 6 + 4 instead of 2k = 6 − 4.

questions.explanation: A point on the graph satisfies the equation. Substitute x = 2, y = k: 3(2) − 2k = 4 ⟹ 6 − 2k = 4 ⟹ 2k = 2 ⟹ k = 1. Getting 8/3 comes from substituting k for x (3k − 4 = 4), i.e. swapping the coordinates.

nodes.title: Coordinate Geometry: The Cartesian Plane
nodes.description: René Descartes' big idea: describe every point in the plane with a pair of numbers. This node sets up the Cartesian plane — two perpendicular axes, four quadrants, and the (x, y) address system — and teaches you to plot points, read coordinates, and reason about signs, axes and distances from the axes. It is the bridge on which algebra and geometry meet, and every graph you ever draw lives here.
learning_outcomes: Can name the axes, origin, quadrants, abscissa and ordinate, and plot any point (x, y) accurately
Can determine the quadrant or axis on which a point lies from the signs of its coordinates
Can read off perpendicular distances of a point from the axes
Can explain why (a, b) and (b, a) are different points when a ≠ b

misconceptions.description: The order of coordinates doesn't matter: (a, b) is plotted by moving b along x and a along y (or treated the same as (b, a)).
misconceptions.signal: Plots (−3, 5) at the location of (5, −3); reads a point's coordinates in the wrong order.
misconceptions.remedy: Physical routine: 'corridor then stairs' — you always walk along the ground floor (x) first, then climb (y). Battleship-style games where a wrong order sinks the wrong ship give immediate, memorable feedback.

misconceptions.description: Any point with a negative coordinate lies in quadrant III (signs are not linked to specific axes).
misconceptions.signal: Places (−3, 5) in QIII 'because it has a minus'; cannot say which quadrant (+,−) belongs to.
misconceptions.remedy: Build the sign map from plotting, not memorisation: plot one point per quadrant, then fill a 2×2 sign table (x sign, y sign → quadrant). Quiz in both directions: point → quadrant and sign pattern → quadrant.

misconceptions.description: A zero coordinate puts the point on the axis of the same name: (0, −4) lies on the x-axis.
misconceptions.signal: Says (0, b) is on the x-axis 'because x = 0'.
misconceptions.remedy: Plot it: (0, −4) means walk 0 along x, then 4 down — you never leave the vertical axis. Generalise by plotting several (0, b) and (a, 0) points and describing each set: the set x = 0 IS the y-axis.

misconceptions.description: Every point must belong to one of the four quadrants.
misconceptions.signal: Forces points like (0, −4) or (5, 0) into a quadrant; treats 0 as negative to make the classification work.
misconceptions.remedy: Refine the map of the plane: quadrants are the four OPEN regions; the axes and origin are boundaries belonging to none. Sorting task with axis points included, requiring extra categories ('on x-axis', 'on y-axis', 'origin').

real_world_hooks: Chess notation (e4!) and Battleship grids are coordinate systems
Google Maps pins: latitude-longitude is a giant coordinate plane wrapped on a sphere
Cinema tickets: row H, seat 12 — order matters, H12 is not 12H
City navigation: '3rd cross, 5th main' in Bengaluru is Cartesian addressing
teaching.video_search: class 9 coordinate geometry cartesian plane quadrants plotting points

questions.prompt: The point (−3, 5) lies in which quadrant?

options.diagnosis: Ignored the signs entirely and placed the point by magnitudes alone.

questions.explanation: x = −3 (move left), y = +5 (move up): left and up is Quadrant II. Choosing QIV means the coordinates were swapped — that is where (5, −3) lives. Sign map: (+,+) I, (−,+) II, (−,−) III, (+,−) IV.

questions.prompt: The point (0, −4) lies

options.diagnosis: Treated the 0 as if it were negative and forced the point into a quadrant.

questions.explanation: Walk 0 units horizontally, then 4 units down: you stay on the vertical (y) axis. Every point with x = 0 lies on the y-axis. Points on the axes belong to NO quadrant — quadrants are the four open regions between the axes.

questions.prompt: The perpendicular distance of the point P(5, 3) from the x-axis is

options.diagnosis: Added the two coordinates; distance from an axis depends on only one coordinate.
Computed the distance from the ORIGIN (√(5²+3²)), not from the x-axis.

questions.explanation: Dropping a perpendicular from (5, 3) to the x-axis lands at (5, 0); its length is the y-coordinate, 3. Distance from the x-axis = |y|; distance from the y-axis = |x| = 5. The √34 answer is the distance to the origin — a different question.

nodes.title: Introduction to Euclid's Geometry
nodes.description: Around 300 BCE, Euclid organised all known geometry into a single logical structure: start from a handful of self-evident statements (axioms and postulates) and derive everything else by pure reasoning. This node introduces that deductive game — definitions, axioms, postulates, theorems — and the famous fifth postulate whose questioning eventually gave birth to entirely new geometries. It teaches you what 'proof' means, which is the operating system for the rest of school geometry.
learning_outcomes: Can distinguish between definitions, axioms/postulates (assumed) and theorems (proved)
Can state and apply Euclid's axioms (e.g. things equal to the same thing are equal to one another) in simple deductions
Can state Euclid's postulates, including the fifth, and its equivalent version: through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel line
Can justify simple statements (e.g. two distinct lines cannot share more than one point) using axioms

misconceptions.description: Axioms are just facts like theorems, and should be (or have been) proved.
misconceptions.signal: Asks for the proof of 'the whole is greater than the part'; labels the angle-sum theorem an axiom because 'it's obviously true'.
misconceptions.remedy: Play the 'why?' regress game: keep asking why until the chain must stop somewhere — those stopping points are axioms, the agreed starting rules. Then sort a mixed list of statements into 'assumed' vs 'proved from the assumed'.

misconceptions.description: A line is the same as a line segment — it has endpoints and finite length.
misconceptions.signal: Talks about 'the length of a line'; treats the edge of the drawing as the end of the line.
