nodes.title: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations
nodes.description: To solve x² + 1 = 0 we extend the real numbers with i, where i² = −1, obtaining complex numbers a + bi with their own arithmetic, conjugates and modulus. Quadratic equations with negative discriminant now have two (conjugate) complex roots — the number system finally makes every quadratic solvable. Complex numbers are indispensable in AC circuit analysis, signal processing and quantum physics.
learning_outcomes: Can compute powers of i by reducing exponents modulo 4
Can add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers, using the conjugate to rationalise quotients
Can find the modulus and conjugate of a complex number and interpret a + bi as a point in the Argand plane
Can solve quadratic equations with negative discriminant and express roots as conjugate pairs
Can explain why rules like √a·√b = √(ab) fail when both a and b are negative

misconceptions.description: Applies the real-number rule √a·√b = √(ab) to negative radicands: √(−4)·√(−9) = √36 = 6.
misconceptions.signal: Multiplies square roots of negatives without first converting to i-form, getting the sign wrong.
misconceptions.remedy: Enforce the discipline 'convert to i BEFORE any arithmetic': √(−4) = 2i, √(−9) = 3i, product = 6i² = −6. Show that the rule √a√b = √(ab) is only guaranteed when at least one of a, b is non-negative.

misconceptions.description: Believes complex numbers can be ordered: writes 3 + i > 2 + i or asks which of i and 1 is larger.
misconceptions.signal: Uses < or > between non-real complex numbers in working.
misconceptions.remedy: Show geometrically that points in a plane have no single 'left-to-right' order that respects arithmetic; contrast with modulus, which CAN be compared. Prove the classic contradiction: if i > 0 then i² = −1 > 0, absurd; similarly i < 0 fails.

misconceptions.description: Treats i² as +1 (or forgets to simplify i² at all), since 'squaring removes the minus'.
misconceptions.signal: Expands (3+2i)(1−i) and leaves −2i² as −2, or turns it into +... with wrong sign; powers of i computed as if period 2.
misconceptions.remedy: Drill the four-cycle i, −1, −i, 1 on a circle diagram; make the student annotate every i² → −1 substitution explicitly in expansions for a while.

misconceptions.description: Computes modulus as |a + bi| = a + b or a² + b² (forgetting the square root).
misconceptions.signal: Writes |3 + 4i| = 7 or 25 instead of 5.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie modulus to distance in the Argand plane and to Pythagoras: it is the hypotenuse of the (a, b) right triangle. Have the student plot the point and measure before computing.

real_world_hooks: AC circuit impedance in electrical engineering is a complex number
The Argand plane: multiplying by i rotates by 90° — the mathematics of rotation in games and graphics
Signal processing behind JPEG images and MP3 audio uses complex exponentials
The history: Cardano and Bombelli 'imagining' numbers to solve cubics in the 1500s
teaching.video_search: complex numbers introduction i squared argand plane class 11

questions.prompt: The value of i⁴⁵ is:

options.diagnosis: Wrote 45 = 4×11 + 1 and computed (i⁴)¹¹ = 1 but dropped the leftover factor i — treated the remainder-1 case as if the remainder were 0.
Off-by-one in the four-cycle: used remainder 3 instead of 1 when dividing 45 by 4.
Treated powers of i as alternating with period 2 (odd power → −1).

questions.explanation: Powers of i cycle with period 4: i, −1, −i, 1. Since 45 = 4×11 + 1, i⁴⁵ = (i⁴)¹¹ · i = 1¹¹ · i = i.

questions.prompt: Compute (3 + 2i)(1 − i).

options.diagnosis: Dropped the −2i² term entirely; expanded only three of the four products.
Sign slip combining the middle terms −3i + 2i; concept of i² likely intact.

questions.explanation: (3 + 2i)(1 − i) = 3 − 3i + 2i − 2i² = 3 − i − 2(−1) = 3 − i + 2 = 5 − i. The key move is i² = −1, which turns −2i² into +2.

questions.prompt: The value of √(−4) × √(−9) is:

options.diagnosis: Converted only one of the two radicals to i-form before multiplying.
Converted correctly to 2i·3i but then simplified i² to i; power-of-i slip.

questions.explanation: Convert first: √(−4) = 2i and √(−9) = 3i, so the product is 6i² = −6. The tempting shortcut √(−4)·√(−9) = √36 = 6 is invalid: the rule √a·√b = √(ab) does not hold when both radicands are negative.

micros.title: The Imaginary Unit and Powers of i
micros.description: Why i is introduced (solving x² + 1 = 0), the definition i² = −1, and the four-cycle i, −1, −i, 1 for reducing any power of i modulo 4.
outcomes: Can state i² = −1 and evaluate i³, i⁴ and negative powers of i
Can reduce iⁿ for large n by dividing the exponent by 4 and using the remainder

question.prompt: The value of i¹⁰³ is:

options.diagnosis: Off-by-one in the four-cycle: used remainder 1 instead of 3 when dividing 103 by 4.
Assumed all large powers of i collapse to 1; only exponents divisible by 4 do.

question.explanation: 103 = 4 × 25 + 3, so i¹⁰³ = (i⁴)²⁵ · i³ = 1 · i³ = −i. Powers of i cycle with period 4 (i, −1, −i, 1) — treating them as period-2 ('odd power → −1') is the classic slip.

micros.title: Adding, Subtracting and Multiplying Complex Numbers
micros.description: Arithmetic with a + bi: combining real and imaginary parts, expanding products like binomials, and substituting i² = −1 explicitly in every expansion.
outcomes: Can add, subtract and multiply complex numbers, simplifying every i² to −1
Can equate real and imaginary parts to solve for unknowns

question.prompt: Compute (2 + 3i)(3 − 2i).

options.diagnosis: Multiplied only the two real parts and the two imaginary parts; FOIL needs all four products.
Sign slip combining the middle terms −4i + 9i; the i² handling was fine.

question.explanation: (2 + 3i)(3 − 2i) = 6 − 4i + 9i − 6i² = 6 + 5i − 6(−1) = 6 + 5i + 6 = 12 + 5i. Treating −6i² as −6 (i.e. i² = +1) loses the +6 and gives 0 + 5i.

micros.title: Conjugates and Division
micros.description: The conjugate a − bi, the key identity z·z̄ = a² + b², and dividing complex numbers by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate.
outcomes: Can find the conjugate of any complex number and compute z·z̄
Can express a quotient of complex numbers in the standard form a + bi

question.prompt: Express (1 + i)/(1 − i) in the form a + bi.

options.diagnosis: Cancelled the (1 + i) against (1 − i) as if they were equal; they are conjugates, not identical factors.
Multiplied by (1 − i)/(1 − i) instead of the conjugate (1 + i)/(1 + i), then mis-simplified the sign.
Divided only the real part by the denominator's real part; division needs the conjugate method, not termwise division.

question.explanation: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator: (1 + i)²/((1 − i)(1 + i)) = (1 + 2i + i²)/(1 + 1) = 2i/2 = i. Check: i(1 − i) = i − i² = 1 + i ✓.

micros.title: Modulus and the Argand Plane
micros.description: Plotting a + bi as the point (a, b), modulus |z| = √(a² + b²) as distance from the origin via Pythagoras, and why complex numbers themselves cannot be ordered.
outcomes: Can plot complex numbers, their conjugates and negatives in the Argand plane
Can compute |z| and explain why |z| values compare even though complex numbers do not

question.prompt: The modulus of 5 − 12i is:

options.diagnosis: Added |5| + |−12|; the modulus is the hypotenuse √(a² + b²), not the sum of the legs.

question.explanation: |5 − 12i| = √(5² + (−12)²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 — the distance from the origin to the point (5, −12). A modulus can never be negative, and 169 is the SQUARE of the modulus.

micros.title: Square Roots of Negative Numbers
micros.description: Writing √(−a) = i√a for a > 0, and the discipline of converting to i-form BEFORE multiplying — because √a·√b = √(ab) fails when both radicands are negative.
outcomes: Can simplify expressions like √(−49) and √(−8) into i-form
Can compute products of square roots of negatives correctly and explain the failing rule

question.prompt: The value of √(−9) × √(−16) is:

options.diagnosis: Converted only one radical to i-form before multiplying; both must become 3i and 4i first.
Reached 3i × 4i = 12i² but then simplified i² to i instead of −1.

question.explanation: Convert first: √(−9) = 3i and √(−16) = 4i, so the product is 12i² = −12. The shortcut √(−9)·√(−16) = √144 = 12 is invalid: √a·√b = √(ab) is only guaranteed when at least one radicand is non-negative.

micros.title: Quadratics with Negative Discriminant
micros.description: Solving ax² + bx + c = 0 when b² − 4ac < 0: the two roots are complex conjugates (−b ± i√(4ac − b²))/2a, and every quadratic now has exactly two roots.
outcomes: Can solve quadratics with negative discriminant and present roots in a + bi form
Can verify that the two roots are conjugates and check them by substitution

question.prompt: The roots of x² + x + 1 = 0 are:

options.diagnosis: Treated the discriminant −3 as +3; a negative discriminant forces an i in the roots.
Dropped the minus of −b in the quadratic formula; the real part must be −b/2a = −1/2.
True over the reals only — in the complex numbers every quadratic has exactly two roots.

question.explanation: Discriminant = 1 − 4 = −3, so x = (−1 ± √(−3))/2 = (−1 ± i√3)/2 — a conjugate pair. Complex numbers exist precisely so that this equation, unsolvable in R, gains its two roots.

nodes.title: Linear Inequalities
nodes.description: Inequalities describe ranges rather than single answers: solving them uses equation-like moves plus one crucial twist — multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. You will express solutions as intervals on the number line and handle systems of simultaneous inequalities. This is the toolkit behind constraints everywhere: budgets, safety limits, eligibility cut-offs, and later, linear programming.
learning_outcomes: Can solve linear inequalities in one variable, reversing the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative
Can express solution sets in interval notation and graph them on the number line
Can solve a pair of simultaneous inequalities and intersect the solution sets
Can translate word problems (marks, budgets, ranges) into inequalities and interpret the solution in context

misconceptions.description: Forgets to reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number.
misconceptions.signal: From −3x > 12 concludes x > −4.
misconceptions.remedy: Test-value habit: after solving, substitute one claimed solution back (x = 0 in −3x > 12 fails instantly). Show on a number line that multiplying by −1 reflects points, which flips left-right order.

misconceptions.description: Treats an inequality like an equation, reporting a single boundary value instead of an interval.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'x = 2' for 5x − 3 < 3x + 1, or shades nothing on the number line.
misconceptions.remedy: Always demand the answer in three synchronized forms — inequality, interval, number-line shading. Ask 'is 0 a solution? is 1.9? is 2?' to force the set-of-many-values view.

misconceptions.description: For a system of inequalities joined by 'and', takes the union of solution sets instead of the intersection.
misconceptions.signal: Combines x > 1 and x < 4 into 'x > 1 or x < 4' (all reals), or shades both regions fully.
misconceptions.remedy: Overlay the two shaded number lines on transparencies (or two colours) and keep only the doubly-shaded part; connect to intersection of sets from the Sets chapter.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles strict vs non-strict boundaries: includes the endpoint for < or excludes it for ≤.
misconceptions.signal: Writes (−∞, 2] for x < 2, or uses a filled dot for a strict inequality.
misconceptions.remedy: Boundary interrogation: 'does x = 2 itself satisfy 5x − 3 < 3x + 1? Check: 7 < 7 is false.' Make open/closed dot choice a verbalised test, not a guess.

real_world_hooks: Minimum marks needed in the final exam to keep a 75% average
Mobile data plans: for how many GB is Plan A cheaper than Plan B?
IPL auction budgets: spending caps as inequalities
Speed limits and safe-dosage ranges as two-sided inequalities
teaching.video_search: linear inequalities one variable interval notation class 11

questions.prompt: Solve for x: −3x > 12.

options.diagnosis: Lost the negative sign on 12/(−3) AND kept the inequality direction; two compounding slips.
Reversed the sign correctly but dropped the negative in −4; arithmetic slip, concept intact.

questions.explanation: Dividing both sides by −3 reverses the inequality: x < 12/(−3) = −4. Sanity check: x = −5 gives −3(−5) = 15 > 12 ✓, while x = 0 gives 0 > 12 ✗.

questions.prompt: The solution set of 5x − 3 < 3x + 1 (x real) is:

options.diagnosis: Reversed the inequality despite dividing by the POSITIVE number 2; misapplies the flip rule, which triggers only for negative multipliers or divisors.

questions.explanation: 5x − 3 < 3x + 1 ⟹ 2x < 4 ⟹ x < 2. Dividing by +2 does NOT flip the sign. The boundary 2 is excluded because the inequality is strict: at x = 2 both sides equal 7.

questions.prompt: Ravi scored 65 and 70 in his first two tests. What must he score in the third test (x) so that his average over the three tests is at least 70?

options.diagnosis: Reasoned 'average 70 means each test needs 70'; never set up the average inequality.
Addition slip: took 65 + 70 = 125, giving 210 − 125 = 85; method right, arithmetic wrong.

questions.explanation: (65 + 70 + x)/3 ≥ 70 ⟹ 135 + x ≥ 210 ⟹ x ≥ 75. 'At least 70' includes 70 itself, so the boundary 75 is included: scoring exactly 75 gives an average of exactly 70.

micros.title: Operations on Inequalities and the Sign Flip
micros.description: Which moves preserve an inequality (adding/subtracting anything, multiplying/dividing by positives) and the one that reverses it: multiplying or dividing by a negative.
outcomes: Can solve one-step inequalities, reversing the sign exactly when multiplying/dividing by a negative
Can verify a solution set by substituting a test value

question.prompt: Solve for x: −2x < 8.

options.diagnosis: Dropped the negative sign on the coefficient and never flipped; two errors that half-cancel.
Flipped correctly but lost the minus on 8/(−2) = −4; arithmetic slip, concept intact.

question.explanation: Dividing both sides by −2 reverses the inequality: x > 8/(−2) = −4. Test x = 0: −2(0) = 0 < 8 ✓, and 0 > −4 ✓ — the test value confirms the flip.

micros.title: Interval Notation and Number-Line Graphs
micros.description: Writing solution sets three synchronized ways — inequality, interval, shaded number line — with open/closed brackets matched to strict/non-strict signs.
outcomes: Can convert among inequality form, interval notation and number-line shading
Can choose open vs closed endpoints by testing whether the boundary value satisfies the inequality

question.prompt: The solution set x ≥ −3 written in interval notation is:

options.diagnosis: Interval points the wrong way — this is x ≤ −3; 'greater than or equal' extends to the right.
∞ is not a number that can be reached, so its bracket is always round, never square.

question.explanation: x ≥ −3 includes the boundary −3 (square bracket) and everything to its right, unbounded above: [−3, ∞). The ∞ side always gets a round bracket.

micros.title: Solving Linear Inequalities in One Variable
micros.description: Multi-step inequalities with brackets and fractions, reported as full interval solution sets — an inequality's answer is a set of many values, not one boundary number.
outcomes: Can solve inequalities like 3(x − 1) ≤ 2(x + 3) and present the answer as an interval and number line
Can state whether specific values belong to the solution set

micros.title: Simultaneous Inequalities: Intersecting Solutions
micros.description: Solving two inequalities that must hold together: solve each, then take the INTERSECTION of the solution sets by overlaying number lines.
outcomes: Can solve 'and'-joined systems and give the combined solution as a single interval
Can explain why 'and' means intersection while 'or' would mean union

question.prompt: The values of x satisfying BOTH x + 2 > 3 AND 2x ≤ 10 form the set:

options.diagnosis: Both endpoints included, but x + 2 > 3 is strict at 1: x = 1 gives 3 > 3, false.

question.explanation: x + 2 > 3 gives x > 1; 2x ≤ 10 gives x ≤ 5. Both must hold, so intersect: 1 < x ≤ 5 = (1, 5]. Taking the union of the two half-lines would cover every real number — the classic 'and'/'or' mix-up.

micros.title: Modelling with Inequalities
micros.description: Translating phrases — 'at least', 'at most', 'between', 'not more than' — into inequalities for marks, budgets and measurement ranges, then interpreting the solution in context.
outcomes: Can set up and solve an inequality from a word problem, choosing strict vs non-strict correctly
Can state the practical meaning of the boundary value

question.prompt: Meena scored 72 and 78 in two tests. What must she score in the third test (x, out of 100) so that her average is MORE than 80?

options.diagnosis: Reasoned 'average above 80 needs each score above 80'; the average inequality was never set up.
Addition slip: 72 + 78 taken as 155, giving 240 − 155 = 85; method right, arithmetic wrong.

question.explanation: (72 + 78 + x)/3 > 80 ⟹ 150 + x > 240 ⟹ x > 90. 'More than 80' is strict, so x = 90 (average exactly 80) does NOT qualify — the boundary stays excluded.

nodes.title: Permutations and Combinations
nodes.description: Counting without listing: the fundamental principle of counting multiplies choices made in sequence, factorials count arrangements, and the twin tools nPr and nCr count ordered selections versus unordered ones. The single most important skill is deciding whether order matters. These techniques power probability, the binomial theorem, and real questions from passwords to tournament fixtures.
learning_outcomes: Can apply the multiplication principle to multi-stage choice problems and the addition principle to exclusive cases
Can compute and manipulate factorials, nPr and nCr, including simplifying quotients of factorials
Can decide from context whether a problem needs permutations (order matters) or combinations (order doesn't)
Can count arrangements with repeated objects (e.g. letters of APPLE) and selections with simple restrictions

misconceptions.description: Uses permutations when order doesn't matter (or combinations when it does) — no test for 'does order count?'.
misconceptions.signal: Computes 10P3 for a committee, or 9C3 for a 3-digit code.
misconceptions.remedy: Institute the two-question checklist before any formula: 'Am I ARRANGING (line, code, ranking → P) or CHOOSING a group (committee, team, handshake → C)?' Verify on a tiny case by explicit listing (choose 2 from {A,B,C}).

misconceptions.description: Adds choices that occur in sequence instead of multiplying them.
misconceptions.signal: For 3 shirts and 4 trousers answers 7 outfits; for a 3-character code adds the options per slot.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the tree diagram for a small case (2 shirts × 3 trousers) and count the leaves — 6, not 5. Verbalise 'for EACH choice of the first, ALL choices of the second are available → multiply'.

misconceptions.description: Remembers nCr as n!/r!, dropping the (n−r)! factor.
misconceptions.remedy: Rebuild the formula from meaning: arrange r of n things (nPr = n!/(n−r)!), then kill the r! orderings of the chosen group. A quick sanity bound helps: nCr can never exceed 2ⁿ.

misconceptions.description: Counts arrangements of repeated letters as all distinct — no division by the repeats' factorial.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 5! = 120 for arrangements of APPLE.
misconceptions.remedy: Physically label the two P's as P₁, P₂, list arrangements of a 3-letter word with a repeat (e.g. 'MOM'), and watch each real word appear exactly 2! times — motivating division by 2!.

real_world_hooks: Number of possible 4-digit UPI PINs and phone lock patterns
IPL playing XI selection from a 15-member squad (combinations) vs batting order (permutations)
Car number plates: how many in one RTO series?
Round-robin tournament: number of matches = nC2 handshakes
Seating arrangements at a wedding table
teaching.video_search: permutations vs combinations fundamental principle counting class 11

questions.prompt: How many 3-digit codes can be formed using the digits 1–9 if no digit repeats?

options.diagnosis: Computed 9³, allowing repeated digits; missed the 'no repetition' condition.

questions.explanation: The three slots have 9, 8, 7 choices respectively (order matters, no repeats): 9 × 8 × 7 = 504 = 9P3. Adding 9 + 8 + 7 = 24 confuses sequential choices with exclusive cases, and 84 = 9C3 ignores that a code is an ORDERED arrangement.

questions.prompt: In how many ways can a committee of 3 members be chosen from 10 people?
questions.explanation: A committee is an unordered group: 10C3 = 10!/(3!·7!) = (10×9×8)/(3×2×1) = 120. 720 = 10P3 counts each committee 3! = 6 times over; 10!/3! forgets the (n−r)! factor; 30 = 10×3 is not a counting principle at all.

questions.prompt: How many distinct arrangements are there of the letters of the word APPLE?

options.diagnosis: Treated the two P's as one letter and computed 4!; collapsed the repeat instead of dividing by 2!.
Divided by 2! twice (or by 4); over-corrected for a single repeated pair.

questions.explanation: APPLE has 5 letters with P repeated twice: 5!/2! = 120/2 = 60. Each genuine word would be counted 2! times if the P's were distinguishable, so we divide 120 by exactly one factor of 2!.

micros.title: The Fundamental Principle of Counting
micros.description: Multiplying choices made in sequence (each stage's options available for every earlier choice) versus adding counts of mutually exclusive cases, seen through tree diagrams.
outcomes: Can apply the multiplication principle to multi-stage problems like codes and outfits
Can recognise when cases are exclusive and must be added instead

question.prompt: A password has 3 characters, each chosen from 5 possible symbols, with repetition allowed. How many passwords are possible?

options.diagnosis: Computed 5 × 4 × 3, imposing 'no repetition' that the problem does not ask for.
Computed 3⁵ — swapped the base and exponent: each of the 3 slots has 5 choices, not the reverse.

question.explanation: Each of the 3 positions independently offers 5 symbols: 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. Adding 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 confuses sequential stages (multiply) with exclusive cases (add).

micros.title: Factorials and Their Algebra
micros.description: n! as the count of arrangements of n distinct objects, the convention 0! = 1, and simplifying factorial quotients like 8!/6! without full expansion.
outcomes: Can evaluate and simplify expressions like 8!/6! and n!/(n−2)!
Can justify 0! = 1 via the pattern n! = n·(n−1)!

micros.title: Permutations: nPr
micros.description: Counting ordered arrangements of r objects from n distinct objects: nPr = n!/(n−r)! derived slot-by-slot from the multiplication principle.
outcomes: Can compute nPr directly and via the slot method for codes, rankings and line-ups
Can solve simple equations involving nPr

micros.title: Arrangements with Repeated Objects
micros.description: Why identical objects shrink the count: n!/(p!·q!·...) for words like BANANA, dividing out the internal reorderings of each repeated letter.
outcomes: Can count distinct arrangements of words with repeated letters
Can explain the division by each repeat's factorial via the labelling argument

question.prompt: How many distinct arrangements are there of the letters of the word BANANA?

options.diagnosis: Divided by 3! for the A's but ignored the two N's; every repeated letter contributes its own factorial.
Divided by 2! only — corrected for the N's but not the three A's.

question.explanation: BANANA has 6 letters with A repeated 3 times and N repeated 2 times: 6!/(3!·2!) = 720/12 = 60. Treating all six letters as distinct overcounts each genuine word 3!·2! = 12 times.

micros.title: Combinations: nCr
micros.description: Counting unordered selections: nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!), built from nPr by dividing out the r! orderings of the chosen group, with the symmetry nCr = nC(n−r).
outcomes: Can compute nCr efficiently, using symmetry to shrink the arithmetic
Can derive nCr = nPr/r! and explain each factor's role

question.prompt: A doubles badminton pair is to be chosen from 12 players. The number of possible pairs is:
question.explanation: A pair is an unordered selection: 12C2 = (12 × 11)/2 = 66. 132 = 12P2 counts each pair twice (order imposed); 12!/2! = 239500800 forgets the (n−r)! factor entirely; 24 = 12 × 2 is not a counting principle.

micros.title: Deciding: Permutation or Combination?
micros.description: The load-bearing skill: interrogating a context — arranging (line, code, ranking → P) versus choosing a group (committee, team, handshake → C) — including mixed problems with restrictions.
outcomes: Can classify a word problem as permutation, combination or multi-stage mix before touching formulas
Can solve selection-then-arrangement problems by chaining C and P steps

question.prompt: From 8 players, a captain and a vice-captain (two different people, distinct roles) are to be chosen. In how many ways can this be done?

options.diagnosis: Computed 8², letting the same person hold both roles; the two picks are without replacement.

question.explanation: The roles differ, so order matters: 8 choices for captain × 7 for vice-captain = 8P2 = 56. 28 = 8C2 would count unlabelled pairs — right answer for 'choose 2 team members', wrong here.

nodes.title: Binomial Theorem
nodes.description: The binomial theorem expands (a + b)ⁿ without multiplying it out: each term is nCr a^(n−r) b^r, with coefficients readable from Pascal's triangle. You will find general terms, middle terms and specific coefficients, and handle expansions like (x − 2y)⁷ where signs alternate. It is the bridge between combinatorics and algebra, and later feeds probability distributions and approximations.
learning_outcomes: Can state and apply the binomial theorem for positive integral n, connecting coefficients to Pascal's triangle and nCr
Can write the general term T(r+1) = nCr a^(n−r) b^r and use it to find any required term or coefficient
Can handle expansions with negative or coefficient-bearing terms like (x − 2y)⁷ and (2x + 3)⁵, applying powers to the whole term
Can count terms in an expansion and locate middle term(s)

misconceptions.description: Believes (a + b)ⁿ = aⁿ + bⁿ — the 'freshman's dream'.
misconceptions.signal: Writes (x + 2)⁵ = x⁵ + 32, or (1.01)ⁿ ≈ 1 + something with no middle terms.
misconceptions.remedy: Falsify with n = 2: (1 + 1)² = 4 ≠ 1² + 1² = 2. Expand (a+b)² and (a+b)³ by hand to SEE the cross terms being born, then present the theorem as bookkeeping for those cross terms.

misconceptions.description: Off-by-one in term indexing: uses r for the r-th term instead of T(r+1) = nCr a^(n−r) b^r, or thinks (a+b)ⁿ has n terms.
misconceptions.signal: For the 4th term uses r = 4; answers 'n terms' when asked how many terms an expansion has.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor on the first term: T₁ corresponds to r = 0, so T(r+1) ↔ r. Have the student write the full expansion of (a+b)³ with r-values 0,1,2,3 labelled under each of its 4 terms.

misconceptions.description: Drops or mishandles the alternating signs in (a − b)ⁿ.
misconceptions.signal: All terms positive in the expansion of (x − 2y)⁷; or negates every term.
misconceptions.remedy: Rewrite (a − b)ⁿ as (a + (−b))ⁿ and carry (−b)^r as a unit; the sign is then (−1)^r, negative exactly for odd r. Check the last term's sign against a quick parity argument.

misconceptions.description: Applies the exponent only to the variable, not the whole term: treats (2x)³ as 2x³.
misconceptions.signal: Coefficient answers off by powers of 2 or 3 in expansions like (2x + 3)⁵.
misconceptions.remedy: Force bracket discipline: write every general term as nCr (2x)^(n−r) (3)^r with brackets intact, and evaluate the numeric parts in a separate line before combining.

real_world_hooks: Pascal's triangle appears in Pingala's ancient Indian prosody (Meru Prastara) — counting syllable patterns
Compound interest growth (1 + r)ⁿ and quick approximations like (1.01)¹⁰
Probability of k heads in n coin tosses uses binomial coefficients
Genetics: offspring trait combinations follow binomial patterns
teaching.video_search: binomial theorem general term pascal triangle class 11

questions.prompt: How many terms are there in the expansion of (x + y)⁴?

options.diagnosis: Computed 2⁴ — confused the VALUE of (1+1)⁴ (sum of coefficients) with the number of terms.
Off-by-one in the other direction (n + 2); knows there's a '+1' somewhere but misplaced it.

questions.explanation: (x + y)ⁿ expands into terms for r = 0, 1, ..., n — that's n + 1 terms. For n = 4: x⁴, 4x³y, 6x²y², 4xy³, y⁴ — five terms.

questions.prompt: The coefficient of x² in the expansion of (x + 2)⁵ is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied 5C2 by 2 instead of 2³; applied the wrong power to the constant.

questions.explanation: General term: 5Cr x^(5−r) 2^r. For x² we need 5 − r = 2, so r = 3: T₄ = 5C3 · x² · 2³ = 10 × 8 × x² = 80x². Forgetting the 2³ gives 10; using r = 2 (off-by-one) gives 5C2·2² = 40.

questions.prompt: The 4th term in the expansion of (x − 2y)⁷ is:
questions.explanation: T₄ = T(3+1) = 7C3 x⁴ (−2y)³ = 35 · x⁴ · (−8y³) = −280x⁴y³. The whole bracket (−2y) is cubed — giving −8, not −2 — and r = 3 (not 4) for the fourth term.

questions.prompt: In the expansion of (a + b)ⁿ the coefficients read the same forwards and backwards, e.g. 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 for n = 4. What is the fundamental reason for this symmetry?

options.text: nCr = nC(n−r): choosing which r of the n brackets contribute a b is the same count as choosing which n − r contribute an a
Because (a + b)ⁿ = aⁿ + bⁿ, and the two end terms aⁿ and bⁿ mirror each other, forcing the whole row to be symmetric
It is a pattern that happens to hold for small n only; for large enough n the middle coefficients stop matching up in pairs
options.diagnosis: Treats Pascal-triangle symmetry as a small-case accident; nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!) is visibly unchanged when r is replaced by n − r, for EVERY n.

options.text: Because the expansion contains exactly n terms, an even count, so pairing the first with the last always matches coefficients

questions.explanation: Each term of (a + b)ⁿ comes from choosing, in each of the n brackets, either a or b. The coefficient of aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ counts the ways to pick WHICH r brackets supply the b — that is nCr. But naming the r brackets that give b is exactly the same act as naming the n − r brackets that give a, so nCr = nC(n−r): the coefficient of aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ equals the coefficient of aʳbⁿ⁻ʳ, and the row is symmetric. (Algebraically, n!/(r!(n−r)!) is unchanged under r ↔ n − r. Note the expansion has n + 1 terms, not n.)

micros.title: Pascal's Triangle and Binomial Coefficients
micros.description: Expanding (a+b)², (a+b)³ by hand to watch cross terms appear, reading coefficients from Pascal's triangle, and identifying each row entry as nCr.
outcomes: Can build Pascal's triangle and match row n to the coefficients of (a+b)ⁿ
Can explain via small cases why (a+b)ⁿ ≠ aⁿ + bⁿ

micros.title: The Binomial Theorem for Positive Integral n
micros.description: The full statement (a+b)ⁿ = Σ nCr a^(n−r) b^r and writing complete expansions, tracking how powers of a fall while powers of b rise, always summing to n.
outcomes: Can write the complete expansion of (a+b)ⁿ for small n with correct coefficients and exponents
Can verify an expansion numerically, e.g. sum of coefficients = 2ⁿ at a = b = 1

question.prompt: Which of the following equals (x + y)³?

options.diagnosis: Middle terms have the wrong degree — every term of (x+y)³ must have total degree 3, but 3xy has degree 2.
Term pattern right, coefficients missing — the middle coefficients 3, 3 come from Pascal's row 1 3 3 1.

question.explanation: (x + y)³ = x³ + 3x²y + 3xy² + y³, coefficients 1 3 3 1 from Pascal's triangle. Dropping the cross terms (x³ + y³) fails instantly at x = y = 1: (1+1)³ = 8, but 1 + 1 = 2.

micros.title: The General Term T(r+1)
micros.description: Using T(r+1) = nCr a^(n−r) b^r to reach any term directly: the k-th term corresponds to r = k − 1, since the first term has r = 0.
outcomes: Can find a specified term of an expansion via the general term without expanding everything
Can find the term containing a given power of x by solving for r

question.prompt: The 5th term in the expansion of (x + y)⁷ is:

options.diagnosis: Used r = 5, reading 'the 5th term' as 'r = 5'; T₅ needs r = 4 because counting starts at r = 0.
Doubly off: r = 2 was used; T₃ = 21x⁵y², two positions before the required term.

question.explanation: T(r+1) with r = 4: T₅ = 7C4 x^(7−4) y⁴ = 35x³y⁴. The first term is r = 0, so the 5th term takes r = 4 — off-by-one is the standard trap (r = 3 gives T₄ = 35x⁴y³).

micros.title: Expansions with Signs and Coefficients
micros.description: Handling (x − 2y)ⁿ and (2x + 3)ⁿ: carrying (−b)^r as a unit so signs alternate as (−1)^r, and raising the WHOLE bracket (2x)^k, not just the variable.
outcomes: Can compute any term of expansions like (x − 2y)⁷ with the correct sign
Can find coefficients in expansions like (2x − 1)⁵, applying the power to the full 2x

question.prompt: The coefficient of x³ in the expansion of (2x − 1)⁵ is:

options.diagnosis: Used 2² instead of 2³ — the exponent on the bracket (2x) slipped by one.

question.explanation: General term: 5Cr (2x)^(5−r) (−1)^r. For x³, 5 − r = 3 so r = 2: 5C2 · 2³ · (−1)² = 10 × 8 × 1 = 80. The sign is (+) because r is even, and the 2 is cubed along with x — writing (2x)³ as 2x³ gives the wrong 20.

micros.title: Counting Terms and Middle Terms
micros.description: An expansion of (a+b)ⁿ has n + 1 terms; locating the single middle term for even n and the two middle terms for odd n, including expansions like (x + 1/x)ⁿ.
outcomes: Can state the number of terms and identify which position(s) are middle
Can compute middle terms, simplifying powers when the terms involve 1/x

question.prompt: The middle term in the expansion of (x + 1/x)⁶ is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the powers as x³·x³ = x⁶; the 1/x contributes x⁻³, so exponents ADD to 3 + (−3) = 0.
Doubled the coefficient believing there are two middle terms to combine; even n = 6 has exactly one middle term.

question.explanation: (x + 1/x)⁶ has 7 terms, so the middle is the 4th: T₄ = 6C3 x³ (1/x)³ = 20 · x³ · x⁻³ = 20 — a constant. Thinking the expansion has 6 terms leads to taking the 3rd term, 6C2 x⁴ x⁻² = 15x².

nodes.title: Sequences and Series: AP, GP, AM-GM, Special Sums
nodes.description: Sequences follow rules; series add them up. Building on arithmetic progressions, you now master geometric progressions — nth term arⁿ⁻¹, finite sums, and the beautiful infinite sum a/(1−r) when |r| < 1 — plus the AM ≥ GM inequality and formulas for Σn, Σn², Σn³. Growth by a constant ratio is the mathematics of compound interest, population growth and radioactive decay.
learning_outcomes: Can identify whether a sequence is an AP, a GP or neither, and find common difference/ratio
Can compute the nth term and the sum of n terms of a GP, and insert geometric means
Can determine when an infinite GP has a finite sum and compute S∞ = a/(1−r)
Can apply AM ≥ GM for two positive numbers and use Σn, Σn², Σn³ to evaluate special series

misconceptions.description: Applies AP formulas to a GP (or vice versa): uses a + (n−1)d on a sequence that multiplies.
misconceptions.signal: For 3, 6, 12, ... writes the 10th term as 3 + 9×3; treats the ratio as a difference.
misconceptions.remedy: Train the first move: compute both consecutive differences AND consecutive ratios for the first three terms; only one will be constant. Say the recipe aloud: 'constant difference → add; constant ratio → multiply'.

misconceptions.description: Off-by-one in term formulas: uses arⁿ or a + nd instead of arⁿ⁻¹ or a + (n−1)d.
misconceptions.signal: Answers are exactly one factor of r (or one d) too large; the 1st term formula gives the 2nd term.
misconceptions.remedy: Test every formula at n = 1: it must return a itself. Build the pattern from a table (term 1: a·r⁰, term 2: a·r¹, ...) so the exponent 'n−1' is seen as 'number of jumps from the start'.

misconceptions.description: Believes every infinite GP has a finite sum, applying a/(1−r) even when |r| ≥ 1.
misconceptions.signal: Computes S∞ for 2 + 4 + 8 + ... as 2/(1−2) = −2 and accepts a negative 'sum' of positive terms.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student add partial sums of 2 + 4 + 8 + ... and watch them explode, then of 8 + 4 + 2 + ... and watch them settle. Make '|r| < 1?' a mandatory pre-flight check before S∞, and celebrate the absurd −2 as a warning story.

misconceptions.description: Uses AM ≥ GM without checking positivity, or believes AM = GM for any pair.
misconceptions.signal: Applies AM-GM to negative numbers; claims (a+b)/2 = √(ab) generally.
misconceptions.remedy: Compute both means for pairs like (1, 9) → AM 5, GM 3 to see strict inequality; identify equality holds only when the numbers are equal; show √(ab) is not even real for a = −1, b = 4.

real_world_hooks: The rice-on-a-chessboard legend: doubling grains is a GP that bankrupts a king
Compound interest and SIP mutual-fund growth are GPs
A ball bouncing to 3/4 of its height each time: total distance is an infinite GP
Viral videos and chain messages: each share triggers r more shares
Radioactive decay and drug concentration in the bloodstream
teaching.video_search: geometric progression sum infinite gp class 11

questions.prompt: The 10th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, 24, ... is:

options.diagnosis: Computed 2⁹ but forgot to multiply by the first term a = 3.

questions.explanation: a = 3, r = 2, so T₁₀ = ar⁹ = 3 × 2⁹ = 3 × 512 = 1536. Using r¹⁰ gives 3072 (off-by-one), and treating the sequence as an AP with 'd = 3' gives 3 + 9×3 = 30.

questions.prompt: The sum of the first 20 terms of the AP with first term 2 and common difference 3 is:

options.diagnosis: Used n instead of n/2 in Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n−1)d]; forgot to halve.
Halved twice — applied n/2 and then divided the final answer by 2 again.

questions.explanation: S₂₀ = (20/2)[2(2) + 19(3)] = 10 × (4 + 57) = 10 × 61 = 610. Using 20 jumps (20×3) instead of 19 gives 640; the n/2 factor comes from pairing terms, and must appear exactly once.

questions.prompt: The sum to infinity of the series 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + ... is:

options.diagnosis: Believes any infinite series must diverge; hasn't internalised convergence for |r| < 1.
Added only the displayed terms (8 + 4 + 2) — computed a partial sum, not the limit.
Multiplied by (1 − r) instead of dividing: computed a(1 − r) = 8 × 1/2.

questions.explanation: Here a = 8 and r = 1/2 with |r| < 1, so S∞ = a/(1 − r) = 8/(1 − 1/2) = 16. Geometrically: 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 0.5 + ... creeps up to, but never passes, 16 — the halves exactly fill the gap.

micros.title: Arithmetic Progressions: Recap and Sigma View
micros.description: Consolidating a + (n−1)d and Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n−1)d], testing every formula at n = 1, and meeting Σ notation for writing series compactly.
outcomes: Can find the nth term and sum of an AP and check formulas at n = 1
Can expand and evaluate simple sigma expressions like Σ(2k + 1)

micros.title: Geometric Progressions and the nth Term
micros.description: Recognising constant-ratio sequences via the difference-vs-ratio test, and the nth term arⁿ⁻¹ where the exponent counts jumps from the first term.
outcomes: Can decide whether a sequence is an AP, a GP or neither by testing differences and ratios
Can compute any term of a GP with arⁿ⁻¹, verifying the formula returns a at n = 1

question.prompt: The 8th term of the GP 2, 6, 18, 54, ... is:

options.diagnosis: Computed 3⁷ but forgot to multiply by the first term a = 2.

question.explanation: a = 2, r = 3, so T₈ = ar⁷ = 2 × 3⁷ = 2 × 2187 = 4374. Using r⁸ gives 13122 (off-by-one in jumps); treating the ratio 3 as a common difference gives 2 + 7×3 = 23.

micros.title: Sum of n Terms of a GP
micros.description: Deriving Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) by the multiply-and-subtract trick, applying it to doubling stories like the chessboard legend, and the special case r = 1.
outcomes: Can compute finite GP sums and reproduce the multiply-by-r derivation
Can handle the r = 1 case, where Sₙ = na

micros.title: Geometric Means
micros.description: The geometric mean √(ab) of two positive numbers, inserting k geometric means between two numbers, and GM as the middle term of a three-term GP.
outcomes: Can compute the GM of two positive numbers and insert geometric means between them
Can use the three-term GP trick a/r, a, ar in problems

micros.title: Infinite GP: Convergence and S∞
micros.description: Watching partial sums settle when |r| < 1 versus explode when |r| ≥ 1; the formula S∞ = a/(1 − r) and its mandatory pre-flight check |r| < 1.
outcomes: Can decide whether an infinite GP has a finite sum before computing anything
Can compute S∞ = a/(1 − r) for convergent GPs, including bouncing-ball style applications

question.prompt: The sum to infinity of the series 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + ... is:

options.text: It does not exist — the series diverges

options.diagnosis: Added only the four displayed terms — a partial sum, not the infinite sum.
Assumed later terms 'don't matter' and kept the first term; here the terms GROW, so they matter more and more.

question.explanation: Here r = 2 with |r| ≥ 1: partial sums 2, 6, 14, 30, ... explode without bound, so no finite sum exists. Blindly applying a/(1 − r) = 2/(1 − 2) = −2 produces a negative 'sum' of positive terms — the formula's absurd output when its |r| < 1 condition is ignored.

micros.title: The AM–GM Inequality
micros.description: For positive numbers, (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab) with equality only when a = b; proving it from (√a − √b)² ≥ 0 and using it for quick min-max facts.
outcomes: Can compute AM and GM of a positive pair and verify AM ≥ GM
Can state the positivity requirement and the exact equality condition

question.prompt: The AM and GM of the numbers 4 and 16 are, respectively:

options.diagnosis: Computed both means correctly but swapped their names; the AM of unequal numbers is always the LARGER of the two.
Took half the difference (16 − 4)/2 = 6 for the AM; the arithmetic mean averages the SUM.

question.explanation: AM = (4 + 16)/2 = 10; GM = √(4 × 16) = √64 = 8. As guaranteed by AM ≥ GM, 10 > 8 — equality would need the two numbers to be equal.

micros.title: Special Sums: Σn, Σn², Σn³
micros.description: The closed forms n(n+1)/2, n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 and [n(n+1)/2]², and combining them with sigma algebra to sum series like Σ k(k + 2).
outcomes: Can evaluate Σn, Σn² and Σn³ for a given n
Can split a polynomial summand with sigma linearity and evaluate the pieces

question.prompt: The value of 1² + 2² + 3² + ... + 10² is:

options.diagnosis: Computed (1 + 2 + ... + 10)² = 55² — that is Σn³'s formula shape, not Σn².
Summed the numbers themselves (Σn), never squaring them.
Used n(n+1)(2n+1)/3 — divided by 3 instead of 6, exactly double the true sum.

question.explanation: Σn² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 = 10 × 11 × 21/6 = 2310/6 = 385. Note 55² = 3025 is Σn³ for n = 10 — the 'square of the sum', a different beast from the 'sum of the squares'.

nodes.title: Straight Lines: Slope, Forms of Equations, Distance
nodes.description: Coordinate geometry turns lines into equations: slope measures steepness as tan of the inclination, and a line can be written in point-slope, two-point, slope-intercept, intercept or general form. Parallel lines share slopes; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1; and the distance from a point to a line has a crisp formula. This algebra-geometry dictionary is the foundation for conic sections, calculus tangents, and linear programming.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the slope of a line from two points or from its inclination, and interpret zero vs undefined slope
Can write the equation of a line in point-slope, slope-intercept, two-point, intercept and general forms and convert between them
Can apply parallelism (equal slopes) and perpendicularity (m₁m₂ = −1) conditions
Can compute the distance from a point to a line and the distance between parallel lines

misconceptions.description: Confuses zero slope with undefined slope: thinks a vertical line has slope 0.
misconceptions.signal: Writes m = 0 for x = 3, or tries y = mx + c form for a vertical line.
misconceptions.remedy: Walk the line physically: flat road = zero slope (no rise), sheer wall = can't walk it, rise/run divides by zero. Pair the graphs of y = 2 and x = 3 and compute rise/run for each from two actual points.

misconceptions.description: Thinks perpendicular lines have equal (or merely reciprocal) slopes instead of m₁m₂ = −1.
misconceptions.signal: Gives the same slope, or the reciprocal without the sign flip, for a perpendicular line.
misconceptions.remedy: Rotate a set square on a coordinate grid: as one arm's slope is 2/3, measure the other's as −3/2. Verify m₁ × m₂ = −1 numerically for several drawn pairs before using it abstractly.

misconceptions.description: Inverts slope as run/rise: Δx/Δy instead of Δy/Δx.
misconceptions.signal: Slope answers are reciprocals of the correct value; steep lines get small slopes.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor slope to meaning: 'how much y changes per unit of x' — like speed is distance per time, not time per distance. Check against steepness intuition: a near-vertical line must have LARGE |m|.

misconceptions.description: Reads slope off an unsolved general form: for 2x + 3y = 6 takes m = 2 (the x-coefficient).
misconceptions.signal: States the slope of ax + by + c = 0 as a, skipping the rearrangement to y = mx + c.
misconceptions.remedy: Make 'solve for y first' a reflex, then derive the shortcut m = −a/b once and verify it against two rearranged examples so the sign and ratio are understood, not guessed.

real_world_hooks: Ramp gradients for wheelchair access (building codes specify maximum slope)
Taxi/auto fare vs distance: slope = rate per km, intercept = base fare
Railway gradients through the Ghats expressed as 1 in 40
Straight-line depreciation of a laptop's value over years
Cricket run-rate charts: required rate as the slope of a chase line
teaching.video_search: straight lines slope forms of equation distance from point class 11

questions.prompt: The slope of the line through the points (1, 2) and (3, 8) is:

options.diagnosis: Computed the rise (8 − 2) but never divided by the run; incomplete formula.
Mixed the subtraction order — used (8 − 2)/(1 − 3); consistency of order slipped.

questions.explanation: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = (8 − 2)/(3 − 1) = 6/2 = 3. The coordinate order must match in numerator and denominator, and the ratio is rise over run — not run over rise.

questions.prompt: The slope of a line PERPENDICULAR to the line 2x + 3y = 6 is:

options.diagnosis: Took the reciprocal but mishandled the sign flip; m₁m₂ = (−2/3)(−3/2) = +1 ≠ −1.

questions.explanation: Rearranged: y = (−2/3)x + 2, so the given slope is −2/3. Perpendicular slope = negative reciprocal = 3/2 (check: (−2/3)(3/2) = −1 ✓). Reading m = 2 straight off 2x + 3y = 6 leads to the wrong −1/2.

questions.prompt: The distance of the point (3, −5) from the line 3x − 4y − 26 = 0 is:

options.diagnosis: Forgot to divide by √(a² + b²) = 5; used only the numerator |3x₁ − 4y₁ − 26|.
Sign slip substituting y = −5: computed 9 − 20 − 26 instead of 9 + 20 − 26.
Used +26 instead of −26 in the numerator: |9 + 20 + 26|/5 = 55/5 = 11. The sign of the constant term slipped, but the division by √(a² + b²) was done correctly.

questions.explanation: d = |3(3) − 4(−5) − 26| / √(3² + (−4)²) = |9 + 20 − 26| / 5 = 3/5. Watch the double negative: −4 × (−5) = +20, and always divide by √(a² + b²).

micros.title: Slope from Two Points and Inclination
micros.description: Slope as rise over run, m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), tied to the inclination by m = tan θ — how much y changes per unit of x, like speed is distance per time.
outcomes: Can compute the slope through two points with consistent coordinate order
Can relate slope to inclination via m = tan θ and to steepness intuition

question.prompt: The slope of the line through (2, 3) and (6, 11) is:

options.diagnosis: Computed the rise 11 − 3 but never divided by the run; the formula is a ratio.
Mixed subtraction order between numerator and denominator — (11 − 3)/(2 − 6); order must match.

question.explanation: m = (11 − 3)/(6 − 2) = 8/4 = 2. Slope is rise over run — Δy per unit Δx; inverting it to run/rise makes steep lines look shallow.

micros.title: Horizontal and Vertical Lines
micros.description: y = c has slope 0 (flat road); x = k has UNDEFINED slope (rise/run divides by zero) and cannot be written as y = mx + c at all.
outcomes: Can write equations of horizontal and vertical lines through a given point
Can explain the difference between zero slope and undefined slope from rise/run

question.prompt: The slope of the vertical line x = 4 is:

options.diagnosis: Read the constant in the equation as the slope; 4 is where the line crosses the x-axis.
Guessed a 'neutral' slope; compute rise/run from two actual points like (4, 0) and (4, 5) to see the zero denominator.

question.explanation: Two points on x = 4, say (4, 0) and (4, 5), give slope (5 − 0)/(4 − 4) = 5/0 — division by zero, so the slope is undefined. Zero slope belongs to the flat HORIZONTAL lines y = c.

micros.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Slope Conditions
micros.description: Parallel lines share slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes multiplying to −1 (negative reciprocals), verified numerically before being used abstractly.
outcomes: Can test parallelism and perpendicularity from slopes
Can find the slope of a line perpendicular to a given line and verify m₁m₂ = −1

question.prompt: A line is perpendicular to y = 4x − 1. Its slope is:

options.diagnosis: Negated without taking the reciprocal; check: 4 × (−4) = −16 ≠ −1.

question.explanation: Perpendicular slopes satisfy m₁m₂ = −1, so m₂ = −1/4 (negative reciprocal of 4). Check: 4 × (−1/4) = −1 ✓. Equal slopes (4) would make the lines parallel, and 1/4 forgets the sign flip: 4 × 1/4 = +1.

micros.title: Point-Slope, Two-Point and Slope-Intercept Forms
micros.description: Writing a line's equation from a point and slope (y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)), from two points, or from slope and y-intercept, and moving fluidly between these forms.
outcomes: Can write the equation of a line from point + slope or from two points
Can convert any of these forms into y = mx + c and read off m and c

micros.title: General Form and Intercepts
micros.description: The general form ax + by + c = 0: extracting slope m = −a/b by solving for y (never by grabbing a coefficient), and the intercept form x/a + y/b = 1.
outcomes: Can rearrange ax + by + c = 0 to find its slope and intercepts
Can write a line from given x- and y-intercepts using the intercept form

question.prompt: The slope of the line 3x + 6y = 12 is:

options.diagnosis: Took −a alone, forgetting to divide by b; the shortcut is m = −a/b, a ratio.
Ratio right, sign lost while moving 3x across; rearrange fully: y = −x/2 + 2.

question.explanation: Solve for y: 6y = −3x + 12, so y = −(1/2)x + 2 — slope −1/2. Reading the x-coefficient (3) straight off the unsolved form skips the rearrangement that the slope definition demands.

micros.title: Distance from a Point to a Line
micros.description: The formula d = |ax₁ + by₁ + c|/√(a² + b²), plus the distance between parallel lines — the absolute value and the √(a² + b²) denominator are both non-negotiable.
outcomes: Can compute the perpendicular distance from a point to a line in general form
Can compute the distance between two parallel lines

question.prompt: The distance of the origin from the line 3x + 4y − 10 = 0 is:

options.diagnosis: Used only the numerator |3(0) + 4(0) − 10|; the denominator √(a² + b²) = 5 was skipped.
Kept the sign of −10 through to the answer; the absolute value makes every distance non-negative.
Divided by a + b = 7 instead of √(a² + b²) = √25 = 5.

question.explanation: d = |3(0) + 4(0) − 10|/√(3² + 4²) = 10/5 = 2. Both guards matter: the absolute value keeps distance positive, and the denominator is the square ROOT of a² + b², not a + b.

nodes.title: Conic Sections: Circle, Parabola, Ellipse, Hyperbola
nodes.description: Slice a double cone at different angles and you get circles, parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas — a single family of curves with standard equations: x² + y² = r², y² = 4ax, x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. You will extract centres, foci, vertices, directrices, axes and eccentricity from these equations. Conics are the shapes of planetary orbits, satellite dishes, headlight reflectors and suspension-bridge cables.
learning_outcomes: Can write the equation of a circle from centre and radius, and complete the square to find them from the general form
Can identify the focus, directrix, axis and latus rectum of a parabola in any of the four standard orientations
Can find vertices, foci, eccentricity and axes lengths for ellipses and hyperbolas in standard form, using c² = a² − b² or c² = a² + b² appropriately
Can classify which conic a given second-degree equation in standard form represents

misconceptions.description: Mixes the focal relations: uses c² = a² + b² for an ellipse (or c² = a² − b² for a hyperbola).
misconceptions.signal: Gets foci outside the ellipse, e.g. (±√34, 0) for x²/25 + y²/9 = 1.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie the relation to geometry: an ellipse's foci are INSIDE (c < a, so subtract); a hyperbola's are beyond the vertices (c > a, so add). Sanity-check every answer by plotting: elliptical foci must lie within the curve.

misconceptions.description: In y² = 4ax, reads the coefficient 4a as a itself, misplacing focus and directrix by a factor of 4.
misconceptions.signal: For y² = 12x states the focus as (12, 0) instead of (3, 0).
misconceptions.remedy: Always solve 4a = coefficient explicitly as a labelled step. Verify with the latus rectum: the chord through the claimed focus should have length 4a = 12 — plugging x = 3 gives y = ±6 ✓, x = 12 fails.

misconceptions.description: Assumes any equation containing both x² and y² is a circle.
misconceptions.signal: Calls x² + 2y² = 4 or x² − y² = 4 a circle.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort a stack of equations by the checklist: equal coefficients & plus sign → circle; unequal & plus → ellipse; minus → hyperbola; only one square → parabola. Graph one of each so the algebraic tags map to distinct shapes.

misconceptions.description: Detaches eccentricity from shape: accepts e > 1 for an ellipse or e = 1 for one, mixing the ranges up.
misconceptions.signal: Reports an ellipse with e = 1.3 without flinching; can't say which conic e = 1 signals.
misconceptions.remedy: Build the e-dial: e = 0 circle → 0 < e < 1 ellipse → e = 1 parabola → e > 1 hyperbola, with a morphing animation. Interpret e as 'how far from circular', so e > 1 for an ellipse becomes visibly impossible.

real_world_hooks: ISRO transfer orbits: satellites move on ellipses with Earth at a focus
Dish TV antennas and solar cookers are parabolic — parallel rays meet at the focus
A cricket ball's flight is (nearly) a parabola
Torch beam on a wall: tilt it and watch circle → ellipse → parabola → hyperbola
LORAN ship navigation uses hyperbolas of constant time-difference
teaching.video_search: conic sections parabola ellipse hyperbola standard equations class 11

questions.prompt: The focus of the parabola y² = 12x is at:

options.diagnosis: Right value of a but wrong axis — y² = 4ax opens along the x-axis, not the y-axis.
Direction slip: positive coefficient means the parabola opens right, focus on the positive x-axis.

questions.explanation: Compare y² = 12x with y² = 4ax: 4a = 12, so a = 3. The parabola opens rightward with focus (a, 0) = (3, 0) and directrix x = −3.

questions.prompt: The foci of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 are:

options.diagnosis: Used a itself as the focal distance — those are the vertices, not the foci.
Correct c but wrong axis; the major axis lies along x since 25 > 9.

questions.explanation: a² = 25, b² = 9, and for an ellipse c² = a² − b² = 16, so c = 4. The major axis is along x (larger denominator under x²), giving foci (±4, 0). Adding instead of subtracting (c = √34 > a) would absurdly place the foci outside the ellipse.

questions.prompt: The equation x² + 2y² = 4 represents:

options.diagnosis: Associated 'two squared terms with different coefficients' with hyperbola; the minus sign, not unequal coefficients, is the hyperbola's signature.
Treats any second-degree curve as a parabola; a parabola has exactly ONE squared variable.

questions.explanation: Divide by 4: x²/4 + y²/2 = 1 — a sum of two squared terms with UNEQUAL positive denominators, i.e. an ellipse (a² = 4, b² = 2). A circle needs equal coefficients; a hyperbola needs a minus sign; a parabola has only one squared variable.

micros.title: Circle: Centre-Radius Form
micros.description: The equation (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² from the distance definition of a circle; writing equations from centre and radius and reading them back, minding the sign of h, k.
outcomes: Can write the equation of a circle from its centre and radius
Can read centre and radius from centre-radius form, handling signs like (x + 2)²

micros.title: Circle: General Form and Completing the Square
micros.description: Converting x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 to centre-radius form by completing the square, finding centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c).
outcomes: Can complete the square to find the centre and radius from a general-form circle
Can determine when a general second-degree equation fails to be a real circle (g² + f² − c < 0)

question.prompt: The centre and radius of the circle x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 = 0 are:

options.diagnosis: Sign flip on the centre: completing the square gives (x − 2)² and (y + 3)², so the centre is (2, −3).
Used the full coefficients instead of halving them; the centre is (−g, −f) with 2g = −4, 2f = 6.
Subtracted 12 instead of adding when moving it across: r² = 4 + 9 + 12 = 25, not 4 + 9 − 12.

question.explanation: Complete the square: (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 12 + 4 + 9 = 25, so centre (2, −3) and radius 5. Each bracket's sign is opposite to the centre coordinate, and the constant moves to the right side with its sign reversed.

micros.title: Parabola: Focus, Directrix and Latus Rectum
micros.description: The four standard parabolas y² = ±4ax, x² = ±4ay: solving 4a = coefficient as an explicit step, then locating the focus, directrix, axis and latus rectum (length 4a).
outcomes: Can identify orientation, focus and directrix for any of the four standard parabolas
Can use the latus rectum to sanity-check the focus position

question.prompt: The focus of the parabola y² = 16x is at:

options.diagnosis: Right a, wrong axis — y² = 4ax opens along the x-axis; x² = 4ay is the one with focus on the y-axis.
Direction slip: the positive coefficient means the parabola opens right, so the focus sits on the positive x-axis.

question.explanation: Compare with y² = 4ax: 4a = 16 gives a = 4, so the focus is (4, 0) and the directrix x = −4. Reading the coefficient 16 as a itself misplaces the focus by a factor of 4.

micros.title: Ellipse: Standard Form and Foci
micros.description: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with a > b: vertices, major/minor axes, and the focal relation c² = a² − b² (subtract, because the foci sit INSIDE, c < a); eccentricity e = c/a.
outcomes: Can extract vertices, foci, axis lengths and eccentricity from a standard ellipse
Can determine the major axis direction from which denominator is larger

question.prompt: The foci of the ellipse x²/16 + y²/9 = 1 are:

options.diagnosis: Gave the vertices (±a, 0); the foci lie strictly between centre and vertices, at distance c = √7.
Correct c but wrong axis — the major axis follows the LARGER denominator, here under x².

question.explanation: a² = 16, b² = 9; for an ellipse c² = a² − b² = 7, so foci (±√7, 0) on the major (x) axis. Adding to get c = 5 > a = 4 would put the foci OUTSIDE the ellipse — geometrically impossible.

micros.title: Hyperbola: Standard Form and Foci
micros.description: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1: two branches, vertices (±a, 0), and the focal relation c² = a² + b² (add, because the foci lie BEYOND the vertices, c > a); eccentricity e = c/a > 1.
outcomes: Can extract vertices, foci, transverse axis and eccentricity from a standard hyperbola
Can justify c² = a² + b² geometrically (foci beyond vertices) and contrast it with the ellipse

question.prompt: The foci of the hyperbola x²/9 − y²/16 = 1 are:

options.diagnosis: Gave the vertices (±a, 0); a hyperbola's foci lie BEYOND its vertices, at c = 5 > 3.
Correct c, wrong axis — the transverse axis follows the POSITIVE squared term, here x².

question.explanation: a² = 9, b² = 16; for a hyperbola c² = a² + b² = 25, so c = 5 and the foci are (±5, 0). Subtracting (ellipse habit) gives √7 < a, which would wrongly pull the foci inside the vertices.

micros.title: Eccentricity: One Dial for All Conics
micros.description: Eccentricity as 'distance from circular': e = 0 circle, 0 < e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola — one parameter morphing the whole conic family.
outcomes: Can compute e = c/a for ellipses and hyperbolas and check it lands in the right range
Can name the conic from its eccentricity alone

question.prompt: A conic section has eccentricity e = 0.5. It must be:

options.diagnosis: A circle is the special case e = 0 exactly; any 0 < e < 1 has already stretched into a proper ellipse.

question.explanation: The eccentricity dial reads: e = 0 circle → 0 < e < 1 ellipse → e = 1 parabola → e > 1 hyperbola. With e = 0.5 strictly between 0 and 1, the conic is an ellipse — hyperbolas require e > 1, never less.

micros.title: Classifying a Conic from Its Equation
micros.description: The checklist for second-degree equations: equal positive squared coefficients → circle; unequal, both positive → ellipse; opposite signs → hyperbola; one squared variable → parabola.
outcomes: Can classify equations like x² + 2y² = 4, x² − 4y² = 4 and y² = 6x at sight
Can normalise an equation (divide by the constant) into a standard form before extracting parameters

question.prompt: The equation x² − 4y² = 4 represents:

options.diagnosis: Ignored the minus sign — an ellipse needs BOTH squared terms positive; the minus is the hyperbola's signature.
A parabola has exactly ONE squared variable; this equation squares both x and y.

question.explanation: Divide by 4: x²/4 − y²/1 = 1 — a difference of squared terms, the standard hyperbola. Containing both x² and y² does not make an equation a circle; the signs and coefficients decide.

nodes.title: Introduction to Three-Dimensional Geometry
nodes.description: Adding a z-axis turns the coordinate plane into coordinate space: points become ordered triples (x, y, z), space splits into eight octants, and the familiar tools upgrade — distance becomes √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²) and the section formula gains a third coordinate. Thinking in 3D coordinates is the gateway to vectors, planes and lines in space, and to how GPS, drones and graphics engines locate anything in the world.
learning_outcomes: Can locate and interpret points (x, y, z), including which coordinate planes and octants they relate to
Can state the coordinates of points on the axes and coordinate planes (which coordinates vanish where)
Can compute the distance between two points in space and use it to classify triangles or verify collinearity
Can apply the section formula (internal division) and midpoint formula in 3D

misconceptions.description: Uses the 2D distance formula in 3D, silently dropping the z-term.
misconceptions.signal: Computes √(Δx² + Δy²) for points with different z-coordinates.
misconceptions.remedy: Derive the 3D formula as Pythagoras applied twice — the box diagonal: floor diagonal first, then up the wall. Have the student compute the diagonal of an actual room to make the third term unforgettable.

misconceptions.description: Mixes up which coordinate vanishes where: thinks a point on the xy-plane has x = 0 or y = 0 (rather than z = 0), or confuses distance-from-plane with distance-from-axis.
misconceptions.signal: Says (2, 3, 0) lies on the z-axis, or that the z-coordinate is the distance from the z-axis.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the classroom corner as the origin: two walls and the floor are the coordinate planes. Physically point: on the floor (xy-plane) you can move in x and y but z = 0. The 'missing' coordinate is the one measuring how far you've LEFT that plane.

misconceptions.description: Misapplies the section formula: swaps which endpoint gets which ratio part, or averages when a ratio is given.
misconceptions.signal: For a 2:1 division gets the point closer to the wrong end; uses the midpoint formula regardless of ratio.
misconceptions.remedy: Mark the segment on a number line first and estimate where 2:1 should fall (two-thirds of the way). The estimate then arbitrates between (2x₂ + x₁)/3 and (2x₁ + x₂)/3 — the ratio parts attach to the OPPOSITE endpoints.

real_world_hooks: The corner of your room as the origin: walls and floor are the coordinate planes
Drone delivery: latitude, longitude, altitude is an (x, y, z) triple
Air traffic control tracks planes in 3D coordinates
3D printers move a nozzle to (x, y, z) positions layer by layer
Chandrayaan's position relative to the lunar surface needs three numbers
teaching.video_search: three dimensional geometry octants distance formula class 11

questions.prompt: A point lies on the xy-plane. Which of its coordinates must be zero?

options.text: None — a point on a plane can have any coordinates
options.diagnosis: Hasn't connected 'lying on a coordinate plane' with a coordinate constraint at all; rebuild with the room-corner model.

questions.explanation: The xy-plane is the 'floor' containing the x- and y-axes; height above it is measured by z. Points on it have z = 0 — the vanishing coordinate is the one NOT named in the plane.

questions.prompt: The distance between the points (1, 2, 3) and (3, 5, 9) is:

options.diagnosis: Computed the sum of squared differences but forgot the final square root.
Squared the z-difference as 6×2 = 12 instead of 6² = 36; got √25 = 5.

questions.explanation: d = √((3−1)² + (5−2)² + (9−3)²) = √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7. Dropping the z-term gives √13 — the 2D shadow of the true distance.

questions.prompt: The point dividing the segment from A(2, −1, 3) to B(5, 2, 9) internally in the ratio 2 : 1 is:

options.diagnosis: Ignored the given ratio and computed the midpoint (1:1 division).
Used the EXTERNAL division formula (m·B − n·A)/(m − n) for an internal division.

questions.explanation: Internal division m:n = 2:1 from A to B: P = ((2·5 + 1·2)/3, (2·2 + 1·(−1))/3, (2·9 + 1·3)/3) = (4, 1, 7). Note P is two-thirds of the way to B, matching the 2:1 estimate; (3, 0, 5) is the 1:2 point — ratio attached to the wrong ends.

questions.prompt: Why does the distance formula become √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²) in three dimensions, rather than keeping the familiar 2D form √(Δx² + Δy²)?

options.text: It is Pythagoras applied twice: the floor diagonal has square Δx² + Δy², and this diagonal then forms a right triangle with the vertical change Δz
The Δz² term is only a safety margin; whenever two points are far apart horizontally, the 2D formula already gives their true distance in space
Because the z-coordinate of each point measures its distance from the z-axis, and that distance must enter the formula alongside Δx and Δy
Actually the vertical change should be added after the root, without squaring, giving √(Δx² + Δy²) + Δz as the full three-dimensional distance
options.diagnosis: Bolts the vertical leg on additively; perpendicular legs combine through their SQUARES (Pythagoras), and lengths only add when the segments are collinear.

questions.explanation: Think of the segment as the diagonal of a box. First walk the floor: the horizontal displacement is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs Δx and Δy, so its square is Δx² + Δy². That floor diagonal and the vertical rise Δz are perpendicular, so Pythagoras applies again: d² = (Δx² + Δy²) + Δz². Dropping Δz² only works when both points share the same z (m1), and the z-coordinate is a point's distance from the xy-PLANE, not from the z-axis (m2).

micros.title: Coordinate Axes and Octants
micros.description: Adding the z-axis: the room-corner model with three mutually perpendicular axes, ordered triples (x, y, z), and the eight octants determined by sign patterns.
outcomes: Can locate a point (x, y, z) relative to the room-corner model
Can name the octant of a point from the signs of its coordinates

micros.title: Points on Coordinate Planes and Axes
micros.description: Which coordinates vanish where: on the xy-plane z = 0, on an axis TWO coordinates vanish — the missing coordinate measures how far you have left that plane.
outcomes: Can state the zero-coordinate conditions for each coordinate plane and axis
Can find the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a coordinate plane or axis

question.prompt: The point (4, 0, 5) lies on:

options.diagnosis: An axis needs TWO zero coordinates; only y is zero here, which pins the point to a plane, not an axis.

question.explanation: y = 0 means the point has not left the xz-plane — the plane spanned by the x- and z-axes. The vanishing coordinate is the one NOT named in the plane; points on the y-axis would instead need x = z = 0.

micros.title: Distance Between Two Points in Space
micros.description: Deriving √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²) as Pythagoras applied twice — the box diagonal: floor diagonal first, then up the wall — and computing distances between points.
outcomes: Can compute the distance between two points in 3D including the z-term
Can reproduce the double-Pythagoras derivation with a room/box picture

question.prompt: The distance between the points (2, 3, 5) and (4, 3, 1) is:

options.diagnosis: Summed the squared differences but forgot the final square root.
Added the absolute coordinate differences 2 + 0 + 4; distance squares each difference before summing.

question.explanation: d = √((4−2)² + (3−3)² + (1−5)²) = √(4 + 0 + 16) = √20 = 2√5. Dropping the z-term (Δz = −4) leaves only √4 = 2 — the flat 2D shadow of the true 3D distance.

micros.title: Applications of the 3D Distance Formula
micros.description: Using distances to classify triangles (isosceles, equilateral, right-angled via Pythagoras), verify collinearity, and find points equidistant from given points.
outcomes: Can classify a triangle in space from its three side lengths
Can test collinearity by checking whether one distance equals the sum of the other two

micros.title: Section and Midpoint Formulas in 3D
micros.description: Internal division in ratio m:n gives ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m+n), ...) — the ratio parts attach to the OPPOSITE endpoints — with the midpoint as the 1:1 special case.
outcomes: Can find the point dividing a segment internally in a given ratio and the midpoint
Can estimate the answer's position first (e.g. 2:1 lands two-thirds along) to catch swapped ratios

question.prompt: The point dividing the segment from A(1, 2, 3) to B(4, 5, 6) internally in the ratio 1 : 2 is:

options.diagnosis: Computed the midpoint, ignoring the 1:2 ratio; the required point is only one-third of the way to B.
Used the EXTERNAL division formula (mB − nA)/(m − n) for an internal division.

question.explanation: P = ((1·4 + 2·1)/3, (1·5 + 2·2)/3, (1·6 + 2·3)/3) = (2, 3, 4) — one-third of the way from A to B, as a 1:2 split demands. (3, 4, 5) is the 2:1 point: the ratio parts got attached to the wrong endpoints.

nodes.title: Limits and Derivatives
nodes.description: Calculus begins here: a limit captures the value a function approaches — which may exist even where the function itself is undefined, as in (x²−4)/(x−2) at x = 2. The derivative is a limit of slopes of secants, giving the exact instantaneous rate of change and the slope of the tangent line. You will evaluate algebraic and trigonometric limits (including sin x/x → 1), differentiate from first principles, and use the sum, product and quotient rules. Every 'rate' in science — velocity, current, growth — is a derivative.
learning_outcomes: Can explain a limit intuitively via left- and right-hand approach, and evaluate limits by substitution where valid
Can resolve 0/0 forms by factoring, rationalising, or standard limits like lim (xⁿ−aⁿ)/(x−a) = naⁿ⁻¹ and lim sin x/x = 1
Can compute a derivative from first principles as the limit of a difference quotient
Can interpret the derivative as instantaneous rate of change and as the slope of the tangent line
Can differentiate polynomials and trigonometric functions using sum, product and quotient rules

misconceptions.description: Equates limit with function value: believes lim x→a f(x) is just f(a), and cannot exist if f(a) is undefined.
misconceptions.signal: Declares lim x→2 (x²−4)/(x−2) 'undefined because you can't put x = 2'.
misconceptions.remedy: Tabulate f at 1.9, 1.99, 1.999 and 2.1, 2.01, 2.001 and watch the values crowd around 4 while f(2) itself doesn't exist. Language shift: the limit is about the JOURNEY (approach), not the destination point.

misconceptions.description: Treats the 0/0 form as an answer: 'it equals 0', 'it equals 1', or 'the limit does not exist'.
misconceptions.signal: Stops at substitution, reports DNE or 0 whenever numerator and denominator both vanish.
misconceptions.remedy: Rebrand 0/0 as 'indeterminate = investigate further', never a verdict. Show three limits that are all 0/0 on substitution yet equal 4, 0 and ∞ respectively, proving the form alone decides nothing.

misconceptions.description: Differentiates products term-by-term: (fg)' = f'g'.
misconceptions.signal: Writes d/dx (x² sin x) = 2x cos x.
misconceptions.remedy: Counterexample first: (x · x)' = (x²)' = 2x, but f'g' = 1·1 = 1. Then motivate the product rule via the growing-rectangle picture (area change = f·Δg + g·Δf) and drill with the 'each factor takes a turn being differentiated' chant.

misconceptions.description: Confuses average rate (secant slope) with instantaneous rate (tangent slope), or computes slope as y/x from the origin.
misconceptions.signal: Answers rate questions with f(b)−f(a) over b−a when the instantaneous rate at a point is asked; divides f(a) by a.
misconceptions.remedy: Zoom-in animation: secants through shrinking intervals visibly rotate into the tangent. Speedometer vs trip-average analogy: 'what does the speedometer read AT this instant?' is the derivative question.

real_world_hooks: Speedometer vs average speed on a Mumbai–Pune drive: instantaneous vs average rate
A batsman's strike rate over the whole innings vs 'momentum' this over
ISRO rocket velocity as the derivative of altitude during launch
Zeno's paradox: how can approaching forever add up to arriving?
COVID case curves: 'the rate of new cases is slowing' is a statement about a derivative
teaching.video_search: limits and derivatives first principles tangent slope class 11

questions.prompt: Evaluate lim x→2 (x² − 4)/(x − 2).

options.diagnosis: Cancelled to x instead of x + 2 — factoring slip (x² − 4 = (x−2)(x+2)).

questions.explanation: Substitution gives 0/0 — indeterminate, so investigate: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = (x−2)(x+2)/(x−2) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2, and lim x→2 (x + 2) = 4. The function is undefined AT 2, yet its limit there exists and equals 4.

questions.prompt: The derivative of x² sin x is:

options.diagnosis: Differentiated only sin x and left x² as a passive constant; product rule not triggered.
Product rule structure right but inserted a minus — possibly contaminated by the quotient rule's numerator.

questions.explanation: Product rule: (fg)' = f'g + fg' with f = x², g = sin x: 2x sin x + x² cos x. Multiplying the separate derivatives (2x)(cos x) is the classic trap — check it fails even for x·x.

questions.prompt: Evaluate lim x→0 sin 4x / x.

options.diagnosis: Pattern-matched 'sin(something)/x = 1' without matching the arguments; the standard limit needs sin 4x over 4x.
Rescaled in the wrong direction — divided by 4 instead of multiplying.

questions.explanation: Write sin 4x/x = 4 · sin 4x/(4x). As x→0, 4x→0, so sin 4x/(4x) → 1, and the limit is 4 × 1 = 4. The standard limit sin θ/θ → 1 applies only when the SAME expression sits inside sin and underneath.

micros.title: Limit Intuition via Tables
micros.description: The limit as the value a function approaches: tabulating f(x) on both sides of a point and watching values crowd a target — which can exist even where f itself is undefined.
outcomes: Can estimate a limit numerically from two-sided tables
Can give an example where lim x→a f(x) exists although f(a) is undefined

question.prompt: Evaluate lim x→3 (x² − 9)/(x − 3).

options.text: It does not exist, because f(3) is undefined

options.diagnosis: Cancelled (x² − 9)/(x − 3) down to x instead of x + 3; refactor: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3).

question.explanation: For x ≠ 3, (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = x + 3, which approaches 6. The function has a hole AT x = 3, but the limit is about the approach, not the destination: values at 2.999 and 3.001 crowd 6.

micros.title: Limit Laws and Algebraic Evaluation
micros.description: Sum, product and quotient laws for limits; direct substitution for polynomials; and resolving 0/0 forms by factoring or rationalising — 0/0 means 'investigate', never a verdict.
outcomes: Can evaluate limits of polynomial and rational functions by substitution where valid
Can resolve 0/0 limits by factoring or by rationalising with a conjugate

micros.title: One-Sided Limits and Existence
micros.description: Left-hand and right-hand limits, and the existence criterion: the limit exists iff both one-sided limits exist and agree — tested on step-like functions such as |x|/x and [x].
outcomes: Can compute LHL and RHL at a point from a formula or graph
Can decide whether a two-sided limit exists and justify with both one-sided values

question.prompt: For f(x) = |x|/x (x ≠ 0), the limit lim x→0 f(x):

options.text: Does not exist, because LHL = −1 but RHL = +1

options.diagnosis: Checked only the right-hand side; for x < 0, |x|/x = −x/x = −1, so the two sides disagree.
Averaged the two one-sided values (−1 and 1); a limit must be a value BOTH sides approach, not a compromise.
Checked only the left-hand side; approach from the right gives +1.

question.explanation: For x > 0, f(x) = 1; for x < 0, f(x) = −1. The one-sided limits are +1 and −1 — they disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist. Existence requires both sides to agree on ONE value.

micros.title: Standard Limits: sin x/x and (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a)
micros.description: The two workhorse limits — sin x/x → 1 as x → 0 (x in radians) and (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) → naⁿ⁻¹ — and the rescaling discipline: sin kx must sit over kx before the limit applies.
outcomes: Can evaluate limits like sin 3x/2x and tan x/x by rescaling to the standard form
Can apply (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) → naⁿ⁻¹ including fractional n

question.prompt: Evaluate lim x→0 sin 3x / 2x.

options.diagnosis: Pattern-matched 'sin(anything)/x → 1'; the standard limit needs the SAME expression inside sin and underneath.
Rescaled in the wrong direction — the factor 3 from sin 3x multiplies, the 2 below divides.

question.explanation: sin 3x/2x = (3/2)·sin 3x/(3x). As x→0, sin 3x/(3x) → 1, so the limit is 3/2. Substituting x = 0 gives the indeterminate 0/0 — a signal to investigate, never the answer 0.

micros.title: The Derivative as Slope and Instantaneous Rate
