micros.description: Secant slopes over shrinking intervals rotating into the tangent: the derivative as the slope of the tangent line and the speedometer-reading instantaneous rate, versus the trip-average rate.
outcomes: Can distinguish average rate (secant slope) from instantaneous rate (tangent slope) in context
Can interpret f'(a) graphically as tangent slope and physically as a rate at one instant

question.prompt: A particle's position is s(t) = t² metres after t seconds. Its INSTANTANEOUS velocity at t = 3 is:

options.diagnosis: Reported the position s(3) = 9, not a rate; velocity asks how fast position is CHANGING.
Differentiated to 2t but then dropped the t; evaluate the derivative AT t = 3.

question.explanation: v(t) = s'(t) = 2t, so v(3) = 6 m/s — the speedometer reading at that instant. Dividing s(3)/3 = 3 gives the AVERAGE velocity over [0, 3], the secant slope from the origin, not the tangent slope at t = 3.

micros.title: Derivative from First Principles
micros.description: Computing f'(x) = lim h→0 [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h for polynomials and simple roots: expand carefully, cancel the h, THEN take the limit.
outcomes: Can differentiate x², x³ and 1/x from first principles, showing every step
Can explain why the h must be cancelled before letting h → 0

question.prompt: Using first principles, the derivative of f(x) = x² is lim h→0 [(x+h)² − x²]/h, which equals:

options.diagnosis: Simplified correctly but stopped before the final step — the limit h → 0 kills the +h.
Expanded (x+h)² as x² + h², leaving h²/h = h → 0; the cross term 2xh carries the whole derivative.
Halved somewhere in the algebra; expanding gives 2xh + h², and dividing by h leaves 2x + h → 2x.

question.explanation: (x+h)² − x² = 2xh + h², so the quotient is 2x + h, and the limit as h → 0 is 2x. Expanding (x+h)² as x² + h² (the distribution error) would leave only h²/h = h → 0 — a wrong derivative of 0.

micros.title: Power, Constant and Sum Rules
micros.description: The power rule d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹, constants passing through, derivatives of sums and differences — differentiating any polynomial term by term.
outcomes: Can differentiate polynomials like 3x⁴ − 2x + 7 fluently
Can differentiate sin x and cos x and combine them linearly with polynomials

question.prompt: The derivative of f(x) = 3x⁴ − 2x + 7 is:

options.diagnosis: The constant 7 survived differentiation; constants have zero rate of change.
Brought the exponent down without multiplying: d/dx x⁴ = 4x³, so the coefficient becomes 3 × 4 = 12.
Multiplied by the old exponent but forgot to reduce it by one; the power rule does both.

question.explanation: Term by term: d/dx 3x⁴ = 12x³, d/dx (−2x) = −2, d/dx 7 = 0. The power rule multiplies by the exponent AND lowers it: nxⁿ⁻¹.

micros.title: Product and Quotient Rules
micros.description: (fg)' = f'g + fg' — each factor takes a turn — and the quotient rule with its order-sensitive numerator; why (fg)' = f'g' fails even for x·x.
outcomes: Can differentiate products like x cos x and quotients like sin x/x correctly
Can produce the counterexample showing (fg)' ≠ f'g'

question.prompt: The derivative of x cos x is:

options.diagnosis: Differentiated only the cos factor, treating x as a constant passenger; both factors take a turn.
Product structure right, but d/dx cos x = −sin x — the minus went missing.

question.explanation: Product rule with f = x, g = cos x: (1)(cos x) + (x)(−sin x) = cos x − x sin x. Multiplying the separate derivatives (1)·(−sin x) = −sin x is the classic trap — it already fails for x·x, where it predicts 1 instead of 2x.

nodes.title: Statistics: Measures of Dispersion, Variance, Standard Deviation
nodes.description: Two datasets can share a mean yet behave completely differently — dispersion measures how spread out the data is. You will compute range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation for ungrouped and grouped data, and compare the consistency of two datasets using the coefficient of variation. Standard deviation is the workhorse of real analytics, from batting consistency to quality control and finance risk.
learning_outcomes: Can compute range, mean deviation (about mean or median), variance and standard deviation for ungrouped and grouped data
Can explain why deviations are squared (or absolute-valued) — raw deviations from the mean always sum to zero
Can predict the effect on mean, variance and SD of adding a constant to, or scaling, every observation
Can compare consistency of two datasets with different means using the coefficient of variation CV = (σ/x̄)×100

misconceptions.description: Conflates variance and standard deviation — reports σ² when σ is asked, or thinks SD can be negative.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 8 when the SD is 2√2; is untroubled by a 'negative SD' after a sign error.
misconceptions.remedy: Emphasise units: if data is in cm, variance is in cm² but SD is back in cm — that's the whole point of the square root. Make writing units after both quantities mandatory for a while; a negative or squared-unit SD then self-flags.

misconceptions.description: Averages raw (signed) deviations from the mean and is puzzled by (or ignores) the inevitable zero.
misconceptions.signal: Computes mean deviation without absolute values, gets 0, and either reports it or fudges signs arbitrarily.
misconceptions.remedy: Prove Σ(xᵢ − x̄) = 0 with a see-saw/balance-point picture: the mean is precisely where deviations cancel. Then present |·| and squaring as the two standard fixes, leading to mean deviation and variance respectively.

misconceptions.description: Compares consistency across datasets using raw SD even when the means differ wildly, instead of the coefficient of variation.
misconceptions.signal: Says the dataset with the smaller SD is 'more consistent' regardless of scale (₹100-scale vs ₹10,000-scale data).
misconceptions.remedy: Show a salary dataset (mean 50,000, SD 500) vs a pocket-money dataset (mean 100, SD 50): smaller SD yet wilder relative swings. Institute the rule: different means → divide out the scale → compare CV = σ/x̄.

misconceptions.description: Thinks shifting every observation by a constant changes the spread: SD(x + 5) = SD(x) + 5.
misconceptions.signal: Adds the constant to the SD after a data-shift question; recomputes everything from scratch and still errs.
misconceptions.remedy: Slide a dot-plot bodily 5 units right on screen: gaps between points are visibly unchanged, so every deviation xᵢ − x̄ survives intact. Contrast with SCALING by k, which stretches gaps and multiplies SD by |k|.

real_world_hooks: Kohli vs a hit-or-miss opener: same average, different SD — who do you pick for a final?
Monsoon rainfall variability across Indian cities with similar annual totals
Quality control: a biscuit factory tracking weight SD on the production line
Mutual fund risk: SD of returns is literally the 'volatility' in the fact sheet
Class marks: same average in two sections, very different spreads
teaching.video_search: variance standard deviation coefficient of variation class 11 statistics

questions.prompt: The variance of the data 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is:

options.diagnosis: Summed the squared deviations but forgot to divide by n = 5.

questions.explanation: Mean = 6. Deviations: −4, −2, 0, 2, 4; squares: 16, 4, 0, 4, 16, summing to 40. Variance = 40/5 = 8 (and SD = √8 = 2√2). Raw deviations sum to 0 — which is why we square them first.

questions.prompt: Each observation in a dataset is increased by 5. The standard deviation of the new dataset:

options.diagnosis: Half-remembered transformation rule — knows 'something non-obvious happens' but SD is exactly unchanged under shifts.
Confused adding a constant with multiplying by one; scaling by k is what multiplies SD by |k|.

questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts every value AND the mean by 5, so each deviation xᵢ − x̄ is untouched — SD unchanged. (The mean increases by 5; only multiplying the data by k rescales the SD.)

questions.prompt: Batsman A has mean score 50 with SD 5; batsman B has mean score 25 with SD 4. Who is more consistent?

options.text: A, because A's coefficient of variation (10%) is lower than B's (16%)
B, because B's SD (4) is smaller than A's (5)
B, because smaller scores fluctuate less in general
options.diagnosis: Judging consistency by the size of the mean itself; neither SD nor mean alone measures relative spread.

options.text: Both are equally consistent since 4 and 5 are nearly equal
options.diagnosis: Treats close raw SDs as equivalent — hasn't normalised by the very different means.

questions.explanation: Consistency across different scoring levels is compared by CV = (σ/x̄)×100: A → (5/50)×100 = 10%, B → (4/25)×100 = 16%. A's scores wobble only 10% of his average, so A is more consistent despite the larger raw SD.

micros.title: Why Dispersion? Range as a First Measure
micros.description: Two datasets with the same mean can behave completely differently — motivating spread measures, starting with range = max − min and its sensitivity to outliers.
outcomes: Can compute the range and explain what it does and does not capture
Can give two datasets with equal means but visibly different spreads

micros.title: Mean Deviation about Mean and Median
micros.description: Why raw deviations from the mean always sum to zero (the balance point), and fixing it with absolute values: mean deviation for ungrouped and grouped data.
outcomes: Can show Σ(xᵢ − x̄) = 0 for a dataset and explain the see-saw picture
Can compute mean deviation about the mean or median for small datasets

micros.title: Variance and Standard Deviation (Ungrouped)
micros.description: Squaring as the other fix for cancelling deviations: variance σ² as mean squared deviation, and SD σ = √variance so the units return to the data's own units.
outcomes: Can compute variance and SD for ungrouped data via deviations from the mean
Can state the unit of each (data in cm → variance in cm², SD in cm) and why SD is never negative

question.prompt: The standard deviation of the data 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is:

options.diagnosis: Summed the squared deviations (4+1+0+1+4) but neither divided by n = 5 nor took the square root.

question.explanation: Mean = 3; squared deviations 4, 1, 0, 1, 4 sum to 10, so variance = 10/5 = 2 and SD = √2. Reporting 2 confuses variance with SD, and 0 comes from averaging the SIGNED deviations, which always cancel.

micros.title: Variance and SD of Grouped Data
micros.description: Extending to frequency distributions: σ² = (1/N)Σfᵢ(xᵢ − x̄)² with class midpoints, and the computational shortcut formula to tame the arithmetic.
outcomes: Can compute variance and SD for a frequency distribution using midpoints
Can apply the shortcut σ² = (1/N)Σfᵢxᵢ² − x̄² and know when it saves work

micros.title: Effect of Shifting and Scaling on Mean and SD
micros.description: Adding a constant slides the whole dot-plot — mean shifts, gaps (and SD) untouched; multiplying by k stretches gaps — mean scales by k, SD by |k|, variance by k².
outcomes: Can predict the new mean, variance and SD after x → x + c or x → kx without recomputing
Can explain with the dot-plot picture why shifts leave SD alone

question.prompt: A dataset has standard deviation 4. If every observation is multiplied by 3, the new standard deviation is:

options.diagnosis: Applied the SHIFT rule to a scaling: multiplying stretches every gap threefold, so SD triples.
Applied k² — that is the VARIANCE factor; SD scales by |k| = 3, giving 4 × 3 = 12.

question.explanation: Scaling by k = 3 stretches every deviation threefold: SD becomes 3 × 4 = 12 (variance goes 16 → 144, a factor of 9). Only ADDING a constant leaves the SD unchanged — and adding 3 to the SD (7) mixes the two rules.

micros.title: Coefficient of Variation and Consistency
micros.description: Comparing spread across datasets with different scales: CV = (σ/x̄) × 100 divides out the mean, making 'more consistent' a fair, unit-free comparison.
outcomes: Can compute CV and use it to rank datasets by consistency
Can explain why raw SD comparisons mislead when means differ widely

question.prompt: Factory A produces a mean of 250 units/day with SD 25; Factory B produces a mean of 50 units/day with SD 10. Which factory is more consistent?

options.text: A, since its CV (10%) is lower than B's (20%)
B, since its SD (10) is smaller than A's (25)
B, because smaller outputs naturally fluctuate less
options.diagnosis: Judged by the size of the mean itself; neither mean nor SD alone measures RELATIVE spread.

options.text: Cannot be compared, since the means differ
options.diagnosis: They CAN be compared — that is exactly what the coefficient of variation is built for.

question.explanation: CV(A) = 25/250 × 100 = 10%; CV(B) = 10/50 × 100 = 20%. A's output wobbles only 10% of its average against B's 20%, so A is more consistent despite the larger raw SD — different scales demand the normalised comparison.

nodes.title: Probability: Random Experiments and the Axiomatic Approach
nodes.description: Probability is rebuilt on set theory: a random experiment has a sample space, events are subsets, and probability is a function obeying three axioms — non-negativity, P(S) = 1, and additivity for mutually exclusive events. From these flow the complement rule P(not A) = 1 − P(A) and the addition rule P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B). This foundation supports everything from weather forecasts to insurance and machine learning.
learning_outcomes: Can describe sample spaces and events as sets for experiments like coin tosses, dice and card draws
Can identify mutually exclusive and exhaustive events and state the axioms of probability
Can apply the complement rule and the addition rule P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B)
Can combine counting techniques (permutations/combinations) with equally-likely outcomes to compute probabilities
Can recognise impossible probability values (outside [0, 1])

misconceptions.description: Equiprobability bias: treats every event as 50-50 ('it either happens or it doesn't') or all outcomes as equally likely even when they aren't.
misconceptions.signal: Says P(rolling a number > 4) = 1/2 'because it happens or it doesn't'; assigns 1/3 each to win/lose/draw in any match.
misconceptions.remedy: Expose the bias with the two-dice sum experiment: sums 2–12 are NOT equally likely (tally 100 rolls, 7 dominates). Enforce the discipline of listing the actual sample space and checking the symmetry claim before dividing counts.

misconceptions.description: Adds probabilities of non-mutually-exclusive events without subtracting the overlap: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) always.
misconceptions.signal: Gets P > 1 for 'king or heart' type questions and doesn't flinch; never mentions P(A∩B).
misconceptions.remedy: Venn-diagram the card deck: shade kings and hearts, watch the king-of-hearts get shaded twice. Tie directly to n(A∪B) from Sets; make 'are they mutually exclusive?' the first written line of every addition-rule solution.

misconceptions.description: Accepts probability values outside [0, 1], e.g. P = 1.4 or P = −0.2, after mechanical arithmetic.
misconceptions.signal: Reports a probability greater than 1 or negative without noticing the impossibility.
misconceptions.remedy: Build the reflex: every probability answer gets range-checked against the axioms before writing it down. Interpret endpoints concretely — 0 = impossible, 1 = certain — so 1.4 reads as 'more certain than certain', an obvious absurdity.

misconceptions.description: Confuses mutually exclusive with exhaustive (or with independent): thinks disjoint events must cover everything, or that 'can't happen together' means 'unrelated'.
misconceptions.signal: Claims P(A) + P(B) = 1 whenever A, B are mutually exclusive; uses the words interchangeably.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort event pairs on a die into a 2×2 grid (exclusive? exhaustive?) with an example in every cell — e.g. {1} and {2} are exclusive but far from exhaustive. Vocabulary precision drills with justification aloud.

real_world_hooks: DLS method and win predictors in cricket broadcasts are probability statements
Ludo and Snakes-and-Ladders: dice sample spaces you've known for years
IMD's '70% chance of rain' — what does it actually claim?
Insurance premiums priced off probabilities of events
Lottery and lucky-draw odds: why the intuition 'I either win or lose' misleads
teaching.video_search: axiomatic probability addition rule sample space class 11

questions.prompt: A fair die is thrown once. The probability of getting a number greater than 4 is:

options.diagnosis: Counted the four outcomes {1, 2, 3, 4} — the complement of the target event (or misread the cutoff as 'greater than 2') — giving 4/6 = 2/3.
Counted only one favourable outcome; treated 'greater than 4' as 'equal to 5' or 'equal to 6' alone.

questions.explanation: Favourable outcomes: {5, 6} — two of the six equally likely faces, so P = 2/6 = 1/3. 'It happens or it doesn't' does NOT make it 1/2; the outcomes, not the descriptions, must be equally likely.

questions.prompt: Given P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A∩B) = 0.2, find P(A∪B).

options.diagnosis: Reported the intersection instead of the union; 'or' and 'and' swapped.
Subtracted everything in sight (0.5 − 0.4 + ... ); formula structure not yet stable.

questions.explanation: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.7. Adding without subtracting the overlap double-counts outcomes in both A and B.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is tossed three times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?

options.diagnosis: Computed P(exactly one head); 'at least one' includes one, two or three heads.
Found the complement P(no heads) correctly but forgot the final step 1 − 1/8.

questions.explanation: The complement of 'at least one head' is 'no heads' = TTT, with probability (1/2)³ = 1/8. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. The complement shortcut beats listing all 8 outcomes — but you must finish the subtraction.

micros.title: Random Experiments and Sample Spaces
micros.description: Describing the full outcome set of an experiment — coins, dice, draws — as a set S, and events as subsets, with careful listing before any probability is computed.
outcomes: Can list sample spaces for multi-stage experiments (three coins, two dice) systematically
Can express events like 'sum is 7' as explicit subsets and count them

micros.title: Types of Events and Event Algebra
micros.description: Complementary events, 'A or B' as union, 'A and B' as intersection, and the precise meanings of mutually exclusive (disjoint) versus exhaustive (covering S).
outcomes: Can build compound events with union, intersection and complement
Can classify event pairs as mutually exclusive and/or exhaustive with justification

question.prompt: A die is rolled once. The events A = {1, 2} and B = {5, 6} are:

options.diagnosis: Definitions swapped: A∩B = ∅ makes them EXCLUSIVE; covering all of S is what exhaustive means.
A and B share no outcomes, so they are certainly mutually exclusive; check A∩B first.

question.explanation: A∩B = ∅, so they cannot happen together — mutually exclusive. But A∪B = {1, 2, 5, 6} misses 3 and 4, so they are NOT exhaustive: disjoint events need not cover everything, and P(A) + P(B) = 2/3 ≠ 1.

micros.title: The Axioms of Probability
micros.description: Probability as a function on events obeying three axioms — P(E) ≥ 0, P(S) = 1, additivity for disjoint events — and range-checking every answer against [0, 1].
outcomes: Can state the three axioms and check whether a proposed assignment of probabilities is valid
Can reject impossible values (negative or above 1) on sight

question.prompt: Which of the following CANNOT be the probability of an event?

options.diagnosis: Perfectly valid — very likely, still within [0, 1].
Any fraction between 0 and 1 is a legitimate probability.

question.explanation: The axioms confine every probability to [0, 1]: 1.2 would be 'more certain than certain'. Note 0 IS allowed — it is the probability of an impossible event — so ruling it out misreads the axioms' range.

micros.title: The Complement Rule and 'At Least One'
micros.description: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) derived from the axioms, and the workhorse pattern: P(at least one ...) = 1 − P(none) — finishing the subtraction every time.
outcomes: Can compute probabilities of complements and 'at least one' events efficiently
Can decide when the complement shortcut beats direct enumeration

micros.title: The Addition Rule
micros.description: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B), inherited straight from n(A∪B) in Sets; the first written line of every solution is 'are the events mutually exclusive?'.
outcomes: Can apply the addition rule with and without overlap, e.g. 'king or heart' from a deck
Can detect the double-count error when an answer exceeds 1

question.prompt: One card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52. The probability that it is a king OR a heart is:

options.diagnosis: Reported P(king AND heart) — the intersection — instead of the union.
Counted only the 13 hearts, forgetting the three kings outside hearts.

question.explanation: P(K∪H) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13; the king of hearts sits in both events and must be subtracted once. Adding to 17/52 counts that card twice.

micros.title: Probability via Counting Techniques
micros.description: Combining nCr counting with equally likely outcomes: P(E) = favourable/total for draws and selections — after verifying the outcomes really are equally likely.
outcomes: Can compute probabilities of card and committee selections using combinations
Can spot and reject bogus 50-50 reasoning by listing or counting the true sample space

question.prompt: Two cards are drawn together from a deck of 52. The probability that BOTH are aces is:

options.diagnosis: Computed (4/52)² — with replacement; drawing together means the second ace comes from 3 of 51 remaining.
Found P(first card is an ace) = 4/52 and stopped; the second card must also be an ace.

question.explanation: P = 4C2/52C2 = 6/1326 = 1/221 (equivalently 4/52 × 3/51). 'Either both are aces or not' does NOT make it 50-50 — the two descriptions are wildly unequal in outcome count.

nodes.title: Relations and Functions: Types, Composition, Invertibility
nodes.description: Functions acquire structure: relations can be reflexive, symmetric, transitive (equivalence relations), and functions can be one-one (injective), onto (surjective) or both (bijective). Composition chains functions together — (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)) — and exactly the bijective functions can be undone by an inverse. Invertibility is the deep idea behind every 'decode', 'undo' and 'solve for x' in mathematics, and behind encryption itself.
learning_outcomes: Can test a relation for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity and identify equivalence relations and their classes
Can prove or disprove that a function is one-one and/or onto, with counterexamples where needed
Can compute compositions g∘f and f∘g, respecting order, and give examples where they differ
Can decide whether a function is invertible and find f⁻¹ explicitly for simple bijections
Can restrict domain/codomain to make a non-invertible function invertible

misconceptions.description: Misreads composition: thinks (g∘f)(x) means g(x)·f(x), or that composition is commutative (f∘g = g∘f).
misconceptions.signal: Multiplies the two function values; computes f(g(x)) when g(f(x)) is asked and expects the same answer.
misconceptions.remedy: Machine-chain picture: f's output conveyor feeds g's input hopper — order is physical. Compute both f∘g and g∘f for f(x) = x+2, g(x) = 3x and display the different results side by side; read g∘f aloud as 'g AFTER f'.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the inverse function with the reciprocal: f⁻¹(x) = 1/f(x).
misconceptions.signal: Writes f⁻¹(x) = 1/(3x − 4) for f(x) = 3x − 4; reads sin⁻¹ as cosec.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two meanings of the exponent −1 on numbers vs functions explicitly. Define f⁻¹ operationally — 'the machine run backwards' — and always verify by composing: f⁻¹(f(x)) must return x, which 1/f(x) spectacularly fails.

misconceptions.description: Believes every function has an inverse, skipping the bijectivity requirement.
misconceptions.signal: Confidently 'inverts' f(x) = x² on R to get √x; never checks one-one or onto.
misconceptions.remedy: Run the backwards machine on f(x) = x²: input 4 — should the output be 2 or −2? The ambiguity IS the failure of one-one. Then show the standard repair (restrict to x ≥ 0), making bijectivity feel like a needed licence, not red tape.

misconceptions.description: Garbles 'one-one' as 'each input has one output' (the definition of a function) rather than distinct inputs having distinct outputs.
misconceptions.signal: Declares f(x) = x² one-one 'because every x gives exactly one x²'.
misconceptions.remedy: Sharpen with arrow diagrams: function-ness is about arrows LEAVING each input (exactly one); one-one is about arrows ARRIVING at each output (at most one). The horizontal line test makes the second condition visual.

real_world_hooks: Encryption/decryption: WhatsApp messages need functions that CAN be undone by exactly one key
Aadhaar enrolment: person → number must be one-one for de-duplication to work
Currency conversion INR→USD and back: composing a function with its inverse
'Same birthday' as a relation on your class: reflexive? symmetric? transitive?
QR codes: encode then decode is f followed by f⁻¹
teaching.video_search: one one onto bijective composition inverse functions class 12

questions.prompt: Let f(x) = x + 2 and g(x) = 3x. Find (g∘f)(2).

options.diagnosis: Added f(2) + g(2) = 4 + 6; invented an operation instead of composing.

questions.explanation: (g∘f)(2) = g(f(2)) = g(4) = 12 — apply f FIRST, then feed its output to g. Reversing the order gives (f∘g)(2) = f(6) = 8, and multiplying values gives f(2)·g(2) = 24; neither is composition in the stated order.

questions.prompt: If f: R → R is f(x) = 3x − 4, then f⁻¹(x) equals:

options.diagnosis: Undid the operations but kept the original sign — subtracted 4 again instead of adding it back.
Reversed each operation's sign but not their ORDER; inverting must unwind last-in-first-out.

questions.explanation: Set y = 3x − 4 and solve for x: x = (y + 4)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 4)/3. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = ((3x − 4) + 4)/3 = x ✓. The reciprocal 1/f(x) fails this check completely.

questions.prompt: Consider f: R → R, f(x) = x². Which statement about its inverse is correct?

options.text: f is not invertible: it is neither one-one nor onto R
f is one-one but not onto, so it is not invertible

questions.explanation: f(2) = f(−2) = 4, so f is not one-one; and no negative number is ever an output, so f is not onto R. Failing both conditions, no inverse exists on R → R. (Restricting to f: [0,∞) → [0,∞) repairs both defects, and only then is √x the inverse.)

micros.title: Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive Relations
micros.description: Test a relation on a set for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity from its defining rule or its list of ordered pairs, producing counterexamples where a property fails.
outcomes: Can check each of the three properties for a relation given as pairs or as a rule
Can produce a specific counterexample pair whenever a property fails

micros.title: Equivalence Relations and Equivalence Classes
micros.description: Recognise relations that are reflexive, symmetric and transitive as equivalence relations, and describe the partition of the set into equivalence classes (e.g. congruence modulo n).
outcomes: Can verify that a relation is an equivalence relation
Can list the equivalence classes of relations like 'a ≡ b (mod 3)' and explain why classes partition the set

micros.title: One-one (Injective) Functions
micros.description: Prove a function is one-one by showing f(x1) = f(x2) forces x1 = x2, or disprove it with two distinct inputs sharing an output; read injectivity off a graph with the horizontal line test.
outcomes: Can prove or disprove injectivity algebraically
Can state the difference between 'every input has one output' (function) and 'distinct inputs have distinct outputs' (one-one)

question.prompt: Which of the following functions from R to R is one-one?

options.text: f(x) = x², because each input x gives exactly one output x²

options.diagnosis: Missed that |−a| = |a| pairs two inputs to one output; did not hunt for collisions.
Ignored periodicity: sin 0 = sin π = 0 already breaks injectivity.

question.explanation: f(x) = 2x + 3 is one-one: 2x1 + 3 = 2x2 + 3 forces x1 = x2. x² fails since f(−1) = f(1) = 1 — 'each input has one output' is the definition of a FUNCTION, not of one-one. |x| and sin x also send distinct inputs to equal outputs.

micros.title: Onto (Surjective) Functions
micros.description: Decide whether every element of the codomain is attained: solve f(x) = y for arbitrary y in the codomain, or exhibit a y with no pre-image. Contrast range with codomain.
outcomes: Can prove or disprove surjectivity for functions like f: R→R, f(x) = x² or f(x) = 2x + 3
Can adjust the codomain to make a given function onto

micros.title: Composition of Functions
micros.description: Compute (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)), feeding the output of the inner function into the outer one, and show with examples that g∘f and f∘g generally differ.
outcomes: Can compute g∘f and f∘g for algebraic and trigonometric functions
Can give an example where g∘f ≠ f∘g and explain why order matters

question.prompt: If f(x) = x² and g(x) = 2x + 1, then (g∘f)(x) equals:

options.diagnosis: Attempted g(f(x)) but distributed 2 over x² + x; algebra slip after a correct setup.

question.explanation: (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)) = g(x²) = 2x² + 1. Computing (f∘g)(x) = (2x+1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1 swaps the order — composition is not commutative — and 2x³ + x² is the PRODUCT g(x)·f(x), which is not composition at all.

micros.title: Invertible Functions and Finding f⁻¹
micros.description: A function has an inverse exactly when it is one-one and onto (bijective). Find f⁻¹ for simple bijections by solving y = f(x) for x, and verify f⁻¹∘f = identity.
outcomes: Can state and apply the bijectivity criterion for invertibility
Can compute f⁻¹ explicitly for functions like f(x) = 3x + 2 or f(x) = (x−1)/(x+2)
Can distinguish f⁻¹(x) from the reciprocal 1/f(x)

question.prompt: The function f: R → R, f(x) = 3x + 2 is invertible. Its inverse f⁻¹(x) is:

options.diagnosis: Reversed only the signs, not the operations; never solved y = 3x + 2 for x.
Undid the operations in the wrong order: added 2 before dividing instead of subtracting first.

question.explanation: Set y = 3x + 2 and solve for x: x = (y − 2)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x − 2)/3. Check: f⁻¹(f(x)) = ((3x+2) − 2)/3 = x. The reciprocal 1/f(x) is a completely different function — f⁻¹ undoes f, it does not divide 1 by it.

micros.title: Restricting Domain and Codomain to Force Invertibility
micros.description: A non-bijective function becomes invertible after restricting its domain (to make it one-one) and shrinking its codomain to the range (to make it onto), e.g. x² on [0, ∞).
outcomes: Can choose a restricted domain and codomain that make functions like x² or sin x bijective
Can explain why the restriction is necessary before an inverse can exist

nodes.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
nodes.description: Sine, cosine and tangent are periodic, so they can only be inverted after restricting to principal branches: sin⁻¹ maps [−1,1] to [−π/2, π/2], cos⁻¹ to [0, π], tan⁻¹ to (−π/2, π/2). You will evaluate principal values, simplify expressions like sin⁻¹(sin x) — which is NOT always x — and use identities such as sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2. These functions are how calculators, surveyors and navigation systems recover angles from ratios, and their derivatives unlock whole families of integrals.
learning_outcomes: Can state the principal-value branches (domain and range) of sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹
Can evaluate principal values such as sin⁻¹(1/2), cos⁻¹(−1/2), tan⁻¹(−1)
Can simplify sin⁻¹(sin x) and cos⁻¹(cos x) when x lies outside the principal branch
Can apply identities like sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 and interpret graphs of inverse trig functions as reflections in y = x

misconceptions.description: Reads sin⁻¹x as the reciprocal 1/sin x (i.e. cosec x).
misconceptions.signal: Converts sin⁻¹(1/2) into 1/sin(1/2) or answers cosec values for inverse-sine questions.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the notations explicitly: sin⁻¹x is 'the angle whose sine is x'; the reciprocal already has its own name, cosec. Read every sin⁻¹ aloud as 'arc sine / angle whose sine is' for several sessions until the misparse dies.

misconceptions.description: Cancels blindly: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x for every x, ignoring the principal range.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 2π/3 for sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3); treats the pair as inverse machines with no restrictions.
misconceptions.remedy: Plot y = sin⁻¹(sin x) over several periods — the sawtooth shape shows the 'cancellation' only holds on [−π/2, π/2]. Teach the two-step repair: find an angle IN the principal range with the same sine (here π − 2π/3 = π/3).

misconceptions.description: Uses wrong principal ranges — e.g. returns a negative angle for cos⁻¹ of a negative number, or an angle beyond π/2 for sin⁻¹.
misconceptions.signal: States cos⁻¹(−1/2) = −π/3, or sin⁻¹(1/2) = 5π/6.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor each branch visually on its graph slice: sin⁻¹ lives in the right half-swing [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹ in the top-to-bottom sweep [0, π]. Range-check every answer against the branch chart before accepting it — cos⁻¹ NEVER outputs negatives.

real_world_hooks: Finding the angle of a ramp or ladder from its measured slope: θ = tan⁻¹(rise/run)
A surveyor recovering the elevation angle of a hilltop from distances
Robotics inverse kinematics: which joint ANGLE achieves this position?
Why your calculator's ASIN button refuses inputs beyond ±1
Satellite dish alignment: elevation angle from latitude via inverse trig
teaching.video_search: inverse trigonometric functions principal values class 12

questions.prompt: The principal value of sin⁻¹(1/2) is:

options.diagnosis: Sign slip: sin(−π/6) = −1/2, not +1/2; positive inputs to sin⁻¹ give angles in (0, π/2].

questions.explanation: sin⁻¹(1/2) asks: which angle in [−π/2, π/2] has sine 1/2? That is π/6. Although sin(5π/6) = 1/2 too, 5π/6 lies outside the principal branch; and sin⁻¹ is not a reciprocal — that's cosec.

questions.prompt: The value of sin⁻¹(sin(2π/3)) is:

options.diagnosis: Knew a range correction was needed but subtracted from the wrong side (used 2π/3 − π or negated); sin(−π/3) = −√3/2 ≠ sin(2π/3).
Halved instead of reflecting; the correction is π − x, not x/2.

questions.explanation: sin(2π/3) = sin(π − 2π/3) = sin(π/3) = √3/2. Since 2π/3 lies outside [−π/2, π/2], sin⁻¹ must return the in-range angle with the same sine: sin⁻¹(√3/2) = π/3. The composition sin⁻¹(sin x) equals x only inside the principal branch.

questions.prompt: If sin⁻¹x = π/5, then cos⁻¹x equals:

options.diagnosis: Used π − π/5: applied a supplementary-angle relation where the identity is complementary (sums to π/2).
Assumed sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹ agree at the same input; they are different angles for the same ratio.
Arithmetic slip in π/2 − π/5 = 5π/10 − 2π/10; method right, fractions wrong.

questions.explanation: For x ∈ [−1, 1], sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2. So cos⁻¹x = π/2 − π/5 = 5π/10 − 2π/10 = 3π/10. The identity reflects the complementarity sin θ = cos(π/2 − θ).

micros.title: What sin⁻¹x Means (and Doesn't)
micros.description: sin⁻¹x is the inverse FUNCTION of a restricted sine, not the reciprocal 1/sin x. Because sine is not one-one on R, its domain must be cut down before an inverse can exist.
outcomes: Can explain why sin, cos, tan need restricted domains to be invertible
Can distinguish sin⁻¹x from cosec x = 1/sin x in notation and meaning

question.prompt: Which statement correctly describes sin⁻¹x?

options.text: The angle in [−π/2, π/2] whose sine is x
1/sin x, the reciprocal of sin x

options.diagnosis: Moved the −1 exponent onto the argument; parsing error in function notation.

options.text: Any angle whose sine is x
options.diagnosis: Ignores the principal branch: without restricting to [−π/2, π/2] there are infinitely many such angles and sin⁻¹ would not be a function.

question.explanation: sin⁻¹ is the inverse of the sine function restricted to [−π/2, π/2]: it returns the unique angle in that interval with the given sine. The reciprocal of sin x is written cosec x — the superscript −1 on a function name means inverse function, not power.

micros.title: Principal-value Branches: Domains and Ranges
micros.description: Memorise and justify the principal branches: sin⁻¹: [−1,1] → [−π/2, π/2], cos⁻¹: [−1,1] → [0, π], tan⁻¹: R → (−π/2, π/2), and why these particular intervals are chosen.
outcomes: Can state domain and range of sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ without error
Can explain why cos⁻¹ needs [0, π] rather than [−π/2, π/2]

micros.title: Evaluating Principal Values
micros.description: Evaluate expressions like sin⁻¹(1/2), cos⁻¹(−1/2), tan⁻¹(−1), landing in the correct principal branch — especially for negative arguments where sin⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ give negative angles but cos⁻¹ gives an angle in (π/2, π].
outcomes: Can evaluate inverse trig expressions at standard values in the correct branch
Can use sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹x and cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x correctly

question.prompt: The principal value of cos⁻¹(−1/2) is:

options.diagnosis: Dropped the negative sign on the argument and evaluated cos⁻¹(1/2).
Confused −1/2 with −√3/2; wrong standard value inside the right branch.

question.explanation: cos⁻¹ takes values in [0, π], never negative. cos⁻¹(−1/2) = π − cos⁻¹(1/2) = π − π/3 = 2π/3, and indeed cos(2π/3) = −1/2. The answer −π/3 uses the sin⁻¹-style branch [−π/2, π/2], which is wrong for cosine.

micros.title: Simplifying sin⁻¹(sin x) and cos⁻¹(cos x)
micros.description: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only when x is inside [−π/2, π/2]; otherwise the answer is the angle in the principal branch with the same sine. Fold arbitrary angles back into the branch using symmetry.
outcomes: Can evaluate sin⁻¹(sin x) and cos⁻¹(cos x) for x outside the principal branch
Can explain why blind cancellation fails using the graph of sin⁻¹(sin x)

question.prompt: sin⁻¹(sin(2π/3)) equals:

options.diagnosis: Folded into the principal branch but flipped the sign; sin(2π/3) is positive so the answer must be positive.
Used sin(2π/3) = 1/2 instead of √3/2; standard-value slip.

question.explanation: sin(2π/3) = sin(π − 2π/3) = sin(π/3) = √3/2. Since 2π/3 lies outside [−π/2, π/2], sin⁻¹ cannot return it: sin⁻¹(√3/2) = π/3. Cancelling sin⁻¹(sin x) to x is only valid inside the principal branch.

micros.title: Identities and Graphs of Inverse Trig Functions
micros.description: Use identities such as sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 and tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2, and interpret the graphs of sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ as reflections of the restricted originals in the line y = x.
outcomes: Can apply sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 to evaluate and simplify expressions
Can sketch inverse trig graphs by reflecting the restricted trig graphs in y = x

nodes.title: Matrices: Operations, Transpose, Invertibility
nodes.description: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers that adds entry-wise but multiplies by a row-into-column rule — an operation that is famously NOT commutative and defined only when inner dimensions match. You will master matrix algebra, transposes, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices, and meet invertible matrices. Matrices encode simultaneous equations, graphics transformations, network links and the entire machinery of modern machine learning.
learning_outcomes: Can state the order of a matrix and decide when sums and products are defined
Can add, scalar-multiply and multiply matrices using the row-by-column rule
Can give examples showing AB ≠ BA and explain why matrix algebra identities differ from number algebra
Can compute transposes and classify matrices as symmetric or skew-symmetric
Can explain why AB = O does not force A = O or B = O, and recognise identity and invertible matrices

misconceptions.description: Assumes matrix multiplication is commutative: AB = BA.
misconceptions.signal: Swaps factor order freely; expands (A+B)² as A² + 2AB + B² without comment.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student compute AB and BA for one small concrete pair and confront the different answers. Then connect to meaning: matrices are TRANSFORMATIONS, and 'rotate then reflect' visibly differs from 'reflect then rotate'.

misconceptions.description: Ports number-algebra identities wholesale: (A+B)² = A² + 2AB + B², (A+B)(A−B) = A² − B².
misconceptions.signal: Uses school identities on matrices without expanding; loses the AB + BA distinction.
misconceptions.remedy: Force the honest expansion (A+B)² = A² + AB + BA + B² and highlight that AB + BA collapses to 2AB only if the pair commutes. Verify the failure numerically with the same pair used for m1.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies matrices entry-by-entry, like addition.
misconceptions.signal: Computes (AB)ᵢⱼ = aᵢⱼ·bᵢⱼ; product of two 2×2s done in four multiplications.
misconceptions.remedy: Teach the row-into-column gesture physically (left hand sweeps a row, right hand a column, dot them). Motivate WHY via composition of linear substitutions — entry-wise product simply doesn't compute the composite.

misconceptions.description: Believes AB = O implies A = O or B = O (no zero divisors), as with numbers.
misconceptions.signal: Cancels matrices from equations: from AB = AC concludes B = C without invertibility.
misconceptions.remedy: Exhibit the classic counterexample [[0,1],[0,0]]² = O with a non-zero matrix. Frame the moral: cancellation is a PRIVILEGE purchased by invertibility, and connect forward to determinants deciding when it's granted.

real_world_hooks: Image filters: every Instagram effect is a matrix acting on pixel data
IPL points table computations as matrix operations on results
Google's PageRank: the web as a giant matrix
Cipher machines: encoding messages by matrix multiplication (Hill cipher)
Neural networks are stacks of matrix multiplications
teaching.video_search: matrix multiplication row column rule non commutative class 12

questions.prompt: If A is a 2×3 matrix and B is a 3×4 matrix, then AB is:

options.diagnosis: Took the INNER dimensions as the answer; those must match and then cancel, leaving the outer pair.
Right dimensions, wrong order — rows of the product come from the LEFT factor.

options.text: Not defined, since A and B have different orders
options.diagnosis: Thinks multiplication needs equal orders like addition does; only the inner dimensions must agree.

questions.explanation: (2×3)·(3×4): the inner 3s match, so the product exists and has the outer dimensions 2×4. Equal orders are required for ADDITION, not multiplication.

questions.prompt: Let A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[2, 0], [1, 3]]. Then AB equals:

options.diagnosis: Row-column bookkeeping slip in the (2,1) entry: used row 2 with the wrong column entries.

questions.prompt: A and B are square matrices with AB = O (the zero matrix). Which conclusion is valid?

options.text: It is possible that neither A nor B is the zero matrix
A = O or B = O necessarily
Both A and B must be zero matrices

questions.explanation: Matrices admit zero divisors: with A = [[0,1],[0,0]] = B, AB = O though neither factor is zero. And BA need not vanish when AB does (for A = [[1,0],[0,0]], B = [[0,0],[1,0]]: AB = O but BA = [[0,0],[1,0]] ≠ O) — another casualty of non-commutativity.

micros.title: Matrix Notation, Order and Types
micros.description: A matrix is a rectangular array a_ij with i indexing rows and j columns. Identify order m×n, equality of matrices, and special types: row, column, square, diagonal, scalar, identity, zero.
outcomes: Can state the order of a matrix and locate the entry a_ij
Can classify matrices by type and use equality to solve for unknown entries

micros.title: Matrix Addition and Scalar Multiplication
micros.description: Add matrices of the same order entrywise and multiply a matrix by a scalar; use the algebra of these operations (commutativity, associativity, additive inverse) to solve matrix equations like 2X + A = B.
outcomes: Can add, subtract and scalar-multiply matrices of matching orders
Can solve simple matrix equations for an unknown matrix X

micros.title: Matrix Multiplication: the Row-by-Column Rule
micros.description: Multiply an m×n matrix by an n×p matrix: the (i,j) entry is the dot product of row i with column j. Check compatibility of orders before multiplying — and never multiply entry-by-entry.
outcomes: Can decide when a product AB is defined and state its order
Can compute 2×2 and 3×3 products accurately with the row-by-column rule

question.prompt: Let A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[2, 0], [1, 3]] (rows listed). Then AB equals:

options.diagnosis: Row-column slip in the (2,1) entry: computed 3 + 4 instead of 3×2 + 4×1.

question.explanation: AB = [[1·2 + 2·1, 1·0 + 2·3], [3·2 + 4·1, 3·0 + 4·3]] = [[4, 6], [10, 12]]. Multiplying entry-by-entry gives [[2, 0], [3, 12]], which is not matrix multiplication, and [[2, 4], [10, 14]] is BA — order matters.

micros.title: Why AB ≠ BA: Matrix Algebra Identities
micros.description: Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive but NOT commutative. Consequently number-algebra identities mutate: (A+B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², and (A+B)(A−B) = A² − AB + BA − B².
outcomes: Can produce a concrete pair with AB ≠ BA
Can expand (A+B)² and (A+B)(A−B) correctly without merging AB and BA

question.prompt: For square matrices A and B of the same order, (A + B)² always equals:

options.diagnosis: Dropped both cross terms entirely — the 'freshman's dream' carried into matrices.

question.explanation: (A+B)² = (A+B)(A+B) = A² + AB + BA + B² by distributivity. The terms AB and BA cannot be merged into 2AB unless A and B happen to commute, which matrices generally do not.

micros.title: AB = O Without A = O or B = O
micros.description: Unlike numbers, matrices have zero divisors: nonzero matrices can multiply to the zero matrix, and AB = AC does not allow cancelling A. Build and verify explicit examples.
outcomes: Can exhibit nonzero A, B with AB = O
Can explain why cancellation fails and connect it to A not being invertible

question.prompt: A and B are 2×2 matrices with AB = O (the zero matrix). Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is possible that A ≠ O and B ≠ O
Necessarily A = O or B = O
Necessarily both A = O and B = O
options.diagnosis: Even stronger version of the no-zero-divisors belief; also fails for numbers (2 × 0 = 0).

options.text: B must be the inverse of A
options.diagnosis: Confused the zero matrix with the identity: AB = I is the inverse condition, not AB = O.

question.explanation: Take A = [[0, 1], [0, 0]] and B = [[1, 0], [0, 0]]: both are nonzero, yet AB = O. Matrices, unlike real numbers, have zero divisors — so AB = O never justifies concluding a factor is zero.

micros.title: Transpose, Symmetric and Skew-symmetric Matrices
micros.description: Form the transpose by swapping rows and columns; use (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. Classify square matrices as symmetric (Aᵀ = A) or skew-symmetric (Aᵀ = −A), and split any square matrix into a symmetric plus skew-symmetric part.
outcomes: Can compute transposes and apply (A + B)ᵀ, (kA)ᵀ, (AB)ᵀ rules
Can verify symmetry/skew-symmetry and write A = (A + Aᵀ)/2 + (A − Aᵀ)/2

micros.title: Identity Matrix and Invertibility
micros.description: The identity matrix I satisfies AI = IA = A. A square matrix A is invertible when some B gives AB = BA = I; the inverse is unique, and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. Verification by direct multiplication.
outcomes: Can verify a proposed inverse by computing AB and BA
Can state and use uniqueness of the inverse and the reversal rule (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹

nodes.title: Determinants: Properties, Adjoint, Inverse, Solving Systems
nodes.description: The determinant condenses a square matrix into a single number that decides everything: invertibility (|A| ≠ 0), the area/volume scaling of the transformation, and solvability of linear systems. You will evaluate 2×2 and 3×3 determinants by cofactor expansion, exploit row/column properties, build inverses via the adjoint A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A|, and solve systems by the matrix method. It is the algebraic gatekeeper between unique solutions and degeneracy.
learning_outcomes: Can evaluate 2×2 and 3×3 determinants by cofactor expansion along any row or column
Can apply determinant properties: effect of row swaps, common factors, identical rows, and |kA| = kⁿ|A|
Can compute minors, cofactors and the adjoint, and find A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A| when |A| ≠ 0
Can use determinants to test consistency and solve systems of linear equations by the matrix method
Can interpret |A| = 0 as the matrix being singular (non-invertible) and compute areas of triangles via determinants

misconceptions.description: Treats the determinant as linear over addition of matrices: |A + B| = |A| + |B|.
misconceptions.signal: Splits determinants across sums of matrices; adds determinants of parts.
misconceptions.remedy: Counterexample immediately: A = [[1,0],[0,0]], B = [[0,0],[0,1]] have |A| = |B| = 0 but |A+B| = |I| = 1. Emphasise that determinant linearity holds only ONE ROW at a time, which is a different (and correct) property.

misconceptions.description: Scales determinants wrongly: |kA| = k|A| instead of kⁿ|A| for an n×n matrix.
misconceptions.signal: For a 3×3 with |A| = 5 answers |2A| = 10.
misconceptions.remedy: Factor k out of each row one at a time, counting a factor of k per row — three rows, three factors, k³. Geometric reinforcement: doubling every edge of a box multiplies volume by 8, not 2.

misconceptions.description: Believes row operations never change a determinant — forgetting that swapping rows flips the sign and scaling a row scales the determinant.
misconceptions.signal: Freely swaps and scales rows while evaluating, reporting the wrong sign or magnitude.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a three-line 'operation ledger': swap → ×(−1); row×k → ×k; row + multiple of another → ×1. Have the student re-evaluate one determinant twice, with and without logging, to see where the sign leaked.

misconceptions.description: Forgets to divide the adjoint by the determinant (A⁻¹ = adj A, not adj A/|A|), or inverts singular matrices.
misconceptions.signal: Reports adj(A) as the inverse; never checks |A| ≠ 0 before 'inverting'.
misconceptions.remedy: Make A·A⁻¹ = I the acceptance test: multiplying A by its adjoint yields |A|·I, visibly off by the factor |A|. Precede every inversion with the ritual line '|A| = ..., ≠ 0, so A⁻¹ exists'.

real_world_hooks: Determinant as area scale factor: how a graphics transform stretches a sprite
Balancing supply-demand equations for two products: unique solution iff determinant ≠ 0
Surveyors computing a triangular plot's area straight from GPS coordinates
Cryptography: a Hill-cipher key matrix must have a nonzero determinant to decode
Structural engineering: singular stiffness matrix = unstable structure
teaching.video_search: determinants adjoint inverse matrix method class 12

questions.prompt: The value of the determinant of [[3, 1], [2, 4]] is:

options.diagnosis: Added the cross products (12 + 2) instead of subtracting; the rule is ad − bc.
Subtracted in the wrong order (bc − ad); a consistent sign convention slip.
Multiplied all four entries (or the two diagonal products) together; determinant structure not yet formed.

questions.prompt: A is a 3×3 matrix with |A| = 5. The value of |2A| is:

options.diagnosis: Used k² — counted a factor of 2 for only two of the three rows.
Computed k·n·|A| = 2·3·5; blended the scaling rule with the matrix order additively.

questions.explanation: |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n×n matrix, since k factors out of each of the n rows: |2A| = 2³ × 5 = 40. Geometrically, doubling all edges of a 3D box scales volume by 8.

questions.prompt: For A = [[4, 3], [2, 2]], the inverse A⁻¹ is:

options.diagnosis: Formed the cofactor matrix but skipped the transpose when building the adjoint.
Negated the wrong entries — swapped the sign pattern between the diagonal and off-diagonal.

questions.explanation: |A| = 4×2 − 3×2 = 2 ≠ 0, so A⁻¹ exists. For a 2×2: swap the main diagonal, negate the off-diagonal: adj A = [[2, −3], [−2, 4]], and A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| = (1/2)[[2, −3], [−2, 4]]. Check: A·A⁻¹ = I ✓ — without the 1/2 you get 2I, not I.

micros.title: 2×2 Determinants and What They Detect
micros.description: Compute |[[a, b], [c, d]]| = ad − bc, connect a zero determinant to the rows being proportional (singular matrix), and to a pair of linear equations having no unique solution.
outcomes: Can evaluate 2×2 determinants quickly and accurately
Can link |A| = 0 to proportional rows and to non-unique solutions of linear systems

micros.title: Minors and Cofactors
micros.description: The minor M_ij deletes row i and column j and takes the determinant of what remains; the cofactor C_ij = (−1)^(i+j) M_ij attaches the checkerboard sign. Fluency here prevents sign errors in every later computation.
outcomes: Can compute any minor and cofactor of a 3×3 matrix
Can reproduce the (−1)^(i+j) sign checkerboard from the formula rather than memory

question.prompt: For A = [[2, 3, 1], [4, 0, 5], [6, 7, 8]] (rows listed), the cofactor C₁₂ is:

options.diagnosis: Gave the minor M₁₂; forgot the sign factor (−1)^(1+2) = −1.
Computed C₂₁ instead of C₁₂; deleted the wrong row and column.
Added the cross products 4×8 + 5×6 instead of subtracting; determinant rule misremembered.

question.explanation: Delete row 1, column 2: M₁₂ = |[[4, 5], [6, 8]]| = 4×8 − 5×6 = 32 − 30 = 2. Then C₁₂ = (−1)^(1+2) × 2 = −2. The checkerboard sign at position (1,2) is negative.

micros.title: Evaluating 3×3 Determinants by Cofactor Expansion
micros.description: Expand a 3×3 determinant along any row or column as Σ a_ij C_ij, choosing the row or column with the most zeros. Confirm the answer is independent of the row chosen.
outcomes: Can expand along any row or column and get the same value
Can pick the expansion line strategically to minimise arithmetic

micros.title: Properties of Determinants
micros.description: Row swaps flip the sign; a common factor of one row comes out once, so |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n×n matrix; identical or proportional rows force zero; |AB| = |A||B| but |A + B| ≠ |A| + |B| in general.
outcomes: Can predict the effect of row operations on a determinant
Can apply |kA| = kⁿ|A| and |AB| = |A||B|, and refute |A+B| = |A|+|B| with a counterexample

question.prompt: A is a 3×3 matrix with |A| = 5. The value of |2A| is:

options.diagnosis: Used k⁴ instead of k³; miscounted the number of rows each carrying a factor of 2.

question.explanation: 2A multiplies EVERY row by 2, and each of the 3 rows releases one factor of 2: |2A| = 2³|A| = 8 × 5 = 40. |kA| = k|A| would be true only if just one row were scaled.

micros.title: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
micros.description: adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix; A · adj A = |A| I, so A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| whenever |A| ≠ 0. A matrix with |A| = 0 is singular and has no inverse.
outcomes: Can compute adj A for 2×2 and 3×3 matrices
Can compute A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| and verify AA⁻¹ = I
Can recognise singular matrices as non-invertible

question.prompt: For A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] (rows listed), A⁻¹ equals:

options.diagnosis: Used |A| = 2 instead of −2; sign slip in ad − bc = 4 − 6.
Formed the adjoint by swapping the diagonal but forgot to negate the off-diagonal entries.

question.explanation: |A| = 1×4 − 2×3 = −2 and adj A = [[4, −2], [−3, 1]] (swap diagonal, negate off-diagonal). So A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| = (−1/2)[[4, −2], [−3, 1]]. Forgetting to divide by |A| gives adj A itself, which fails AA⁻¹ = I.

micros.title: Solving Linear Systems by the Matrix Method
micros.description: Write a system as AX = B and solve X = A⁻¹B when |A| ≠ 0. When |A| = 0, use (adj A)B to distinguish inconsistent systems from ones with infinitely many solutions.
outcomes: Can solve 2- and 3-variable systems via X = A⁻¹B
Can classify a system as unique / inconsistent / infinite using |A| and (adj A)B

nodes.title: Continuity and Differentiability
nodes.description: Continuity at a point demands three things: f(a) exists, the limit exists, and they are equal — 'the pen never leaves the paper'. Differentiability is stronger: the graph must also be smooth, so |x| is continuous everywhere yet not differentiable at its corner. You will test piecewise functions, then differentiate everything in sight — composites via the chain rule, implicit relations, exponential and logarithmic functions, and parametric forms. This is the technical engine room of calculus.
learning_outcomes: Can test continuity at a point via left limit, right limit and function value, including for piecewise functions
Can determine parameter values that make a piecewise function continuous
Can explain with examples why differentiability implies continuity but not conversely (|x| at 0)
Can differentiate composite functions with the chain rule, including trig, exponential and logarithmic compositions
Can perform implicit differentiation, logarithmic differentiation and parametric differentiation, and compute second derivatives

misconceptions.description: Believes every continuous function is differentiable — smoothness comes free with unbrokenness.
misconceptions.signal: Claims |x| is differentiable at 0 'because the graph is connected'; never checks corners or cusps.
misconceptions.remedy: Zoom in on |x| at 0: a differentiable graph flattens into its tangent line under zoom, but the corner stays a corner forever. Compute the left (−1) and right (+1) difference-quotient limits to certify the failure, then bank the hierarchy: differentiable ⊂ continuous.

misconceptions.description: Reduces continuity to 'f(a) is defined' or to 'the limit exists', dropping the equality requirement.
misconceptions.signal: Declares a function continuous after checking only one of the three conditions; accepts a hole-with-dot-elsewhere graph as continuous.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a three-item checklist stamped on every problem: value ✓ limit ✓ equal ✓. Show the three distinct failure modes graphically (missing point, jump, misplaced dot) and have the student name which condition each violates.

misconceptions.description: Chain rule amputation: differentiates the outer function but forgets to multiply by the inner derivative.
misconceptions.signal: Writes d/dx sin(x²) = cos(x²); d/dx e^(3x) = e^(3x).
misconceptions.remedy: Onion-peeling protocol: name the layers u = x², y = sin u in writing, then multiply dy/du · du/dx explicitly for a dozen problems before allowing shortcuts. Numerically verify one case (slope of sin(x²) at x = 1 ≈ 1.08, not 0.54) to prove the factor is real.

misconceptions.description: Checks differentiability of a piecewise function by plugging the point into a one-sided derivative formula, never comparing both sides.
misconceptions.signal: At a boundary point computes the derivative of just one piece and declares the function differentiable; or matches function values and assumes derivatives match too.
misconceptions.remedy: Two-column ritual at every junction: left derivative | right derivative, computed separately, then compared. Reinforce with a graph where the pieces MEET (continuous) but at different slopes — visibly a kink, hence not differentiable.

real_world_hooks: Income-tax slabs: the tax function is continuous but has corners at slab boundaries
A cricket ball's bounce: position is continuous, velocity jumps — differentiability lost at impact
Electricity tariffs and cab surge pricing as piecewise functions
Zooming into a smooth curve on your phone map until it looks straight — that's differentiability
Temperature through the day: continuous, but the rate flips sign at the afternoon peak
teaching.video_search: continuity differentiability chain rule class 12

questions.prompt: At x = 0, the function f(x) = |x| is:

options.diagnosis: Equates the corner with a break; the graph is unbroken at 0 — only smoothness fails.
Reverses the implication; differentiability ALWAYS forces continuity, so this combination is impossible for any function.

questions.explanation: lim x→0 |x| = 0 = f(0), so f is continuous. But the difference quotient has left limit −1 and right limit +1, so no single derivative exists — a corner. Continuity is necessary but not sufficient for differentiability.

questions.prompt: The derivative of sin(x²) with respect to x is:

options.diagnosis: Differentiated the inner function INSIDE the outer one; chain rule layers collapsed into each other.
Chain rule executed fully but with the sign of d(sin)/dx flipped — mixed up with the derivative of cos.

questions.explanation: Layers: y = sin u, u = x². dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²). Omitting the inner derivative 2x is the single most common chain-rule error.

questions.prompt: f(x) = kx + 1 for x ≤ 5 and f(x) = 3x − 5 for x > 5. For what value of k is f continuous at x = 5?

options.diagnosis: Matched the SLOPES of the two pieces instead of their values; that's a (failed) differentiability condition, not continuity.
Solved 5k = 10, dropping the '+1' from the left piece while equating.
Evaluated the right piece as 3(5) = 15, dropping the −5; solving 5k + 1 = 15 gives k = 14/5.

questions.explanation: Continuity at 5 needs left value = right limit: 5k + 1 = 3(5) − 5 = 10, so 5k = 9 and k = 9/5. Matching coefficients of x (k = 3) would be aiming at equal slopes — a different, stronger condition that this function cannot satisfy simultaneously.

micros.title: Continuity at a Point: the Three-part Test
micros.description: f is continuous at a exactly when the left limit, right limit and f(a) all exist AND are equal. Apply the test to piecewise and rational functions, and classify what fails when a function is discontinuous.
outcomes: Can run the three-part continuity test at a point
Can name which ingredient fails (limit missing, value missing, or unequal) in a discontinuity

question.prompt: Define f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3 and f(3) = 4. Is f continuous at x = 3?

options.text: No: the limit is 6 but f(3) = 4, and the two must be equal
Yes, because the limit as x → 3 exists
No, because f is not defined at x = 3
options.diagnosis: Did not read the definition: f(3) IS defined (as 4); the failure is the mismatch, not a missing value.

question.explanation: For x ≠ 3, f(x) = (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3) = x + 3, so the limit at 3 is 6. Continuity needs limit = value: 6 ≠ 4, so f is discontinuous at 3. Having a defined value, or an existing limit, is necessary but not sufficient — they must agree.

micros.title: Choosing Parameters for Continuity of Piecewise Functions
micros.description: Given a piecewise function with an unknown constant (e.g. f(x) = kx² for x ≤ 2, f(x) = 3 for x > 2), equate the one-sided limits and the value at the joint to solve for the constant.
outcomes: Can set up and solve the matching equation at the junction point
Can verify the resulting function is continuous by re-running the three-part test

micros.title: Differentiability Implies Continuity — Not Conversely
micros.description: Differentiability at a point requires equal left-hand and right-hand derivatives. Every differentiable function is continuous, but |x| at 0 is continuous with a corner: continuity does not buy smoothness.
outcomes: Can check differentiability by comparing one-sided derivatives
Can state and instantiate the one-way implication with |x| at 0

question.prompt: At x = 0, the function f(x) = |x| is:

options.diagnosis: Reversed the implication: differentiability is the STRONGER condition and always brings continuity with it.
Misread the V-shaped graph as broken; |x| has no jump at 0, only a corner.

question.explanation: |x| → 0 as x → 0 from both sides and |0| = 0, so it is continuous. But the left-hand derivative is −1 while the right-hand derivative is +1; since they differ, f′(0) does not exist. Corners are continuous, not smooth.

micros.title: The Chain Rule for Composite Functions
micros.description: Differentiate f(g(x)) as f′(g(x)) · g′(x): outer derivative evaluated at the inner function, times the inner derivative. Drill on trig, power and nested compositions until the inner factor is never dropped.
outcomes: Can differentiate compositions like sin(x²), (3x² + 1)⁵, cos³x
Can handle double compositions such as sin(cos(x²))

question.prompt: The derivative of sin(x²) with respect to x is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by the inner derivative but never differentiated the outer sine to cosine.
Differentiated the inner function INSIDE the argument instead of multiplying outside; chain rule structure garbled.

question.explanation: With outer f(u) = sin u and inner u = x²: d/dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · d/dx(x²) = 2x cos(x²). Stopping at cos(x²) amputates the chain — the inner derivative 2x must multiply the result.

micros.title: Implicit Differentiation and Inverse Trig Derivatives
micros.description: Differentiate relations like x² + y² = 25 term-by-term, attaching dy/dx to every y-derivative via the chain rule, then solve for dy/dx. Derive and use d/dx sin⁻¹x = 1/√(1−x²) and d/dx tan⁻¹x = 1/(1+x²).
outcomes: Can find dy/dx from an implicit relation
Can differentiate expressions containing sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹

micros.title: Derivatives of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
micros.description: Use d/dx eˣ = eˣ, d/dx ln x = 1/x, d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a, combined with the chain rule for forms like e^(3x²) and ln(sin x).
outcomes: Can differentiate exponential and logarithmic compositions
Can explain why aˣ needs the extra ln a factor

micros.title: Logarithmic Differentiation
micros.description: For functions of the form u(x)^v(x) or unwieldy products/quotients, take ln of both sides, differentiate implicitly, and multiply back by y. The classic: d/dx xˣ = xˣ(1 + ln x).
outcomes: Can differentiate xˣ and similar variable-power functions
Can decide when logarithmic differentiation is the efficient route

micros.title: Parametric Differentiation and Second Derivatives
micros.description: For x = f(t), y = g(t), compute dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); iterate carefully for d²y/dx² by differentiating dy/dx with respect to t and dividing by dx/dt again. Compute second derivatives of explicit functions.
outcomes: Can compute dy/dx for parametric curves like x = a cos t, y = a sin t
Can compute second derivatives, including the parametric case

nodes.title: Applications of Derivatives: Rates, Monotonicity, Maxima and Minima
nodes.description: Derivatives go to work: related rates connect dA/dt to dr/dt through the chain rule; the sign of f′ tells where a function increases or decreases; and critical points, filtered through the first- or second-derivative test, locate maxima and minima. The crown jewels are optimisation problems — largest area, least cost, fastest route. This chapter is where calculus starts earning its keep in physics, economics and engineering.
learning_outcomes: Can solve related-rates problems by differentiating a geometric relation with respect to time
Can determine intervals of increase and decrease from the sign of f′
Can find critical points and classify them using the first- or second-derivative test
Can recognise critical points that are NOT extrema (e.g. x³ at 0) and check endpoints for absolute extrema on closed intervals
Can set up and solve optimisation word problems, verifying the nature of the optimum

misconceptions.description: Believes f′(c) = 0 guarantees a maximum or minimum at c.
misconceptions.signal: Marks every critical point as an extremum; never tests the sign change; x³ at 0 called 'a minimum'.
misconceptions.remedy: Keep x³ at 0 on permanent display: slope zero, yet the curve sails through rising on both sides. Require a verdict line for each critical point — sign chart of f′ or sign of f″ — before any max/min label is granted.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the sign of f with the sign of f′: 'f is positive here, so f is increasing here'.
misconceptions.signal: Reads increase/decrease off whether the graph is above the x-axis rather than off its slope.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast plots: f(x) = 1/x on (0, ∞) is positive yet decreasing; f(x) = x on (−∞, 0) is negative yet increasing. Drill the sorting question 'positive or increasing?' on graph snippets until the two attributes decouple.

misconceptions.description: In related-rates problems, differentiates with respect to the space variable (or substitutes values BEFORE differentiating), missing the chain rule through time.
misconceptions.signal: From A = πr² writes dA/dt = 2πr with no dr/dt factor; plugs r = 5 into A first and differentiates a constant.
misconceptions.remedy: Enforce the sequence: relate variables symbolically → differentiate w.r.t. t (every variable earns a d/dt) → THEN substitute numbers. Annotate each term with units (cm²/s vs cm/s) so a missing dr/dt shows up as a units mismatch.

misconceptions.description: Hunts absolute extrema on a closed interval only among critical points, ignoring the endpoints.
misconceptions.signal: On [0, 3] reports the local minimum as absolute even when f(3) is larger/smaller; endpoints never evaluated.
misconceptions.remedy: Institute the candidate-list method: absolute extrema live among {critical points} ∪ {endpoints} — build the full table of values every time. A graph where the max sits at the interval's edge makes the omission visceral.

real_world_hooks: Minimising the metal in a tin can of fixed volume — real packaging economics
A ladder sliding down a wall: how fast does the top drop as the base slides?
Maximum height and range of a cricket ball or ISRO launch trajectory
Economics: marginal cost/revenue and profit maximisation where MR = MC
Air pollution balloons: rate of volume change as a balloon inflates
teaching.video_search: applications of derivatives maxima minima related rates class 12

questions.prompt: The function f(x) = x² − 4x + 5 is increasing on:

options.diagnosis: Solved f′(x) < 0 by mistake, or flipped the inequality when isolating x; the interval found is where f DECREASES.
Solved 2x − 4 > 0 as x > 4; dropped the coefficient 2 when dividing.

questions.explanation: f′(x) = 2x − 4 > 0 ⟺ x > 2, so f increases exactly on (2, ∞). Note f(x) = (x−2)² + 1 is positive EVERYWHERE, yet it decreases until x = 2 — positivity of f and increase of f are unrelated properties.

questions.prompt: The radius of a circle is increasing at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area increasing when the radius is 5 cm?

options.diagnosis: Substituted dr/dt where r belongs: computed 2π(2) instead of 2π(5)·2; variables and rates swapped.

questions.explanation: A = πr² ⟹ dA/dt = 2πr·(dr/dt) = 2π(5)(2) = 20π cm²/s. Forgetting the dr/dt factor gives 10π (units would wrongly be cm²), and 25π is just the AREA value πr² — a quantity, not a rate.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x³, which statement about x = 0 is correct?

options.text: It is a critical point but NOT a local maximum or minimum
It is a local minimum since f′(0) = 0
It is a local maximum since f′(0) = 0
It is not a critical point since f′(0) ≠ 0
options.diagnosis: Differentiation slip: f′(x) = 3x² does vanish at 0; recompute before classifying.

questions.explanation: f′(x) = 3x² is zero at x = 0, so 0 is critical. But f′ > 0 on BOTH sides (no sign change), so f is increasing through 0 — a point of inflexion with horizontal tangent, not an extremum. f′(c) = 0 is necessary, never sufficient, for an interior extremum.

micros.title: Derivative as an Instantaneous Rate of Change
micros.description: Interpret dy/dx as the rate of change of y with respect to x in applied units — marginal cost, velocity, rate of area growth with radius — and evaluate rates at specific instants.
outcomes: Can compute and interpret a rate of change with correct units
Can translate 'rate of change of A with respect to r' into dA/dr

micros.title: Related Rates: Differentiating Through Time
micros.description: When two quantities are linked by a geometric relation, differentiate the RELATION with respect to time t using the chain rule, and only then substitute the instant's values. Balloons, ladders, melting cubes.
outcomes: Can set up dA/dt = (dA/dr)(dr/dt)-style chains from a geometric formula
Can explain why substituting values before differentiating destroys the problem

question.prompt: The radius of a circle is increasing at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area increasing when the radius is 5 cm?

options.diagnosis: Reported the AREA πr² at r = 5, not its rate of change; never differentiated.
Computed 2π(dr/dt) — forgot the factor r when differentiating πr².

question.explanation: A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr · dr/dt = 2π(5)(2) = 20π cm²/s. Substituting r = 5 BEFORE differentiating gives A = 25π, a constant whose derivative is 0 — the classic related-rates trap.

micros.title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions via the Sign of f′
micros.description: f is increasing where f′ > 0 and decreasing where f′ < 0. Solve the inequality f′(x) > 0, present intervals of monotonicity, and keep the sign of f itself firmly separate from the sign of f′.
outcomes: Can find intervals of increase/decrease by solving f′(x) > 0 and f′(x) < 0
Can articulate why the sign of f says nothing about monotonicity

question.prompt: The function f(x) = x² − 4x + 5 is increasing exactly on:

options.diagnosis: Solved f′(x) < 0 (or flipped the inequality); found the decreasing interval instead.
Differentiated incorrectly to x − 4 (or solved 2x > 4 as x > 4); the correct root of f′(x) = 2x − 4 is x = 2.

question.explanation: f′(x) = 2x − 4 > 0 ⟺ x > 2, so f increases on (2, ∞). Note f(x) = (x−2)² + 1 is positive EVERYWHERE, yet f still decreases on (−∞, 2): positivity of f and increase of f are unrelated properties.

micros.title: Critical Points and the First-derivative Test
micros.description: Find points where f′ = 0 or f′ fails to exist, then classify them by the SIGN CHANGE of f′: + to − gives a local max, − to + a local min, no change (like x³ at 0) gives neither.
outcomes: Can locate critical points and run the first-derivative sign test
Can exhibit a critical point that is not an extremum

question.prompt: For f(x) = x³, we have f′(0) = 0. At x = 0 the function has:

options.text: Neither a local maximum nor a local minimum

options.diagnosis: Confused 'not an extremum' with 'not a critical point': f′(0) = 0 makes x = 0 critical by definition.

question.explanation: f′(x) = 3x² ≥ 0 on both sides of 0 — the sign of f′ does not change, so x³ keeps rising through the origin. f′(c) = 0 is necessary for an interior extremum but never sufficient; the sign change is what decides.

micros.title: The Second-derivative Test
micros.description: At a critical point c with f′(c) = 0: f″(c) < 0 means local max, f″(c) > 0 means local min, and f″(c) = 0 is inconclusive — fall back to the first-derivative test.
outcomes: Can classify critical points using f″
Can recognise the inconclusive case f″(c) = 0 and switch tests

micros.title: Absolute Extrema on a Closed Interval
micros.description: On [a, b], the absolute maximum and minimum occur at critical points OR at the endpoints. Build the candidate list (critical points inside the interval plus both endpoints), evaluate f at each, and compare.
outcomes: Can execute the closed-interval method completely, endpoints included
Can discard critical points that fall outside the interval

question.prompt: The absolute maximum value of f(x) = x³ − 3x on the interval [0, 3] is:

options.diagnosis: Used the critical point x = −1 (where f = 2), which lies OUTSIDE [0, 3].
Evaluated only the left endpoint x = 0; never compared all candidates.

question.explanation: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1; only x = 1 lies in [0, 3]. Candidates: f(0) = 0, f(1) = −2, f(3) = 27 − 9 = 18. The absolute maximum is 18, attained at the ENDPOINT x = 3 — checking only critical points would wrongly return −2.

micros.title: Optimisation Word Problems
micros.description: Translate a story (maximum area, minimum cost, fastest route) into a one-variable function using the constraint, find and classify its critical points, and answer in context with the nature of the optimum verified.
outcomes: Can set up the objective function and eliminate a variable via the constraint
Can verify max/min with a derivative test and state the answer with units

nodes.title: Integrals: Techniques and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
nodes.description: Integration reverses differentiation: an indefinite integral is a whole family of antiderivatives, differing by the constant C. You will build a toolkit — substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions, and standard forms leading to logs and inverse trig — then meet the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, which computes definite integrals as F(b) − F(a) and welds together the tangent problem and the area problem. It is arguably the single most powerful equation in mathematics.
learning_outcomes: Can find antiderivatives of standard functions and always include the constant of integration
Can integrate by substitution, recognising when an integrand contains a function and its derivative
Can integrate by parts, choosing u by the ILATE heuristic, and handle products like x·eˣ
Can evaluate definite integrals via the Fundamental Theorem as F(b) − F(a), respecting order and sign
Can use partial fractions and properties of definite integrals (e.g. ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a−x)dx) to simplify evaluation

misconceptions.description: Drops the constant of integration — believes d/dx and ∫ cancel exactly, so each function has ONE antiderivative.
misconceptions.signal: Writes ∫x² dx = x³/3; loses solution families in differential equations later.
misconceptions.remedy: Differentiate x³/3, x³/3 + 7 and x³/3 − 42 and watch all three collapse to x²: the reverse journey cannot know which one you left from. Graph the family as parallel curves; make a missing +C cost a mark ritually.

misconceptions.description: Integrates products factor-by-factor: ∫f·g dx = (∫f dx)(∫g dx).
misconceptions.signal: Writes ∫x eˣ dx = (x²/2)eˣ; never reaches for parts or substitution.
misconceptions.remedy: Differentiate the claimed answer and watch the product rule spray extra terms — it cannot reproduce the integrand. Mirror the lesson from differentiation: products need their own machinery (integration by parts), which is the product rule run backwards.

misconceptions.description: Reverses direction: differentiates instead of anti-differentiating (∫x² dx = 2x), or applies the power rule with the exponent going down.
misconceptions.signal: Power drops by one under an integral sign; ∫cos x dx = −sin x (differentiated instead).
misconceptions.remedy: Institute the verification loop: every integral answer must be differentiated back to the integrand before submission. The habit is self-correcting — 2x differentiates to 2, not x², and the error surfaces immediately.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles the Fundamental Theorem: computes F(a) − F(b), adds F(b) + F(a), or appends +C to definite integrals.
misconceptions.signal: Definite integral answers off by sign, or doubled; writes '7 + C' for a definite integral.
misconceptions.remedy: Verbalise F(b) − F(a) as 'net change from a to b — end minus start', like a trip odometer. Show the constant cancelling: (F(b)+C) − (F(a)+C) kills C, so definite integrals are numbers, not families.

real_world_hooks: Odometer from speedometer: integrating speed over time recovers distance
Total rainfall from a rain-intensity graph during a monsoon downpour
ISRO: integrating thrust acceleration to get a rocket's velocity profile
Electricity bill: energy = integral of power drawn over the month
