Area of an irregular plot of farmland as an integral
teaching.video_search: integration substitution by parts fundamental theorem class 12

questions.prompt: ∫x² dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Raised the power but forgot to divide by the new exponent; differentiate back to see 3x², not x².

questions.explanation: The power rule for integration raises the exponent and divides by it: ∫x² dx = x³/3 + C. The +C is essential — every function of the form x³/3 + constant has derivative x². Always check by differentiating.

questions.prompt: Evaluate ∫₁² 3x² dx.

options.diagnosis: Antiderivative taken as 3x³ — forgot to divide by the new exponent (3x³/3 = x³); then 24 − 3 = 21.

questions.explanation: ∫3x² dx = x³, so the definite integral is [x³]₁² = 2³ − 1³ = 8 − 1 = 7. It is end-value MINUS start-value: forgetting to subtract F(1) gives 8; adding gives 9.

questions.prompt: ∫x eˣ dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Sign slip inside integration by parts: added ∫eˣ dx instead of subtracting it.
Treated eˣ as if it absorbs the integral unchanged and x as a passive constant; parts never applied.

questions.explanation: By parts with u = x, dv = eˣdx: ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C = (x − 1)eˣ + C. Verify by differentiating: (x − 1)eˣ + eˣ = x eˣ ✓. Integrating the factors separately — (x²/2)(eˣ) — fails this check.

questions.prompt: Priya writes ∫2x dx = x² + 1 and Rahul writes ∫2x dx = x² − 7. Each checks by differentiating and recovers 2x. What is the correct conclusion?

options.text: Both are antiderivatives: differentiation kills any added constant, so the antiderivatives of 2x form the family x² + C, any two differing by a constant
Neither is right: ∫2x dx is exactly x², because integration and differentiation are inverse operations that pair each function with ONE antiderivative
Both are wrong for a different reason: ∫2x dx = 2, since under the integral sign the power should come down in front and then reduce by one
At least one must contain an algebra slip, because two genuinely different functions can never share exactly the same derivative at every point
options.diagnosis: Assumes differentiation is one-to-one; it is many-to-one — all vertical shifts of a curve have identical slopes, so distinct functions can share a derivative.

questions.explanation: Differentiate both answers: d/dx(x² + 1) = 2x and d/dx(x² − 7) = 2x. The constant contributes zero slope, so differentiation erases it — and the reverse journey cannot know which constant was erased. Hence 2x has an entire FAMILY of antiderivatives, x² + C, whose graphs are vertical translates of one another; any two members differ by a constant. That is precisely why the indefinite integral must carry +C: writing ∫2x dx = x² alone silently discards every other member of the family.

micros.title: The Antiderivative Idea and the Constant of Integration
micros.description: Integration reverses differentiation: F is an antiderivative of f when F′ = f. Because constants die under d/dx, every answer carries + C — a whole family of curves, one for each constant.
outcomes: Can antidifferentiate power functions with the reversed power rule (exponent up, then divide)
Can explain why + C is mandatory and what it represents geometrically

question.prompt: ∫ x² dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Raised the power but forgot to divide by the new exponent 3.

question.explanation: The power rule in reverse: raise the exponent to 3, divide by 3, and add the constant: ∫x² dx = x³/3 + C. Check by differentiating: d/dx(x³/3 + C) = x². Answering 2x differentiates instead of integrating; omitting + C loses infinitely many antiderivatives.

micros.title: The Table of Standard Integrals
micros.description: Command the standard forms: xⁿ, 1/x, eˣ, aˣ, sin x, cos x, sec²x, 1/(1+x²), 1/√(1−x²) — each verified by differentiating the claimed answer, with special care on signs (∫sin x dx = −cos x + C).
outcomes: Can quote and apply the standard integral table accurately, signs included
Can verify any table entry by differentiation

micros.title: Integration by Substitution
micros.description: When the integrand contains a function AND (a constant multiple of) its derivative, set u equal to the inner function so du absorbs the derivative factor: ∫2x cos(x²) dx becomes ∫cos u du.
outcomes: Can spot the u–du pair and carry out the substitution completely
Can convert back to x and verify by differentiating

question.prompt: ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Sign flipped: confused ∫cos u du = sin u with ∫sin u du = −cos u.
Substituted u = x² but never let du = 2x dx absorb the factor 2; double-counted it.

question.explanation: Let u = x², so du = 2x dx — the 2x in the integrand is exactly du. Then ∫cos u du = sin u + C = sin(x²) + C. Differentiate to confirm: cos(x²)·2x. Multiplying the pieces' separate integrals (x²·sin(x²)) is not a valid rule.

micros.title: Integration by Parts
micros.description: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du, with u chosen by ILATE (Inverse trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential). Handles products like x·eˣ, x·sin x, ln x that substitution cannot touch.
outcomes: Can choose u and dv sensibly and execute the formula
Can handle repeated application and the ∫eˣ(f + f′) shortcut

question.prompt: ∫ x eˣ dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Sign slip in the parts formula: used uv + ∫v du instead of uv − ∫v du.
Treated x as a constant that integration ignores; only integrated the eˣ factor.

question.explanation: Take u = x (algebraic before exponential in ILATE), dv = eˣ dx: ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C. Check: d/dx(xeˣ − eˣ) = eˣ + xeˣ − eˣ = xeˣ. Integrating each factor separately and multiplying — (x²/2)eˣ — is not a valid rule: differentiation of products needs the product rule, so integration of products needs parts.

micros.title: Integration by Partial Fractions
micros.description: Split a proper rational function with factorable denominator into simpler fractions — A/(x−a) + B/(x−b), with repeated-factor and quadratic-factor patterns — then integrate each piece to logarithms and arctangents.
outcomes: Can decompose rational integrands with distinct and repeated linear factors
Can integrate the resulting pieces, e.g. ∫dx/((x−1)(x+2))

micros.title: The Definite Integral as a Limit of Sums
micros.description: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the limit of Riemann sums: slice [a, b] into n strips, sum the strip areas f(xᵢ)·Δx, and let n → ∞. This is what the integral MEANS; the Fundamental Theorem is what makes it computable.
outcomes: Can set up a Riemann sum for a simple function and pass to the limit
Can interpret the definite integral as signed area accumulated from a to b

micros.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
micros.description: If F′ = f on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a): upper-limit value minus lower-limit value, in that order, and no + C. The bridge between antiderivatives and areas.
outcomes: Can evaluate definite integrals via F(b) − F(a) with correct order and signs
Can explain why the constant of integration cancels in definite integrals

question.prompt: ∫₁² 2x dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Evaluated F(2) = 4 only; forgot to subtract the lower-limit value F(1) = 1.

question.explanation: An antiderivative of 2x is x². By the Fundamental Theorem: ∫₁² 2x dx = [x²]₁² = 2² − 1² = 4 − 1 = 3. Subtracting in the wrong order gives −3; adding gives 5. And a definite integral is a NUMBER — no + C appears.

micros.title: Properties of Definite Integrals
micros.description: Exploit structure instead of computing: swapping limits flips the sign, ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a−x)dx, splitting at an interior point, and even/odd symmetry on [−a, a] (odd integrands give 0).
outcomes: Can apply the king property f(x) → f(a−x) to evaluate resistant integrals
Can use even/odd symmetry and limit-splitting to shortcut evaluation

nodes.title: Applications of Integrals: Areas Under Curves
nodes.description: The definite integral becomes a measuring tool: the area under a curve is ∫y dx, the area between two curves is the integral of (upper − lower), and regions bounded by parabolas, circles and lines yield to careful setup. The crucial subtlety is that a raw definite integral counts area below the x-axis as negative — geometric area requires splitting at the crossings and taking absolute values. Sketch first, integrate second.
learning_outcomes: Can sketch the region described by curves and lines before setting up any integral
Can compute the area under a curve between two ordinates using a definite integral
Can split an integral at x-axis crossings and combine absolute values to get true geometric area
Can compute the area between two curves by integrating (upper − lower) between intersection points found algebraically

misconceptions.description: Discards or mangles regions below the x-axis: reports a negative 'area' or silently drops the negative lobe.
misconceptions.signal: States an area as −2; for sin x on [0, 2π] computes only the first arch and answers 2.
misconceptions.remedy: Shade both lobes of sin x on [0, 2π] in different colours and ask 'is the lower pool of paint less real?'. Establish the protocol: find the crossings, integrate each piece, add |values| — and that any final negative area means a setup error.

misconceptions.description: Equates the plain definite integral with geometric area even when the curve crosses the axis: ∫₀²π sin x dx = 0, 'so the area is 0'.
misconceptions.signal: Reports 0 area for visibly shaded regions; never splits the interval at roots of the function.
misconceptions.remedy: Distinguish the two questions explicitly — NET signed accumulation vs PAINT needed. Compute both for the same curve and tabulate them side by side so the student owns both concepts rather than merging them.

misconceptions.description: Integrates (f − g) between curves without establishing which is on top (or without finding intersections), yielding sign errors or wrong limits.
misconceptions.signal: Gets a negative between-curves area and just flips the sign at the end without understanding; uses guessed limits.
misconceptions.remedy: Make the sketch non-negotiable: mark intersection points by solving f = g, test one x between them to crown the upper curve, then write ∫(upper − lower). The 'test a point' step converts guessing into verification.

real_world_hooks: Land area of a river-bounded field: the boundary is a curve, the survey is an integral
Cricket wagon wheels and Manhattan charts: area under a run-rate curve is total runs
Cross-sectional area of a dam or road embankment from its design curves
Work from a force-displacement graph in physics is literally area under the curve
Velocity-time graphs: area above vs below the axis = forward vs backward displacement
teaching.video_search: area under curve between curves definite integral class 12

questions.prompt: The area under the line y = 2x, above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 3 is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied base by height (3 × 6) as if the region were a rectangle; the region is a triangle — the integral supplies the missing 1/2 automatically.
Applied an extra factor of 1/2 to the already-correct integral; double-counted the triangle formula on top of ∫2x dx.
Evaluated y(3) = 6 — reported the height of the region, not its area.

questions.explanation: Area = ∫₀³ 2x dx = [x²]₀³ = 9. Geometric check: the region is a right triangle with base 3 and height 6, area = ½ × 3 × 6 = 9 ✓. The integral IS the triangle formula here — don't apply ½ twice.

questions.prompt: The total area enclosed between y = sin x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2π is:

options.diagnosis: Reported the length of the interval; area needs the integral of the function, not the width of the window.

questions.explanation: ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2 (upper arch) and ∫_π^{2π} sin x dx = −2 (lower arch). The signed total is 0, but geometric area = |2| + |−2| = 4. Splitting at the crossing x = π is what separates 'net accumulation' from 'area'.

questions.prompt: The area of the region enclosed between the curves y = x² and y = x is:

options.diagnosis: Added the two individual integrals (1/2 + 1/3) instead of subtracting lower from upper.
Integrated only one curve (x²) over [0,1]; the enclosed region needs the difference of the two.

questions.explanation: Intersections: x² = x at x = 0, 1. On (0, 1), the line y = x is above y = x² (test x = ½: 0.5 > 0.25). Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹ = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. Integrating (x² − x) instead gives −1/6 — the sign says 'you subtracted upper from lower'.

micros.title: Sketching the Region Before Integrating
micros.description: Draw the curves, lines and axis limits first: find intercepts and intersection points, decide where each curve sits relative to the axis and to the other curve. The sketch dictates the limits and the integrand.
outcomes: Can sketch regions bounded by a parabola/circle/line combination
Can find intersection points algebraically to serve as integration limits

micros.title: Area Under a Curve Between Two Ordinates
micros.description: For f ≥ 0 on [a, b], the area between the curve, the x-axis and the ordinates x = a, x = b is ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. Also compute areas against the y-axis via ∫ x dy.
outcomes: Can compute the area under a non-negative curve as a definite integral
Can switch to y-integration when the region is naturally bounded by y-limits

micros.title: Handling Regions Below the Axis
micros.description: The definite integral counts area below the x-axis as negative. For true geometric area, split the integral at every axis crossing and add ABSOLUTE values of the pieces — never let lobes cancel.
outcomes: Can locate axis crossings and split the integral there
Can report total geometric area as the sum of absolute lobe areas

question.prompt: The total area enclosed between the curve y = sin x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2π is:

options.diagnosis: Summed absolute lobe sizes but attached a stray negative sign; area can never be negative.

question.explanation: ∫₀^π sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^π = (−(−1)) − (−1) = 2 and ∫_π^{2π} sin x dx = −2. The plain integral over [0, 2π] is 0 because the lobes cancel — but the GEOMETRIC area is |2| + |−2| = 4. Split at the crossing x = π and add absolute values.

micros.title: Area Between Two Curves
micros.description: Find the intersection points, establish which curve is on top over the interval, and integrate (upper − lower). If the curves swap positions, split the integral at the swap point.
outcomes: Can find intersections and identify the upper curve on each sub-interval
Can compute areas like the region between y = x and y = x²

question.prompt: The area of the region enclosed between y = x and y = x² is:

options.diagnosis: Added the two integrals (1/2 + 1/3) instead of subtracting lower from upper.
Integrated only the line y = x over [0, 1]; forgot to remove the region under the parabola.

question.explanation: The curves meet where x = x², i.e. x = 0 and x = 1, and on (0, 1) the line lies above the parabola (at x = 1/2: 0.5 > 0.25). Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. Integrating (x² − x) — lower minus upper — produces the impossible negative area.

micros.title: Areas of Standard Regions: Circles, Ellipses, Parabola–Line
micros.description: Assemble the full toolkit on classic board configurations: area of a circle or ellipse by integration (using symmetry and quarter-regions), and mixed regions like a parabola cut by a chord.
outcomes: Can derive the area of a circle x² + y² = a² or ellipse by integrating a quarter and multiplying by 4
Can compute the area between a parabola and a chord line

nodes.title: Differential Equations: Separable and First-order Linear
nodes.description: A differential equation relates a function to its derivatives — it describes how something changes and asks you to recover the thing itself. You will read off order and degree, solve separable equations by gathering each variable to its own side, and solve first-order linear equations dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) with the integrating factor e^∫P dx. General solutions carry arbitrary constants; initial conditions pin down particular solutions. This is the native language of physics, biology and economics: growth, decay, cooling, circuits, epidemics.
learning_outcomes: Can determine the order and degree (when defined) of a differential equation
Can verify that a given function is a solution of a differential equation
Can solve separable equations, keeping the arbitrary constant and simplifying it legitimately
Can solve dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) using the integrating factor e^∫P dx
Can apply initial conditions to extract particular solutions and model growth/decay situations

misconceptions.description: Confuses order with degree: order is the highest derivative present; degree is the power of that highest derivative (in polynomial form).
misconceptions.signal: For (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ = 0 answers 'order 3' or 'degree 2'; swaps the two labels under pressure.
misconceptions.remedy: Two-question drill on many examples: 'How DEEP does differentiation go?' (order) then 'What POWER sits on that deepest derivative?' (degree). Flag the trap that other, lower derivatives' powers (like the 4 here) are pure distractors.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles arbitrary constants: drops C entirely, adds a separate C to both sides and cancels them, or expects the count of constants to equal the degree instead of the order.
misconceptions.signal: Presents y = x as 'the' solution of dy/dx = y/x; writes ln y + C = ln x + C ⟹ y = x.
misconceptions.remedy: Show the one-parameter family y = Cx as a fan of lines all satisfying the equation, so losing C visibly loses almost every solution. Rule: integrate both sides, write ONE constant on one side immediately, and rename combined constants honestly (C₂ − C₁ = C).

misconceptions.description: Bungles the integrating factor: uses ∫P dx itself (without exponentiating), or e^P without integrating.
misconceptions.signal: For dy/dx + (2/x)y = x writes IF = 2 ln x or e^(2/x) instead of e^(2 ln x) = x².
misconceptions.remedy: Drill the three-step chant 'integrate P → exponentiate → multiply through', writing each artifact separately. Verify the factor works: after multiplying, the left side must collapse to d/dx(IF·y) — if it doesn't, the factor is wrong.

misconceptions.description: Separates variables illegally: moves terms additively across dy/dx, or divides by expressions that could be zero without noting lost solutions.
misconceptions.signal: From dy/dx = x + y writes dy = x dx + y... then integrates; loses y = 0 solutions when dividing by y.
misconceptions.remedy: Test separability first: can the RHS be written as f(x)·g(y)? (x + y cannot.) When dividing by g(y), park the case g(y) = 0 in a margin note and check at the end whether constant solutions were lost.

real_world_hooks: Chai cooling on the table follows Newton's law of cooling — a separable equation
Population growth of a city and compound interest are dy/dt = ky in disguise
Carbon dating an archaeological find from its decay equation
Epidemic spread curves (as seen during COVID) come from differential equations
A parachutist's terminal velocity: solving dv/dt = g − kv
teaching.video_search: differential equations separable integrating factor class 12

questions.prompt: The order and degree of the differential equation (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ + y = 0 are:

options.diagnosis: Took the highest power appearing ANYWHERE; degree reads the power of the HIGHEST-ORDER derivative only.
Read the order off the largest exponent (4) rather than the deepest derivative (second).

questions.explanation: The highest derivative present is d²y/dx² → order 2. Its power (with the equation polynomial in derivatives) is 3 → degree 3. The exponent 4 on the FIRST derivative is a deliberate distractor — degree only looks at the highest-order derivative.

questions.prompt: The general solution of dy/dx = y/x (x, y > 0) is:

options.diagnosis: Integrated the x-side as if the equation were dy = (1/x)... treated y on the right as a constant instead of separating dy/y = dx/x.
Sign slip while separating: wrote dy/y = −dx/x, giving ln y = −ln x + C₁, i.e. xy = C.

questions.explanation: Separate: dy/y = dx/x. Integrate: ln y = ln x + C₁, so y = e^{C₁}x = Cx — a one-parameter family of lines through the origin. Cancelling the constants to get y = x keeps only ONE member of the family; a sign slip (dy/y = −dx/x) would give the hyperbolas xy = C instead.

questions.prompt: The integrating factor of the differential equation dy/dx + (2/x)y = x (x > 0) is:

options.diagnosis: Integrated 2/x as 2x — power-rule slip on 1/x, whose integral is ln x, not x²/2 scaled.

questions.explanation: P(x) = 2/x, so ∫P dx = 2 ln x, and IF = e^{2 ln x} = e^{ln x²} = x². Check: multiplying through by x² gives x²y′ + 2xy = x³, whose left side is exactly d/dx(x²y) ✓ — the collapse test every integrating factor must pass.

questions.prompt: A bacterial culture grows according to dy/dx = ky, whose general solution is y = Ce^(kx). Why must a measurement such as y(0) = y₀ be supplied before the model can predict the population at a later time?

options.text: The equation only fixes HOW y changes; every value of C gives a curve obeying that growth law, and the initial measurement selects which curve this culture follows
It need not be supplied: the equation alone determines y, since the constant C disappears when you differentiate and so it has no real effect on the solution
Because the equation has degree 1, its solution carries one constant; an equation of second degree would instead need two separate measurements to pin down
Because substituting x = 0 into the general solution forces C = 0, so a measurement is needed to restore the constant that the substitution eliminated
options.diagnosis: Thinks x = 0 kills C; in fact y(0) = Ce⁰ = C, so the initial value doesn't destroy the constant — it directly EQUALS it, which is exactly how y₀ pins C down.

questions.explanation: dy/dx = ky is a statement about slopes: at every point, the growth rate is proportional to the current size. Infinitely many curves satisfy that — y = Ce^(kx) for every C — forming a fan of solutions. The differential equation cannot distinguish a dish seeded with 100 bacteria from one seeded with a million; only a measurement can. Substituting x = 0 gives y(0) = Ce⁰ = C, so C = y₀ and the particular solution is y = y₀e^(kx). (The number of arbitrary constants matches the ORDER of the equation — here first order, one constant — not its degree.)

micros.title: Order and Degree of a Differential Equation
micros.description: Order = highest derivative present; degree = the power of THAT highest derivative once the equation is polynomial in its derivatives (and undefined otherwise). Two different dials — do not cross the wires.
outcomes: Can read off order and degree, including when radicals must first be cleared
Can recognise equations where the degree is not defined

question.prompt: For the differential equation (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ + y = 0, the order and degree are respectively:

options.diagnosis: Took the highest power appearing ANYWHERE; degree is the power of the highest-ORDER derivative only.
Read the exponent 4 on dy/dx as an order; order counts differentiation, not powers.

question.explanation: The highest derivative present is d²y/dx² → order 2. The equation is polynomial in derivatives, and that highest derivative carries power 3 → degree 3. The power 4 sits on the lower-order dy/dx and is irrelevant to the degree.

micros.title: Verifying Solutions of Differential Equations
micros.description: Substitute a candidate function into the equation: differentiate it as many times as needed and check the identity holds for all x. Verification builds the meaning of 'solution' before any solving technique.
outcomes: Can verify that a given function satisfies a given differential equation
Can show a candidate FAILS to be a solution by exhibiting the mismatch

micros.title: General vs Particular Solutions
micros.description: The general solution of an order-n equation carries n independent arbitrary constants; initial conditions pin them down to a particular solution. The number of constants matches the ORDER, not the degree.
outcomes: Can distinguish general from particular solutions and count constants correctly
Can apply an initial condition to extract the particular solution

micros.title: Solving Separable Equations
micros.description: Rewrite dy/dx = g(x)h(y) as dy/h(y) = g(x) dx — a multiplicative separation, never additive — integrate both sides, keep ONE arbitrary constant, and simplify it legitimately (e.g. e^C → A).
outcomes: Can separate variables correctly and integrate both sides
Can manage the constant of integration through exponentials and note solutions lost by division

question.prompt: The general solution of dy/dx = 2xy is:

options.diagnosis: Integrated the right side with respect to x while treating y as a constant — the variables were never separated.
Integrated 2x incorrectly as 2x again; ∫2x dx = x², not 2x.

question.explanation: Separate: dy/y = 2x dx. Integrate: ln|y| = x² + C₁, so y = ±e^(C₁) e^(x²) = C e^(x²). Dropping the constant gives only ONE solution curve out of infinitely many; the constant must ride along from the moment of integration.

micros.title: First-order Linear Equations and the Integrating Factor
micros.description: For dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x), multiply through by IF = e^(∫P dx) — integrate P FIRST, then exponentiate — so the left side collapses to d/dx(y·IF); then y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C.
outcomes: Can compute the integrating factor correctly
Can solve equations like dy/dx + y/x = x² end to end

question.prompt: The integrating factor of the differential equation dy/dx + (1/x)y = x², for x > 0, is:

options.diagnosis: Used P(x) itself as the integrating factor; skipped both the integration and the exponentiation.

question.explanation: IF = e^(∫P dx) = e^(∫dx/x) = e^(ln x) = x (for x > 0). Both steps are essential: integrate P to get ln x, THEN exponentiate. Multiplying the equation by x gives d/dx(xy) = x³, which integrates immediately.

micros.title: Modelling with Differential Equations: Growth and Decay
micros.description: dy/dt = ky yields y = y₀e^(kt): exponential growth (k > 0) or decay (k < 0). Fit k and y₀ from data, and answer doubling-time / half-life style questions for populations, investments and radioactivity.
outcomes: Can derive y = y₀e^(kt) from dy/dt = ky with an initial condition
Can solve applied growth/decay problems including doubling time

nodes.title: Vector Algebra: Dot and Cross Products
nodes.description: Vectors carry magnitude and direction, and two different 'multiplications' extract different geometry: the dot product a·b = |a||b|cos θ is a SCALAR measuring alignment (zero means perpendicular), while the cross product a×b is a VECTOR perpendicular to both, with magnitude |a||b|sin θ equal to the parallelogram's area (zero means parallel). You will compute both in component form, find projections, angles, areas and unit normals. This is the working mathematics of forces, torques and 3D graphics.
learning_outcomes: Can represent vectors in component form, compute magnitudes, unit vectors and section-formula combinations
Can compute dot products, use them to find angles and projections, and characterise perpendicularity by a·b = 0
Can compute cross products via the determinant rule, use |a×b| for areas, and characterise parallelism by a×b = 0
Can state which product yields a scalar and which a vector, and that a×b = −(b×a) while a·b = b·a

misconceptions.description: Adds magnitudes when adding vectors: |a + b| = |a| + |b| regardless of directions.
misconceptions.signal: Claims two forces of 3 N and 4 N always total 7 N; triangle inequality never mentioned.
misconceptions.remedy: Walk the displacement: 3 km east then 4 km north lands you 5 km away, not 7. Let the student drag two arrows in an applet through angles 0° to 180° and watch |a+b| slide between 7 and 1 — equality only when perfectly aligned.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the output TYPES of the two products: expects a·b to be a vector, or a×b to be a number.
misconceptions.signal: Writes a·b with i, j, k components; reports |a×b| when the vector a×b is asked, or vice versa.
misconceptions.remedy: Attach each product to its geometric deliverable: dot = 'how much alignment?' (one number), cross = 'the axis perpendicular to both, sized by area' (an arrow). Type-check every equation: a scalar can never equal a vector, so errors become syntax errors.

misconceptions.description: From a·b = 0 concludes a = 0 or b = 0, missing perpendicularity (and symmetrically for a×b = 0 missing parallelism).
misconceptions.signal: Treats zero products like zero products of numbers; surprised that i·j = 0 for two 'perfectly good' vectors.
misconceptions.remedy: Make i·j = 0 and i×i = 0 canonical examples: nonzero vectors with vanishing products. Reframe zero as INFORMATION — dot zero says 'perpendicular', cross zero says 'parallel' — rather than as degeneracy.

misconceptions.description: Treats the cross product as commutative: a×b = b×a.
misconceptions.signal: Swaps factors freely in cross products; sign of the normal vector comes out random.
misconceptions.remedy: Right-hand rule physically, both orders: curling from a to b points the thumb opposite to curling from b to a, so a×b = −(b×a). Contrast in the same breath with the dot product, which IS symmetric, to prevent overcorrection.

real_world_hooks: Work done = force · displacement (dot); torque on a spanner = r × F (cross)
A boat crossing a river: velocity vectors add tip-to-tail, not magnitude-to-magnitude
Cricket fielding: the throw to the keeper as a 3D displacement vector
Game engines light surfaces using the normal vector from a cross product
ISRO thrust vectoring: resolving engine force along and across the flight path (projection)
teaching.video_search: dot product cross product geometric meaning class 12 vectors

questions.prompt: If a = 2i + 3j − k and b = i − j + 2k, then a·b equals:

options.diagnosis: Sign slip on the k-term: (−1)(2) taken as +2; components multiplied right, one sign lost.
Sign slip on the j-term: took (3)(−1) as +3, giving 2 + 3 − 2 = 3; the k-term's sign was handled correctly.

questions.explanation: a·b = (2)(1) + (3)(−1) + (−1)(2) = 2 − 3 − 2 = −3. The dot product is a SCALAR — a single signed number measuring alignment — never a vector of component products.

questions.prompt: a and b are NON-ZERO vectors with a·b = 0. What must be true?

options.text: At least one of a, b is the zero vector

options.diagnosis: Swapped the zero conditions of the two products: it is a×b = 0 that signals parallel vectors.
Assumes all products vanish together; for perpendicular vectors the cross product is at its LARGEST (|a||b|).

questions.explanation: a·b = |a||b|cos θ = 0 with both magnitudes nonzero forces cos θ = 0, i.e. θ = 90°. Perpendicular nonzero vectors (like i and j) have zero dot product — and simultaneously the maximal cross product, since sin 90° = 1.

questions.prompt: For a = i + j and b = i − j, the cross product a × b equals:

options.diagnosis: Computed the dot product instead: a·b = (1)(1) + (1)(−1) = 0 — or assumed that perpendicular vectors make the cross product vanish too; the zero conditions of the two products are swapped.

questions.explanation: a × b = det[[i, j, k], [1, 1, 0], [1, −1, 0]] = i(1·0 − 0·(−1)) − j(1·0 − 0·1) + k(1·(−1) − 1·1) = −2k. Computing b × a instead gives +2k (anticommutativity), and the answer must be a VECTOR along k, not the bare number −2.

micros.title: Vectors in Component Form: Magnitude and Unit Vectors
micros.description: Write vectors as xi + yj + zk, compute magnitude |a| = √(x² + y² + z²), build the unit vector a/|a|, and distinguish vectors (magnitude + direction) from scalars.
outcomes: Can compute magnitudes and unit vectors in 3D
Can identify equal, collinear and coinitial vectors from components

micros.title: Vector Addition and the Section Formula
micros.description: Add vectors componentwise (triangle/parallelogram law) — magnitudes do NOT simply add unless the vectors are parallel. Use the section formula (mb + na)/(m + n) for points dividing a segment.
outcomes: Can add and subtract vectors and interpret the triangle law geometrically
Can find position vectors of internal/external division points

question.prompt: Vectors a and b are perpendicular with |a| = 3 and |b| = 4. Then |a + b| equals:

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the magnitudes; that bounds |a − b| for parallel vectors, not this sum.
Multiplied the magnitudes — confused vector addition with some product.

question.explanation: |a + b|² = |a|² + |b|² + 2a·b = 9 + 16 + 0 = 25, so |a + b| = 5 — the Pythagorean diagonal of the rectangle with sides 3 and 4. Magnitudes add to 7 only when the vectors point the SAME way; direction always matters.

micros.title: The Dot Product: a Scalar from Two Vectors
micros.description: a·b = |a||b|cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ — the output is a NUMBER. Use it to find the angle between vectors; it is commutative and distributes over addition.
outcomes: Can compute dot products in component form
Can extract cos θ = a·b/(|a||b|) and interpret its sign

question.prompt: If a = 2i + 3j − k and b = i − j + 2k, then a·b equals:

options.diagnosis: Sign slip: computed 2 + 3 − 2 by ignoring the negative components.
Dropped the third term (−1)(2) = −2 from the sum; incomplete expansion.

question.explanation: a·b = (2)(1) + (3)(−1) + (−1)(2) = 2 − 3 − 2 = −3. The dot product is a SCALAR — multiplying matching components and summing collapses everything to a single number; 2i − 3j − 2k keeps the terms as a vector, which is a type error.

micros.title: Projection of One Vector on Another
micros.description: The scalar projection of a on b is a·b/|b|, the vector projection is (a·b/|b|²)b. Interpret as the shadow of a along b's direction.
outcomes: Can compute scalar and vector projections
Can explain the difference between the two and when each is asked for

micros.title: Perpendicularity and the Zero Dot Product
micros.description: For nonzero vectors, a·b = 0 means a ⊥ b — not that either vector vanishes. Use this test to find unknowns making vectors perpendicular and to verify orthogonality of i, j, k.
outcomes: Can test and impose perpendicularity via a·b = 0
Can state the correct logic: a·b = 0 ⟹ a = 0 or b = 0 or a ⊥ b

question.prompt: a and b are NONZERO vectors with a·b = 0. What can you conclude?

options.diagnosis: Swapped the tests: parallel vectors give a×b = 0; parallel NONZERO vectors have a·b = ±|a||b| ≠ 0.
Invented a magnitude condition; the dot product vanishing constrains the ANGLE (cos θ = 0), not the lengths.

question.explanation: a·b = |a||b|cos θ. With both magnitudes nonzero, the product can only vanish through cos θ = 0, i.e. θ = 90°. Unlike real-number multiplication, a zero dot product does not force a zero factor — perpendicularity is the third way.

micros.title: The Cross Product via the Determinant Rule
micros.description: a×b = |i j k; a₁ a₂ a₃; b₁ b₂ b₃| — the output is a VECTOR perpendicular to both, with |a×b| = |a||b|sin θ. It is anti-commutative: a×b = −(b×a).
outcomes: Can compute cross products with the determinant expansion
Can state and use a×b = −(b×a) and check the result is perpendicular to both inputs

question.prompt: If a × b = 3i − j + 2k, then b × a equals:

options.diagnosis: Confused anti-commutativity with the products cancelling; b × a is the opposite VECTOR, not zero.

question.explanation: The cross product is anti-commutative: b × a = −(a × b) = −3i + j − 2k. Swapping two rows of the defining determinant flips its sign. And the output is a vector — √14 is merely the common MAGNITUDE of both products.

micros.title: Applications of the Cross Product: Areas and Parallelism
micros.description: |a×b| is the area of the parallelogram on a and b (half it for the triangle); a×b = 0 for nonzero vectors means they are parallel. Compute areas of triangles from vertex coordinates.
outcomes: Can compute parallelogram and triangle areas via cross products
Can test collinearity/parallelism with a×b = 0

nodes.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry: Lines and Planes
nodes.description: Vectors turn spatial geometry into computation: a line is r = a + λb (a point plus a direction), specified by direction ratios or the normalized direction cosines with l² + m² + n² = 1. You will find angles between lines using their direction vectors, the shortest distance between skew lines, and work with planes through their normal vectors — including the distance from a point to a plane. This is the geometry of flight paths, laser alignment and 3D modelling.
learning_outcomes: Can convert direction ratios to direction cosines by dividing by the magnitude, and verify l² + m² + n² = 1
Can write vector and Cartesian equations of a line through a point with a given direction, or through two points
Can compute the angle between two lines from their direction vectors and test parallel/perpendicular conditions
Can find the shortest distance between skew lines and the distance from a point to a plane
Can relate the angle between a line and a plane to the angle with the plane's normal (complementary angles)

misconceptions.description: Uses direction ratios directly as direction cosines, skipping normalisation by the magnitude.
misconceptions.signal: States the direction cosines of ratios 2, −1, 2 as (2, −1, 2); l² + m² + n² comes out as 9 and no alarm rings.
misconceptions.remedy: Install the checksum: direction cosines MUST satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1 — have the student verify it on every answer. Connect cosines to meaning: they are literal cosines of angles with the axes, so none can exceed 1 in magnitude.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the angle a line makes with a plane with the angle it makes with the plane's NORMAL (they are complements).
misconceptions.signal: Uses cos θ = |b·n|/(|b||n|) for a line-plane angle without converting; answers off by exactly 90° − θ.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the side-view triangle: line, its shadow in the plane, and the normal — the line-plane angle sits between line and shadow, and line-normal is its complement. Anchor the formula sin θ = |b·n|/(|b||n|) to that picture rather than to memory.

misconceptions.description: Garbles parallel/perpendicular tests: e.g. declares planes parallel when their normals are perpendicular, or lines perpendicular when direction ratios are proportional.
misconceptions.signal: Applies a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂ = 0 as a parallelism test; mixes up proportionality vs zero dot product.
misconceptions.remedy: Route every test through the carrier vectors: planes inherit behaviour from their NORMALS, lines from their DIRECTIONS. Parallel ⟺ vectors proportional; perpendicular ⟺ dot product zero. Two worked contrasts side by side lock the mapping.

misconceptions.description: Computes point-to-plane distance without dividing by |n|: uses |ax₁ + by₁ + cz₁ + d| alone.
misconceptions.signal: Distances come out |n| times too large; answer changes if the plane equation is scaled by 2, and the student doesn't notice the inconsistency.
misconceptions.remedy: Expose the scale bug: 6x − 3y + 2z = 4 and 12x − 6y + 4z = 8 are the SAME plane but give different unnormalised 'distances'. Dividing by |n| restores invariance — tie to the unit-normal form of the plane equation.

real_world_hooks: Two flight paths over an airport: skew lines and their minimum separation (air-safety distance)
A mobile tower's guy-wires: angles between cables and the ground plane
Laser levelling on a construction site: point-to-plane distances
Drone waypoint navigation: lines in space via point + direction
Docking at the ISS: aligning a spacecraft's approach line with the docking plane's normal
teaching.video_search: three dimensional geometry lines planes direction cosines class 12

questions.prompt: The direction cosines of a line with direction ratios 2, −1, 2 are:

options.diagnosis: Divided by the SQUARED magnitude (4+1+4 = 9) instead of its square root 3.
Divided by the sum of absolute values (2+1+2 = 5) instead of √(sum of squares).

questions.explanation: Magnitude = √(2² + (−1)² + 2²) = √9 = 3, so (l, m, n) = (2/3, −1/3, 2/3). Checksum: (2/3)² + (1/3)² + (2/3)² = 9/9 = 1 ✓ — direction cosines must always pass this test.

questions.prompt: The distance of the point (2, 5, −3) from the plane 6x − 3y + 2z − 4 = 0 is:

options.diagnosis: Divided by |n|² = 49 rather than |n| = 7; normalised twice.
Sign slip on the z-term: 2(−3) taken as +6, giving |12 − 15 + 6 − 4| = 1 in the numerator.

questions.explanation: d = |6(2) − 3(5) + 2(−3) − 4| / √(6² + 3² + 2²) = |12 − 15 − 6 − 4| / √49 = 13/7. The division by |n| = 7 is what makes the answer independent of how the plane equation is scaled.

questions.prompt: A line makes an angle of 30° with a plane. The angle between the line and the plane's normal is:

options.diagnosis: Took the supplement (180° − 30°) instead of the complement; the normal stands at 90° to the plane, not 180°.
Believes a line is always perpendicular to a plane's normal — that holds only for lines LYING IN the plane.

questions.explanation: The normal is perpendicular to the plane, so (line, normal) + (line, plane) = 90°. With the plane angle 30°, the normal angle is 60°. This is why the line-plane formula uses sin θ where the line-line formula uses cos θ.

micros.title: Direction Ratios and Direction Cosines
micros.description: Direction ratios a, b, c fix a line's direction up to scale; direction cosines l, m, n are the ratios NORMALISED by √(a² + b² + c²), so that l² + m² + n² = 1 always.
outcomes: Can convert direction ratios to direction cosines by dividing by the magnitude
Can verify l² + m² + n² = 1 and recover the angle each axis makes

question.prompt: A line has direction ratios 2, −3, 6. Its direction cosines are:

options.diagnosis: Divided by the sum of absolute values 2 + 3 + 6 = 11 instead of the root-sum-of-squares.
Reported the squared cosines (which sum to 1) instead of the cosines themselves.

question.explanation: The magnitude is √(2² + (−3)² + 6²) = √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7, so (l, m, n) = (2/7, −3/7, 6/7). Check: 4/49 + 9/49 + 36/49 = 1. Raw ratios are only proportional to the cosines — they must be normalised.

micros.title: Equations of a Line in Space
micros.description: Write a line through point a with direction b as r = a + λb, and in Cartesian symmetric form (x−x₁)/a = (y−y₁)/b = (z−z₁)/c; also through two given points. Convert fluently between the two forms.
outcomes: Can write vector and Cartesian equations of lines from point + direction or two points
Can translate between the vector and symmetric forms

micros.title: Angle Between Two Lines; Parallel and Perpendicular Tests
micros.description: cos θ = |b₁·b₂|/(|b₁||b₂|) from the direction vectors. Lines are parallel when direction ratios are proportional and perpendicular when a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂ = 0 — keep the two tests straight.
outcomes: Can compute the angle between lines from direction ratios
Can apply the proportionality test for parallel and the zero-dot-product test for perpendicular

question.prompt: Two lines have direction ratios (1, 2, 2) and (2, 1, −2). The lines are:

options.diagnosis: Computed cos θ with a wrong dot product or magnitudes; the dot product here is exactly 0.
Coincidence requires proportional ratios AND a shared point; neither condition holds.

question.explanation: Dot product of directions: (1)(2) + (2)(1) + (2)(−2) = 2 + 2 − 4 = 0, so the lines are perpendicular. Parallelism would need proportional ratios (1/2 = 2/1 = 2/−2 fails immediately).

micros.title: Shortest Distance Between Skew Lines
micros.description: Skew lines neither meet nor run parallel. The shortest distance is |(a₂ − a₁)·(b₁×b₂)|/|b₁×b₂| — the projection of the connecting vector onto the common perpendicular direction b₁×b₂.
outcomes: Can classify a pair of lines as intersecting, parallel or skew
Can compute the shortest distance between skew lines with the formula

micros.title: Equations of a Plane
micros.description: A plane is fixed by its normal n: r·n = d (normal form) or ax + by + cz + d = 0 in Cartesian form, where (a, b, c) are the normal's direction ratios. Build plane equations from a point and normal, or three points.
outcomes: Can write a plane's equation from point + normal and read off the normal from ax + by + cz + d = 0
Can test whether points lie on, or lines lie in, a given plane

micros.title: Angle Between a Line and a Plane
micros.description: The line's direction meets the plane's NORMAL at some angle θ; the angle with the plane itself is the complement 90° − θ, computed via sin φ = |b·n|/(|b||n|). Parallel/perpendicular tests follow from the normal.
outcomes: Can compute the angle between a line and a plane via the normal
Can state why the line–normal and line–plane angles are complementary

question.prompt: A line makes an angle of 30° with the normal to a plane. The angle between the line and the plane is:

options.diagnosis: Treated 'angle with the plane' as always a right angle; only a line ALONG the normal is perpendicular to the plane.
Subtracted from 180° instead of 90°; used supplement instead of complement.

question.explanation: The angle with the plane and the angle with its normal always add to 90°: the plane lies at right angles to the normal. So the required angle is 90° − 30° = 60°. Reporting 30° hands in the line–normal angle by mistake.

micros.title: Distance from a Point to a Plane
micros.description: Distance from (x₁, y₁, z₁) to ax + by + cz + d = 0 is |ax₁ + by₁ + cz₁ + d| / √(a² + b² + c²) — the division by |n| is what converts the raw substitution into a genuine length.
outcomes: Can compute point-to-plane distances with correct normalisation
Can find the distance between parallel planes via a point on one of them

question.prompt: The distance from the point (1, 1, 1) to the plane x + 2y + 2z − 3 = 0 is:

options.diagnosis: Divided by |n|² = 9 instead of |n| = 3; squared the normaliser.
Substituted +3 instead of −3 for the constant term; sign of d mishandled.

question.explanation: Numerator: |1 + 2(1) + 2(1) − 3| = |2| = 2. Normal magnitude: √(1² + 2² + 2²) = √9 = 3. Distance = 2/3. Skipping the division by |n| leaves the un-normalised value 2, which has no geometric meaning as a length.

nodes.title: Linear Programming
nodes.description: Linear programming optimises a linear objective Z = ax + by subject to linear constraints: graph the inequalities, intersect them into a feasible region, and use the corner-point theorem — the optimum, if it exists, occurs at a vertex. Unbounded regions demand one extra check before declaring victory. Born from wartime logistics, LP now schedules airlines, blends diets, allocates factory time and routes deliveries.
learning_outcomes: Can translate a word problem into decision variables, a linear objective function and linear constraints
Can graph the constraints and identify the feasible region, including non-negativity restrictions
Can apply the corner-point method: find vertices, evaluate Z at each, and select the optimum
Can handle unbounded regions correctly, checking whether the candidate optimum is genuine via the open half-plane test

misconceptions.description: Believes the optimum can sit anywhere in the feasible region (or at its 'centre'), so tests arbitrary interior points.
misconceptions.signal: Evaluates Z at a scatter of interior points and picks the best; never enumerates vertices.
misconceptions.remedy: Slide the objective line Z = c interactively across the region: it exits the region at a corner (or an entire edge), never at an interior point. Level-line intuition makes the corner-point theorem feel inevitable instead of arbitrary.

misconceptions.description: Evaluates the objective at intersection points that are NOT in the feasible region (constraint lines crossing outside it).
misconceptions.signal: Vertex list includes points violating some constraint; 'optimal' point fails substitution into the constraints.
misconceptions.remedy: Add a verification column to the vertex table: every candidate must satisfy ALL constraints before Z is computed. Shade the infeasible side of each line in grey so illegal intersections are visually dead on arrival.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles unbounded regions: either declares 'no optimum ever exists', or blindly trusts the corner-point value without the half-plane check.
misconceptions.signal: Refuses to minimise over an unbounded region; or reports a 'maximum' that the region actually exceeds beyond every bound.
misconceptions.remedy: Work one example each way: a minimum that DOES exist on an unbounded region, and a maximum that doesn't. Teach the decisive test: after finding candidate value M, check whether the open half-plane (Z beyond M) intersects the region — empty means M is genuine.

misconceptions.description: Shades the wrong side of a constraint line, or forgets the non-negativity constraints x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
misconceptions.signal: Feasible regions extend into negative quadrants; region on the wrong side of ≤ lines.
misconceptions.remedy: Test-point ritual: substitute (0,0) (or another off-line point) into every inequality and shade the side that passes. Physically box the first quadrant first whenever x, y ≥ 0 appear — production quantities can't be negative.

real_world_hooks: A tailor with limited cloth and stitching hours maximising profit on shirts vs kurtas
Diet problems: cheapest thali meeting protein and calorie requirements
Airline crew and train timetable scheduling are industrial-scale LPs
A dabbawala-style delivery fleet minimising cost under route constraints
Farm planning: allocating acres between two crops under water and labour limits
teaching.video_search: linear programming corner point method feasible region class 12

questions.prompt: In a linear programming problem with a bounded feasible region, the maximum of the objective function Z occurs:

options.text: At a corner point (vertex) of the feasible region
At the centre of the feasible region
At any interior point where Z is large
At the feasible point farthest from the origin
options.diagnosis: Conflates the objective function with distance; for Z = x − 2y, points NEAR the origin can beat far ones.

questions.explanation: The corner-point theorem: on a bounded feasible region, a linear objective attains its maximum and minimum at vertices (possibly along a whole edge, but always including a vertex). Level lines of Z sweep across the region and last touch it at a corner.

questions.prompt: The corner points of a feasible region are (0,0), (4,0), (0,5) and (2,4). The maximum of Z = 3x + 4y is:

options.diagnosis: Evaluated only the axis vertices (4,0) and (0,5); the mixed vertex (2,4) was skipped.
Maximised 3x alone using (4,0); the y-term's contribution to Z was ignored.

questions.explanation: Z(0,0) = 0; Z(4,0) = 12; Z(0,5) = 20; Z(2,4) = 6 + 16 = 22. The maximum is 22 at (2,4). Every listed vertex must be evaluated — and only listed (feasible) vertices count; a point like (4,3) giving 24 lies outside the region.

questions.prompt: A feasible region is UNBOUNDED and the smallest value of Z = x + 2y over its corner points is 6. When is 6 actually the minimum of Z?

options.text: When the open half-plane x + 2y < 6 has no point in common with the feasible region
Never — an unbounded region cannot have a minimum
Always — the smallest corner value is automatically the minimum
Only if the region also contains the origin

questions.explanation: On unbounded regions the corner-point method needs a final check: draw x + 2y < 6. If that open half-plane misses the region entirely, no feasible point beats 6, so 6 is the true minimum; if it intersects the region, Z dips below 6 and no minimum exists at the corners. Unboundedness threatens maxima and minima differently — each case needs this test, not a blanket rule.

micros.title: Formulating a Linear Programming Problem
micros.description: Extract decision variables from the story, write the linear objective function Z to maximise or minimise, and translate every resource limit and requirement into a linear constraint — including x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
outcomes: Can define variables and write the objective function from a word problem
Can list ALL constraints including non-negativity

micros.title: Graphing Constraints and the Feasible Region
micros.description: Plot each constraint line, shade the correct half-plane (test with the origin), and intersect all shaded regions with the first quadrant to obtain the feasible region — the set of all allowed decisions.
outcomes: Can shade the correct side of each constraint using a test point
Can identify the feasible region and its vertices from the graph

question.prompt: Which point lies in the feasible region determined by x + y ≤ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0?

options.diagnosis: Checked only the non-negativity conditions; 3 + 2 = 5 violates x + y ≤ 4.
Satisfies neither x + y ≤ 4 nor y ≥ 0; substitution never performed.

question.explanation: (1, 2): 1 + 2 = 3 ≤ 4 ✓, 1 ≥ 0 ✓, 2 ≥ 0 ✓ — all three constraints hold. (−1, 3) satisfies x + y ≤ 4 but breaks x ≥ 0: the non-negativity constraints are real constraints and must be checked every time.

micros.title: The Corner-point Method
micros.description: For a bounded feasible region, the optimum of a linear objective occurs at a VERTEX: find all corner points (intersections that actually lie in the region), evaluate Z at each, and pick the best.
outcomes: Can find corner points by solving pairs of boundary equations and discarding infeasible intersections
Can evaluate Z at every vertex and identify maximum and minimum

question.prompt: The corner points of a bounded feasible region are (0, 0), (5, 0), (3, 4) and (0, 6). The maximum of Z = 4x + y over the region is:

options.diagnosis: Evaluated Z at only some vertices, or assumed the 'highest-looking' corner wins without comparing all four values.
Picked the vertex with the largest coordinate instead of the largest Z; Z weights x four times y here.

question.explanation: Z at the corners: (0,0) → 0, (5,0) → 20, (3,4) → 16, (0,6) → 6. The maximum is 20 at (5, 0). A linear objective over a convex polygon always peaks at a vertex — interior points like (2, 2) with Z = 10 can never beat the best corner.

micros.title: Optima on Unbounded Feasible Regions
micros.description: With an unbounded region the corner-point value is only a CANDIDATE: the optimum exists iff the open half-plane beyond it (Z > M for max, Z < m for min) shares no point with the region. Run this check every time.
outcomes: Can perform the open half-plane test on an unbounded region
Can decide whether a candidate optimum is genuine or the problem has no optimum

question.prompt: Minimising Z = x + 2y over an UNBOUNDED feasible region, the smallest corner-point value is 6. What must you do before declaring 6 the minimum?

options.text: Check whether the open half-plane x + 2y < 6 has any point in common with the feasible region; 6 is the minimum only if it has none
Nothing — the smallest corner value is always the minimum
Conclude no minimum exists, since unbounded regions never have optima
Evaluate Z at a few interior points to see if anything smaller appears

question.explanation: On an unbounded region the region may stretch into territory where Z keeps decreasing forever. The definitive test: intersect the region with the OPEN half-plane x + 2y < 6. Empty intersection → 6 is the true minimum; non-empty → no minimum exists. Unbounded regions sometimes do and sometimes don't have optima — only the test decides.

micros.title: Applied LPP: Diet, Manufacturing and Transport
micros.description: Solve complete board-style problems end to end: formulate from the story, graph, run the corner-point method, and interpret the optimal vertex as a real decision (units to produce, packets to buy).
outcomes: Can solve a full two-variable LPP word problem from text to interpreted answer
Can sanity-check the answer against the constraints and context

nodes.title: Probability: Conditional Probability, Bayes' Theorem, Random Variables
nodes.description: Probability learns from information: P(A|B) re-weights chances given that B occurred, the multiplication rule chains events, and independence means P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B). Bayes' theorem reverses conditionals — from P(evidence|cause) to P(cause|evidence) — the logic behind medical testing and spam filters, where base rates routinely humiliate intuition. Random variables then attach numbers to outcomes, with probability distributions and means (expected values) to summarise them.
learning_outcomes: Can compute conditional probabilities from the definition P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) and from two-way tables
Can apply the multiplication rule and test events for independence via P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B)
Can distinguish independent events from mutually exclusive events with examples
Can apply the total probability theorem and Bayes' theorem to reverse conditional probabilities
Can construct the probability distribution of a discrete random variable and compute its mean (expected value)

misconceptions.description: Swaps the conditional: treats P(A|B) as equal to P(B|A).
misconceptions.signal: Reports a test's accuracy P(positive|disease) as the answer to 'given a positive, what's the chance of disease?'.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two with a stark verbal pair: P(rain | monsoon month) vs P(monsoon month | rain). Then run one Bayes computation with concrete counts (a 10,000-person table) so the student SEES the two conditionals come out wildly different.

misconceptions.description: Equates independence with mutual exclusivity: 'independent events can't happen together'.
misconceptions.signal: Sets P(A∩B) = 0 for independent events; claims disjoint events are independent 'because they don't affect each other'.
misconceptions.remedy: Flip it: mutually exclusive events are MAXIMALLY dependent — knowing A happened tells you B certainly didn't. Verify with numbers: P(A)P(B) > 0 ≠ 0 = P(A∩B) for disjoint events with positive probabilities. Independence means information about one leaves the other's probability UNCHANGED.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies unconditionally: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) even for dependent events (e.g. drawing without replacement).
misconceptions.signal: Two aces without replacement computed as (4/52)², not (4/52)(3/51).
misconceptions.remedy: Slow-motion the second draw: the deck now has 51 cards and 3 aces — the sample space itself changed. Make the general rule primary — P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A) — with plain multiplication as the special case earned only by verified independence.

misconceptions.description: Base-rate neglect: ignores the prior in Bayes problems, so a 90%-accurate test 'means' 90% chance of disease after a positive.
misconceptions.signal: Answers near the test's accuracy regardless of how rare the condition is; shocked by the true answer.
misconceptions.remedy: Natural frequencies beat formulas: of 10,000 people, 100 have the disease → 90 true positives; of 9,900 healthy → 990 false positives. Only 90 of the 1,080 positives are real (~8%). Build the tree BEFORE the formula, every time.

real_world_hooks: Medical screening: why a positive result for a rare disease is less scary than it sounds
Spam filters: Bayes' theorem deciding if 'lottery winner!' mail is junk
Cricket: probability a batsman scores 50+ GIVEN the team batted first (conditional from data tables)
Insurance and expected value: how premiums are priced
Weather app 'chance of rain' updating as new radar evidence arrives

questions.prompt: Given P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A∩B) = 0.2, find P(A|B).

options.diagnosis: Computed P(A∪B) = 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.2; union and conditional formulas interchanged.

questions.explanation: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) = 0.2/0.5 = 0.4 — condition on B by dividing by B's probability. Dividing by P(A) instead gives P(B|A) = 0.2/0.6 = 1/3, a different question; and 0.3 = P(A)P(B) wrongly presumes independence.

questions.prompt: A and B are INDEPENDENT events with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. Then P(A∩B) is:

options.diagnosis: Applied the addition rule to an 'and' question; union and intersection swapped.
Computed P(A∪B) = 0.3 + 0.4 − 0.12 — right machinery, but answered the union instead of the intersection.

questions.explanation: For independent events, P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12. Independence does NOT mean the events can't co-occur — that's mutual exclusivity, and disjoint events with positive probabilities are never independent.

questions.prompt: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects it with probability 0.9 in the diseased, but also gives a false positive with probability 0.1 in the healthy. If a random person tests positive, the probability they actually have the disease is:

options.diagnosis: Computed the numerator P(disease ∩ positive) but never divided by the total probability of testing positive.
Reported the prior unchanged — the positive test result was given no evidential weight at all.

questions.explanation: Bayes: P(D|+) = (0.01×0.9) / (0.01×0.9 + 0.99×0.1) = 0.009/0.108 = 1/12 ≈ 8.3%. In a town of 10,000: 90 true positives vs 990 false positives — only 90 of 1,080 positives are real. The rarity of the disease (base rate) drags the answer far below the test's 90% accuracy.

micros.title: Conditional Probability from the Definition
micros.description: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) re-scales probability to the world where B has happened. Compute it from given probabilities and from two-way tables, and keep P(A|B) firmly distinct from P(B|A).
outcomes: Can compute conditional probabilities from the definition and from tables
Can explain with an example why P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) in general

question.prompt: Given P(A) = 0.8, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A∩B) = 0.2, the value of P(A|B) is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied P(A∩B) by P(B) instead of dividing; formula inverted.
Added 0.2 + 0.5; no conditional structure used at all.

question.explanation: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) = 0.2/0.5 = 0.4. Dividing by P(A) instead gives P(B|A) = 0.2/0.8 = 0.25 — the swapped conditional. The event AFTER the bar supplies the denominator.

micros.title: The Multiplication Rule for Dependent Events
micros.description: P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A): the second factor must be CONDITIONED on the first event having happened. Essential for without-replacement draws, where the sample space shrinks between picks.
outcomes: Can chain conditional probabilities for sequential draws without replacement
Can decide when the second factor needs updating and when it does not

question.prompt: Two cards are drawn from a standard 52-card pack WITHOUT replacement. The probability that both are kings is:

options.diagnosis: Updated the denominator to 51 but kept 4 kings for the second draw; forgot one king left the pack.
Added 4/52 + 4/52; used the addition rule where the multiplication rule belongs.

question.explanation: P(K₁∩K₂) = P(K₁)·P(K₂|K₁) = (4/52)(3/51) = (1/13)(1/17) = 1/221. After the first king leaves, only 3 kings remain among 51 cards. Squaring 4/52 (= 1/169) pretends the draws are independent, which without replacement they are not.

micros.title: Independent Events vs Mutually Exclusive Events
micros.description: A and B are independent when P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) — knowing one occurred doesn't change the other's probability. Mutually exclusive events CANNOT co-occur, and (for positive-probability events) are never independent.
outcomes: Can test independence numerically with P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B)
Can articulate the difference between independent and mutually exclusive with examples

question.prompt: A and B are INDEPENDENT events with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. Then P(A∩B) equals:

options.text: 0, because independent events cannot occur together

options.diagnosis: Added the probabilities — that computes P(A∪B) for mutually exclusive events, not P(A∩B) for independent ones.
Took min(P(A), P(B)) or assumed B ⊂ A; no multiplication performed.

question.explanation: Independence MEANS P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2. It is mutually EXCLUSIVE events that cannot co-occur (P(A∩B) = 0). Independent events with positive probabilities always can — one happening simply tells you nothing about the other.

micros.title: The Theorem of Total Probability
micros.description: When events E₁, ..., Eₙ partition the sample space, P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ): the overall probability of A is the prior-weighted average over the scenarios. Tree diagrams make the sum visible.
outcomes: Can compute P(A) across a partition using a tree diagram
Can verify the partition is genuine (exhaustive and mutually exclusive) before applying the theorem

micros.title: Bayes' Theorem: Reversing the Conditional
micros.description: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) / Σ P(Eⱼ)P(A|Eⱼ): update a prior in the light of evidence. The denominator is the total probability of the evidence; the prior must never be ignored, however accurate the 'test'.
outcomes: Can set up the Bayes numerator and total-probability denominator correctly
Can explain base-rate neglect with a rare-disease example

question.prompt: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects it with probability 0.9 in the diseased, but also gives a false positive with probability 0.1 in the healthy. A randomly chosen person tests positive. The probability they actually have the disease is:

options.diagnosis: Reported the joint probability P(disease AND positive); never divided by the total probability of testing positive.
Reported the denominator P(positive) itself as the answer; Bayes fraction left unassembled.

question.explanation: P(D|+) = P(D)P(+|D) / [P(D)P(+|D) + P(D′)P(+|D′)] = (0.01)(0.9) / [(0.01)(0.9) + (0.99)(0.1)] = 0.009/0.108 = 1/12 ≈ 0.083. Despite the '90% accurate' test, the disease is so rare that most positives are false — ignoring the 1% base rate inflates the answer tenfold.

micros.title: Discrete Random Variables and Probability Distributions
micros.description: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome; its probability distribution lists each value with its probability, all probabilities non-negative and summing to 1. Build distributions for coin, die and card experiments.
outcomes: Can construct the distribution table of a discrete random variable
Can use Σpᵢ = 1 to find an unknown probability in a table

micros.title: Mean (Expected Value) of a Random Variable
micros.description: E(X) = Σ xᵢpᵢ: the probability-weighted average of the values — the long-run average per trial, not the most likely single outcome. Compute and interpret means of small discrete distributions.
outcomes: Can compute E(X) from a distribution table
Can interpret the mean as a long-run average, including non-attainable values like 3.5 for a die

question.prompt: A random variable X takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.3, 0.5, 0.2 respectively. The mean E(X) is:

options.diagnosis: Averaged the values (0 + 1 + 2)/3, ignoring the probabilities entirely.
Summed the values of X; probabilities never entered the computation.
Reported the largest probability instead of the weighted average of the values.

question.explanation: E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ = 0(0.3) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.2) = 0 + 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9. Each value is weighted by how often it occurs; the unweighted average (0+1+2)/3 = 1 would only be right if all three values were equally likely.
